title: 生活中的律動 Rhythms in Life
description:
生活中各種現象都是有跡可循的,物理則是探究這些現象運作的根本法則,本課程主要透過簡單物理原理,探討生活相關的議題,包含運動、科技、人體健康、大腦運作、生活環境等,並以物理定理方式解釋許多平日會看到的自然現象以及生物體運作的道理,讓不同背景的學生能透過自然科學的角度了解這個世界。
本課程為"線上"與"實體"並行,線上部分為演講課(每周進行),實體部分為討論課(兩周一次),線上課程網站為google classroom,修課同學請用政治大學 g suite帳號 "學號"@g.nccu.edu.tw加入,google classroom課程網站,115生活中的律動 (代碼:zbygte64 ),連結
https://classroom.google.com/c/ODY3NDI3NDk1NjEz?cjc=zbygte64
The questions about how and why things happen in our daily lives involve physical principles. Physics are related to many interesting aspects including sport science of the ball game, modern electronic technology, health science, life science, and environments. This course not only introduces the relation between physical principles and these phenomena, but also explains how they work.
This is a hybrid class given partly online and partly in class. Lecture will be given online (weekly) and students need to attend in class discussion (every 2 weeks). The online class uses google classroom under NCCU g suite package. Students need to join the online class website using NCCU g suite account. The website will be announced before class.
objectives:
藉由系統化的介紹,促使不同科系學生理解物理與日常生活的關聯性。傳達物理與日常生活的關聯性,激發學生對物理科學的興趣;透過簡單物理原理,解釋上述生活中看到的議題,使同學將課堂知識,轉化為生活中的知識,讓不同科系同學認識科學中的基本道理,主題強調物理與生活的關聯性,解釋物理發展如何應用於日常生活,整合了物理、統計、醫學、生物等學科,讓學生了解跨領域科學的應用。
以考試、每周測驗與主題報告為學習成效評估標準
This course is intended to provide undergraduate students (particularly students not in physics background interested in science) with an introduction to the fundamental concepts of physics in the context of examples from our daily lives. Topics include physics in bio-medical applications, environmental, sport science, electrical technology. The purpose is to help students from different background to learn how physical principles guide and constrain life, and to understand multidisciplinary science applications
The grade will be evaluated by exam, weekly quiz, and report.

description:
本課程將物理學融入歷史的脈絡中。沿著人類文明發展的軸線,及藉由各時代主要物理學家的生平與貢獻,來解釋各種物理現象及其時代背景,了解物理學對歷史的重大衝擊。

title: 大腦與我 The Brain and I
description:
本課程將於一學期內深入探討大腦的運作及其與身體的關聯,內容分為四大單元:
第一單元:「微觀的腦」,介紹大腦的基本結構、功能及發育過程。
第二單元:「腦與身體的協作」,探討外界訊息如何傳遞至大腦,並了解大腦如何協調身體各部位的運作,包括感官功能與肢體移動的控制。
第三單元:「腦與心智」,介紹大腦的高等認知功能,涵蓋學習、記憶、情緒、動機等心理過程,以及性別差異的影響。
第四單元:「失控的腦」,探討與大腦相關的疾病,包括成癮、精神疾患與神經退化性疾病的症狀、成因與治療,並關注大腦健康及社會醫療層面的議題。
本課程旨在讓學生全面了解大腦的運作與健康,並引發對大腦及心理健康的深入思考。
objectives:
使學生了解大腦的基本結構、發育過程及神經傳導原理,並掌握大腦不同區域的功能。
培養學生對大腦如何處理感官訊息與控制肢體運動的深入理解,並探索大腦如何與身體協同工作。
使學生掌握大腦在高等認知功能中的角色,涵蓋學習、記憶、情緒與動機,並探討性別差異對心智的影響。
使學生理解大腦功能失調對認知、情緒與行為的影響,並認識成癮、精神疾患及神經退化性疾病的成因、症狀與治療方式。

title: 科技與人文社會 Technology and Human Society
description:
本課程提供「科技與人文社會」(Science, Technology and Society; STS) 領域的概論。STS 是一個正在發展,但對於人類的發展與進步有著顯著影響力的學科。STS 主要在探索科學、科技及社會之間錯綜複雜的互動關係;與傳統科學不同的是,STS 並沒有特定標準答案,或在回應科技/ 科學是好或不好的問題,STS 更強調的是社會、政治、文化、物質條件如何形塑科技/科學產物, 甚至如何影響社會。
欲修習本課之學生必須主動、積極地參與課程討論,不論是在課堂上的發言,或是每堂課必須繳交的發言單,透過聽、說、讀、寫、想的修煉,學生必須對於授課內容、同儕學習、課前閱讀進行反思,以形成自己的論述及觀點,以達到通識教育的目的。

title: 數位遊戲與社會 Digital Games and Society
description:
*第一堂課必須出席才能修習此堂課程。;另外期末報告您這組報告時您一定要上台出席不然以0分計。
娛樂是什麼?什麼樣的情境下會覺得有愉悅感?還是一種更高層次的欣賞?
媒體娛樂在人類生活中扮演不可或缺的角色,這些包含了電視、電影、音樂、電台、網路、電子遊戲,以及行動娛樂像是手機或是平板,就算是許多餐廳也都是以媒體娛樂的主題來設計及呈現。在這樣一個世代中,媒體娛樂如何融入並影響人類的傳播行為、關係、以及社會架構?而品牌又如何藉由娛樂的形式塑造其形象,並達到說服的效果?
數位遊戲是現在娛樂媒體產業中持續成長、營收最高的產業。到底為什麼會有遊戲呢?是因為前人無聊而發明的「玩具」,還是另有典故呢?若你對於遊戲的歷史及現今遊戲產業的發展有興趣,想要在體驗遊戲時能夠有不同的反思及思考層次,或是想要更瞭解遊戲在社交、心理、文化及教育層面的影響,不論你是個超厲害的Hard-core玩家,或是偶爾滑滑手機的輕鬆玩家,這堂課都歡迎你。我們將會從不同的角度來瞭解遊戲,包括從科技的發展(體感互動、虛擬實境)、傳播心理及教育等面向剖析遊戲對於個人及社會的影響。此外,遊戲於說服、或是在醫療復健、新聞、健康運動、及社會議題改變的應用,將會有精彩的遊戲案例呈現與討論。我們同時也會探討電競及遊戲實況等玩家文化,若你想要修習專屬遊戲設計或程式設計,建議修習其他課程

title: 睡眠與健康 Sleep and Health
description: 這門課程將帶領學生探索睡眠的科學基礎,理解其對身心健康的影響,並學習如何透過科學方法改善睡眠品質。學生將透過睡眠日誌記錄與測驗認識自身睡眠狀況,並學習如何定義與測量睡眠。我們將探討環境、行為與生物時鐘對睡眠的影響,並理解清醒與睡眠的微妙平衡。並將關注壓力、情緒與時間管理對睡眠的影響,釐清睡眠迷思,並認識各類睡眠障礙,如失眠、晝夜節律失調與呼吸障礙等,探討其與其他疾病如心血管疾病、情緒疾患、神經退化性疾病的關聯性,幫助學生建立健康的睡眠習慣。
objectives:
理解睡眠的科學基礎:掌握睡眠的定義、結構,並分析其對身心健康的影響。
學習睡眠評估與調適方法:透過睡眠日誌與測量工具認識自身睡眠狀況,並學習改善策略。
分析影響睡眠的因素:探討環境、行為、生物時鐘與心理因素對睡眠的影響,學習維持健康作息的方法。
認識與解析睡眠障礙:了解失眠、晝夜節律失調、呼吸障礙等問題,並探討其與其他疾病的關聯性。
建立健康的睡眠習慣:運用科學知識改善個人與他人的睡眠品質,提升生活與學習效率。
grading:

期末報告:30%

title: 俄國文化與社會 Russian Culture and Society
description: 蘇聯解體後,台灣與俄羅斯在經貿、文化等各方面的交流日益密切。一般人對俄羅斯的印象,仍停留在一個地處冰天雪地的神秘國度,然而俄羅斯在文學、音樂、舞蹈、戲劇等文化方面的成就卻是舉世公認的。為了揭開這文化大國的神秘面紗,本課程將概括介紹俄羅斯文化的各個層面,及其當前所面臨的社會、婦女等問題。
objectives: 本課程目標為使學生對俄羅斯文化與社會有真確的了解,同時培養學生對多元文化的欣賞及尊重,並以分組報告的方式培養同學們溝通及協同合作的能力。
grading: 課堂參與、上網互動學習15%、作業20%、期中考30%、期末報告35%,凡點名5次不到者學期成績以零分計。

title: 生活中的資訊資源與應用 Everyday Life Information and Application
description:
本課程以「生活議題中的資訊資源、資料判讀與AI輔助分析」為核心,協助學生理解個人、社會與國家在全球政治、經濟、文化、科技與永續發展系統中的位置。課程將以國際經貿、科技發展、人才培育、創新創業、產業動態、能源供需、永續治理與公共政策等議題為情境,引導學生認識國內外重要資訊資源與開放資料庫,並學習如何運用生成式AI與資料分析工具進行資訊檢索、資料整理、議題分析、趨勢觀測與知識表達。
本課程強調,AI並非取代人類判斷的答案機器,而是協助學生進行資訊探索、資料整理、觀點比較、問題形成與分析反思的學習夥伴。因此,課程將結合資訊素養、資料素養與AI素養,培養學生在面對大量、複雜且快速變動的資訊環境時,能夠辨識資訊品質、理解資料脈絡、檢驗AI生成內容的可信度,並提出具有證據基礎與公共關懷的分析觀點。
本課程以科學、技術、經濟、貿易、產業、人才、能源與永續發展等重要趨勢作為議題場景,透過「問題界定、資訊蒐集、AI輔助整理、資料分析、脈絡解讀、批判反思與成果表達」的學習流程,協助學生建立整合量化資訊與質性脈絡的分析能力。課程將依序帶領學生完成四項核心訓練:第一,認識國內外重要資料庫與開放資料來源;第二,學習使用AI工具輔助檢索策略設計、資料摘要、關鍵概念整理與視覺化構想;第三,根據主題進行資訊與數據的蒐集、整理、分析與驗證;第四,從資料分析結果進一步探討議題脈絡、發展趨勢及其背後的制度性、社會性與技術性原因。
課堂將透過案例講授、資料庫實作、AI提示設計、資料判讀練習、小組討論與期末專題報告,引導學生理解資訊如何影響日常生活、公共決策與未來社會發展。學生須在課程中學習如何負責任地使用生成式AI,包括揭露AI使用方式、檢核AI生成內容、避免不當依賴、尊重著作權與資料隱私,並建立具有倫理意識與批判能力的AI協作能力。
objectives:
本課程旨在建立學生對資訊、資料與AI生成內容的敏感度,並培養其運用資訊資源分析生活與公共議題的基礎能力。完成本課程後,學生應能達成以下學習成效:
掌握基礎資訊資源與資料庫檢索能力
學生能認識並操作國內外重要資料庫,包括OECD Statistics、WTO、World Bank、政府開放資料平台、教育部統計、經濟部統計、科技政策相關資料庫及其他公共資訊來源。
建立資料判讀與資訊品質評估能力
學生能判斷資訊來源的可信度、完整性、時效性、偏誤與適用範圍,並理解資料背後的蒐集邏輯、分類架構與制度脈絡。
培養AI輔助資訊分析與實作能力
學生能運用生成式AI工具進行檢索策略設計、資料摘要、概念比較、議題拆解、趨勢觀察、報告架構規劃與初步視覺化構想,同時具備檢核AI生成內容的能力。
培養國際視野與公共議題分析能力
學生能從經濟、貿易、科技、人才、能源、創新與永續等議題中,分析不同國家、產業與社會群體所面臨的發展條件與挑戰。
建立批判思考與負責任AI使用素養
學生能辨識AI生成內容可能產生的錯誤、幻覺、偏誤與過度簡化問題,並能透過資料來源驗證、交叉比對與倫理反思,形成具證據基礎的判斷。
完成以生活議題為核心的資訊分析專題
學生選定一項生活或公共議題,整合資料庫、開放資料、AI輔助分析與人工判讀,完成一份具資料證據、議題脈絡與政策或行動建議的期末報告。
grading:

期末報告:35%

title: 窺探科技中的語言應用 Exploring Language Application in Daily Technology
description:
(暫定)
日常生活中不離語言的使用,語言以各種形式出現於說話、報章雜誌、廣告、符號等等,並與目前人工智慧的發展息息相關。此課程將探索生活中的語言使用、及其於科技結合實例之議題,例如討論為何機器人的回應總是很罐頭、為何機器需要斷詞及詞類標註、為何需要句法剖析樹、是否同樣一套機器模型或是資料處理流程就足以應付所有語言等議題,以及在既有已釋出的自然語言處理平台或軟體所產出的結果 (e.g., CKIP CoreNLP、Weka等) 在學界及業界的應用討論。透過網路平台或軟體的使用,本課程將讓學生體驗針對同一種語言 (e.g., 英文及中文) 不同斷詞系統之間輸出的結果為何不同,其優缺點、及背後當初設計的初衷和考量是什麼;對於不同的情緒分類方式,對於訓練模型自動判斷產品評論好壞又會有哪些不同影響;或者對於客服機器人的回覆方式可以採用或是設計哪些語言策略,使得整體對話流更加順暢等議題內容。
期末展演將鼓勵學生自行發掘科技生活中的任何語言現象,可使用現有網路語言處理工具或自行以程式語言處理資料進一步做輔助,分析其語境、發生緣由、統整歸納語言規則,及做出可行性高的實質應用思考,並與班上同學分享交流,促進思考發想。
(備註: 課程中每週需要自行攜帶筆電上課以便於實作,會於課程中學習如何寫簡易程式語言)
objectives:
認識語言學於生活及科技之密切結合及其應用
培養人文科學角度之批判性思考及創造力
增強與社會之連結度
學習將專案發想實際化以提出具執行潛能的計畫案
能夠自己撰寫簡易程式語言
grading:
(暫定)

In-Class discussion (50 %): in-class participation and group discussion
Final Presentation (30 %): oral presentation (15%) + final report (15%)

title: 那些動物教我的事 Things We Learned from Animals
description:
※ 本課程排定三次體驗參與單元,其中兩次(第15、16週)課程時間將另行安排於週六進行,選課前請同學確認可接受配合課程設計和安排。
在這個全球暖化的世界,又遭疫症肆虐的地球,人類如何跟自然世界和其他物種共存,是重要且急切的議題。最新近的跨領域學術研究也在思考「後人類」和「人類世」的問題。動物與人互相依賴 的需要越來越重要,而兩者之界線越來越模糊。課程分三個單元,每單元五課的形式進行:
單元一、動物丶科學丶生命科學
單元二、動物與人類之共存與異同: 智性丶倫理丶生死
單元三丶動物想像丶哲思丶與舞動
課程沒有門檻,只要是對自身或物動有興趣以多方角度思考的同學皆適宜。
objectives:
課程目標
本課程透過跨領域的合作與探討,結合生命科學、生理醫學、心理學、哲學及表達藝術等多元視角,深入思考動物在人的生命與文化中的意義。課程旨在培養學生以謙遜而開放的態度,理解「動物的人性」與「人的動物性」,並探討兩者之間的差異與連結。藉由跨學科的交流與反思,學生將能拓展對人與動物共存關係的理解,並培養批判性思維與倫理意識。

1.上課參與: 出席及課堂參與 20%, 準時繳交作業10%
2. 每次上課課後作業考評: 70%

title: 語言與認知神經科學概論 Introduction to Language and Cognitive Neuroscience
description:
本課程以語言學概念爲支柱,融入認知心理學及神經科學觀點,探討人類語言的各個面向。 循序介紹人類語言的本質,涵蓋語意、語音、句法結構、和各種語言歧義現象,討論涉及語 言及非語言領域的認知功能(顏色、數量、空間/時間、社會認知),如類別化現象,及支持語言處理(從單詞語彙、語句、到語境整合)過程的大腦機制。課程後段介紹語言與其他非語言認知的交互作用、語言功能失調,語言學習的相關認知神經功能、及人類語言演化。課程針對每週的週次議題,介紹經典的研究案例和當前新的研究結果,討論這個領域中目前已知及未知的部分,帶入課間小組討論,藉由同學間的意見交換,理解科學探討的歷程和跨領域研究的挑戰,培養邏輯思維和人文關懷。
*加簽規則:教師將於第一週課堂介紹課程內容後、現場進行抽籤 (將以在遞補名單上的同學為優先)。
欲加簽的同學請先詳閱課程大綱及課程要求、出席第一週課堂。
objectives:
課程目標:
本課程旨在介紹人類語言的特性、涉及語言處理的認知系統及大腦神經機制。透過討論語言 的各種面向、和與非語言認知系統的關聯,希冀從多元角度讓同學瞭解人類語言的本質,及語言學、認知心理學、神經科學之間的跨領域互動交流。此外,各主題的討論中將採用科學 方法做論證,針對各個議題,將用不同的案例帶入課間討論、從意見交換中、培養同學批判性思考和邏輯論述的能力、體會科學研究精神。
學習成效:透過此課程,同學應能:
瞭解人類語言的本質及語言的各個面向
認識語言相關的認知功能及大腦機制
理解語言及非語言認知之間的交互作用
培養獨立思考的能力、運用科學方法和邏輯思維理解跨領域研究的重要及挑戰
grading:

title: 台灣近現代社會文化史 Relationship of Taiwan's Cultural History and Its Modern Society
description:
本課程以日治中期至1945年戰後的台灣為中心,探究在台灣文化發展的情形。而文化的發展,不管是外來的或是土生的,都必然與當時的國內外社會情況緊密相連。因此,本課程將探討各個年代的社會狀況之特色。
本課程以1945-1971年退出聯合國、1970年代、1980年代與1990年代作為討論的分斷點。各個年代或時期在其國內外的狀態變化下,各有其不同的特色。本課程每堂課即依各年代所發生之主要事件為主軸,展開對這些事件之社會學與歷史性的討論,再擴及當時社會與文化的發展脈絡,及其所產生的變化。
另一方面,1970年代末乃至1980年代,台灣的經濟起飛奠定了日後消費社會的形成,以及民主化運動的發展。但此一課題另有「台灣經濟史」等課程作更詳盡的討論,是以本課程在經濟發展這方面僅加以略提,而以文化社會方面為主。
*本堂課可加簽。
objectives:
本課程的目的即在於探討各個年代的社會狀況之特色,以及在該社會背景下,台灣文化市場乃至在台灣發展的本土文化、外來文化的狀態與變化,以期深化對台灣社會文化發展脈絡的理解。
由於僅用年代、文字、講授歷史事件易流於表層的意義,本課程重視敘事化與脈絡的產生,並希望學生能發揮想像力,設身處地在那個歷史的年代。本課程將使用一些影片,並請同學分組就影片進行討論。希望能藉此培養學生歷史敘事的能力。
grading:
1、課堂表現30%,以出席率(一次點名未到扣5分)與小組討論貢獻度計算
2、作業70%:小組報告30%,個人報告各20%
a) 分組報告:4000字為原則,以論文格式寫作(有標題、分節、有註釋),需有主軸問題意識。同時,每位組員須各別交上對其他人的工作分配比例評分表。
b) 期末個人報告:2500-3000字為原則。以論文格式寫作(有標題、分節、有註釋),需有主軸問題意識。
*本課程會使用PPT,並會上傳簡版PPT,但上課只能用手抄筆記(可用平板)。這個規定的意義,請參考:Sherry Turkle (2018),《重新與人對話:迎接數位時代的人際考驗,修補親密關係的對話療法》(台北:時報出版),頁263-283。
摘錄請看:【你是在抄筆記,還是在作筆錄?】〔聯絡資訊已移除〕

title: 抵抗!理論和實踐 Resistance in Theory and Practice
description:
What does it mean to resist existing structures of oppression? What strategies and tactics are possible? What forms of solidarity emerge through moments of resistance?
This course explores resistance primarily through literature, social theory, and law. It defines resistance in the broadest sense, examining how activists, artists, lawyers, and protesters have used cultural, political, social, and economic strategies to challenge existing legal structures.
objectives:
Students will develop confidence in writing and speaking.
Students will understand key theories of resistance in philosophy, political thought, and law.
Students will explore different tactics of resistance, from civil disobedience to armed struggle.
Students will examine the role of literature, art, and culture in movements of resistance.
Students will analyze case studies of resistance across different contexts and histories.
grading:
Students are evaluated according to their participation with in-class activities, attendance, quizzes on reading, and a final creative project. Students who feel anxious about their English ability should not be afraid, as mistakes related to fluency will not be punished, and effort will be rewarded.
Participation (Attendance, Participation) 50%
Students are expected to participate in interactive activities, court hearings, role plays.
Reading Quizzes – 10%
Students will be quizzed on basic comprehension of readings. One quiz grade will be dropped.
Midterm Project (asylum mock trial) 15%
Students will participate in a mock asylum hearing. Students will be given time to prepare for this hearing.
Final Theater Project 25%
Students will complete a final theater project on the theme of resistance for the semester. Students will be given time to prepare for this project.
Some themes that students can choose from:
Indigenous resistance
Slavery and Carceral Resistance
Civil Rights Movement
Environment
Feminism
Culture and Aesthetics
Violent resistance / Guerilla Warfare
Strikes / Labor Organizing
Migration
Gender, Sexuality, and Queer culture

title: 氣候變遷對社會韌性的挑戰 Climate Resilience in Motion
description:
Limiting global warming requires rapid and far-reaching transitions across energy, land use, urban infrastructure, and industrial systems. At the same time, intensifying climate impacts make adaptation and resilience an equally urgent priority. Effective climate action therefore requires more than technological solutions: it demands an understanding of climate risk, socio-technical change, governance, investment, justice, and public participation.
Using Taiwan as a central case while drawing on international experience, this course integrates natural- and social-science perspectives to examine how societies can move from climate commitments to effective mitigation and adaptation. Students analyze emission profiles, hazards, exposure, vulnerability, and sectoral transition pathways while exploring planetary boundaries, sustainability transitions, climate justice, and absorptive, adaptive, and transformative resilience.
Lectures, discussions, current climate news briefings, field-based learning, group projects, and hands-on exercises are combined throughout the course. Interactive tools—including Energy Policy Simulator, En-ROADS, climate-risk maps, and climate board games—help students test policy choices, identify trade-offs, and design practical action. The course culminates in a team-based Climate Resilience Action Project that translates evidence and theory into an implementable response for a community, sector, organization, or place in Taiwan.
objectives:
Explain the relationships among climate mitigation, adaptation and resilience.
Interpret emissions, climate-hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and adaptive-capacity data, with particular attention to Taiwan.
Use scenario simulators, databases, and risk-mapping tools to compare policy pathways and communicate uncertainty.
Evaluate mitigation and adaptation options in terms of feasibility, co-benefits, trade-offs, maladaptation risks, and climate justice.
Co-design and communicate an evidence-based climate resilience action plan with an implementation pathway and measurable indicators.
grading:

Final Group Work | 40% | 3 to 5 students to form a group to study the climate action that required to decarbonize a specific sector, industry or city by 2050.
Participation | 15% | The activeness of the students in the class discussion, and gaming and model practice. nAttendance, which will be checked on eight unannounced occasions during the semester. nEach student is allowed: •One absence without prior notice; and •One personal leave requested before class. These allowances will not reduce the attendance score. However, if a student exceeds either allowance, the attendance component of the participation grade will be recorded as zero.
CLASS ASSIGNMENTS | 15% | THERE WILL BE THREE ASSIGNMENTS DURING THIS SEMESTER National emission profile analysis and carbon footprint in your daily life. Reflection of Energy Security Discussion. A practice in questionnaire design for the final report topic, accompanied by a critical analysis of media representations of climate news.

title: 創新媒體與創意 Innovative Media and Creativity
description:
隨著生成式AI(Gen-AI)、XR與虛擬製作(Virtual Production)等技術導入, 影音媒體產業將經歷重大轉型,觀眾持續增加跨平台影音使用,應用GenAI、虛擬科技將帶來影音創新及創意突破:加速新型態影音產製速度,提升內容沉浸感和社交臨場感。透過新興科技加持的新形態影音,若能結合適當品牌策略與跨平台社群行銷,創新影音內容得以迅速擴散,快速吸引觀眾目光,增強網路聲量和影響力。
本課程以「影音創意」與「科技融合」為核心,本學期與專家產學合作,教導同學如何創造虛擬角色(virtual avatars or influencers),並將其應用於影音內容,結合社群媒體行銷,進而經營自媒體品牌,用來達到有效溝通台灣重要議題之策略目的。課程目標是讓學生執行創新影音專案時,學習到企劃、提案、製作、經營、社群互動和數據分析等整合實務經驗,嘗試為觀眾帶來沉浸式、擬人化之社交影音體驗。
同學將組成創意製作小組,共同創作Avatar。透過策略性經營自媒體品牌,本學期題目希望針對台灣文化社會關懷、永續發展SDGs、兒少節目 或人權性平等主題發揮,須超越泛娛樂化和個人秀網紅形式,需有知識內容含金量+觀眾互動反饋+社會實踐。同學將嘗試以虛擬角色結合生成式AI工具,策劃、製作與推播影音及社群內容,再搭配跨平台行銷手法,藉以讓內容迅速擴散,進而引發關注與互動。
本課程結合產學合作,邀請業界專家指導學生從創建虛擬角色、運用新科技製作實驗性創新影音與社群內容,並獲得專業回饋。學生將在實作與發表中累積新媒體時代所需的跨域創意與實戰能力,達成「學中做、做中學」的目標,為未來媒體職涯鋪路。
objectives:
為因應新媒體科技變化,本課程培養具創新思維及創意企製能力影音專業人才,課程規劃分為兩大主軸:1. 知識理解:認識AI與XR等新興技術對影音產製與行銷模式的影響,聚焦於掌握虛擬角色製作與生成式AI科技趨勢和發展脈絡。2.實作應用:學生將學習虛擬角色製作及GenAI工具使用,經營小組自媒體品牌,透過社群平台行銷推廣、觀眾互動與數據回饋進行成效分析,完整體驗內容企劃、製作、經營與評估的流程。
其課程目標:
1. 協助學生了解GenAI和虛擬Avatar影音新科技發展,以及它們對影音產業及生態所帶來衝擊,同時了解思考影音媒體結合新科技進行創新、調整或轉型之作法與成效。
2. 結合GenAI和虛擬Avatar影音新科技規劃自媒體影音品牌、企製內容,並進行社群行銷,結合知識、know-how及實作經驗,最後以數據評估成效,邀請專家講評企製內容。
3. 透過影音作品,提高對人文社會議題思考力及媒體表達力。
學期間安排活動 (工作坊、演講、參訪和高峰會):
1. 專家講演 GenAI & Vtuber (Ubitus: 日商優必達Ubitus商務總監許朝欽)、AI工具製作虛擬AVATAR及影音
2. 公視數位發展部 Vtuber及虛擬主播參訪
3. 參與”亞洲新媒體高峰會”(亞洲新媒體高峰會已成為NMEA每年固定舉辦的重點活動之一。每年年底NMEA邀集國內外的產業專家共聚一堂,舉行為期兩天的產業高峰會,會上針對內容產業最前沿的趨勢與議題進行討論,激發產業內外的跨界創新合作)
grading:
本通識課程提供學生對於使用GenAI科技應用於媒體內容產製(影音及社群媒體行銷)第一手經驗,每組同學們均可以用GenAI產出圖文、社群媒體內容、長短影音等,教學評量方式如下:
成績考核: 平時成績: 100%
1. 參與(10%):出席 、討論、課堂作業 (5%)
2. 虛擬角色設計報告(10%):每組PPT分享 (報告虛擬角色與品牌在影音和社群應用規畫)
3. 企劃書提案 (15%):口頭報告 (5%); 書面報告(10%) 透過自媒體品牌結合虛擬角色、影音及社群媒體,傳播重要台灣文化社會議題(如兒少、永續、健康等)
4. 虛擬角色社群內容 (20%)(社群平台設計規劃+ >10 篇社群圖文、短影音)
5. 虛擬角色影音作品 (25%)(累計>10mins) (2個以上影音作品)
6. 期末報告 (20%):口頭報告 (5%); 書面報告(15%) (指標:整體規劃、內容呈現;品牌力、影響力及成效 (質量評估 eg: 數據或網路口碑)
Extra: 小組互評 (+-5%):自媒體團隊期末組內表現互評,可加減總分 5 分 (最後總分)

title: 東協的整合與發展 The ASEAN Integration and Development
description: This course is designed to provide an overview for Southeast Asia in term of the historical development and integration processes of the ASEAN community, prospects and challenges. We explore the variations in regional growth of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member within 10 countries (Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Indonesia, Brunei, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar). This course is aimed to bring students into a deeper approach about ASEAN community. A map will be constructed throughout the course with selective socio- economic conditions for comparison and better understanding.
objectives:
Students will benefit through the insightful knowledge and the sharing of best practices. By the end of the course, students will be able to obtain the following knowledge:
Identity and diversity of SEA: geopolitical importance and local uniqueness
The four distinct waves of cultural influence: China, India, European Colonizers, and the Islam
Social transformation after the Western colonialism
Historical development of ASEAN: Journey to community building
Rationales of ASEAN community
ASEAN Political-Security Community (APSC)
ASEAN Economic Community (AEC): Milestones
ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community (ASCC)
ASEAN opportunities and challenges
Taiwan's New Southbound Policy toward the ASEAN economies
grading:
The final grades are determined by 2 parts as following:
Attendance: 70%
Written exam:30%
Please note: Active participation in class discussions, especially during the Q&A sections/ Kahoot, may enhance your final grade.

title: 國小學生課後關懷與輔導 After-school Tutorial Service for Elementary School Students
description: 本課程旨在發揮個人所學,落實專長訓練,讓同學學習如何幫助國小學生,特別是弱勢家庭,學習妥善運用課後在校時間,進行作業與體能發展、人際互動、生活藝術的學習。本課程與台北市課後照顧協會合作,同學們亦可經由與該組織之互動,了解非營利組織的運作與服務規劃、管理,不僅可以強化淑世情懷,有助於開拓眼界,也確立以服務為目的的人生觀。
grading: 實習表現:輔導學生的積極度30%,服務出席準確性10%。學生須參與至少18小時的服務活動。 課堂參與(含討論課):20%,學生必須出席課堂活動(實體&線上): 包含第一至三週課堂說明,期中討論報告(將於第8週~10週)舉行,及期末口頭報告(最後兩週)。以及線上教材的作業回應。 服務輔導紀錄與期末口頭報告:40%(依輔導的詳實度、反思深度與論點豐富度評量) (4)服務與輔導紀錄須於實習的第一、三、五次服務完成的一週內分批寄給教師,最後將完整記錄與期末報告的投影片上傳至數位教學網。

title: 圖書館實務及創意管理 Library Practices and Innovative Management
description:
本課程以圖書館的核心功能與實務運作為主軸,引導學生從「保存文化記錄、捍衛知的權利、統整資訊資源、滿足資訊需求」等面向,認識圖書館在知識保存、資訊服務、文化傳承與社會教育中的角色。課程內容結合數位典藏、文獻保存、知識自由、無障礙閱讀、資訊組織、館藏檢索、AI資料庫、閱讀推廣與圖書館空間設計等主題,協助學生理解圖書館如何回應不同使用者的資訊需求,並在數位科技與社會變遷中持續創新服務。
本課程除透過課堂講授與圖書館導覽,使學生理解圖書館實務的基本概念與運作方式外,也將安排圖書館資源與資料庫檢索課程,培養學生資訊搜尋、資源運用與問題分析能力。期末則以小組合作方式,選擇一項圖書館實務議題,從問題觀察、現況分析到具體改善方案,提出具創意與可行性的圖書館實務規劃報告,藉此培養學生對圖書館服務與管理的創意思考能力。
objectives:
1.認識圖書館核心功能與社會角色
引導學生理解圖書館在保存文化記錄、捍衛知的權利、統整資訊資源與滿足資訊需求等面向的功能,認識圖書館作為知識保存、資訊服務、文化傳承與終身學習機構的重要性。
2.理解圖書館實務運作與服務內涵
協助學生認識數位典藏、文獻保存、知識自由、無障礙閱讀、資料徵集、資訊組織、特藏資料、校史檔案、閱覽典藏與推廣活動等圖書館實務主題,掌握圖書館服務與管理的基本概念。
3.培養資訊檢索與圖書館資源運用能力
透過數位館藏檢索、特藏資料介紹、AI資料庫與輔助學習工具等課程活動,培養學生運用圖書館資源、搜尋資訊、評估資訊與解決問題的能力。
4.發展圖書館創意管理與實務規劃能力

title: 動物權:理論與實踐 Animal Rights: Theory and Practice
description:
包括人為氣候變遷在內的全球生態環境裂化徵狀正一一浮現之際,人類在不改變其與動物之關係的情況下,是否有存續機會?人類對待動物的方式是哲學問題、經濟問題、科學問題、還是政治問題?
野保與動保吵不停,究竟該如何看待並解決流浪動物問題?
以辛格與里根之辯論*貫串,輔以金利卡與唐納森的「動物公民」**觀念,本課程探究每位同學作為一個世界公民,其與地球、自然、其他物種之關係。
本課程隔週週三上課,每次兩小時。
*1975年彼得.辛格(Peter Singer)出版《動物解放》,主張既然人類透過奴隸制度剝削其他人類、透過性別歧視壓制女性的觀念及行為漸遭汰除,人類也應該開始反省對其他動物的剝削利用,調整其完全排除其他物種利益考量的「物種歧視」觀念及行為。1983年湯姆‧里根(Tom Regan)出版The Case for Animal Rights,認為雖然《動物解放》倡議停止剝削動物,但彼得.辛格是從功利主義出發,用利益的加減計算得出動物虐待剝削「淨利為負」;據以得出不應虐待剝削動物之結論。對里根而言,這是對於動物權利的一種否定。一如人類個人為其生命的唯一主體,對其經歷的事物之意義具有唯一主觀的感受詮釋能力,動物亦然。因此,一如人類具備不可侵犯的基本權利,動物亦然。
**《動物公民:動物權利的政治哲學》,白舜羽譯,貓頭鷹書房出版,2021
objectives: 透過課程內容、討論、隨堂測驗、作業、指定讀物以及測驗,學習並反思資本主義社會與動物的關係。
grading:
課堂參與(點名or隨堂作業)、作業、測驗、心得均佔相同比例。
缺課該次0分。有請假60分。有醫生證明或公假單該次不計分。

title: 自主學習專題:Stand-Up Comedy 單口喜劇創作與表達 Seminar in Self-Directed Learning: Stand-Up Comedy: Creation and Expression
description:
單口喜劇俗稱脫口秀, 因校內的課程以往都較偏學術性, 加上有其他同學也對單口喜劇有興趣, 故開設這門課程希望可以訓練學生口說和創作能力, 以應付未來在職場上人際關係之間溝通的技巧。
我們會以許多週的創作課程,來訓練學生對於開口前先快速擬定講稿, 並且也有訓練口條與台風的課程, 最後的成果發表會要求學生用這 16 週所學的知識上台講述 3 分鐘的脫口秀。
成果發表會提供學生實作和實踐的機會,學生也會在寫稿的當中, 開始了解自己的價值觀。上台講述對於一般人是一件極度挑戰的事情, 可以利用此機會達成人生的一個成就。藉由單口喜劇的內容可以覺察時事脈動, 了解當今社會大眾所關注的議題為何。
objectives:
1. 學習創作脫口秀
2. 學習深入觀察議題的能力
3. 學習脫口秀技巧, 能透過脫口秀方式, 吸引人關注議題
grading:
平時成績(出席率、平時上課表現) 20%(表現好加分,缺席扣分)
期中校外教學 心得500-1000字 30%
期末成發 50%
weeklyText:
課程 2 小時
每週練習、創作時間請同學估有 3 小時以上的投入
【第一週】前導: 課堂內容介紹 (包括自我介紹、對課程的想像、單口喜劇演員在做什麼)
【第二週】
何謂喜劇?喜劇風格、單口喜劇的歷史演進?新手要如何開始?
【第三週】
學習說話、表達——如何有效表達自己的想法?精準表達語句、在舞台上的肢體動 作、吸引觀眾注意的技巧等)(笑話結構、one liner)
【第四週】
初階寫作:如何撰寫文案?如何從生活中經驗變成有趣的段子?什麼才好笑 (態度修辭、one liner練習) 五
【第五週】
初階寫作(二)(三分鐘段子) 如何建立穩健台風?訓練台風、同學嘗試上台 成果演練及指導(一)(檢視上週文案作業+老師建議)
【第六週】
學習舞台上的臨場反應(如何與觀眾互動、如何面對觀眾的疑問、觀眾沒反應時如何 應對?
【第七週】
彈性課程——校外教學/邀講者演講(卡米地、23 open mic 改成星期三) 成果演練及指導(二)
【第八週】
學習成為觀眾(進階三分鐘練習、尋找人設)(也可選這週去看卡米地)
【第九週】
(進階寫作二)
【第十週】
(表演課) 學習精準選題?(如何從一項議題中提煉精華?如何捕捉「笑點」?)
【第十一週】
摸索冒犯的「界線」:當單口喜劇遇上道德兩難(如何彩排)(run show) 成果演練及指導(三)
【第十二週】
脫口秀表演的大小事(談論冒犯、炎上、公關危機)公關、自媒體

期末分組成果發表

期末分組成果發表

期末成果發表

title: 計算思維與人工智慧 Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence
description:
本課程旨在介紹計算思維與人工智慧的基本概念、原理和應用,為之後修習資訊相關課程奠下基礎。21世紀數位時代,如何具有應用人工智慧技術能力,培養計算思維是第一步,因為計算思維是分析問題、制定解決方法的思考過程,其中解決的步驟得依循電腦運算邏輯,因此在有了抽象思考能力後,將進一步介紹電腦具體運作架構,兩者的結合將由人工智慧程式應用來加以練習,此外也將介紹人工智慧的發展歷程和未來趨勢,以及人工智慧對社會、經濟和文化的影響。
加退選說明: 若選課人數達上限135人,仍有多人候補;實習課週五 67節隔週上課,必點名,所以時間不能配合,麻請退選,給後補同學機會;之後退簽,需具名特殊原因,不然不退簽。
​加簽說明: 本學期不開放加簽,若加退選沒選上者,可於往後學期嘗試看看。
本課程會介紹程式,但不是全部,想要學程式設計,建議 程式設計概論 / Programming 101 by 邱淑怡, 郭正佩
objectives: 首先認識計算思維,搭配電腦數位架構介紹,進一步理解計算思維在電腦中運作方式,此思維進一步深化到人工智慧領域,課程將介紹人工智慧中機器如何學習的基礎知識,搭配程式實作,讓學生有初步設計其專業領域智能系統的能力;此外課程將分析人工智慧對社會文化影響,並探討相關的倫理問題。
grading:

title: 計算思維與人工智慧 Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence
description: 本課程旨在介紹計算思維與人工智慧的基本概念、原理和應用,為之後修習資訊相關課程奠下基礎。21世紀數位時代,如何具有應用人工智慧技術能力,培養計算思維是第一步,因為計算思維是分析問題、制定解決方法的思考過程,其中解決的步驟得依循電腦運算邏輯,因此在有了抽象思考能力後,將進一步介紹電腦具體運作架構,兩者的結合將由人工智慧程式應用來加以練習,此外也將介紹人工智慧的發展歷程和未來趨勢,以及人工智慧對社會、經濟和文化的影響。
objectives: 首先認識計算思維,搭配電腦數位架構介紹,進一步理解計算思維在電腦中運作方式,此思維進一步深化到人工智慧領域,課程將介紹人工智慧中機器如何學習的基礎知識,搭配程式實作,讓學生有初步設計其專業領域智能系統的能力;此外課程將分析人工智慧對社會文化影響,並探討相關的倫理問題。

title: 詞彙學 Chinese Lexicology
description:
課程會對華語詞彙進行全面性的介紹。在本課程中,我們會針對以下幾個華語詞彙呈現的特性進行深入介紹與探討: (a) 華語中關於字、詞、詞組的概念;(b) 華語中關於字、詞、詞組的界線;(c) 華語詞彙的建構以及其內部結構;(d) 漢字與華語詞彙的不對稱性;(e) 華語詞彙與華語語法的互動;(f) 華語詞彙的功能性; (g) 華語詞彙與詞意等面向。本課程除了幫助學生建立華語詞彙的基本觀念之外,也會透過課堂討論來引導學生觀察日常生活中的詞彙現象進行描述,並適時結合一些當代華語的相關語言研究內容,幫助學生掌握華語詞彙的研究脈絡;本課程同時也會不時以中英對比的方式(如詞彙形式、語法差異)進行不同語言之間的比較與說明,幫助學生掌握華語詞彙與華語語法的互動以及培養學生具有能力洞察不同語言之間的差異,以期未來能反饋到華語教學實務上。
This course provides an introduction to Chinese morphology. In particular, we look at many different aspects in which the features of Chinese morphology manifest: (a) the concept of Chinese words; (b) the internal structure and boundary of Chinese words; (c) the formation of Chinese words; (d) the relation between Chinese characters and Chinese words; (e) the interaction between Chinese words and Chinese grammar; (f) the function of Chinese words; (g) the lexical meaning of Chinese words; (h) loan words and the development of new words in Chinese; (i) the relation between Chinese words and culture. Overall, this course offers a foundation (regarding the knowledge of Chinese words) for students who aspire to become a Chinese-as-a-second-language teacher so that they can apply the learned knowledge to their teaching of Chinese in the future.
objectives:
本課程會對華語詞彙進行全面性的介紹。在本課程中,我們會針對以下幾個華語詞彙呈現的特性進行深入介紹與探討: (a) 華語中關於字、詞、詞組的概念;(b) 華語中關於字、詞、詞組的界線;(c) 華語詞彙的建構以及其內部結構;(d) 漢字與華語詞彙之間的不對稱性;(e) 華語詞彙與華語語法的互動;(f) 華語詞彙的功能性; (g) 華語詞彙與詞意等面向。本課程除了幫助學生建立華語詞彙的基本觀念之外,也會透過課堂討論來引導學生觀察日常生活中的詞彙現象進行描述,並適時結合一些當代華語的相關語言研究內容,幫助學生掌握華語詞彙的研究脈絡;本課程同時也會不時以中英對比的方式(如詞彙形式、語法差異)進行不同語言之間的比較與說明,幫助學生掌握華語詞彙與華語語法的互動以及培養學生具有能力洞察不同語言之間的差異,以期未來能反饋到華語教學實務上。
Course Objectives
This course provides an introduction to Chinese morphology. In particular, we look at many different aspects in which the features of Chinese morphology manifest: (a) the concept of Chinese words; (b) the internal structure and boundary of Chinese words; (c) the formation of Chinese words; (d) the relation between Chinese characters and Chinese words; (e) the interaction between Chinese words and Chinese grammar; (f) the function of Chinese words; (g) the lexical meaning of Chinese words; (h) loan words and the development of new words in Chinese; (i) the relation between Chinese words and culture. Overall, this course offers a foundation (regarding the knowledge of Chinese words) for students who aspire to become a Chinese-as-a-second-language teacher so that they can apply the learned knowledge to their teaching of Chinese in the future.
Learning Outcomes
1. To better understand (a) the key features of Chinese morphology; and (b) the interaction between Chinese words and other components such as meaning, grammar and Chinese culture
2. To develop the teaching and communication skills of applying the learned knowledge about Chinese words to teaching of Chinese.
3. To develop the analytical skills of recognizing the morphological differences between Chinese and other languages, and elaborating on how Chinese words interact with meaning, grammar and Chinese culture.
4. To develop critical thinking skills.

title: 旅行與台灣歷史 Travel and Taiwan's history
description:
※本課程為大學部選修課程!
※本課程所用數位工具適合一般文科生,不需程式寫作能力。
※本學期數位工具為AI Agent,非一問一答之AI,而是建立代理系統,協助策劃臺灣歷史主題的自助旅行計畫。(我也不會,所以請專家來教我們,我跟大家一起學)
本課程為台灣史研究所開設的「臺灣與近代世界」跨領域學程科目之一,亦為一般選修學分。
本課程同時加入國立政治大人文創新學程 / 創新與創造力學程,與本校資訊科學系廖文宏老師共創課程,在一般歷史課程之外(內容),加入數位工具的學習與應用課程(數位),培養歷史與科技之間的跨界運用與反思能力,藉以強化在未來數位時代中的人文素養。
objectives:
1、藉由不同時空的旅行,理解臺灣史的各個面向。
2、藉由不同旅行的比較,理解背後的文化意涵。
3、熟悉數位工具發展趨勢,企畫與批判臺灣史主題的自助旅行計畫。

title: 選修英文:閱讀與口語訓練(ETP專班) English Elective:Reading & Oral Training(ETP)
grading:
Class time will be devoted to reading, discussion, collaborative inquiry, and speaking activities. To participate effectively, you are expected to complete the assigned readings and preparation before class and to take an active role in pair work, group work, and whole-class discussions.
Your final grade will be based on the following course components:
Weekly Inquiry Forum: 20%
Midterm Inquiry Presentation: 20%
Personal Interest Talk: 20%
Final Synthesis Presentation: 20%
Class Participation: 20%
For group assignments, grades will reflect both the quality of the group’s overall work and each member’s individual contribution. Individual grades may therefore differ within the same group.
ASSIGNMENTS AND REQUIREMENTS
Attendance and Participation
Attendance is essential because much of the learning in this course takes place through discussion and interaction. Your participation grade will be based on your attendance, preparation, and active contribution to the learning of the class.
Participation includes taking part in pair and group discussions, responding to questions, sharing ideas and interpretations, listening and responding to classmates, and contributing constructively to student-led activities. Quality of participation is more important than simply speaking frequently.
Reading and Preparation
Assigned readings should be completed before class. You may also be asked to complete short preparation tasks, reflection questions, or other activities related to the readings. These tasks are designed to help you participate meaningfully in class discussions and inquiry activities.
Weekly Inquiry Forum
Each student will participate in one group-led Weekly Inquiry Forum. Rather than giving a conventional presentation or summarizing the assigned reading, the group will use the week’s core question and reading to develop its own interpretation and lead the class in a 30-minute inquiry session.
The forum should include relevant textual evidence, the group’s own perspective, and meaningful opportunities for classmates to participate, respond, and discuss.
Personal Interest Talk
Each student will give a 3–5 minute individual talk on a topic of personal interest. The topic may be something you enjoy, know well, care about, or simply want to introduce to the class. The purpose of this activity is to develop confidence, ownership, and an individual speaking voice.
Midterm Inquiry Presentation
The midterm project will ask you to investigate a question connected to the first half of the course and the theme of The World That Shapes Us. You will work collaboratively to develop a focused inquiry, gather relevant evidence, and present your findings and interpretation to the class.
Final Synthesis Presentation
The final project will ask you to bring together ideas from the second half of the course and, where appropriate, make connections across the semester. The emphasis will be on synthesis, interpretation, and developing a thoughtful response to the larger question of what it means to remain human in a changing world.
Detailed instructions and grading criteria for major assignments will be provided separately.

title: 選修英文:學術聽說訓練(ETP專班) English Elective: Academic_Listening_&_Speaking(ETP)
description: This course, which is conducted in English, is designed for high-intermediate to advanced English learners. It is based on a content-based syllabus, utilizing lectures on topics from different academic disciplines and related reading materials. The authentic content provides both a context for the practice of important language skills and a basis for the exploration of high-interest topics for learners. The course covers diverse issues and integrates vocabulary, grammar, listening and speaking skills necessary for academic success. Throughout the semester, students are encouraged to improve their academic listening and speaking ability by listening to lectures and participating in discussions, as well as practicing note-taking and summarizing.
objectives:
This course will help students to
- build discipline- or topic-related vocabulary
- improve listening skills both in everyday and academic settings
- develop learning strategies and study skills for academic success
- reinforce academic discussion and communicative skills
- develop effective note-taking and summarizing skills
- deliver informative talks / presentation in today’s academic and professional world
- expand critical thinking
- be aware of cultural differences and similarities
Learning Outcomes for Lecture Comprehension and Note-taking
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
- predict lecture content and organization
- listen for the lecturer’s main points and for the general organizational framework
- make guesses when information is missed
- evaluate and decide what is and is not important during a lecture
- note key words, and use abbreviations and symbols
- organize information and visually represent the relationship between ideas
- note most numbers and statistics
Learning Outcomes for Informative Talks & Presentation
By the end of the course, while presenting, students will be able to:
- consider the audience and have clear objectives (to inform, to amuse, to persuade, to train, etc.)
- have a clear structure and link the parts together
- address academic issues successfully with a variety of resources
- consider the timing
- speak clearly at the right speed
- use appropriate language
- maintain eye contact with the audience
- use body language effectively
- appear confident and positive
- make clear visual aids to support messages
- use the equipment professionally
grading:
ATTENDANCE, PUNCTUALITY & ASSIGNMENT/EXAM POLICIES
Attendance is important, and students are expected to come to class ON TIME! (Attendance/Lateness policy will be explained in the first class.) Students who are absent for more than half of total class hours without an appropriate reason will receive zero for both Attendance and Class Performance portions, and CANNOT partake in the final exam. All required assignments must be submitted to the instructor before the due dates. Note that NO assignments will be accepted after the deadline. The quizzes CANNOT be made up (except for sick leave), and NO make-up final exam will be given unless you have received the instructor’s permission in advance.
To successfully complete the course, you must participate in assigned activities and take quizzes and the final exam. Your final grade is determined by the following course components:
Participation: 20% (Attendance 10% + Class performance 10%)
Quizzes: 20%
Assignments: 20%
Presentations: 20% (group 10% + individual 10%)
Final exam: 20%
Participation
Your participation grade will be based on your attendance, homework preparation, and the
contribution you make to the learning experience of others. Contribution includes your questions to
the instructor, insights and comments regarding class content, answers to the instructor’s questions,
and reactions to other students’ contributions in class.
Quizzes
Throughout the semester, 4 quizzes will be given in class, including 3 listening quizzes and 1 speaking
task. The listening quizzes contain lecture listening, note-taking and comprehension questions,
and students are required to give their responses orally in the speaking task. More details will be
provided in class.
Assignments
You will give 3 short Informative Talks (ITs) on topics discussed this semester (2 to your group
members and 1 to the whole class). Each IT focuses on a relevant subtopic of your choice, lasts five
minutes, and may include visual aids. Before the class, you need to upload the outline to the class
website. When you give your IT during class time, the other group members will then
practice note-taking strategies and give you feedback when the IT is finished. Note that your
feedback (e.g., notes and comments) will also need to be uploaded to the class website afterwards.
NO assignments will be accepted after the deadline, which is the end of each unit. Besides these IT assignments, you need to comment on other students' speaking task performance (Week #11) and give suggestions. More details will be
provided in class.
Presentations
You will give one Group Presentation (GP) and one Individual Presentation (IP). For the group
presentation, each group will report on an assigned topic. The presentation should last approximately
20 minutes, followed by a 5-minute class discussion. Before the presentation, each group needs to
upload their PowerPoint slides to the class website. While presenting, each group will be evaluated by
the instructor as well as by their peers. For the individual presentation, each student will be assigned
by the instructor to give a 5-minute informative talk (on one of the chosen topics) with PowerPoint
presentation in front of the whole class. More details will be provided in class.
Final Exam
The final exam contains a listening test and an integrated speaking test. The listening test includes
lecture listening, note-taking, and comprehension questions. In the integrated speaking test, you will
be required to give your responses orally. You will need to demonstrate your ability to respond to
the questions clearly and coherently and the ability to accurately convey the information about what
you have read or listened to.
*** The grading rubrics for the group presentation/speaking test/note-taking exercise (attached below) will be available on the class website.

title: 選修英文:英文寫作(ETP專班) English Elective:Essay_Writing(ETP)
description: This course is an introduction to academic writing and literacy through the fundamentals of essay writing with an emphasis on genre knowledge and audience awareness. The course, which is conducted in English, incorporates lectures and discussion sessions making class-time full of activity. Writing assignments provide students opportunities to practice writing skills while exploring current issues through their own interests and experiences. Students learn ways to approach writing assignments, how to find an interesting topic, and how to go through the process of writing a powerful essay in English. An assigned textbook is used as a guide, but other materials and references will be made available on the course blog.
objectives:
In this class, learners will practice writing as a process of invention and revision that anyone can master with effort. Students will review basic paragraph structure and then learn about common rhetorical forms. They will practice several types of essays including narrative, comparison/contrast, cause-effect, and argument. Literacy skills are incorporated as learners search online sources, learn to cite them, and create a reference list. In sum, students will gain a foundational understanding of English composition and learn the writing process as they develop their own writing and revising toolkit.
By the end of the semester, those who have satisfactorily completed the course requirementswill be able to identify a compelling topic, decide how to treat it in writing, and compose a strong and thoughtful essay to explore or argue it. Students will be familiar with elements of good academic compositions including organization, thesis statements, and clarity of ideas. Finally, students will learn the mechanics of academic writing such as document format, and citations and reference lists.
grading:
Your final grade will be determined by the following course components:
Participation/Homework assignments: 15% (attendance, late to class, out-of-class assignments)
Expository/Benefits Essay (out-of-class – including drafts and AI version): 15%
Process Essay (in-class test): 35%
Cause-Effect Essay (in-class test): 35%
Participation/Homework assignments: 15%
Attendance and coming to class on time = 5%
Out-of-class assignments = 10%
There are two main written assignments (the business letter and the academic paragraph). These assignments will be explained in class, but students must check Moodle for complete details on all assignments (including writing practice from the textbook). Please bring the following items to each class:
The textbook (required)
Lined paper for writing practice (loose-leaf paper, not a bound notebook)
FAQ about Participation:
What happens if I miss the first class?
Please inform the teacher that you will be absent on the first day of class by sending me an email. Students who miss the first day of class must write two make-up papers.
Time yourself for 15 minutes and write a self-introduction by hand, including topics such as your major, interests, writing experience, interesting life experiences, and future goals. Do not use help tools to correct your grammar. I need a sample of your typical writing style.
Write a summary of the key points of the Day One PPT, which will be posted on Moodle. You can write this assignment by hand.
What are we going to do for homework?
There are a few writing assignments that complete activities which we start in class - such as writing a business letter, completing an academic paragraph, the process essay, or other practice writing activities. We may also do pre-writing activities for homework that will prepare you to write an essay in class. In addition to writing activities, students will complete assigned exercises in the textbook. Therefore, having the textbook is a requirement for participation and will be checked in the third week.
Do we need to buy the complete textbook? Can’t we make photocopies of the book chapters we use?
We will be using quite a bit of the textbook in both practice activities and learning from the essay model examples, so you would need to photocopy most of the book, which is illegal by copyright laws unless the publisher gives permission. This textbook also functions partly as a workbook and reference book, so it is worth it to use for study and improvement of essay writing skills. Students are also required to bring the textbook to each class even though we may not use it in every class.
Can we get an ebook?
It is allowed to buy an ebook version of the textbook, but students with the ebook may need to write answers to activities on a separate piece of paper, or use your Apple Pen to fill in the blanks of assignments in your e-textbook. Students must be ready to prove they bought the ebook by showing the professor.
Other than assignments, what else is included in the participation grade?
Attendance is mandatory. If a student has three or more unexcused absences, he/she will fail the course. Coming to class on time is also important. Coming late cannot be made up and if a student is late three times, it equals one unexcused absence. The main component of this hands-on writing course is practice. Students are required to participate in writing practice alone and with a partner. This ensures peer feedback and mutual encouragement in your writing journey.
How do we submit assignments?
Please print out the assignment, including any pre-writing, etc. I want to have the paper-version of your writing because I want to write comments all over the paper and also show grammar errors. The only assignment that I will accept as an email attachment is a make-up essay. Minor assignments may be written by hand, except for the business letter. Major assignments must be typed and printed out (essay, double-spaced; outline and pre-writing, single-spaced).
Out-of-class assignments:
Expository/Benefits Essay (out-of-class): 15%
The expository essay is how students learn the foundation of essay writing. This assignment is completed in stages. The first stage is the first draft, using the basic essay format. The second stage is expanding the essay according to our instruction in class. The third stage is an additional draft with more changes. The final draft considers all of what we have learned in class to make it the best essay you have ever written. Please type and print out the final draft of the assignment, including the detailed outline and the final draft of the essay. The early drafts and pre-writing may be handwritten.
SPECIAL NOTE ON ASSIGNMENTS AND AI:
The first draft of all out-of-class assignments must be your own writing without grammar checks, translations, AI, or other help tools. In other words, they must include all of your errors. No grammar will be graded on those assignments. If a first-draft assignment is turned in with no errors OR if that assignment appears that some sentences have been fabricated by AI or other writing help tools, the paper will not be accepted and will not be allowed to be made up.
However, on some writing assignments, students will be asked to use AI (using Chat-GPT or other AI tool) to correct their grammar. In this case, they must write the first draft by themselves without help tools and then have AI rewrite it with correct grammar. Students must turn in both the original version and the AI version. They will analyze these two versions in class to check for patterns of grammar errors. (AI version assignments = academic paragraph and expository essay) Again, grammar will not be graded on out-of-class assignments, but it will be graded on in-class tests. Therefore, students are encouraged to improve their grammar using this method before the first in-class exam.
Process Essay (in-class test): 35%
Students will prepare to write a process essay following procedures learned in class. Students will then use part of their prepared material from class to write the essay without the use of digital help tools. They will have three hours to write this essay in class. This essay tests the student’s ability in proper structure of the essay and outline format as well as language use (grammar and vocabulary).
Cause-Effect Essay (in-class test): 35%
The final exam tests the student’s advanced essay writing ability to organize body paragraphs in their own way and to persuasively produce a cause-and-effect essay on a particular phenomenon. The topic will be given in class on the day of the test, but it will be a topic that everyone has experience with. The final exam will be the fufillment of the objective from the first day of class: to compose a detailed outline and essay from blank page to finished product without the help of digital writing tools.

title: 跨界實驗室 X Lab
description:
【重要說明】
1. 優先開放人創學程與創創學程學生修課。
2. 第一堂課需親到才算選到,缺席者請自行退選。
【課程簡介】
此刻與過去 或許都在未來之中 而過去也包含了未來
~T. S. Eliot
2006年起,政大師生翻轉上課形式,設計了一個以直覺、感情與感官為主的教育實驗,前四年叫做「創意學程」,第五年起更名「X書院」,歷經「人文創新學程」和「人文創新數位虛擬學院」等不同階段,兩年前正式成立「政大X實驗學院」。
有人把「X」唸成「差」,挺好的,成績差、人際差,都沒關係;有人以為「X」是漏字,挺好的,所有被排擠的、被丟掉的、被忽略的,都可以在這裡暫時安置。追本溯源,「Χ」來自數學方程式的「未知」。因此,作為X實驗學院入門課,「跨界實驗室」的目標就是:找到門,推開它,走出去!
第一道門是走出自己的舒適圈,踏上未知之旅;第二道門,是認識五位守門人陳文玲、劉冠妏、陳囿蓉、黃彥晨和唐京睦,創造一個師生互為主體、涵融陰陽動能的學習體驗;第三道門,是閱讀《榮格自傳》,逐章逐節瞭解瑞士心理學家榮格早年、中年與晚年的發展,透過探究原型(Archetypes)、人格類型(Personality Types)與個體化歷程(Individuation)等相關理論,往內打開自己,並據此逐步完成期末創作「自己之書」,回應如何在這個不停變動的世界裡整合自我、安身立命
objectives:
一位教育者必須以此為目標,即是將託付給他的一群孩子造就成許許多多且各異的人;若是他的教養誤將一個人分裂成兩個人,兩個彼此爭執的人,也勝過於延續普遍的企圖,即是將所有的學生都教育成一種人...... 如此一來,自然而然會有一種截然不同的學校產生,一種沒有考試與競爭的學校,不會與生活斷了聯繫,而是不斷地走向生活。這種學校不會扼殺正在萌生中的個性,而是提供每個人機會,貫徹其天性最深處之願望的學校。~《慢讀里爾克》
【守門人講師群】
陳文玲|政大X實驗學院教授兼副院長(與廣告系合聘),以榮格心理學為基調,設計系列「探索自我X藝術表達」的體驗課程 ,以人工行動回應人工智慧,試圖在教育現場創造非A即B的「第三種」可能性。
劉冠妏|信仰著「我的一生是一個無意識自我充分發揮的故事」的諮商心理師。從成長文化中的文學世界走入西方心理學世界,面對個人自我以及其所處環境的探究與理解,在以認識自我為同心圓下,窺探著一層層關係的激盪與迴響。
陳囿蓉|心理師、藝術創作者。以夢與圖像為路徑,帶領人探索無意識與自我轉化。長期陪伴心靈探索者進入象徵世界,練習與內在對話。
黃彥晨|政大X實驗學院專案總監,擅長塔羅占卜、芳香療法、戲劇與五感體驗......更鍾愛於意象綻放於身體、感官與心靈的流動時刻,也期待將這樣跨邊界、詩意、活著的經驗分享給他人。
唐京睦|政大創意學程第四屆學生,政大廣電系與企管系雙主修畢,香氣工作者,塔羅與占星研究者,擅長在意象與體驗之間,打開創作與互動的空間。
【目標與成效】
練習工具:經由「自由書寫」與「曼陀羅繪圖」兩種創意表達工具,認識意象與象徵
調和平衡:透過體驗性工作坊,認識陰性原則和陽性原則的發展與困境,調和內在與外在平衡
學習理論:搭配榮格心理學理論,逐章閱讀《榮格自傳》
完成習作:仿照《榮格自傳》的架構,回看過往、想像未來,完成期末創作「自己之書」
grading:
出席參與 30%
期末創作 30%
期末聯展 30%
期末自評 10%

title: 傳統精緻藝術再創新-故宮博物院專案實作 Reinnovation of Chinese Classical Arts
description:
AI 可以生成作品,但無法生成觀點。文化創新的起點,不是 Prompt,而是理解文物。
本課程為政治大學與國立故宮博物院合作開設之跨領域專案實作課程,以故宮典藏文物為創作起點,透過文化研究、創意思考、手作原型(Prototype)與 AI 等多元創作方法,探索傳統藝術在當代的新可能。
課程不同於直接利用 AI 生成作品,而是引導學生從理解文物的歷史背景、美學特色與文化意涵開始,發掘值得重新詮釋的觀點,再透過手作原型反覆測試、討論與修正,逐步形成創作方向,最後運用 AI 與數位工具提升作品的完成度,讓科技成為深化創意的媒介,而非取代思考的捷徑。
本課程採專案式學習,由學生組成團隊,從故宮文物及相關文化主題中發展創作議題,並依作品需求自由選擇最適合的媒介形式,成果不限於動畫,可涵蓋互動體驗、數位敘事、展覽、裝置藝術或手作與數位融合等多元表現。
課程由吳彥杰老師負責課程設計與專案指導,並與國立故宮博物院合作,邀請故宮專家分享文物知識、策展觀點與文化詮釋,另安排手作工作坊及跨領域創作者共同參與指導,協助學生完成從文物理解到創作實踐的完整歷程。
objectives:
本課程以「理解、詮釋、原型、創作、協作、反思」作為核心學習歷程,引導學生完成一項結合文化理解與當代創作的跨領域專案。修課完成後,學生預期能具備以下能力:
1. 文化理解(Understand)
能理解故宮文物的歷史背景、文化意涵與美學特色,並從不同角度分析其文化價值,建立創作所需的研究基礎。
2. 文化詮釋(Interpret)
能從文物與文化主題中提出值得被重新看見的觀點,將歷史知識轉化為具有當代意義的創作概念,而非僅停留於內容介紹或形式模仿。
3. 原型設計(Prototype)
能運用手作 Prototype(原型)將抽象想法快速具體化,透過製作、測試、討論與修正,逐步發展作品方向,理解原型作為創作思考工具的價值。
4. 創作實踐(Create)
能依據創作目的選擇適切的媒介與工具,包含 AI、動畫、互動媒體、展覽、裝置藝術或其他數位形式,完成兼具文化內涵與創作觀點的作品。
5. 跨域協作(Collaborate)
能與不同專長背景的成員共同規劃、分工與溝通,整合人文、藝術、設計與科技等多元知識,完成跨領域創作專案。
6. 創作反思(Reflect)
能於創作歷程中持續檢視自己的研究、詮釋與創作選擇,適時修正方向,並反思 AI 與創作者在文化創作中的角色與價值。

title: 旅行與台灣歷史 Travel and Taiwan's History
description:
※本課程為大學部選修課程!
※本課程所用數位工具適合一般文科生,不需程式寫作能力。
※本學期數位工具為AI Agent,非一問一答之AI,而是建立代理系統,協助策劃臺灣歷史主題的自助旅行計畫。(我也不會,所以請專家來教我們,我跟大家一起學)
本課程為台灣史研究所開設的「臺灣與近代世界」跨領域學程科目之一,亦為一般選修學分。
本課程同時加入國立政治大人文創新學程 / 創新與創造力學程,與本校資訊科學系廖文宏老師共創課程,在一般歷史課程之外(內容),加入數位工具的學習與應用課程(數位),培養歷史與科技之間的跨界運用與反思能力,藉以強化在未來數位時代中的人文素養。
objectives:
1、藉由不同時空的旅行,理解臺灣史的各個面向。
2、藉由不同旅行的比較,理解背後的文化意涵。
3、熟悉數位工具發展趨勢,企畫與批判臺灣史主題的自助旅行計畫。

title: 初級越語 Basic Vietnamese
description:
本課程為讓初學者了解擁有詞彙、聽、說、讀、寫的基本知識,有效幫助學生運用口說及寫作交流廣泛的議題。本課程將運用越語介紹越南當地各種文化面向。
This course for beginners is aimed to provide students with basic knowledge in major skills of Vietnamese competency used in a broad range of topics in both oral and written communication. The class is designed in various cultural aspects of Vietnam life through the use of Vietnamese language.
objectives:
本課程目標學生了解越語文法句型的基本知識、日常單字及片語。每節課程會進行越語聽、說、讀、寫實際練習。另外、本課程將教導學生掌握越語古今文化之獨特性。選修本課程,學生將建立以下基礎:
The goals of this course are to master the basic knowledge of grammatical sentence patterns, daily vocabulary and phrases. Each lesson has drills and exercises to improve major skills of Vietnamese language. Moreover, the purposes of Vietnamese lectures are to provide students the grasp of distinctive features of Vietnam culture, both ancient and modern. Upon the completion of elementary course, students will establish the foundation of Vietnamese as follow:
發音Pronunciation:
深入理解語音系統及越語音節結構。
Understand in-depth the phonetic system and its syllable structure.
擁有標準越語發音。
Be able to pronounce Vietnamese words correctly.
詞彙Vocabulary:
獲得日常對話中的基礎詞彙。
Gain basic words in daily conversations.
文法Grammar:
時態標示(đã, đang, sẽ)、句型、數字、時間、日期與季節、量詞(cái, quả, trái, quyển...)、疑問詞( khi nào/bao giờ, tại sao, được không)、。。。
Tense markers (đã, đang, sẽ), sentence patterns, numbers, time, date and seasons, classifiers (cái, quả, trái, quyển...), interrogative words (khi nào/bao giờ, tại sao, được không...)...
聽力Listening:
能夠傾聽與理解熟悉的主題之基本對話,包含初級越語範圍中的詞彙和語法。
Be able to listen and comprehend basic conversations in familiar topics within the limits of vocabulary and grammar acquired in this course.
口說Speaking:
能夠回答簡單問句、在熟悉情境中表達自我。
Be able to answer simple questions and express oneself in familiar situations.
閱讀Reading:
能夠閱讀和理解運用基礎詞彙書寫的熟悉主題短文章。
Be able to read and understand short passages on familiar daily topics written in basic vocabulary.
寫作Writing:
能夠在基礎詞彙和語法有限範圍內聽寫、書寫簡單句子和簡短文章,例如自己對未來四年的計畫、日常工作段落等。
Be able to write dictations, simple sentences and short passages in familiar topics within the limit of basic vocabulary and grammar-for example: topics of future plan, daily routine...
文化知識Cultural knowledge:
使用基礎越語例如越南節日、歌謠的文化價值等,習得一般文化知識。
Acquire the general cultural knowledge through the use of Vietnamese language at basic level with regards to the cultural manner of expressions, Vietnam national holidays, sayings...
越語檢定標準Vietnamese language proficiency level:
達到A1(初級標準)
Successful students will be able to acquire A1 (Pre-elementary level)
grading:
學生需於課前將詞彙記熟,文法與閱讀複習,以便於課堂上進行討論與練習。課堂作業繳交將以寄送E-mail方式交予講師。最終成績將依以下4個部分判定:
Students are responsible for memorizing vocabulary, reviewing grammar, and reading materials before class in order to reserve valuable in-class time for oral practice. All assignments are sent to instructor's email prior to the deadlines. The final grades are determined by 4 parts as following:
出席率與參與度(討論,課堂活動,截止日期): 40%
Attendance and participation (discussion, in-class activities, meeting deadlines)
回家作業 (聽力-閱讀 -寫作): 30 %
Weekly Homework ( listening – reading –writing)
考試:30 %
Written exam

title: 東南亞社會與文化中的基督宗教 Christianity in the Southeast Asian Context
description:
宗教除了超越性的向度,也具現世性和臨在性,因此種種關於宗教的認識和詮釋均無法脫離所處脈絡。宗教在東南亞社會扮演重要角色,其政教關係、宗教間的關係以及所謂的「宗教自由」往往不是相對世俗化、自由宗教市場的台灣社會的脈絡所能理解。另一方面,社會系統其實受一個獨立的文化系統塑造和控制,文化體系是價值觀、符號、信仰的複雜交織體,宗教正是價值觀、符號、信仰的集合,因而與文化交織。基督宗教雖被認為來自西方,但已深植本土,且是東南亞某些國家為人所知的元素之一。
早在伊斯蘭傳入東南亞地區以先,基督宗教的亞述東方教會在七世紀就已進入馬來半島和蘇門答臘北部,然而十三到十五世紀,伊斯蘭開始在馬來世界(Nusantara)發展,基督宗教早期據點逐漸消失。歐洲大航海時代揭開序幕以後,天主教隨著葡萄牙殖民勢力進入,與伊斯蘭在這塊區域展開傳教競爭。在1557年佔領澳門後,葡萄牙以此為中心向交趾支那(越南)、高棉、暹羅傳教。而後新教海權國家荷蘭、英國等也挾其殖民勢力在東南亞傳教。對東南亞許多國家而言,基督宗教與殖民勢力可謂緊密相關,但也代表某種現代性;而在一些海洋東南亞國家,伊斯蘭被視為反殖民的力量,與基督宗教迥然有別,因此產生某種對立。在二戰後紛紛獨立的東南亞國家的社會和文化處境下,與殖民勢力相關的基督宗教扮演什麼樣的角色?還有今日強調非西方的「世界基督教」(World Christianity)研究視野下,在不同的東南亞國家,基督宗教又產生何種多元性和在地性?一般論及東南亞與宗教時少有涉及基督宗教,然而基督宗教在許多東南亞國家往往是第二或第三大宗教(在菲律賓和東帝汶更是人數最多的宗教),且具影響力,在某些地方更是身份認同的象徵。
作為宗教研究所和東南亞文化與宗教跨領域學程一部分,本課程將先概述東南亞歷史文化,並讓同學對基督宗教有基本認識,之後分別探討幾個東南亞國家的基督宗教概況以及與社會和文化有關的議題、案例。此外,本課程也預計籌劃校外參訪,認識在本地的東南亞基督宗教群體。
objectives: 國人一般提及東南亞的宗教,如數家珍的不外乎上座部佛教、伊斯蘭、印度教。除提及菲律賓,基督宗教往往被忽視。本課程具東南亞文化和世界宗教通識的意義,嘗試以基督宗教為切入點認識東南亞的社會與文化,同時也期盼提升修讀者對基督宗教及其現況的基礎認識,尤其是它在世界各地的多元性與異質性,單以西方基督宗教為模版已不足夠。另外,基於特殊時空脈絡所致東南亞各國各族文化在台灣的落戶與交融,台灣社會將來可望具備較諸其他東亞國家更傑出的東南亞文化識讀潛力。作為現代公民,相信培養多元文化視野以及對世界宗教的認識將是不可或缺的一環,本課程盼望能承擔部分責任。

title: 歐盟經貿法 European Union Economic Law
description:
歐盟乃一不斷發展之動態統合過程,不同學說試圖解釋此一新興現象與演進背景。歐盟政經統合已發展至貨幣同盟階段,並推動共同外交暨安全政策、銀行聯盟、資本市場聯盟、能源聯盟、單一數位經濟市場並規劃財政聯盟等,形成最高整合層次的區域經貿整合組織,歐盟自稱為「超國家組織」。歐盟法律與政策皆是27個會員國利益相互激盪、競爭、辯證及調和之結果,代表歐洲集體智慧與創意巧思。歐盟乃WTO正式會員,並積極參與國際組織活動,據此,歐盟政策不但規範其所屬會員國,也深深影響國際規則發展動向,值得吾人共同關心,參考借鑑。
歐盟是以內部市場及對外貿易取得最大成就。本課程將介紹歐盟經貿專題,包括共同貿易政策、歐盟新一代FTA政策、貨幣政策、歐元、數位策略、人工智慧法(AIA)、數位服務法(DSA)、數位市場法(DMA)、防治假訊息、食品安全,COVID-19因應、俄烏戰爭因應、氣候變遷與能源安全、人權條款、歐盟對外關係、對等關稅與歐美關係、歐中關係、地緣政治變遷對歐盟的影響,以及台歐經貿關係等議題。這些議題皆是國際學術主流議題,頗具時效性及挑戰性。
本課程也將從事下列專題研究:
(1) 歐盟共同貿易政策:本課程共同貿易政策專題研究將討論:歐盟共同貿易政策、新一代FTA政策、國家安全與歐盟外資審查機制、歐盟晶片與半導體發展策略、歐盟與我國及中國大陸之經貿關係、中美競爭地緣政治對歐盟的影響等重要議題。
(2) 歐盟經貿法專題:歐盟碳邊境調整機制(CBAM)、ESG企業責任,以及俄烏戰爭對歐盟能源安全與歐俄能源貿易關係的影響等議題。
(3) 歐盟數位策略、AIA、DSA及DMA、數位歐元、防治假訊息專題。
objectives:
經濟區域整合已經是現今世界最重要的經濟貿易發展趨勢,歐盟自1950年代起,就開啟建構經濟整合的列車,逐步朝向深化及廣化方向發展。本課程提供一研究機會以從事歐盟經貿政策之法律、政治、經貿分析,以瞭解歐盟此一發展最為成功之超國家組織,WTO會員以及世界最大市場之特殊經貿暨銀行政策風貌。
在後冷戰時期,國際經濟已成為各國對外關係的主軸,以爭取本國最大利益及財富,並做為各國權力、地位及影響力之重要後盾。歐盟乃世界第一大經濟體,擁有近4.5億人口,對國際經貿規則的發展有重大影響力。歐盟也是台灣重要貿易伙伴、出口市場及外資及技術來源。本課程將討論歐盟一些重要經貿議題,包括:歐盟共同貿易政策、新一代FTA政策、歐元、氣候變遷與能源安全、CBAM、ESG企業責任、數位策略、晶片與半導體發展策略、人工智慧、數位貿易、俄烏戰爭對歐盟經貿政策的影響、台歐貿易關係等議題,以提升對歐盟經貿了解,培養具有歐洲觀及歐洲專業的高階人才,並提高歐洲學養及國際競爭力。
grading:
宜具備歐洲聯盟一般常識;
評分採取課堂討論、口頭及課堂書面報告、考試、期末書面報告及上課出席狀況等方式。另外,鼓勵:1. 定期上歐盟網站瀏覽,了解歐盟最新發展,並在課堂上做討論;2. 出席國內外歐盟主題研討會或工作坊;3. 博士生在國內外歐盟相關學術研討會提交論文,或投稿期刊,以培養歐盟研究能力,並提高歐盟研究水準。

title: 歐洲文化與文明 European Cultures and Civilization
description: 盱衡現下,後冷戰時代地緣政治抬頭,全球化的態勢轉趨區域性發展,但各地區仍牽一髮動全身。歐洲自工業革命以降,向以文化霸權自居,此自有其悠久而豐厚的文化與文明底蘊,為了整合並鞏固歐陸強權,遂有歐盟誕生。然而,由於文化歧異、種族多元、宗教衝突、勞動糾紛、難民遷徙、能源爭奪、恐怖主義等問題紛至沓來,不僅造成內部矛盾,外在衝突亦迭有所聞,俄烏戰爭的爆發更將問題推升極致。近年來,甚而有學者和觀察家開始提出歐洲是否面臨困境與衰退。但不論如何,探討歐洲歷來文明與文化問題的來由,唯有追本溯源才是正確的方向。本課程將以單元主題形式,摘取吾人側重之議題,給予不同角度的研讀,期能透過此課程幫助同學整合過往學習基礎,進一步探討歐洲文化與文明之諸多問題,並加以辯證思考。
objectives:
一、課程目標:
本課程設計以單元主題為基礎架構,在全球性的視野格局下,透過指定教材內容之研讀,從中摘取關鍵議題,藉以挖掘蘊含於歐洲文化與文明發展中的相關問題。此外,搭配影視教材之交叉印證,期能建立多方視角的討論可能。
本學期主要探討單元主題內容:中世紀專題、工業革命專題、希特勒專題。
二、學習成效:
1) 從關鍵性議題的探討,建立關於歐洲文化與文明之深度思考。
2) 建立批判性觀點,並能有辯證性的思考認知。
3) 具備觀察、分析並統合歐洲各層面訊息之能力,並能深入比較與借鏡。
grading:
*評量工具與策略、評分標準成效
一、分組報告(40%):分組報告組別分配按修課人數訂定之。重點說明:
(1) 針對該單元主題範圍,自行擇定分組興趣主題、
(2) 以各別專業方向進行深度研析報告、
(3) 側重明確之主題架構與團隊合作彙整成效、
(4) 本課程可按需要使用AI輔助工具,但須適時揭露使用方式與範圍、
(5) 以中文進行現場報告。
二、期中考、期末考 (10%+10%):範圍為指定導讀教材與上課PPT。
(1) 20題單選題線上測驗:考題為英文 。(除非有重大原因並提出證明,否則錯過考試均以零分計)
(2) 單元分組導讀 (20%):閱讀資料為英文,導讀為中文。
三、出缺席與其他(20%):請透過學校指定管道辦理請假手續。

title: 歐盟法導論 Introduction to European Union Law
description:
歐盟乃一不斷發展之動態統合過程,不同學說試圖
解釋此一新興現象與演進背景。歐盟政經統合已發
展至貨幣同盟階段,並推動共同外交暨安全政策。
歐盟乃由里斯本條約以及歐盟相關法律所創造而成
立,歐盟法律因此在歐洲整合過程扮演一項關鍵角
色。歐盟法律皆是會員國利益相互激盪、競
爭、辯證及調和之結果,代表歐洲集體共識與創意
巧思。
歐盟法律不但據此規範其所屬會員國,也深深影響
國際規則發展動向,值得吾人共同關心,參考借
鑑。本課程提供歐盟法律之基礎知識,藉以瞭解歐
盟此一發展最為成功的超國家組織,世界最大市場
及新經濟強權的超國家法律之特殊風貌。
本課程講授範圍主要包括:歐盟法律的發展背
景、歐盟法律的法源與種類、歐盟超國家法律的特
徵、歐盟法律一般原則、歐盟的主要機構與立法程
序、歐洲法院與歐盟統合、歐盟法律與會員國法律
的競合關係等項議題,並討論里斯本條約、歐
洲基本權利憲章等法律文件,以及相關歐盟AI、GDPR、氣候變遷等法制。
本課程之進行,以研讀英文文獻為主。希望同學能
透過相關文獻閱讀與報告之準備,對於歐盟基本原
理原則與歐盟未來發展有基本之瞭解。
本課程屬於歐盟研究學分學程課程之一。
objectives: 使學生具備對於歐盟法基本原則與法制之瞭解
grading:
期中案例摘要個人報告 50%
期末筆試或小組報告 50%

依上課後指定教材,分為:(每週除上課外,建議投入學習時數為三小時,包括課前預習與課後複習)
1. 課程簡介
2.歐盟之發展歷史
3.歐盟之機構
4.歐盟之機構運作

8.歐盟法律秩序:歐盟法自主性

title: 國際關係理論 International Relations Theory
description:
The world is changing faster than our maps of it. Hegemonic competition now spans chips and shipping lanes; wars are redrawing borders in Europe and the Middle East; great-power rivalries stretch across the Indo-Pacific and Asia-Pacific regions; artificial intelligence advances by the month; and the climate system is breaching thresholds once thought to be decades away. We now live in a world of unknowns, where yesterday’s certainties expire before the semester ends. In such a world, no subject is more critical than International Relations: it is the discipline that asks why states fight or cooperate, why international orders rise and unravel, and how power, ideas, and institutions shape the fates of nations—and of all of us who live in them. This course might not offer you predictions. But it will attempt something more durable: to equip you with the theories and analytical tools needed to ask better questions of a world that refuses to stand still.
Against this backdrop, this graduate seminar is intended to provide an advanced introduction to the major theoretical traditions, analytical approaches, contemporary problems, and emerging frontiers in International Relations (IR). As a seminar, the course expects each student to complete the assigned readings before coming to class and to participate actively in course discussions and simulation activities.
Rather than organizing the course exclusively around the traditional “isms,” the course proceeds in four stages. Part I (Long-Standing Foundational Paradigms) examines the foundational theoretical traditions of IR, including realism, liberalism, institutionalism, constructivism, critical approaches, and psychological and behavioral extensions. Part II (New Analytical Perspectives) turns to the analytical toolkits that reoriented the field around domestic politics and strategic interaction, as well as to theorizing from outside the great powers. Part III (Critical Phenomena in Modern International Relations) applies theory to the central empirical problems of contemporary world politics: war and political violence, the global economy, energy, and geopolitical and economic competition. Part IV (New Frontiers: Challenges of the Anthropocene) confronts the planetary and technological transformations—climate change and migration, emerging technologies, and artificial intelligence—that test the limits of inherited IR theory. The course will also feature invited talks, which will be announced later in the semester.
Throughout the course, students will be asked to identify the assumptions, causal mechanisms, scope conditions, and empirical implications of competing theories. The aim is to encourage students to read critically, participate actively, connect theory to evidence, and design original research.
objectives:
Master the core concepts, debates, and theories of contemporary IR.
Identify the principal actors, mechanisms, and international dimensions of each substantive area.
Apply IR theory to analyze current international developments.
Design and write an original, theoretically grounded research paper.
grading:
Weights may be adjusted before the term begins.

weeklyText:
Note: The number of readings of each week might seem challenging, so there is a chance of adjusting the required amount. Send your feedbacks to me from now on and I will consider potential adjustment by week 2.
Week 1(9/10) — Introduction — What Is IR Theory? Science, Paradigms, and Levels of Analysis
Goal: Course logistics, the role of theory in social science, the levels-of-analysis problem, and the politics of paradigms.
1. Kenneth N. Waltz, Man, the State, and War (New York: Columbia University Press, 1959), Introduction and ch. 1.
2. Jack Snyder, “One World, Rival Theories,” Foreign Policy, no. 145 (2009): 52–62.
3. David A. Lake, “Why ‘Isms’ Are Evil: Theory, Epistemology, and Academic Sects as Impediments to Understanding and Progress,” International Studies Quarterly 55, no. 2 (2011): 465–480.
Central Question: What makes an explanation a theory of international relations, and what are the appropriate units and levels through which world politics should be explained?
Week 2 — Realism — Anarchy, Power, the Security Dilemma, and International Order
Classical and structural realism; offensive vs. defensive realism; hegemonic order and power transition; the contemporary polarity debate.
1. John J. Mearsheimer, The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (New York: W. W. Norton, 2001), chs. 1–2.
Recommended to read & conpare/contrast the following reading: Kenneth N. Waltz, Theory of International Politics (Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1979), chs. 5–6.(this is not required)
2. Rosato, Sebastian. 2026. “Competition Under the Security Dilemma.” International Security 50(4): 36–73.
3. Graham Allison, "The Thucydides Trap: Are the U.S. and China Headed for War?," The Atlantic, September 24, 2015; Robert Gilpin, "The Theory of Hegemonic War," Journal of Interdisciplinary History 18, no. 4 (Spring 1988): 591–613; C. Raja Mohan, "The Multipolar Delusion," Foreign Affairs, February 19, 2026.
Central Question: Is great-power competition primarily produced by capabilities, intentions, status, technological change, or the structural uncertainty inherent in anarchy?
Week 3 — Liberalism, International Institutions, and Global Governance
Neoliberal institutionalism and the study of international cooperation, institutional design, global governance, and the rise—and contemporary crisis—of the liberal international order.
1. Keohane, John J. Robert O. After Hegemony: Cooperation and Discord in the World Political Economy (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1984), ch. 4+ ch.6(most critical).
2. Robert O. Keohane. 2001. “Governance in a Partially Globalized World.” American Political Science Review 95(1): 1–13; Barbara Koremenos, Charles Lipson, and Duncan Snidal, “The Rational Design of International Institutions,” International Organization 55, no. 4 (2001): 761–799.)
3. David A. Lake, Lisa L. Martin, and Thomas Risse. 2021. “Challenges to the Liberal Order: Reflections on International Organization.” International Organization 75(2): 225–257; Jeff D. Colgan and Robert O. Keohane. 2017. “The Liberal Order Is Rigged: Fix It Now or Watch It Wither.” Foreign Affairs 96(3): 36–44; Goddard, Stacie E., Ronald R. Krebs, Christian Kreuder-Sonnen, and Berthold Rittberger. 2025. “Liberalism Doomed the Liberal International Order.” Foreign Affairs.
Recommended to read Ikenberry, G. John. 2018. “The End of Liberal International Order?” International Affairs 94(1): 7–23..(this is not required, but this give you a sense about what LIO is about)
Central Question: Can liberal institutions create durable cooperation and international order in a world still defined by anarchy, unequal power, and domestic political conflict?
Week 4 — Constructivism and Beyond: Norms, Identity, Critique, Everyday Politics, and Psychology
The social construction of anarchy, identity, and security, joined with feminist and racial critiques of the discipline and with the political psychology and behavioral revolution in IR. The week also explores how international politics is constituted through everyday practices, affect, and lived experience.
1. Alexander Wendt, “Anarchy Is What States Make of It: The Social Construction of Power Politics,” International Organization 46, no. 2 (1992): 391–425; Nyman, Jonna. 2021. “The Everyday Life of Security: Capturing Space, Practice, and Affect.” International Political Sociology 15(3): 313–337.
2.J. Ann Tickner, “Hans Morgenthau’s Principles of Political Realism: A Feminist Reformulation,” Millennium 17, no. 3 (1988): 429–440; Brown OR. The Underside of Order: Race in the Constitution of International Order. International Organization. 2024;78(1):38-66. doi:10.1017/S0020818324000018
Recommend to read Bulley, D. (2026). Fair play? Hostile environments and everyday immigration ethics. Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1080/1369183X.2026.2675344; (Not required, but it is helpful to make sense of everyday politics)
3. Emilie M. Hafner-Burton, Stephan Haggard, David A. Lake, and David G. Victor, “The Behavioral Revolution and International Relations,” International Organization 71, no. S1 (2017): S1–S31; Wayne, Carly, Mitsuru Mukaigawara, Joshua D. Kertzer, and Marcus Holmes. 2025. “Diplomacy by Committee: Assessing Resolve and Costly Signals in Group Settings.” American Journal of Political Science 69(4): 1218–1234;
Recommended to read Landau-Wells M. Building from the Brain: Advancing the Study of Threat Perception in International Relations. International Organization. 2024;78(4):627-667. doi:10.1017/S0020818324000328((Challenging the field: this is not required, but highly recommended))
Recommended to read Kertzer, Joshua D., Ryan Brutger, and Kai Quek. 2024. “Perspective Taking and the Security Dilemma: Cross-National Experimental Evidence from China and the United States.” World Politics 76(2): 334–378..(this is not required, but highly recommended)
Central Question: Where should IR explanations begin—with social structures and shared meanings, with everyday practices and power relations, or with the cognitive processes of individuals?
Week 5(10/7) — Mid-term Examination
Take-home examination covering Part I (Weeks 1–4). No assigned readings.
PART II — NEW ANALYTICAL PERSPECTIVES
Week 6 — Strategic Choice and Domestic Politics — Open Economy Politics, Bargaining and War, and the Democratic Peace
The strategic-choice reorientation of the field: domestic sources of foreign economic policy (OEP), rationalist explanations for war, and regime type/democratic peace.
1. David A. Lake and Robert Powell, “International Relations: A Strategic-Choice Approach,” in Strategic Choice and International Relations (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1999), 3–38; James D. Fearon, “Rationalist Explanations for War,” International Organization 49, no. 3 (1995): 379–414.
2. Lake, David A. 2009. “Open Economy Politics: A Critical Review.” Review of International Organizations 4(3): 219–244; Frieden, Jeffry A. 1991. “Invested Interests: The Politics of National Economic Policies in a World of Global Finance.” International Organization 45(4): 425–451.
3. Bueno de Mesquita, Bruce, James D. Morrow, Randolph M. Siverson, and Alastair Smith. 1999. “An Institutional Explanation of the Democratic Peace.” American Political Science Review 93(4): 791–807.; Schultz, Kenneth A. 1999. “Do Democratic Institutions Constrain or Inform? Contrasting Two Institutional Perspectives on Democracy and War.” International Organization 53(2): 233–266.
Central Question: How do preferences, strategic interaction, and domestic institutions combine to shape international economic and security outcomes?
Week 7 — IR Theory of Middle Powers and Small States
How small and middle powers acquire a theoretical place in a great-power-centric discipline: agency under power asymmetry, autonomy, hedging, soft balancing, role adaptation, and international order—with particular attention to Global South perspectives on nonalignment and strategic autonomy.
1. Robert O. Keohane, “Lilliputians’ Dilemmas: Small States in International Politics,” International Organization 23, no. 2 (1969): 291–310; Long, Tom. 2017. “Small States, Great Power? Gaining Influence through Intrinsic, Derivative, and Collective Power.” International Studies Review 19(2): 185–205
recommend: Peter J. Katzenstein, Small States in World Markets: Industrial Policy in Europe (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1985), ch. 1.
2.Efstathopoulos, Charalampos. 2023. “Global IR and the Middle Power Concept: Exploring Different Paths to Agency.” Australian Journal of International Affairs 77(2): 213–232; Michael Beckley. 2026. “The Middle Power Delusion: Not Choosing Is Not an Option.” Foreign Affairs, May 25, 2026; Umar, Ahmad Rizky Mardhatillah. 2023. “The Rise of the Asian Middle Powers: Indonesia’s Conceptions of International Order.” International Affairs 99(4): 1459–1476.
3.Michalski, Anna, Douglas Brommesson, and Ann-Marie Ekengren. 2024. “Small States and the Dilemma of Geopolitics: Role Change in Finland and Sweden.” International Affairs 100(1): 139–157; Paul, T. V., Kai He, and Anders Wivel. 2025. “Soft Balancing in the Regions: Causes, Characteristics and Consequences.” International Affairs 101(1): 3–15.
Core questions: Is “middle power” or “small state” a structural position defined by capabilities, a role identity, a diplomatic strategy, or a relational condition?How can small and middle powers exercise meaningful agency under conditions of structural power asymmetry?
PART III — CRITICAL PHENOMENA IN MODERN INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS
Week 8 — Interstate War, Civil War, and Political Violence
Organized as a ladder of levels: the bargaining framework at the state level, civil war at the group level, and leaders at the individual level. (Send your TOPIC of Final paper this week.)
1. Christopher Blattman, Why We Fight: The Roots of War and the Paths to Peace (New York: Viking, 2022), Introduction and ch. 1.; Elizabeth N. Saunders, "Politics Can't Stop at the Water's Edge," Foreign Affairs 103, no. 2 (March/April 2024)
2.Barry R. Posen. 2025. “Putin’s Preventive War: The 2022 Invasion of Ukraine.” International Security 49(3): 7–49; Andrew S. Lim and James D. Fearon, "The Conventional Balance of Terror: America Needs a New Triad to Restore Its Eroding Deterrence," Foreign Affairs 104, no. 3 (May/June 2025): 104–122
3. James D. Fearon and David D. Laitin, “Ethnicity, Insurgency, and Civil War,” American Political Science Review 97, no. 1 (2003): 75–90; Barbara F. Walter, “The Critical Barrier to Civil War Settlement,” International Organization 51, no. 3 (1997): 335–364.
recommend but not required: Stathis N. Kalyvas, The Logic of Violence in Civil War (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006), ch. 1.
recommend but not required: Scott Wolford, "The Bargaining Framework and Russia's Invasion of Ukraine," Conflict Management and Peace Science 41 (2024).
Chantal Berman, Killian Clarke, and Rima Majed, "From Victims to Dissidents: Legacies of Violence and Popular Mobilization in Iraq (2003–2018)," American Political Science Review 118, no. 1 (2024): 213–234.
Core questions: Why do wars begin, how are they deterred, why do civil wars emerge, and why are they difficult to terminate?
Week 9 — International Political Economy — Trade, Money, and Finance
Systemic IPE: the structure of trade, monetary power and currency hierarchy, central banking, and financial governance.
1. Charles P. Kindleberger, The World in Depression, 1929–1939 (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1973), chs. 1, 14.; Joseph S. Nye, Jr., “The Kindleberger Trap,” Project Syndicate, January 9, 2017, https://www.project-syndicate.org/commentary/trump-china-kindleberger-trap-by-joseph-s--nye-2017-01?barrier=accesspay.
2. Benjamin J. Cohen, Currency Power: Understanding Monetary Rivalry (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2015), chs. 1; Binder, Andrea. 2024. “Outsourcing Empire: International Monetary Power in the Age of Offshore Finance.” International Studies Quarterly 68(4): sqae123.
3. Joanne Gowa and Edward D. Mansfield, “Power Politics and International Trade,” American Political Science Review 87, no. 2 (1993): 408–420
Core Question: Does globalization constrain states, empower particular domestic coalitions, or create new forms of monetary and financial state power?
Week 10 — Energy Politics and Security
Oil and international conflict; the resource curse; energy statecraft; and the geopolitics of the energy transition — critical minerals, supply chains, and the transformation of energy interdependence.
1. Jeff D. Colgan, “Fueling the Fire: Pathways from Oil to War,” International Security 38, no. 2 (2013): 147–180.;Depledge, Duncan. 2023. “Low-Carbon Warfare: Climate Change, Net Zero and Military Operations.” International Affairs 99(2): 667–685
2. Llewelyn Hughes and Phillip Y. Lipscy, “The Politics of Energy,” Annual Review of Political Science 16 (2013): 449–469.
3. Michael L. Ross, “What Have We Learned about the Resource Curse?,” Annual Review of Political Science 18 (2015): 239–259.
recommend: Sim, Li-Chen, and Farkhod Aminjonov. 2025. “Corridors, Pipelines and Electrons: Modalities of Economic Engagement by Central Asia with the Indo-Pacific.” International Affairs 101(4): 1213–1235.
Week 11 — Economic Security, Weaponized Interdependence, Geopolitics/Geopolitical Economy, and Geoeconomics
From economic statecraft to weaponized interdependence; sanctions, export controls, investment screening, and the security–economy nexus in an era of great-power rivalry
Albert O. Hirschman, National Power and the Structure of Foreign Trade (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1945), ch.1-2; Kenneth A. Schultz and Barry R. Weingast, "The Democratic Advantage: Institutional Foundations of Financial Power in International Competition," International Organization 57, no. 1 (2003): 3–42.
Henry Farrell and Abraham L. Newman, "Weaponized Interdependence: How Global Economic Networks Shape State Coercion," International Security 44, no. 1 (2019): 42–79; Cha, Victor D. 2023. “Collective Resilience: Deterring China’s Weaponization of Economic Interdependence.” International Security 48(1): 91–124.
Anton Malkin and Tian He, "The Geoeconomics of Global Semiconductor Value Chains: Extraterritoriality and the US–China Technology Rivalry," Review of International Political Economy 31, no. 2 (2024): 674–699.Andrew B. Kennedy, "The Process of Paradigm Change: The Rise of Guided Innovation in China," Review of International Political Economy 31, no. 4 (2024): 1220–1244 ;
Recommended (not required): David A. Baldwin, Economic Statecraft (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1985), ch. 1; Daniel W. Drezner, "The Hidden Hand of Economic Coercion," International Organization 57, no. 3 (2003): 643–659; Nikhil Kalyanpur, "An Illiberal Economic Order: Commitment Mechanisms Become Tools of Authoritarian Coercion," Review of International Political Economy 30, no. 4 (2023): 1238–1262; Kennedy, A. B. (2023). The Resilience Requirement: Responding to China’s Rise as a Technology Power. Survival, 65(1), 115–128. https://doi.org/10.1080/00396338.2023.2172858 (
PART IV — NEW FRONTIERS: CHALLENGES OF THE ANTHROPOCENE
Week 12 — The Politics of Climate Change and Migration
Climate change as the emblematic Anthropocene challenge: environmental scarcity and conflict; climate-induced displacement and the limits of the refugee regime; the existential politics of decarbonization; and the Anthropocene critique of IR itself.
Anthony Burke, Stefanie Fishel, Audra Mitchell, Simon Dalby, and Daniel J. Levine, “Planet Politics: A Manifesto from the End of IR,” Millennium 44, no. 3 (2016): 499–523.
Eckersley, Robyn. 2023. “(Dis)order and (In)justice in a Heating World.” International Affairs 99(1): 101–119; Robert O. Keohane and David G. Victor, “The Regime Complex for Climate Change,” Perspectives on Politics 9, no. 1 (2011): 7–23
McDonald, Matt. 2026. “Climate Change and National Security: What Drives the Agenda?” International Studies Quarterly 70(2): sqag026;
recommend: Idean Salehyan and Kristian Skrede Gleditsch, “Refugees and the Spread of Civil War,” International Organization 60, no. 2 (2006): 335–366.
Core Question:Can state-centric IR adequately explain a planetary crisis whose causal processes, victims, responsibilities, and political agents do not conform to national borders?
Week 13 — Emerging Technologies and World Politics
How technological change reshapes power, security, and governance: networks, cyber conflict, the information order, semiconductors, and autonomous weapons.
Herrera, Geoffrey L. 2006. Technology and International Transformation: The Railroad, the Atom Bomb, and the Politics of Technological Change. Albany: SUNY Press. Introduction and Ch.2
Burdette, Zachary. 2025. “The U.S.-China Military Balance in Space.” International Security 49(4): 71–118.
Hutto, James Wesley, and James Patton Rogers. 2026. “The Drone Revolution: Towards a Synthesis in the Drone Debate.” European Journal of International Security 11(2): 145–165.
Schneider, Jacquelyn, Benjamin Schechter, and Rachael Shaffer. 2023. “Hacking Nuclear Stability: Wargaming Technology, Uncertainty, and Escalation.” International Organization 77(3): 633–667.
Core Problem: Are new technologies exogenous shocks to the international system? What are the potential changes in international system?
Week 14 — The Challenges and Opportunities of AI in Global and International Relations
Artificial intelligence and the balance of power; AI in military and diplomatic decision-making; governance of frontier AI; and what machine intelligence means for IR theory itself.
Feldstein, S. (2023). The Consequences of Generative AI for Democracy, Governance and War. Survival, 65(5), 117–142. https://doi.org/10.1080/00396338.2023.2261260
Avi Goldfarb and Jon R. Lindsay, “Prediction and Judgment: Why Artificial Intelligence Increases the Importance of Humans in War,” International Security 46, no. 3 (Winter 2021/22): 7–50.
Michael C Horowitz, Erik Lin-Greenberg, Algorithms and Influence Artificial Intelligence and Crisis Decision-Making, International Studies Quarterly, Volume 66, Issue 4, December 2022, sqac069, https://doi.org/10.1093/isq/sqac069
Maschmeyer, Lennart. 2026. “Deception and Detection: Why Artificial Intelligence Empowers Cyber Defense over Offense.” International Security 50(3): 86–126.
Core Problem: Does AI change only the capabilities available to existing actors, or could it alter the fundamental assumptions of IR concerning agency, rationality, power, and strategic interaction?
Week 15 — Student Presentations
Presentation of final research papers with peer commentary. No assigned readings.
Week 16(December 24) — Conclusion
Synthesis across the four parts: what survives of the paradigms, what the new frontiers demand, and where the field is going. Final papers due per course schedule.

title: 數位行銷與博物館科技 Digital Marketing and Museum Interactive Technology
description:
【當文化遇上 AI 與 XR:解鎖沉浸式策展與科技行銷新思維】
從智慧博物館到沉浸式展演,AI 與 XR(AR/VR/MR)正在重塑未來的文化體驗!暑期遍訪巴黎各大博物館,以及東京 teamLab Planets 以及曼谷商場,將帶給大家滿滿的他山之石案例。
本課程帶你站上文化與科技的交會點。我們不只聊策展創意,更實戰結合 AI、XR、互動科技 與 數位行銷策略,深度剖析國內外成功案例(數位博物館、新媒體藝術、品牌行銷)。
這門課能帶給你什麼?
科技轉譯力: 善用 AI 與 XR 打造虛實整合的多感官體驗。
跨域整合力: 貫通策展理念、技術選用與行銷思維。
實戰應用力: 透過專題實作與案例剖析,掌握業界第一線動態。
一次掌握「文化內容設計」、「互動科技策劃」與「數位行銷實務」三大硬實力,成為未來文創科技領域搶手的跨域人才!
李昀叡|科碼新媒體 執行長 深耕互動科技領域逾 20 年,帶領團隊連續三年榮獲「台灣科技 50 強」國際殊榮。擅長將前沿科技融入文化內容,跨越實體與數位的邊界,打造兼具藝術感與商業價值的沉浸式體驗。
近期操刀包含「國家檔案館」、「台東探索館」及「國立臺灣史前文化博物館 XR 體驗」等大型指標性專案,累積豐富的智慧博物館與新媒體策展實務經驗。本次將結合最新巴黎博物館考察洞察,一手傳授第一線科技轉譯力與數位行銷心法,帶領學員掌握 AI 與 XR 時代的跨域關鍵競爭力。
objectives:
課程目標:

深化業界實務理解與觀察力:藉由邀請業師分享真實案例,提升實務知識與應用觀點。

title: 台灣原住民族文化概論 Introduction of Indigenous Cultures in Taiwan
description: 本課程旨在認識與探究台灣原住民族文化,涵蓋南島語系民族起源、神話傳說、民族認定、社會組織、命名制度、宗教信仰、民族文學、民族藝術、文化教育、文化資產、民族文化政策、傳統知識體系等面向。課程透過民族誌文獻閱讀、紀錄片解析、議題探究、專題報告等方式,引導學生理解台灣原住民族文化的現況與發展,並培養學生對當代原住民族文化議題的思辨能力。
objectives:
一、課程目標:本課程引導學生認識台灣原住民族的多元文化,培養閱讀與分析民族誌的素養,並提升探究當代原住民族文化議題的能力。
二、學習成效:學生具備台灣原住民族文化之系統性理解,並能思考原住民族文化在當代社會當中的實踐與應用。

title: 阿美族語(一) Languages of Taiwan Aborigines – ’Amis (I)
description: 本課程為基礎阿美語,主要教學目標在於教授阿美族語書寫符號、其對應之語音符號及正確發音部位、拼寫規範、熟記阿美族語300~400個基本詞彙、日常生活會話、基本語法結構,加強學習者的聽、說、讀、寫的基本能力,培育以族語與人進行日常生活溝通之能力。
objectives:
課程目標:
本課程全程規劃為一學年,分上下二學期;本學期阿美語教學則依序從語音符號系統、音韻結構、正音教學、拼寫規範、聽寫訓練、詞彙結構、語法結構、溝通及會話訓練。第一學期的目標使學生都能通過初級族能力認證,第二學期通過中級族能力認證,以達成未來升學或出國深造之學程基本要求。
本期學習成效:
1. 正音:能夠正確發出族語書寫符號所代表之語音。
2. 透過聽寫訓練,我口說我寫正確一致。
3. 能夠分辨詞彙輕、重音位置。
4. 習得基本詞彙300~400詞。
5. 能夠了解句法結構和語序。
6. 能以簡短句型進行日常生活的溝通及會話。
7. 具備通過族語初級認證測驗之能力。

title: 布農族語(一) Languages of Taiwan Aborigines-Bunun(I)
description:
本學期課程主旨在幫助同學認識並能開口說布農族語言,以提升布農族語言的溝通使用能力。教學內容除了簡單的平常性生活用語,也兼顧簡單的語法結構與相關布農族歷史文化的族語詞彙及其應用,過程中擬併同族語歌謠、戶外教學、耆老族語訪談來進行,同時視班上同學的族語程度,盡量使用族語進行教學,以創造族語環境的氛圍。
為鼓勵修課同學參加族語認證考試,課程中,將針對認證考試的內容及項目,透過模擬試題的設計及練習,增加修課同學具備參加中高級認證考試的能力。
objectives:
課程目標
1. 提升同學在布農族語之聽、說、讀、寫之能力。
•聽力:視班上同學族語程度,老師盡量使用族語進行教學。
•朗讀:老師帶領同學朗讀布農族語之詞彙及句子。
•閱讀:老師提供簡單的族語短句或短文,請同學閱讀並試著翻譯
•寫作:老師說族語詞彙及短句,請同學以族語記音寫作。以及請同學作
族人耆老的訪談,學生做族語口述之族語逐字記音。
•口說:請同學盡量以族語(混夾帶漢語亦可)回答問題,或進行分組之
族語議題對話(混夾帶漢語亦可)。
2. 鼓勵同學參加12月初之族語中高級認證測驗。
預期學習成效
一、經過課程的教導及學習,學生在聽族語、了解族語及運用族語的能力提升。
二、經過課程的教導及學習,學生在說族語、族語對話、族語溝通的能力提升。
三、經過課程的教導及學習,學生在讀族語、朗讀族語及講解族語的能力提升。
grading:
評量方式
1. 出席、上課表現(20%)
2. 族語小考總和(30%)
3. 個人報告(戶外教學學習單、筆記、作業等)(20%)
4. 期末簡易測驗(30%)

title: 原住民族與國家發展 The Development of Indigenous Peoples and Modern States
description:
本課程是原住民族發展學分學程之核心課程。此學程的目的是為了整合民族行政與法規事務、語言文化教育及南島國際視野與在地實驗之學習與經驗,將其運用在原住民族發展之思考,並探討原住民族與國家間的關係及當代多元文化治理的典範。
本課程包含三個部分:第一部分原住民族與國家發展之相關學理;第二部分為台灣原住民族與國家發展經驗的反思;第三部分是國際經驗的學習與交流。
本年度課程有兩個副主題:「災害治理」以及「碳治理」。針對這兩個副主題,本課程邀請台灣與國際的學者進行專題講座,向學生介紹這兩個議題對原住民族發展所帶來的挑戰,並對於國家與原住民族之間的複雜權力關係進行反思。
*本課程為臺灣原住民族發展學分學程中民族教育次專長之必修課程
objectives:
本課程包含三個部分:首先介紹原住民族發展與現代國家之關係的相關學理論述,並融入副主題之討論;第二部分透過專題講座帶入副主題在台灣原住民族發展與國家互動經驗的理解與反思;第三部分透過線上專題講座進行國際經驗的學習與交流,這部分將主要以英文進行。
透過前述的課程安排,本課程希望幫助學生掌握相關學理基礎,了解台灣當前發展的現況,也能認識國際間的經驗,將學習之成果應用在台灣原住民族與國家發展相關議題的分析及未來的展望。
選修本課的學生須具備基本的英文聽說能力,以充分參與線上國際講座。
