title: 近代日本的形成與發展 The Formation and Development of Modern Japan
description:
本課程是以「公論」、天皇、立憲政治三者為主軸,來探究從幕末維新期至第二次世界大戰結束為止近代日本的形成與發展,進而思考近代日本天皇制國家的本質,以及國家與社會的統合問題。
在此所謂的「公論」,意指以打破江戶時期世襲身分制為前提的人才登用及政治參與。而「公論」又與天皇制國家的建立與立憲政治的形成密不可分。因此,本課程的重點將放在幕末「公論」慣習的發生、天皇大權的摸索,以及近代「天皇的官僚」、明治憲法體制、家族國家觀、政黨政治的形成與發展上。
同時,鼓勵同學從臺灣之「他者」的角度,重新思考日本近代史、甚至是日治時期的臺灣史或同一時期的東亞史。
以有中級日語閱讀能力及基本日本近代史知識者為佳。
課程進度及課堂口頭發表的方式,會依同學的日語能力適時調整。
objectives:
1.理解近代日本天皇制國家、社會的形成及其構想。
2.理解19世紀以來日本立憲主義的建構過程及其特徵。
3.透過課堂的平時的口頭發表及討論,培養統整論點及分析能力。
4.透過撰寫期末書面報告,訓練論文寫作能力。
※期末書面報告之要求:本學期的主題,自由選擇;需遵循論文寫作格式(問題意識、本論、結論、注釋、出處)。
中日文不拘(中文:至少6000字,日文:至少6500字)。
※旁聽生須得到任課教師的同意,並且必須要預習及參與課堂討論,若未能做到此要求,任課老師會適時拒絕旁聽。

title: 日本神話與文化 Japanese Mythology and Culture
description: 「神話」不單僅止於是上古諸神的神靈故事,更是人們對於天地開闢、人類由來等、始祖出現、禮儀民俗等等的說明與解釋。因此,「神話」可說是一個民族最根源的生活與信仰的體現,更是建構該民族文化的重要基盤。本課程企圖透過日本神話的故事,解析其背後所蘊含的文化意義。
objectives: 本課程主要以『新編日本古典文學全集—古事記』『新編日本古典文學全集—日本書紀』為文本,介紹日本著名的神話故事。並配搭中西進『日本神話の世界』(筑摩書房、 2013)、中西進『神話力—日本神話を創造するもの』(桜楓社、1991)等書籍,進行神話解析,以期學習者在孰悉神話故事之上,進一步學習日本古代之風俗民情、社會、精神與文化。這將是一門綜合神話學、民俗學、考古學、歷史學等多元角度之神話課程。建議修課同學需具備閱讀日文文本之能力。

title: 日本古典文法1 Grammar of Ancient Japanese Literature I
description:
日本古典文法是一套和現代日文大不相同的文法體系,卻又是現代日文的根源與先驅。現存日文的相關資料中,除了日本古典文學等領域之外,台灣殖民文學、近現代日本文學、台日政治史等相關文獻,甚至是日本媒體廣告、動漫中,也存在著為數不少的古典文法。因此培養解讀日本古文的能力,不僅是有助於學習者理解日語文法體系的歷史脈絡、掌握日語的特色,更是進行日本研究、理解日本文化時的重要先行工作。本課程分上下學期,欲修下學期課程者,請務必修上學期課程。
教材: 教師自製教材
objectives:
(一)本課程之課程目標:
習得日語古典文法之基礎知識
認識著名之日本古文文章。
習得基本知閱讀古文能力。
建立現代與古典一脈相承的語法體系與概念。
奠定處理日治時代文獻資料的能力。
理解日本媒體、動漫等文化產業中的古文表現。
(二)基於上述之課程目標,本課程主要以古文讀解、活用語之文法為主,由淺入深進行教學以及實作練習。內容可分以下五部份:
古文讀音之介紹與練習
形容詞活用
形容動詞活用
動詞活用
(三)透過前述之課程目標和課程內容,本課程預計能為學習者帶來以下的學習成就:
能夠解讀日本古文,理解日語文法體系的歷史脈絡、掌握古典日語的特色。
了解現代日語和古文之異同點。
處理日本古典文獻。
處理古文與現代日文混用的文獻。
處理圖書館、出版社以及台灣總督府所留存之日治時代文獻。
處理日本媒體、動漫等文化產業中的古文表現。
grading:
每單元預計進行約四週,上課時會先進行文法結構之系統教學,進而搭
配文章做練習。
每單元會先複習現代日語之文法結構,再循序近入古典文法,借此理解現代日語和古文一脈相承之系統。
兩次筆試。

description:

보고서의 내용은 자유롭게 정하되, 예를 들면 다음과 같습니다.
(i) 한국어 또는 중국어의 지역적 변이를 조사한 뒤,
(ii) 방언 지도를 작성하고,
(iii) 해석 및 한국어학에의 시사점을 제시함.

title: 韓國學研究課題(文學與歷史)—韓國古典文學研究 Korean Studies Research Project (Literature & History) — Studies on Classical Korean Literature
description: 本課程旨在初步介紹韓國文學史重要著作,以及韓國各朝代文學流變與代表作品。課程共分為三個部分,第一部分安排兩週韓國文學史精讀,閱讀幾本韓國文學史著作;第二部分依時代先後依序介紹古代文學、三國時代及南北國時代詩歌及散文、高麗時代詩歌及散文、朝鮮時代諺文與漢文詩歌及散文,其中《訓民正音》創制後,朝鮮時代文學明確區分出國文學與漢文學,各有其特色及代表作品;第三部分為期末報告,以課程中所介紹的作者、作品或文類、時代為主題,撰寫發表。
objectives:
1.初步了解各時代韓國文學的發展。
2.正確認識韓國文學與文化,藉此理解韓國人的思維模式。
3.藉由大量閱讀文獻、論文,養成資料吸收、分析及批判思考的能力。
4.利用期末報告的撰寫訓練論文寫作技巧,並鼓勵發表論文。
grading:
1.課堂出席與論文討論:20%
2.指定論文提要:20%
3.作品選讀分析:20%
4.期末報告:40%

title: 韓國學研究課題(社會與文化)—從語言看韓國文化 Korean Studies Research Project (Society & Culture) — Korean Culture through Korean Language
description: 이 강의는 한국어 사용에서 나타나는 다양한 언어 현상을 한국 사회와 문화를 이해하는 출발점으로 삼는다. 특정 이론이나 학문 분야에서 출발하기보다, 실제 언어 사용에서 포착되는 현상을 탐구하고 그 속에 담긴 사회문화적 의미를 해석하는 방식으로 수업을 전개한다. 이를 위해 언어 연구의 다양한 이론과 분석 관점을 유연하게 활용한다. 학생들은 이 과정을 통해 언어로 한국문화를 읽는 눈을 기르고, 실제 언어 자료를 바탕으로 독자적인 문화 연구를 수행하는 기초 역량을 갖춘다. 언어와 사회·문화의 관계에 관심이 있는 학생, 실제 언어 자료(어휘, 담화 등)의 분석에 기반한 학위논문을 구상하는 학생에게 특히 유용하다.
objectives:
1. 한국어 사용에서 나타나는 다양한 언어 현상을 탐구 대상으로 인식하고 관찰할 수 있다.
2. 언어 연구의 다양한 이론과 분석 관점을 활용하여 언어 현상에 담긴 사회문화적 의미를 해석할 수 있다.
3. 한국어의 언어 현상을 자신의 언어·문화 환경과 비교하며 성찰할 수 있다.
4. 실제 언어 자료를 바탕으로 연구 문제를 설정하고 독자적인 문화 연구를 수행할 수 있다.
grading: 발제30%; 발표(소논문) 30%; 주제20%; 아니면10%; Cc참여10%

title: 中東專題研究 Seminar in Middle East
description: Middle Eastern studies includes a wide spectrum of important topics. For the purpose of helping students earn a comprehensive idea of the scopes of the Middle Eastern studies, this course aims at discussing various crucial research topics related to the Middle East. The course consists of 6 parts, religion, society, culture, politics, economy, and gender.
objectives: At the end of the class, students will learn various important topics related to the Middle Eastern studies, and have the abilities to develop their own research agenda on the Middle East.
grading:
Group presentation (10%)
Participation in seminar (35%)
A 3000 words essay related to the Middle East conflict (50%).
Attendenance (5%).
Students who are absent from three or more classes in this course may receive no credit.
Plagiarism will be given zero marks for the course.

title: 研究方法與論文寫作 Research Methodology and Thesis Writing
description: This course is designed for students at postgraduate level. It helps students to establish a basic understanding about qualitative research and qualitative research methods. By completing the course, students are expected to have the ability to conduct independent research. Besides, significant issues discussed by the participants include: ontology and epistemology, positivist and post-positivist approaches to international studies, the formulation of research questions, data (texts) collection, and strategies for writing a critical literature review.
objectives:
The course aims to give students a grounding in the basic principles of qualitative research methodology. It provides students with an introduction to the major methods of qualitative data collection and analysis, how qualitative data are actively constructed and interpreted by a researcher and an appreciation of the practical and epistemological concerns raised by qualitative data collection.
On successful completion of this course students should be able to:
Demonstrate an ability to conduct independent research
Collect qualitative data
Conduct research in a manner which is consistent with professional practice
grading:
Class Participation and Presentation: 30%
Mid-term Essay (3,000 words): 30%
Final Essay (5,000 words): 40%
Students are required to submit their mid-term and final essays in Week 8 and Week 16, respectively. All written work must be submitted in BOTH electronic and hard copy formats.
Electronic submission: Email a copy to the lecturer (〔聯絡資訊已移除〕) by the due date.
Hard copy submission: Submit a printed copy to the main administration office of Master Program of Middle Eastern and Central Asian Studies by the due date.
Late submissions will be penalized at 5% per day. No extensions will be given. If you are unable to submit your work on time, you must submit it as soon as you can with written evidence for the reason for lateness.

title: 後共民主化 Post-Communist Democratization
description: The collapse of authoritarian rule in Southern Europe, Latin America and East Asia which began in the 1970s, the breakdown of Communist regimes in East Europe and the former Soviet Union which began in 1989, and the recent color revolutions and the Arab Spring which began in the 2000s, have revived interest in the study of democratization. Despite its initial achievements, some setbacks remain. The longstanding debates on the causes, patterns and consequences of democratization and autocratization remain unresolved. The course mainly explores the ongoing process of democratization in the post-communist countries in both theory and practice and investigates factors contributing to democratic resilience and backsliding.
objectives:
The course aims to address the following questions to advance understanding of democracy: Does the literature of transition from authoritarian regimes shed light on the developmental trend and pattern of Soviet-type regime transition? Is the liberal democratic order in crisis? What explains the persistence and vulnerability of existing authoritarian regimes? How can democracy be effective and sustainable?
Students are introduced to contending perspectives on the major issues of post-communist democratization.
grading:
Class participation (25%): Students are expected to attend regularly, to read the assigned readings, and to actively participate in class discussions.
Presentations (25%): Each student is required to give three ten-minute oral presentations. The first two are to present reviews of the assigned readings of the weekly topic, and the final one is to present the research proposal of the final paper.
Final paper (50%): Each student is required to write a research paper (5,000-8,000 words) related to the topics covered in the course.

title: 俄國政府與政治 Russian Government and Politics
description: 本課程的授課內容著重自1991年蘇聯解體以來,後共俄羅斯的憲政體制變革,政治權威與政權本質,政治制度設計、運作與影響,以及政治轉型之相關議題。在俄國威權統治的歷史脈絡與政治實踐,2020年總統延任修憲與菁英延續,以及2022年以來俄烏戰爭的衝擊下,普欽主政時期俄國的政治展望,在內外環境的變動下,始終圍繞著政治穩定性與脆弱性的爭辯。
objectives:
本課程旨在探討以下問題:俄國基本的政治體制為何,具有哪些特性?如何界定與解釋俄國的政權類型與統治的正當性?有哪些因素或重要議題影響俄國政治發展的變與常?
本課程以問題導向方式,培養學生從不同的角度進行思辯論述,以期具備理論應用、現勢分析與學術研究的能力。

title: 伊斯蘭文明:議題與討論 Islamic Civilisation: Seminars
description: This course addresses the conceptualisation of the human cultural phenomena termed Islamic civilisation. While a number of the subjects that characterise Islamic civilisation will be covered, the focus of this course centres on the ways through which the historical cultural phenomena in the regions where Islam constitutes the mainstream religion are analysed, diagnosed, and understood by academics and laymen. Students will be guided to reflect on the present conceptualisation of Islam and invited to formulate better approaches to the complexity and diversity of Islamic world.
objectives: By the end of the course, students will learn: 1) the current conceptual categories through which Islamic art, philosophy, and culture are construed; 2) the problems inherent in such conceptual categories; and 3) to reconceptualise the human cultural phenomena termed Islamic civilisation.

title: 現代伊斯蘭思想專題 Special Topic on Modern Islamic Thoughts
description:
本課程從伊斯蘭世界面對西方殖民主義衝擊的全球歷史宏觀脈絡,探討晚近兩百年穆斯林回應西方列強所帶來的現代文明之各種新思潮,聚焦於嘗試調和伊斯蘭傳統與西方現代文明的思想流派為主,全盤西化或全面復古的相反兩極則不在本課程討論的範圍。授課內容分三個單元,第一單元鋪陳伊斯蘭世界從殖民到後殖民時期近兩百年的思想史脈絡,以「後殖民主義」(postcolonialism)的批判史觀為宏觀探索的視角,但不排除對伊斯蘭現代史的其他史觀與視角;第二單元聚焦於殖民時期的思想家與學派,伊斯蘭學界概括為「伊斯蘭現代主義」(Islamic modernism)的各家學說;第三單元聚焦於後殖民時期的思想家與學派,泛稱「新傳統主義」(Neotraditionalism)的各家學說。後兩單元皆就遜尼派與什葉派分開討論,遜尼派又分中東與南亞兩大系統,前者以埃及的「穆斯林兄弟會」(Ikhwan al-Muslimun)為主;後者以巴基斯坦的「伊斯蘭協會」(Jama`at-i-Islami)為主;什葉派則聚焦於伊朗,分別探討宗教學者與世俗知識階層的伊斯蘭新思潮。
本課程將集中在遜尼派與什葉派影響力較大的思想與運動流派,針對其歷史淵源、思想內涵,及其所在國家的政治社會情況作整體考察,同學們既可研讀個別思潮與運動領導者的原著,又可研讀分析這些流派的重要研究著作,以便對當前伊斯蘭復興運動各種議題有充分理解並發展個人的批判性分析。
若修習本課程的同學過去未曾修過伊斯蘭相關課程,請參閱「伊斯蘭教:歷史與主題」課程所列指定教材,利用暑假期間進行課前研讀,以便初步掌握相關的概念與歷史脈絡。
objectives:
當代遍及伊斯蘭世界的「復興運動」(或譯「復振運動」,revivalist movement),經常被西方學界或媒體冠上「宗教激進主義」(religious radicalism)、「恐怖主義」(terrorism)、「原教旨主義」(fundamentalism)等貶抑的稱謂,加上全球反恐與反移民的右翼思潮崛起,導致針對上述思潮與運動對當代穆斯林社會的實質意義為何,缺乏不帶偏見預設的論述空間。本課程企圖將當代伊斯蘭復興運動從思想面及歷史-政治社會形構面加以探究,並將其源頭上溯至十九世紀伊斯蘭現代改革運動,務使修課同學獲得分析該運動較完整的認識架構。
透過研讀現代伊斯蘭復興思潮與各別國家或區域實踐的原典與研究著作,以便對當代伊斯蘭復興運動兼具內在思想深度與外部歷史及政治社會脈絡的整體性理解,並可進行跨國、跨區域、跨宗派的比較研究。此外,也鼓勵修課同學以本課程所提供的研究架構與問題意識,反思自身所探索的宗教傳統之類似的回應現代性之思潮與運動,並在課堂上進行對話,以便開展跨宗教的傳統與現代性交涉之比較研究。

或派別的一本著作或某一觀念為主題,撰寫一篇研究論文,字數不少於一萬字。

title: 中亞現存游牧傳統 Living Nomadic Traditions in Central Asia
description: This graduate course examines nomadic traditions of Central Asian peoples as living, evolving practices rather than relics of the past. Drawing on ethnography, oral history, material culture studies, and contemporary fieldwork, students will explore how nomadic ways of life—pastoral herding, portable architecture, oral epic poetry, seasonal migrations, and traditional crafts—continue to shape daily life, identity, and community across the region today. Special attention is given to how nomadic heritage is negotiated, preserved, and transformed in the context of modernization, urbanization, and state-building in the post-Soviet era. The course combines thematic lectures with guest seminars by scholars and practitioners from Central Asia.
objectives:
Course Objectives:
To introduce students to nomadic traditions as dynamic, living cultural systems in Central Asia
To examine the material, social, and symbolic dimensions of nomadic life—from yurts and herding to oral poetry and ritual
To analyze how nomadic traditions are preserved, adapted, or contested in modern Central Asian societies
To develop students' ability to use ethnographic and comparative methods in analyzing non-Western cultural practices
To foster cross-cultural understanding through direct engagement with scholars and practitioners from the region
Learning Outcomes:
Students will be able to identify and describe key nomadic traditions across different Central Asian groups
Students will critically analyze the relationship between nomadic heritage and contemporary identity politics
Students will demonstrate understanding of how material culture, oral traditions, and everyday practices intersect
Students will develop comparative analytical skills applicable to cultural studies and area studies research
Students will engage productively with primary sources—including oral testimonies, ethnographic texts, and cultural artifacts
grading:
Presentations and reports (25%)
Mid-term Exam (25%)
Final Essay — 2,000–2,500 words on a nomadic tradition of the student's choice, with comparative analysis to their own cultural context (40%)
Attendance (10%)

title: 俄烏衝突研究 Special Topics on the Russia-Ukraine Conflict
description: The ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict represents a defining moment in 21st-century history, offering the world unprecedented opportunities to advance theoretical understanding, develop innovative methodologies, and contribute to knowledge that will inform policy and practice for decades to come. With such a “critical historical moment”, however, we have learned not only the mass media but also many scholars analysis have continuously failed to access critical information so to give insightful views on the undergoing international unrest and international power conflict normally invisible during peacetime. In face of all kinds of biased war information and propaganda, this war therefore provides a unique laboratory but also a challenging task for understanding how political institutions, identities, and relationships stage warfare under extreme duress. This course aims to revisit selected aspects of researches on the Russia-Ukraine conflict, through class discussion and then to develop an insightful approach for understanding the origins of geopolitical tensions, conflict prevention, humanitarian response, and international security. Hopefully the course participants can contribute to evidence-based policy-making and humanitarian practice, providing further research with broader social impact beyond academic circles.
objectives:
Firstly, students to learn how recent scholarship emphasise the importance of Realist and Liberal theories provide competing explanations for the conflict’s origins and development. Comparative analyses using these frameworks help illuminate different aspects of the war’s causes and conduct.
Secondly, through learning the phenomenological approaches to own valuable knowledge for studying critical thinking in academic institutions during the war; in addition, students are also expected to check on qualitative thematic analysis has been employed to understand coping strategies among key findings.
Thirdly, theoretical frameworks such as constructivist approaches offer insights into identity formation and perception-based motivations in the conflict. This theoretical framework emphasises how Russian and Ukrainian identities have shaped the war’s trajectory.
In addition, students may experience how a proper politico-sociological analysis in understanding the war’s impact on Ukrainian society. Research methodologies include semi-structured interviews with displaced populations, and survey research examining social attitudes during wartime.
In general, developing expertise in Russia-Ukraine conflict studies positions young scholars at the forefront of an emerging and important academic specialisation. As the conflict’s implications continue to unfold over decades, scholars with deep understanding of its insightful dimensions will be increasingly valuable to academic institutions, policy organizations, and international agencies.

title: 國際政治研究 Study of International Politics
description:
這是一門討論課,其目的是在各位同學對國際關係領域已有相當瞭解後,
對若干國際政治專題做進一步的探討。因此,所列出之閱讀資料只是幫助我們對問題的瞭解。各位同學自然可以,也應該,找尋主題的相關資料。同時,我們要本著求真求實、求融會貫通的精神,研究相關專題,不必為一人、一家、一派所束縛。
除對重要理論做深入探討外,亦將針對二次大戰後的國際政治發展及主要國家之國家安全政策與外交政策進行析評。
國際政治的理論與實務有其連續性與發展性。上課時間主講人將適時分發相關報導、分析、評論文章,供同學們閱讀、思考,俾使理論與當前實務相結合。
除課堂討論與報告外,每位同學必須在學期中(期中考試週)提出一篇三千字左右的思考性論文,並於學期結束時繳交一篇一萬字左右的研究性論文,作為學期成績。思考性論文與研究性論文均應限於國際關係之範疇。
grading: 成績之計算大致為:課堂參與、討論及報告:40%;思考性論文20%;學期報告研究性論文40%。本科目不舉行期中考試。期中考試週照常上課,並繳交思考性論文。本科目無期末考試,期末考試週前一週繳交學期研究性論文。

title: 俄國史研究 Study of Russian History
description:
俄羅斯歷史自九世紀基輔羅斯肇建起,至二十一世紀俄羅斯聯邦之重塑,其發展脈絡始終深刻牽動全球地緣政治的格局變化;而俄羅斯民族獨特的歷史韌性與精神性格,亦形塑當今多極化世界的複雜面貌。
本課程採專題研討方式,自基輔羅斯立國切入,循序剖析蒙古統治、莫斯科崛起、「第三羅馬」論述、沙皇專制體制、帝國西化與擴張、文化黃金時代、農奴解放、蘇聯興衰至當代「新俄羅斯」之演進歷程。期能引導修課學生深化歷史脈絡之研析,建構獨立的學術批判思維,並為後續發展俄國各領域研究奠定堅實之理論與知識基礎。
objectives:
1. 有效運用各領域學研資源
2. 觀察探索教育學習新模式
3. 培養深度閱讀及評析素養
4. 形塑終身與自主學習態度
5. 奠定論文寫作與發表能力

2. 兩次期中報告(40%)
3. 期末報告(30%)

title: 吉爾吉斯語(一) Kyrgyz 1
description: This course is designed for students who have little or no prior knowledge of the Kyrgyz language and aims to introduce students to the basic structure and grammar of Kyrgyz, as well as develop listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills. Students will also gain an understanding of Kyrgyz culture, customs, and traditions.
objectives:
Course Objectives:
The objectives of this course comprise
to provide students with the fundamental knowledge of the Kyrgyz language, including basic vocabulary and grammar,
to enable them to convey basic information and conduct simple conversations.
to develop students' abilities to understand and produce simple texts in Kyrgyz, as well as provide them with an understanding of Kyrgyz culture, customs, and traditions.
Learning Outcomes:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
Use basic Kyrgyz vocabulary and grammar to hold simple conversations and convey basic information
Understand and produce simple spoken and written texts in Kyrgyz
Demonstrate sound understanding of culture, customs, and traditions

Class Participation: 20%
Homework Assignments: 20%
Mid-term Examination: 30%
Final Examination: 30%

title: 伊朗文化專題 Topics on Iran Culture
description: 本課程的主要目的是視伊朗為一個國家、一個仍在延續的文明的發源地以及伊斯蘭和中東文化運動的引擎,以此向學生介紹。由於語言障礙以及西方視角在伊朗問題上的普遍性,學生們經常難以找到關於伊朗的第一手資料。大多數學者傾向於複製西方學者對伊朗的解釋,這導致他們無法對伊朗形成平衡、中立和客觀的認識。我將力求在解釋中避免任何主觀因素,並清楚地描繪伊朗作為一個國家及其政府的全貌。
objectives: 修此課之學生將可對伊朗這個國家、對伊斯蘭、對藝術與文化有全面性的瞭解。並進而對中東與伊斯蘭世界具備判斷的能力。
grading:
出席率20%
參與課程互動的踴躍程度30%
課堂報告40%

title: 中東歐與俄羅斯經濟發展比較研究 Comparative Studies on Economic Development in the CEE and Russia
description: 蘇聯、東歐國家在一九八九年後陸續由共產計劃經濟轉型為市場經濟體,這些曾為國際社會中的所謂轉型經濟體已歷經多年市場經濟轉型發展,本課程將透過對其轉型模式和經濟社會發展之進程進行探討比較,以利學生熟悉和掌控中東歐國家和俄羅斯的經濟現狀與脈動,如中東歐國家由轉型為市場經濟體到加入歐盟;俄烏武裝衝突後國際政經架構變動下的中東歐與俄國之經濟發展等,加強學生對此區域之認知,培育相關經貿專才。
objectives: 學生學習本課程將透過專題討論以及期中與期末報告的實作練習,獲取探索、思考之研究能力,以期後續得以自主終身學習,並從專題討論中熟悉和掌控中東歐國家與俄羅斯之經濟現狀與脈動,熟諳市場經濟運作機制和洞察複雜的國際政經社會對個體經濟發展之影響,獲得具備對此區域經貿分析的能力,厚植個人未來職涯發展實力。
grading:
期中報告:30% 期末報告:40 %
平時成績(時事分享、專題實作和作業、上課參與情形):30%
weeklyText: 1.課程介紹與研究範疇認定 2.冷戰時期的東歐國家與蘇聯(影帶輔助教學) 3.八零年代末的政經瓶頸與改革(課前作業:自行看影帶”司馬庫斯”思考共產經營模式的優缺點)(指定閱讀:經濟激進轉型策略理論篇) 4.後共產主義國家經濟轉型模式:比較經濟體制、轉型意涵、激進與演進轉型(課前預習 - 指定閱讀:經濟激進轉型策略理論篇及波蘭個案) 5.激進經濟轉型模式:內涵及其模式選擇之國際組織影響力 6.個案實證:波蘭工潮、自由化與轉型發展(影帶輔助教學)(課前預習 - 指定閱讀:經濟均衡發展策略-俄國案例) 7. 俄國經濟震撼療法轉型困境與經濟發展(影帶輔助教學) 8. 波蘭與俄羅斯激進轉型比較(課前預習 - 閱讀匈牙利經濟之參考文獻) 9. 匈牙利「新經濟機制」的現代政經意義及其轉型現狀(課前預習 - 閱讀捷克經濟之參考文獻) 10. 捷克「布拉格之春」、「天鵝絨革命」及其轉型發展(影帶輔助教學)(課前預習 -閱讀巴爾幹半島國家經濟之參考文獻) 11. 巴爾幹半島:南斯拉夫、斯洛文尼亞、馬其頓等(課前預習 - 指定閱讀:經濟均衡發展策略) 12. 市場化機制之比較:自由化(如國際化下的金融、資本市場)、穩定化與私有化(私有化模式與成長率、不均關係)(請同學自行在家看哈佛大學”正義:一場思辨之旅”課程中第三講主題1自由選擇權,思考課稅重分配) 13. 經濟發展理論-所得分配、社會不均(課前預習 - 指定閱讀:經濟整合策略之發展與趨勢) 14. 轉型經濟體之經濟發展問題:生產結構、所得分配、經濟成長等(課前預習 - 指定閱讀:經濟整合策略之發展與趨勢) 15. 中東歐與俄國參與國際經濟之效應比較:中東歐加入歐盟之效應、俄烏武裝衝突與俄國經濟發展 16. 期末報告(書面報告加口頭報告)

title: 俄國現勢專題 Current Situation of Russia
description:
蘇聯曾於冷戰時期與美蘇並列兩大超強,是共產主義國家,但於1991年解體後,各個加盟共和國獨立,東歐也脫離其箝制,開始民主轉型,整個社會政經體制的轉變對於各個國家的衝擊是相當巨大。尤其俄羅斯聯邦,其領土跨越歐亞兩大洲,其特殊的地理位置,具有特殊的地緣政治優勢及文化發展。
本課程定位為俄羅斯研究基礎課程,鑒於很多學生在大學時期都不是俄羅斯政經研究專業,所以藉由本課程在一學期內建立學生對俄羅斯政治經濟和區域問題的基礎,以利學生未來在俄研所修習課程時,能更加瞭解自己未來的研究走向。
本課程的設計: 每堂課二小時,第一小時分享俄羅斯時事,第二小時針對現勢挑選一俄羅斯專題文章做分析探討。
objectives: 旨在透過資料的閱讀及討論,讓學生充分了解蘇聯解體後的俄羅斯的國家政經和區域發展,培養與提昇同學對該國家的理解與分析能力。
grading:
學生每人每周需準備一個俄羅斯時勢,課堂口頭報告
學生成績由課堂口頭報告(40%)、學期書面報告(50%)與平時上課參與(10%)決定。課堂報告需針對每星期指定之教材與主題,學期報告題目可自行決定,以課堂標題或案例為主題。同學應於期中前決定議題,並且蒐集相關資料,於期末考週課堂口頭報告,並繳交三頁內之報告大綱,並於規定期限內繳交期末報告,以8000~15000字為準,須有註釋,必須符合學術報告體例。

title: 選修英文:表演藝術產業英文 English Elective: English for Performing Arts Industries
description:
Performing Arts and Productions is an interdisciplinary course designed to immerse students in the creative, collaborative, and technical processes that bring live performance to life. Whether rooted in theatre, dance, or multimedia performance, the performing arts demand a unique combination of imagination, discipline, communication, and craft. This course provides students with a comprehensive introduction to these practices, allowing them to develop both their artistic voice and their understanding of production workflows used in contemporary performance environments.
Across sixteen weeks, students will explore the foundational elements of performance, including movement, voice, improvisation, character creation, and ensemble work. Through guided workshops, students will learn how the performer uses the body and voice as expressive tools, and how physicality, gesture, rhythm, and breath contribute to storytelling. These sessions emphasize experiential learning, encouraging students not only to analyze performance but to embody it through active participation.
Beyond performer training, the course introduces essential production skills that help transform creative ideas into staged realities. Students will gain exposure to directing principles, stagecraft, lighting and sound basics, stage management, and visual design. By understanding each component of production, students experience the collaborative nature of performance-making—where performers, directors, designers, and technicians work together toward a unified artistic vision. This holistic approach helps students appreciate the interconnectedness of all roles and fosters respect for the diverse expertise required to create a successful performance.
A significant emphasis of the course lies in process over product. Students are encouraged to experiment, take creative risks, and reflect on their learning journey. Weekly tasks—ranging from short improvisations to script analysis and movement composition—build students’ confidence and deepen their understanding of the artistic process. These tasks also prepare students for the larger midterm and final performance projects, where they apply accumulated skills to create original or adapted work.
The final weeks of the course focus on rehearsal methods and production integration. Students will experience firsthand the rhythm of a rehearsal room, learning how to incorporate feedback, solve creative problems, and collaborate efficiently under time constraints. Technical rehearsals introduce students to cueing, transitions, and the layering of design elements, providing a practical understanding of how technical choices enhance performance. The course culminates in a final showcase where students present their work to an audience, demonstrating their growth and their ability to transform ideas into compelling stage moments.
Ultimately, Performing Arts and Productions aims to empower students with creative agency, body awareness, communication skills, and collaborative mindset. Whether students hope to pursue further studies in performing arts or simply wish to explore creative expression, the course offers a supportive environment to discover their artistic capacities. By the end of the semester, students will not only have developed a foundational toolkit for performance and production but will also have gained confidence in expressing themselves, collaborating with others, and engaging deeply with the creative process.
objectives:
The primary goal of Performing Arts and Productions is to equip students with a foundational understanding of how performance is created, rehearsed, and realized on stage. Throughout the course, students will develop core performance skills—such as body awareness, vocal expression, improvisation, character building, and ensemble collaboration—while also gaining insight into the technical and organizational elements that support a production. By engaging with both artistic and production-focused practices, students learn to think as performers, directors, designers, and creative collaborators.
Another key goal is to cultivate confidence, creativity, and critical thinking. Students will be encouraged to explore their own artistic voices, take risks, and reflect on their process. Through weekly exercises and peer feedback, they will learn how to communicate effectively, respond to direction, and work within a team—skills that extend beyond the performing arts into many professional fields. The course also aims to foster an appreciation for the interdisciplinary nature of performance, helping students understand how movement, text, music, space, lighting, and visual design interact to shape meaning on stage.
The final representation of learning will take the form of a collaborative performance showcase presented in Week 16. Students will work in groups to rehearse and present a short performance piece—either an original devised work or a selected scene developed earlier in the semester. This final showcase allows students to apply all aspects of their training: performance technique, script or movement analysis, staging, production planning, and basic technical integration. It is also an opportunity for students to experience the full arc of a production process—from conception to rehearsal to public presentation.
Through this final performance, students demonstrate not only their artistic growth but also their ability to work collaboratively, integrate feedback, manage production challenges, and transform creative ideas into a polished stage piece.
grading:
Assessment Suggestions
Participation & attendance (20%)
In-class exercises & Assignments (20%)
Midterm ensemble performance (20%)
Final performance (40%)
Mid term:
Mid Term Performance Viewing & Critical Feedback
Theme: Watching professional performance and sharing the feedback
Purpose of the Midterm
The midterm assessment focuses on helping students broaden their artistic awareness by watching a live performance or a professionally recorded stage/screen production. Students will learn how to analyse artistic choices, identify performance techniques, and articulate constructive feedback. This process strengthens their understanding of how theory and practice merge in real-world performance contexts.
Pre-Class Preparation
Students must watch one performance before class. Options may include:
A live theatre, dance, or interdisciplinary show
A recorded professional production available through online platforms
A student or university production approved by the instructor
Students take brief notes while watching:
What stands out?
Which performance techniques affect the storytelling?
How do lighting, sound, set, and costume contribute to the mood?
What emotions or messages does the performance communicate?
In-Class Activities
Group Sharing (5-10 min):
Students share initial impressions in small groups, focusing on personal reactions and standout moments.
Structured Feedback Workshop:
Using the “What–How–Why” model:
What did you notice? (Observation)
How was it executed? (Technique)
Why did it work or not work? (Impact)
Discussion Topics:
Performance quality and character embodiment
Use of space, movement, and gestures
Vocal clarity and emotional expression
Effectiveness of visual design (lights, props, costumes)
Overall storytelling and audience engagement
Key takeaways for students’ own final projects
Mini Reflection Writing
Students write a short reflective paragraph summarizing:
One element they admired and hope to borrow in their own performance
One aspect they think could be improved and why
What they learned about being an audience member
Final Project Explanation
The final project is designed to integrate all the performance, production, and creative skills students have learned throughout the course. Each student or small group will choose one scene from an existing play and adapt it into a new performance piece, demonstrating their understanding of acting, movement, staging, script adaptation, and basic production design.
1. Scene Selection
Students may select:
A scene from a classical or modern play
A short excerpt from a contemporary script
A monologue or duologue that can be expanded
A short movement-based or physical theatre scene with text
Students must receive instructor approval to ensure the scene is appropriate in length, content, and feasibility.
2. Adaptation Requirements
Students must creatively reinterpret the chosen scene using at least three elements learned in the course, such as:
Movement composition (levels, tempo, physical storytelling)
Voice techniques (projection, tone, character voice)
Improvisation (added moments or transitions)
Choreography or ensemble movement
Stagecraft basics (lighting concept, sound cues, props)
Script adaptation (condensing, modernizing, re-contextualizing)
Screen-performance techniques (for recorded elements or multimedia integration)
Marketing strategies (strong promotional concept)
The goal is not to copy the original scene exactly but to transform it into a fresh, meaningful, and performable piece.
3. Performance Requirements
Each final performance should:
Be 10-15 minutes long
Show clear artistic intention and creative choices
Demonstrate collaboration (if group-based)
Incorporate blocking, character work, timing, and emotional clarity
Include at least one simple design element (sound, light, prop, costume, or multimedia)
The performance will take place in Week 16 during the final showcase.
4. Promotional Materials
To strengthen their understanding of arts marketing, students will also create:
A. Performance Flyer
The flyer must include:
Title of the adapted scene
Original playwright + “Adapted by ___”
Short description (50–80 words)
Performance date, time, and location
Performers’ names
A visually appealing design that reflects the tone or theme of the piece
Students may use Canva or other simple design tools.
B. Invitation Message
Students must create a short invitation to send to classmates, teachers, or friends. This message should:
Introduce the performance
Highlight what is unique about the adaptation
Encourage the audience to attend

title: 選修英文:創意寫作 English Elective: Creative Writing
description: This course is an introduction to creative writing and literacy through the fundamentals of writing non-fiction, fiction, and poetry with an emphasis on genre knowledge and audience awareness. The course, which is conducted in English, incorporates lectures and discussion sessions making class-time full of activity. Writing assignments provide students with opportunities to practice and improve their writing skills while designing topics based on their own interests and experiences. Students learn ways to approach writing assignments and how to use their writing ability to express themselves creatively in a variety of genres in English. Based on the lectures, lessons, and in-class practice, students will create a portfolio of creative work to present at the end of the semester.
objectives: In this class, learners will practice writing as a process of invention and revision that anyone can master with effort. The course is taught with a particular emphasis on helping non-native-speaking students improve their general English writing skills and language use/sentence structure within the context of creative writing. As with academic writing, students will learn the importance of structure for each writing piece, providing the framework for creative expression. The course is divided into two main sections: creative non-fiction and short-story fiction with additional instruction and practice in screenwriting and poetry. In creative non-fiction, students will learn how to compose travel writing, features/human interest articles, and memoir/personal experience compositions. In fiction, students will learn how to compose a short story, which includes character-creation, world-building, plotting, genre, voice, and dialogue. In addition to non-fiction and fiction skills, students will learn a variety of other creative writing methods, such as composing scenes for film and theater, writing poetry such as haiku and free-verse, and creative journaling. By the end of the course, students will become more confident in their English writing skills and be able to transfer this confidence into any form of writing, whether non-academic or academic.
grading:
Your final grades will be determined by the following course components:
Participation: 15% (including attendance, coming on time to class, in-class writing practice, partner contribution)
Out-of-class assignments: 15% (includes travel writing, feature writing, and memoir)
Representative Work (includes presentation of non-fiction work at the end of the semester: graded on changes based on feedback and model): 15%
Creative Non-Fiction Exam: 30%
Creative Fiction Assignment (process with final draft written in class): 25%
Participation:
Students will be graded on the following aspects of participation:
Attendance. Students are required to come to class. If a student has three unexcused absences or more, he/she will fail the course. Students can make up the participation for being absent by writing an extra assignment and sending it as an attachment by email to the instructor.
Coming to class on time. Students must come to class on time. If they are late three times, it equals one unexcused absence. Every time a student is late, it affects his/her participation, unless it was an emergency. Students cannot make up for coming late.
In-class writing practice: Students must bring lined paper to class and write their practice writing on it. It will be collected by the teacher after class. Students will improve their writing by practicing writing in class. Often this includes partner collaboration on written assignments. It will also include analysis of your novel that you read for homework.
Out-of-class assignments: The following are the assignments that will be started in class and/or finished for homework if they couldn’t be completed in class.
Descriptive writing practice
Travel writing assignment
Feature writing assignment
Memoir writing assignment
Screenplay
Poem
Partner interaction: It is important for students to give each other feedback and encouragement on their writing. Therefore, those who do not participate or interact with a partner will fail participation. Writers become better writers with help from other writers or feedback from readers. Therefore, students are required to help each other improve!
Representative Work: (out-of-class project)
Based on one of the creative projects that students have learned this semester, they must rewrite one project that represents their own creativity, called the Representative Work. They may choose to rewrite one of the following projects for this assignment (listed below). Students are expected to improve their first draft based on the teacher's feedback and comparison with the model. Therefore, improvements should go beyond correcting grammar errors. Consider adding more to each paragraph.
Travel Article (on a place they have traveled to)
Feature Article (interviewing a person and writing about him or her)
Memoir (about a personal experience in which you learned a valuable life lesson)
This grade includes a final presentation at the end of the semester to present your representative work to the class, sharing a portion or all (if there is time) of the writing, discussing the background of the content, and the creative inspiration behind the reason for choosing this work to represent your creativity.
Creative Non-Fiction Exam: (in-class exam)
This first in-class exam is a test of the creative non-fiction modes that have been taught and practiced in class. These include travel writing, features writing, and a memoir/personal experience composition. Students will write according to the topic presented on the day of the exam and include an outline to show the structure of their work. Students’ writing will be judged on outline structure, creative introductions, supporting body paragraphs, creative conclusions, and language use.
Short Story: (out-of-class/in-class project)
Students will learn to write a fictional short story. They have the freedom to choose their own genre (suspense, horror, romance, fantasy, etc.). Through guided instruction, students will create a map of the world in which the story takes place. They must also create a main character and a villain for their story, and include at least one minor character. Then they will plot out a story using the model presented in class. Students’ writing will be judged on pre-writing effort and creativity (map/plot structure/character development), creative introductions, dialogue usage, story in five acts, and language use. Absolutely no AI or help tools may be used on the pre-writing phase. Students will write the final draft of their story in class. To make sure that students complete the final draft within the time limit in class, students must come prepared! They can only start their final draft after all the pre-writing work has been completed and checked by the teacher.

title: 選修英文:科技英文 English Elective: English for Information Technology
description:
In today's digital era, where information technology is ever-present and artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, it is crucial for individuals to possess tech-savviness and stay updated with the latest IT trends. The English for Information Technology course is specifically tailored to introduce cutting-edge topics in information technology that directly align with the needs of the Millennials.
This one-semester 3-credit-hour course is designed for high-intermediate/advanced students of English as a foreign language. This is not a course that aims to teach students information technology knowledge. Rather, it is designed to allow students to transform their English language knowledge into the communication skills necessary for careers in the IT field or any profession. In addition, students are encouraged to think about and consider ethical issues and related topics in information technology. Students will also learn how to discover and discuss new and trending information technologies. A considerable emphasis will be put on training students to create an academic research poster on a topic on issues related to information technology.
objectives:
The primary goal of this course is to allow students to maximize their English listening, speaking, and writing abilities while exploring a wide range of topics in information technology. The course will be conducted entirely in English.
Learning outcomes:
Upon completion of the course, students are expected to have:
broadened their knowledge of trending technologies and their applications,
possessed an awareness of the global information technology field,
learned the skills to share expertise and credentials effectively,
learned the skills to communicate in English in the IT workplace,
learned how to search and organize information regarding emerging IT,
learned how to create an academic research poster,
learned the skills to present research findings/results in speaking and in writing,
upgraded their English presentation skills.
By the end of this course, students are expected to be able to demonstrate their knowledge on different topics covered in class by using topic-related vocabulary words and phrases appropriately.
grading:
All materials, including the written text, handouts, and any information spoken in class or written on the board, are expected to be reflected in your work. Take notes and study the handouts. Keep all of the work you do during the course until after the final grades have been announced.
You are expected to:
participate actively in all in-class activities and discussions;
preview assigned materials;
attend each class AND be on time;
conduct two oral presentations;
hand in all written assignments;
take the final examination.
Your final grades are determined by the following course components:
Participation (attendance, class discussion, activity, etc.): 20%
Written assignments: 30%
Presentations 30%
Final examination: 20%
ATTENDANCE, PUNCTUALITY & ASSIGNMENT POLICIES
Attendance and punctuality are required for all class sessions.
Any absence will be counted against your records unless a leave of absence is requested to the instructor by email, prior to or by the end of the absent day.
Exams can only be made up or rescheduled for valid reasons (see the University’s policy regarding make-up exams).
LEARNING TASKS & ASSIGNMENTS
Participation
Class participation refers to your active involvement in the class activities including your insights and comments regarding class content, responses to the instructor’s questions, and reactions to other students’ contributions.
Assignments
In addition to the periodic in-class assignments, individual or group-based, you will complete two major assignments: (1) create your own LinkedIn profile, (2) write a professional email reply to a client using AI as a support tool.
(1) For the LinkedIn profile, you will be asked to give a quick and accurate description of yourself as a professional. You will be given samples to help you prepare your own LinkedIn Summary.
(2) For the client email reply, you are given a scenario involving a difficult customer interaction. You will use AI to help draft a response, then revise and improve it based on what you've learned about tone, clarity, and professional email conventions.
All assignments are to be handed in on the due dates. Late submissions will be penalized 5% per day late, up to a maximum penalty of 20%. The grading rubrics for the writing assignments are available on the course Moodle.
Presentations
You will give ONE individual and ONE group presentation on IT related topics: (1) pitch a startup idea and launch an IT product/service, (2) present your academic research poster.
(1) Individual presentation (approximately 5 minutes): Imagine you are launching your own IT startup. You will open with a short pitch, then present your product or service, highlighting its key features and benefits for a specific audience. The presentation ends with a brief Q&A session in which you respond to questions about your product.
(2) Group presentation (approximately 10 minutes): You will be asked to produce an academic research poster to display your research on IT topics. The poster should be written in a formal style and referenced. Different structures and styles will be discussed in class.
All presentation materials should be uploaded to Moodle. Specific guidelines and grading rubrics will be provided in class.
Final exam
The final exam is a paper-&-pencil exam. All materials, including the vocabulary list, readings, handouts, and video exercises provided in class throughout the semester will potentially be included. No make-up exam will be given unless you obtain the instructor’s permission in advance.

title: 選修英文:傳播英文 English Elective: English for Mass Communication
description:
English for Mass Communication has been designed with the aim of nurturing students’ expertise in English communication, fostering their ability to think creatively, solve problems, and effectively practice communication. By enrolling in this course, students can anticipate the acquisition of valuable skills that will enhance their prospects for future academic pursuits and employment.

Specific units included in the design encompass a wide range of subjects, including an overview of communication applications, multimedia production of English communication such as podcast creation, video production, script development, and so on.
Through active participation in this course, students will not only improve their English language proficiency, but also gain hands-on experience in applying their mass communication skills in real-life scenarios. The knowledge and expertise they acquire throughout this course will prove advantageous as they pursue further educational or career opportunities.
objectives:
This course has been carefully designed to offer students the chance to enhance their ability to effectively convey their messages to an audience when communicating in English. Students will receive ongoing support and guidance to address any challenges they encounter throughout the course.
The objectives & learning outcomes of the course include:
Enhancing students’ ability to deliver compelling public speeches and presentations.

Boosting students’ confidence in carrying out practical communication tasks.
Providing students with opportunities to observe and analyze information and interactions across various communication mediums.
grading:

Your final grades are determined by the following course components:

The grading rubric for the written test is available on the class website. No make-up exams will be given unless you have received the instructor’s permission in advance.
The use of generative AI tools

title: 選修英文:閱讀與口語訓練 English Elective: Reading & Oral Training
description: Reading and Oral Training is a one-semester course for high-intermediate to advanced learners of English. The course, which is conducted in English, is designed to acclimate students to using English as a tool for advanced communication. During the course, students will enhance their reading and speaking skills through lectures, pair/group discussions, oral presentations, role-play, writing assignments, watching films, and other in-class activities. Students will become familiar with different communication styles and methods of organization for handling discussion and presentation of contemporary issues through a combination of reading materials and speaking exercises on various subjects from different sources, such as novels, news media, blog posts, and academic articles. Students will also learn to summarize texts, analyze structure (through outlining), compare and contrast, and give opinions, which can be extended to more advanced reading skills, e.g. identifying facts and opinions, and making inferences in class.
grading:
Class time will be devoted to activities that allow you to practice and interact in English. To successfully complete the course, you must prepare the assigned homework prior to class and actively participate in class discussions and pair/group work. Your final grades are determined by the following course components:
Attendance & participation: 15%
Quizzes: 10%
Oral presentations: 20%
Written assignments: 35%
Final Exam: 20%
ASSIGNMENTS AND REQUIREMENTS
Attendance & participation
You are required to attend classes regularly and on time. Absences (including sick leave and personal leave), tardiness, or early departure will damage your attendance grade. Contact me about your absence before class if you must miss class.
Your participation grade will be based on your homework preparation, and the contribution you make to the learning experience of others. Contribution includes your in-class questions to the instructor, insights and comments regarding class content, answers to the instructor’s questions, and reactions to other students’ contributions. Speaking up in class, either being called or voluntarily, will add points to your participation grade. Try to catch any opportunity to speak up in class to earn bonus points! Writing down your responses to questions on Moodle Discussion Boards will also add points to your participation grade.
In-class quizzes
Six pop quizzes based on assigned readings will be given in class. Missed quizzes CANNOT be made up.
Written assignments
Six written assignments based on the course readings will be assigned. The assignments may ask you to respond to key issues in the readings, write summaries, analyze passages or write short compositions comparing/contrasting cultural issues. You are required to complete the assignments at home by due dates so that you can join discussions in class. Late submission will lead to lower grades of your assignment. You need to upload the images of all the writings you have done for the course to Moodle regularly. I will use these files as reference when I evaluate your writing performance at the end of the semester.
Oral presentations
You will give two types of oral presentations during the semester:
In-class group discussions: In these discussions, you will share opinions, discuss questions brought up by the instructor or your classmates, and/or present your written assignment work.
Individual oral presentation during midterm exam week: You will give a 5-7 minute formal presentation recommending your favorite book to the class. More detailed guidelines for this assignment can be seen on our Moodle course page.
See the attachment for the grading rubric for the individual oral presentation.
Final Exam
The Final Exam consists of written responses to critical thinking questions based on lecture content and assigned readings in the course throughout the semester.

title: 選修英文:閱讀與口語訓練 English Elective: Reading & Oral Training
grading:
Class time will be devoted to reading, discussion, collaborative inquiry, and speaking activities. To participate effectively, you are expected to complete the assigned readings and preparation before class and to take an active role in pair work, group work, and whole-class discussions.
Your final grade will be based on the following course components:
Weekly Inquiry Forum: 20%
Midterm Inquiry Presentation: 20%
Personal Interest Talk: 20%
Final Synthesis Presentation: 20%
Class Participation: 20%
For group assignments, grades will reflect both the quality of the group’s overall work and each member’s individual contribution. Individual grades may therefore differ within the same group.
ASSIGNMENTS AND REQUIREMENTS
Attendance and Participation
Attendance is essential because much of the learning in this course takes place through discussion and interaction. Your participation grade will be based on your attendance, preparation, and active contribution to the learning of the class.
Participation includes taking part in pair and group discussions, responding to questions, sharing ideas and interpretations, listening and responding to classmates, and contributing constructively to student-led activities. Quality of participation is more important than simply speaking frequently.
Reading and Preparation
Assigned readings should be completed before class. You may also be asked to complete short preparation tasks, reflection questions, or other activities related to the readings. These tasks are designed to help you participate meaningfully in class discussions and inquiry activities.
Weekly Inquiry Forum
Each student will participate in one group-led Weekly Inquiry Forum. Rather than giving a conventional presentation or summarizing the assigned reading, the group will use the week’s core question and reading to develop its own interpretation and lead the class in a 30-minute inquiry session.
The forum should include relevant textual evidence, the group’s own perspective, and meaningful opportunities for classmates to participate, respond, and discuss.
Personal Interest Talk
Each student will give a 3–5 minute individual talk on a topic of personal interest. The topic may be something you enjoy, know well, care about, or simply want to introduce to the class. The purpose of this activity is to develop confidence, ownership, and an individual speaking voice.
Midterm Inquiry Presentation
The midterm project will ask you to investigate a question connected to the first half of the course and the theme of The World That Shapes Us. You will work collaboratively to develop a focused inquiry, gather relevant evidence, and present your findings and interpretation to the class.
Final Synthesis Presentation
The final project will ask you to bring together ideas from the second half of the course and, where appropriate, make connections across the semester. The emphasis will be on synthesis, interpretation, and developing a thoughtful response to the larger question of what it means to remain human in a changing world.
Detailed instructions and grading criteria for major assignments will be provided separately.

title: 選修英文:閱讀與口語訓練 English Elective: Reading & Oral Training
description: Reading and Oral Training is a one-semester course for high-intermediate to advanced learners of English. The course, which is conducted in English, is designed to acclimate students to using English as a tool for advanced communication. During the course, students will enhance their reading and speaking skills through lectures, pair/group discussions, oral presentations, role-play, writing assignments, watching films, and other in-class activities. Students will become familiar with different communication styles and methods of organization for handling discussion and presentation of contemporary issues through a combination of reading materials and speaking exercises on various subjects from different sources, such as novels, news media, blog posts, and academic articles. Students will also learn to summarize texts, analyze structure (through outlining), compare and contrast, and give opinions, which can be extended to more advanced reading skills, e.g. identifying facts and opinions, and making inferences in class.
grading: Class time will be devoted to activities that allow you to practice and interact in English. To successfully complete the course, you must prepare the assigned homework prior to class and actively participate in class discussions, online discussions, and pair/group work. Your final grades are determined by the following course components: Attendance: 10% Participation: 12% Moodle worksheets: 3% (Due 9/24 13:30) Individual speech: 10% Interview video: 15% + 5% (Video Task) Start-up presentations (Final): 15% Group presentation (Chapter): 15% Midterm: 15% ASSIGNMENTS AND REQUIREMENTS Attendance & participation Your attendance mark is based on the average minutes you are present in class, and the mark will be calculated with 100-point scale , whereas participation grade will be based on homework preparation, and the contribution you make to the learning experience of others. Contribution includes your in-class questions to the instructor, insights and comments regarding class content, answers to the instructor's questions, and reactions to other students' contributions. You will need to submit proper document in order for the instructor to mark your absence as an excused leave. If the final mark for the attendance is lower than 80, this attendance mark will be zero. Humans in Our Life: Writing You will interview someone you do not know. Think of the questions you might be asking before you choose your interviewee. Write up the person's story in writing. You also have to gain this person's consent to take photos of him/her. It is suggested that his/her story is worth reading and the readers can learn something. You will also have to add your own self-reflection on the story. Oral presentations You will give three types of oral presentations during the semester: 2 group presentation, individual speech (Daily Dedication), and poster session (short story). Group Presentation 1 (20%): Each group will take up one chapter of the book and use 25-30 minutes to lead the discussion regarding the chapter of your choice. Group Presentation 2 (15%): Each group will try to think of a feasible business they are going to establish. The presentation should be 15-20 minutes. Individual Speech (10%): Each person will choose their own topic to introduce to the audience. Everyone will present their own presentation on the same day as its our class's TEDx Talk. It should be 3-4 minutes long. Interview Video Task (15%): In a group of 5-6 people, choose a traditional job that is underrated or invisible to most people, and make a video to describe the job. The video should be 12-15 minutes long, and everyone should take a speaking role. You are not required to be seen in the video, but who's speaking should be known for the viewers. See the attachment for the grading rubric for these presentations. All rubrics will be announced on Facebook. Mid-term exam: 15% The exam is based on an assigned reading that will be distributed a week earlier or two. Class discussion will be given a week ahead for you all to brainstorm what you can connect to. The exam is mainly on testing your critical thinking skills; therefore, as long as your ideas are conveyed successfully, grammar and sentence structures do not matter much.

title: 選修英文:學術聽說訓練 English Elective: Academic Listening & Speaking
description: This course, which is conducted in English, is designed for high-intermediate to advanced English learners. It is based on a content-based syllabus, utilizing lectures on topics from different academic disciplines and related reading materials. The authentic content provides both a context for the practice of important language skills and a basis for the exploration of high-interest topics for learners. The course covers diverse issues and integrates vocabulary, grammar, listening and speaking skills necessary for academic success. Throughout the semester, students are encouraged to improve their academic listening and speaking ability by listening to lectures and participating in discussions, as well as practicing note-taking and summarizing.
objectives:
This course will help students to
- build discipline- or topic-related vocabulary
- improve listening skills both in everyday and academic settings
- develop learning strategies and study skills for academic success
- reinforce academic discussion and communicative skills
- develop effective note-taking and summarizing skills
- deliver informative talks / presentation in today’s academic and professional world
- expand critical thinking
- be aware of cultural differences and similarities
Learning Outcomes for Lecture Comprehension and Note-taking
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
- predict lecture content and organization
- listen for the lecturer’s main points and for the general organizational framework
- make guesses when information is missed
- evaluate and decide what is and is not important during a lecture
- note key words, and use abbreviations and symbols
- organize information and visually represent the relationship between ideas
- note most numbers and statistics
Learning Outcomes for Informative Talks & Presentation
By the end of the course, while presenting, students will be able to:
- consider the audience and have clear objectives (to inform, to amuse, to persuade, to train, etc.)
- have a clear structure and link the parts together
- address academic issues successfully with a variety of resources
- consider the timing
- speak clearly at the right speed
- use appropriate language
- maintain eye contact with the audience
- use body language effectively
- appear confident and positive
- make clear visual aids to support messages
- use the equipment professionally
grading:
ATTENDANCE, PUNCTUALITY & ASSIGNMENT/EXAM POLICIES
Attendance is important, and students are expected to come to class ON TIME! (Attendance/Lateness policy will be explained in the first class.) Students who are absent for more than half of total class hours without an appropriate reason will receive zero for both Attendance and Class Performance portions, and CANNOT partake in the final exam. All required assignments must be submitted to the instructor before the due dates. Note that NO assignments will be accepted after the deadline. The quizzes CANNOT be made up (except for sick leave), and NO make-up final exam will be given unless you have received the instructor’s permission in advance.
To successfully complete the course, you must participate in assigned activities and take quizzes and the final exam. Your final grade is determined by the following course components:
Participation: 20% (Attendance 10% + Class performance 10%)
Quizzes: 20%
Assignments: 20%
Presentations: 20% (group 10% + individual 10%)
Final exam: 20%
Participation
Your participation grade will be based on your attendance, homework preparation, and the
contribution you make to the learning experience of others. Contribution includes your questions to
the instructor, insights and comments regarding class content, answers to the instructor’s questions,
and reactions to other students’ contributions in class.
Quizzes
Throughout the semester, 4 quizzes will be given in class, including 3 listening quizzes and 1 speaking
task. The listening quizzes contain lecture listening, note-taking and comprehension questions,
and students are required to give their responses orally in the speaking task. More details will be
provided in class.
Assignments
You will give 3 short Informative Talks (ITs) on topics discussed this semester (2 to your group
members and 1 to the whole class). Each IT focuses on a relevant subtopic of your choice, lasts five
minutes, and may include visual aids. Before the class, you need to upload the outline to the class
website. When you give your IT during class time, the other group members will then
practice note-taking strategies and give you feedback when the IT is finished. Note that your
feedback (e.g., notes and comments) will also need to be uploaded to the class website afterwards.
NO assignments will be accepted after the deadline, which is the end of each unit. Besides these IT assignments, you need to comment on other students' speaking task performance (Week #11) and give suggestions. More details will be
provided in class.
Presentations
You will give one Group Presentation (GP) and one Individual Presentation (IP). For the group
presentation, each group will report on an assigned topic. The presentation should last approximately
20 minutes, followed by a 5-minute class discussion. Before the presentation, each group needs to
upload their PowerPoint slides to the class website. While presenting, each group will be evaluated by
the instructor as well as by their peers. For the individual presentation, each student will be assigned
by the instructor to give a 5-minute informative talk (on one of the chosen topics) with PowerPoint
presentation in front of the whole class. More details will be provided in class.
Final Exam
The final exam contains a listening test and an integrated speaking test. The listening test includes
lecture listening, note-taking, and comprehension questions. In the integrated speaking test, you will
be required to give your responses orally. You will need to demonstrate your ability to respond to
the questions clearly and coherently and the ability to accurately convey the information about what
you have read or listened to.
*** The grading rubrics for the group presentation/speaking test/note-taking exercise (attached below) will be available on the class website.

Assignments

Each talk on the academic field will focus on a relevant subtopic of your choice, last five minutes, and include PowerPoint slides. Before or after the class, you need to upload the slides and then give your online feedback on your partners’ talks after this activity. More details will be provided in class.

title: 選修英文:英文寫作 English Elective: Essay Writing
description: 論文寫作課程旨在幫助學生撰寫大學程度的論文。我們將首先提供一系列論文範例,並分析其結構、內容、詞彙和語法結構。隨著課程的深入,學生將了解優秀論文的通用標準,並能根據這些標準評估自己的作品。我們希望學生在意識到自身能力與預期目標之間的差距後,能夠制定策略性學習計畫並據此改進。在講解關鍵概念之後,我們將安排課堂限時寫作練習和課後寫作作業,幫助學生鞏固所學。隨後,我們將對這些論文進行討論,引導學生進行自我修改,進而提升論文品質。
objectives:
到學期結束時,完成課程要求的學生應達到以下程度:
具備論文寫作原則與策略的知識
熟悉並有使用常用寫作資源(如線上字典、同義詞庫、生成式人工智慧等)的經驗。
大學生普遍了解其寫作標準和要求,以及
同儕互評和自我修改能力以及修改技巧。
grading:
參與率(20%)
積極參與對您在本課程中的成功至關重要。參與方式包括:
定期出勤,
積極參與課堂討論和同儕回饋
對Moodle討論區做出有意義的貢獻,
與同儕進行建設性互動,以及
樂於分享想法、提出問題並認真思考回饋。
因為寫作是透過對話和修改而發展的,所以整個學期都需要持續、認真地參與。
論文一:比較(20%)
這篇比較論文的寫作計畫為期三週。你需要就相關的比較主題撰寫兩篇課堂習作。在兩稿之間,你需要根據同伴和人工智慧的回饋來修改你的作品。我們期望你的作品在第一次課堂習作的基礎上有所進步。
本次作業旨在評估您以下方面的能力:
清楚比較和/或對比兩個或多個主題,
保持邏輯結構和段落統一性,
運用有效的過渡語和比較性語言,
詞彙運用精準,語法準確。
論文二:因果關係(20%)
在本次作業中,你將分析特定問題或情況的起因和/或影響。你將遵循同樣的三週週期,準備並分析案例,完成兩篇課堂限時寫作,並根據回饋修改草稿。
本文旨在評估你以下方面的能力:
提出清晰明確的論點,
建立合乎邏輯的因果關係,
提供詳細的解釋和支持,
保持邏輯連貫性、清晰度和語言準確性,
在草稿的基礎上進行改進,最終形成修訂版。
論文三:討論(20%)
本次作業要求你從多個角度探討一個有爭議的問題或一個多角度討論的話題,提出平衡的論點,最終得出合理的結論。你將遵循同樣的三週循環,分析範文,在課堂上撰寫論證草稿,並利用同伴和人工智慧的回饋來完善你的論點。這篇論文將直接銜接你的最終論證論文。
本次作業旨在評估您以下方面的能力:
對不同觀點進行平衡客觀的概述,
批判性地評估證據和反駁論點,
形成一個細緻入微且論證充分的結論,
保持學術客觀性、連貫性和語言精確性,
將回饋意見納入考量,以加深草稿之間的批判性分析。
最終論證論文(20%):
最終論證論文是一個貫穿整個學期的項目,它整合了你在論文1-3中培養的各項技能。完成論文1後,你將開始構思你的主題。完成論文2後,你將制定一個結構化的大綱。完成論文3後,你將完成一份完整的初稿,並參與同儕互評。最後一周將安排一次面對面的面試,屆時你將向同學們展示並討論你的論點。你的主題應該反映你真正關心的問題(例如,校園生活、社會議題、與更廣泛議題相關的個人經驗)。你的論點必須反映你自己的思考和表達。人工智慧可以在修改和潤飾語言的過程中提供幫助,但所有的觀點和論證都必須是獨一無二的。
本次作業旨在評估您以下方面的能力:
提出一個有理有據且重點突出的論點,
組織一個連貫且論點充分的論點,
對回饋做出有意義的回應
在清晰度、深度和準確性方面做出實質修改,以及
在面試過程中進行有意義的討論。

title: 選修英文:英文寫作 English Elective: Essay Writing
description: This course is an introduction to academic writing and literacy through the fundamentals of essay writing with an emphasis on genre knowledge and audience awareness. The course, which is conducted in English, incorporates lectures and discussion sessions making class time full of activity. Writing assignments provide students with opportunities to practice writing skills while exploring current issues through their own interests and experiences. Students learn ways to approach writing assignments and go through the process of writing an academic essay in English. An assigned textbook is used as a guide, but other materials and references are available on the course Moodle.
objectives:
In this course, students will practice writing as a process of invention and revision that anyone can master with effort. The course starts with a review of basic paragraph structure before moving on to common types of essays including cause-effect, comparison, and argument essays. By the end of the semester, students who have successfully completed the course requirements will be able to write thoughtful and well-organized essays. They will have a solid understanding of key components of academic writing, including organization, thesis statements, and clarity of ideas. grading:
All materials, including the written text, handouts, and any information spoken in class or written on the board, are expected to be reflected in your work. Attendance & participation (discussion, peer review, free writing activity, etc.): 20%

ATTENDANCE, PUNCTUALITY & ASSIGNMENT POLICIES

Exams cannot be made up or rescheduled unless you provide documentation of a true emergency.

Free writing

Writing assignments
In addition to the free writing activities and other miscellaneous writing tasks in class, you will write four major assignments, including a classification essay, a cause-effect essay, a comparison essay, and an argument essay. You will develop each of these essays over several weeks. Topic options will be suggested by the class and will address social, political, cultural, or environmental issues relevant to your local contexts or NCCU.
When writing the essays, you are expected to apply the writing skills and language learned in class. description: This course is an introduction to academic writing and literacy through the fundamentals of essay writing with an emphasis on genre knowledge and audience awareness. objectives:
In this class, learners will practice writing as a process of invention and revision that anyone can master with effort. Students will review basic paragraph structure and then learn about common rhetorical forms. They will practice several types of essays including narrative, comparison/contrast, cause-effect, and argument. In sum, students will gain a foundational understanding of English composition and learn the writing process as they develop their own writing and revising toolkit.
By the end of the semester, those who have satisfactorily completed the course requirementswill be able to identify a compelling topic, decide how to treat it in writing, and compose a strong and thoughtful essay to explore or argue it. Students will be familiar with elements of good academic compositions including organization, thesis statements, and clarity of ideas. Finally, students will learn the mechanics of academic writing such as document format, and citations and reference lists.
grading:
Your final grade will be determined by the following course components:
Participation/Homework assignments: 15% (attendance, late to class, out-of-class assignments)
Expository/Benefits Essay (out-of-class – including drafts and AI version): 15%
Process Essay (in-class test): 35%
Cause-Effect Essay (in-class test): 35%
Participation/Homework assignments: 15%
Attendance and coming to class on time = 5%
Out-of-class assignments = 10%
There are two main written assignments (the business letter and the academic paragraph). These assignments will be explained in class, but students must check Moodle for complete details on all assignments (including writing practice from the textbook). Please bring the following items to each class:
The textbook (required)
Lined paper for writing practice (loose-leaf paper, not a bound notebook)
FAQ about Participation:
What happens if I miss the first class?
Please inform the teacher that you will be absent on the first day of class by sending me an email. Students who miss the first day of class must write two make-up papers.
Time yourself for 15 minutes and write a self-introduction by hand, including topics such as your major, interests, writing experience, interesting life experiences, and future goals. Do not use help tools to correct your grammar. I need a sample of your typical writing style.
Write a summary of the key points of the Day One PPT, which will be posted on Moodle. You can write this assignment by hand.
What are we going to do for homework?
There are a few writing assignments that complete activities which we start in class - such as writing a business letter, completing an academic paragraph, the process essay, or other practice writing activities. We may also do pre-writing activities for homework that will prepare you to write an essay in class. In addition to writing activities, students will complete assigned exercises in the textbook. Therefore, having the textbook is a requirement for participation and will be checked in the third week.
Do we need to buy the complete textbook? Can’t we make photocopies of the book chapters we use?
We will be using quite a bit of the textbook in both practice activities and learning from the essay model examples, so you would need to photocopy most of the book, which is illegal by copyright laws unless the publisher gives permission. This textbook also functions partly as a workbook and reference book, so it is worth it to use for study and improvement of essay writing skills. Students are also required to bring the textbook to each class even though we may not use it in every class.
Can we get an ebook?
It is allowed to buy an ebook version of the textbook, but students with the ebook may need to write answers to activities on a separate piece of paper, or use your Apple Pen to fill in the blanks of assignments in your e-textbook. Students must be ready to prove they bought the ebook by showing the professor.
Other than assignments, what else is included in the participation grade?
Attendance is mandatory. If a student has three or more unexcused absences, he/she will fail the course. Coming to class on time is also important. Coming late cannot be made up and if a student is late three times, it equals one unexcused absence. The main component of this hands-on writing course is practice. Students are required to participate in writing practice alone and with a partner. This ensures peer feedback and mutual encouragement in your writing journey.
How do we submit assignments?
Please print out the assignment, including any pre-writing, etc. I want to have the paper-version of your writing because I want to write comments all over the paper and also show grammar errors. The only assignment that I will accept as an email attachment is a make-up essay. Minor assignments may be written by hand, except for the business letter. Major assignments must be typed and printed out (essay, double-spaced; outline and pre-writing, single-spaced).
Out-of-class assignments:
Expository/Benefits Essay (out-of-class): 15%
The expository essay is how students learn the foundation of essay writing. This assignment is completed in stages. The first stage is the first draft, using the basic essay format. The second stage is expanding the essay according to our instruction in class. The third stage is an additional draft with more changes. The final draft considers all of what we have learned in class to make it the best essay you have ever written. Please type and print out the final draft of the assignment, including the detailed outline and the final draft of the essay. The early drafts and pre-writing may be handwritten.
SPECIAL NOTE ON ASSIGNMENTS AND AI:
The first draft of all out-of-class assignments must be your own writing without grammar checks, translations, AI, or other help tools. In other words, they must include all of your errors. No grammar will be graded on those assignments. If a first-draft assignment is turned in with no errors OR if that assignment appears that some sentences have been fabricated by AI or other writing help tools, the paper will not be accepted and will not be allowed to be made up.
However, on some writing assignments, students will be asked to use AI (using Chat-GPT or other AI tool) to correct their grammar. In this case, they must write the first draft by themselves without help tools and then have AI rewrite it with correct grammar. Students must turn in both the original version and the AI version. They will analyze these two versions in class to check for patterns of grammar errors. (AI version assignments = academic paragraph and expository essay) Again, grammar will not be graded on out-of-class assignments, but it will be graded on in-class tests. Therefore, students are encouraged to improve their grammar using this method before the first in-class exam.
Process Essay (in-class test): 35%
Students will prepare to write a process essay following procedures learned in class. Students will then use part of their prepared material from class to write the essay without the use of digital help tools. They will have three hours to write this essay in class. This essay tests the student’s ability in proper structure of the essay and outline format as well as language use (grammar and vocabulary).
Cause-Effect Essay (in-class test): 35%
The final exam tests the student’s advanced essay writing ability to organize body paragraphs in their own way and to persuasively produce a cause-and-effect essay on a particular phenomenon. The topic will be given in class on the day of the test, but it will be a topic that everyone has experience with. The final exam will be the fufillment of the objective from the first day of class: to compose a detailed outline and essay from blank page to finished product without the help of digital writing tools.
