description:
本課程雖以「創作」為名,但實際上並不會教「創作」本身,而是更偏向實作練習,讓同學在課程結束後,不會被技術限制,而能在創作上更加自由
本課程將以 Unity3D 作為主要的開發工具。雖然 Unity3D 經常被用於遊戲開發,但本課程的教材將以「非遊戲」的方式來進行設計,旨在拆解各項遊戲引擎中的元素,帶領各位實際操作「互動新媒體領域」經常使用到的觀念與技術,以期待同學們未來在實作上可以有更彈性的思考
—
本課程將會包含較廣泛的概念,除了 Unity3D 軟體本身的基礎操作概念以外,還會包含 3D 建模、動畫、動態演算法、Shader、API 呼叫等概念。授課時,比起仔細教導各項技術細節,本課程更傾向於讓同學掌握整體的概念,因為當代的 AI 技術已經成了最好的實作導師。只要同學具備正確的觀念理解,便可以藉由 AI 輕易的取得正確、可執行的程式碼,甚至架構概念清晰時,也可以在不調整程式碼的情況下進行完整的專案實作
因此,本課程的設計為,在上課時,同學可以帶著輕鬆的心情到教室,老師會以手把手的方式,帶同學走過一遍整個實作的過程,讓同學理解這項技術的實際用法為何。但若要能夠實際應用到自己的創作、實作中,則有賴同學在課後自行摸索練習。因此本課程的課程不需預習,也可帶著輕鬆的心情來課,但會需要花費較多時間進行課程後的練習實作
—
另外,在軟體開發中應用 AI 將會是未來的重要技能與趨勢,因此本課程將會高度鼓勵同學使用 AI。課程中會試著帶同學申請學生版的免費 AI 服務,但由於各公司政策經常有變,因此難以保證該免費服務足夠使用,也期待當課程中需要購買付費 AI 服務時,同學能以購入課本的心態來進行付費
objectives:
數位技術:
理解如何使用 Unity3D 進行製作
廣泛理解各項「互動新媒體」中的技術概念
了解如何利用 AI 來協助撰寫程式
人文藝術:
課程中會有作品與藝術家案例,藉由大量的觀看,來建立審美的概念框架
課程中會包含大量的創作練習,藉由大量的創作,來了解自身的創作能量
grading:
每周作業繳交(50%)
每週作業互評(30%)
期末專案繳交(20%)
期末專案互評(10%)
每週作業的部分,要透過課程專用平台進行繳交,並系統會派發讓同學們進行互評
作業繳交的分數,有交即有分;互評的部分則以同學之間的評分為準
(但因為同學通常不會給到滿分,因此總分有 110 計算)

title: 機器人與AI互動專題:理論與研究 Seminar on Human-Robot Interaction and Human-AI Interaction: Theories and Research
description:
請注意:此門課程將以英語授課,所有的課間報告與討論也將以英文進行。Note: This course will be taught in English. All the in-class presentations and discussions will also be in English.
This seminar course explores advanced theories and research in Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) and Human-AI Interaction (HAI). Students will examine cutting-edge studies and core concepts in the field, including interaction dynamics, social implications, and the evolving roles of robots and AI agents in human environments. Through in-depth discussions and analyses of academic papers, students will critically evaluate the theoretical and empirical foundations of HRI and HAI while considering their applications in diverse contexts. The course also emphasizes understanding how these technologies influence communication, collaboration, and social structures.
objectives:
By the end of this course, students will:
Understand foundational and emerging theories in HRI and HAI.
Develop a comprehensive knowledge of key frameworks and concepts in the field.
Critically analyze academic literature.
Engage with research papers to evaluate methodologies, findings, and implications.
Examine social and ethical impacts of HRI/HAI technologies.
Discuss how robots and AI agents shape societal norms and values.
Apply theoretical insights to real-world scenarios.
Consider how research findings can inform future design and applications.
Communicate academic ideas effectively.
Lead and contribute to seminar discussions with clear and critical perspectives.
grading:
The total score of 100 points will be the accumulation of these activities:
Leading a class (20%): Each student will lead one class over the course of the semester. (Students may form a team to co-lead. I will decide the size of the teams in the first week.) The class lead(s) will be responsible for the assigned readings and, if preferred, selecting 1-2 additional articles for students to read that apply concepts from that week’s readings to current work in Human-AI Interaction (HAII), Human-Robot Interaction (HRI), Computer-mediated communication (CMC), human-computer interaction (HCI), or a related area. Readings must be assigned to the rest of the class a week in advance. During the class session, the student(s) will be the class lead(s) to lead the discussion. The class lead(s) are encouraged to include multiple activities and up-to-date examples (such as short videos, memes, recent popular SNS posts, other student’s online discussion) to facilitate the discussion.
Online Discussion (15%): Each week (except for Week 1, team project presentation, team project data collection, and final poster sessions), students are expected to post comments on the topic in the online forum set up for that week.
Each post should include (a) a short description of one surprising or interesting point from the readings assigned for that week, something you did not know before or had not thought deeply about; and (b) some implications of this interesting point for your own research or experience. Posts should be about 150-300 words and must be completed by 6 PM one day before the class to receive credit.
Students should also comment on two other student's posts by 10 PM one day before the class to receive full credit.
Each student is allowed to miss two weeks without any need for explanation, but no late submission will be accepted. If a student misses more than two assignments, no excuses will be accepted for subsequent missed assignments.
Team Research Projects (55%): Students will work in teams to conduct a research project on an HRI or HAII topic. This project can be design-oriented, theoretical analysis, or related to human’s behavior related to intelligent agents.
Students are expected to work on:
Idea Pitch (5%): Students will prepare 2-3 research topics, why they find these topics interesting and important, supported by key previous studies (2-4 for each topic). Every research topic should be less than 1 page, double spaced, excluding tables and figures.
Midterm Research Proposal Presentation (15%): Students will present (1) one chosen research topic, (2) a refined introduction of research motivation supported by a brief literature review (with clear definitions of the main concepts, and at least 4 relevant studies), and (3) proposed research methods. The presentation should be between 8-12 minutes, followed by 5 minutes of Q&A.
Final Poster Session (15%): Each research project team will present its research and results to the class via a short oral presentation and a poster. Students also need to prepare a 1-2 minute of short video and upload it onto YouTube to attract attention to their research. Further details will be provided later in the semester.
Final Report (20%): Students will write a report of the project using standard report-writing style (e.g., introduction, related work (literature review), hypotheses, method, results, discussion). The research report should be 10-15 pages, double spaced, excluding tables and figures.
Class participation (10%):
Active participation is essential for this course. Students are expected to come to each class prepared, having read and taken notes on the assigned materials. You may be called on to summarize the main arguments, strengths, weaknesses, or critiques of any assigned reading.
To receive full participation credit, each student must contribute verbally at least twice per class session. Simply attending class without speaking will result in zero points for participation that day.
Each student may miss up to two classes without explanation. However, no additional absences will be excused, regardless of the reason. In addition, students must not miss the class sessions during which they are responsible for leading discussions, presenting team projects, collecting data, or participating in the final poster session.
Bonus (2%): Participating in any user studies related to communication, design, psychology, and human-computer interaction at NCCU will lead to +0.5 of the final semester points. Students can participate in up to 4 studies. (If a study takes more than 30 minutes, it counts as 2 studies.)

title: 近代物理學 Modern Physics
description:
「近代物理學」課程旨在介紹20世紀以來物理學的重大突破,包括相對論和量子力學。本課程為「電子物理學士學位學程」必修課程之一,開放給全校非學程同學選修,也開放給校外人士隨班附讀。選修本課程的學生應具備微積分及普通物理的知識。
相對論:高速的世界與彎曲的時空
當物體接近光速時,時間會變慢,長度會縮短,呈現出奇幻的時空現象。一對雙胞胎在地球上原本同齡,其中一人搭乘太空船進行高速旅行,返航時發現自己依然年輕,而留在地球上的兄弟姊妹卻已經白髮蒼蒼。原因在於,假設當太空船以 0.8 倍光速飛行時,太空船上經過的三十年,地球上可能已經過了五十年。
另一方面,重力主導著日月星辰的運行,但我們將理解,重力並非傳統意義上的力,而是時空幾何的表現。質量告訴時空如何彎曲,時空告訴質量如何運動。
量子力學:顛覆直覺的微觀世界
在原子與基本粒子的尺度中,世界與日常經驗截然不同,量子事件以機率的方式被描述,並呈現出疊加與不確定性等特性。我們驚訝地發現,量子世界不再像古典物理那樣,只要知道系統的初始條件,就能根據物理定律精確預測未來。
粒子的能量是量子化的,對應不同的量子態。許多量子現象更是超乎我們的直覺:量子穿隧讓粒子有機會穿越古典物理中無法跨越的障礙;量子糾纏讓兩個粒子彷彿具有心電感應一般;量子疊加則是量子計算的核心。
我們將理解,量子力學居然與太陽的核融合、元素週期表與化學反應息息相關;而從半導體、雷射、核磁共振、電子顯微鏡到量子電腦,量子力學不僅改變了人類理解自然的方式,也深刻影響著現代科技。
objectives:
1.理解近代物理與古典物理的不同
2.訓練獨立思考的能力,提升自身科學素養,亦可作為之後專業課程的基礎。
3.學習近代物理學在多學科領域及科技發展中的應用。

title: 電磁學(一) Electromagnetism(I)
description:
Electromagnetism is one of the four fundamental interactions in nature. It is of great importance to learn the subject for understanding many natural phenomena.The goal of the course is to give an introduction and fundamental understanding of static electromagnetic fields and electromagnetic wave. Moreore, the course will equip students with the mathematical tools and fundamental laws in electromagnetism for more advanced subjects, such as electrodynamics and antenna theory. To build up the mathematical skills and exercise the electromagnetic knowledge, in-class exercises, quizzes and bi-weekly homework will be assigned to students.
電磁學是四大力學之一,為了解自然現象的重要一環。本課程將介紹靜電學、靜磁學以及電磁波,目標是幫助學生建立數學工具並瞭解電磁學基本定律,未來可以再學習更高階的課程,如電動力學、天線理論。為幫助學生更熟悉,課程會以線上教學影片以及實體課堂練習並行,學期中會安排小考。
objectives:
In the end of the course, the students will be able to explain the basic laws in electromagnetics, master vector analysis, solve static electromagnetic problems in vacuum and in matter, solve for the time-varying fields. These knowledge and techniques can be applied in more advanced studies and applications.
學生能夠解釋電磁學的基本定律、熟悉向量分析、解真空及物質中的電磁學問題,並奠基電磁學在工程應用的基礎。

title: 電子學(一) Electronics(I)
description:
講授電子學基礎知識,介紹電子元件的運作原理,涵蓋半導體、二極體、金氧半場效電晶體,雙極接面電晶體,並介紹分析各種基本放大器電路的方法。
本課程採線上與實體並行模式,每周課程進度為一次線上講授以及實體習題講解,線上課程網站為google classroom,修課同學請用政治大學 g suite帳號 "學號"@g.nccu.edu.tw加入,google classroom課程網站,115電子學一 (代碼: edtwf7v6),連結 https://classroom.google.com/c/Nzk4MTM1Njc3MTMy?cjc=edtwf7v6
This course introduces fundamental knowledge of electronics including semiconductor, diode, metal oxide semiconductor field effect transistor and bipolar junction transistor. The lecture also introduces the concepts of circuit analysis for different types of amplifiers.
This class will be given in hybrid online and in class mode. Students are required to take online lecture and attend in class exercise weekly. Online class will be conducted using google classroom under NCCU g suite package. Students can join the google classroom using NCCU g suite account, which is in the form of “student 〔聯絡資訊已移除〕”. The website will be announced before class.
objectives:
本課程目標在於使學生了解基本的半導體電子元件特性以及電子電路的分析方法,修習本課程將會建立半導體電子元件的基本知識,並能夠將其應用在電子電路的分析上。
The object of the course is to introduce the electronic devices including diode and transistor, and to develop the ability to analyze electronics circuits. The students who take this class will learn basic knowledge of electronic devices and be able to analyze electronics circuit.
grading:
每周習題(40%)、學期評量考試(40%)、每周線上評量(20%)

2. 藉由實驗課建立動 手作實驗的能力及分析數據的能力以培養對物理之興趣。

title: 工程數學(二) Engineering Mathematics (II)
description:
「工程數學(二)」旨在介紹物理中常用的數學觀念。
本系列課程就像一列園區小火車,依序遊覽多元的物理與工程主題,包括力學、電學、磁學、光學、熱力學與流體力學,並延伸至量子力學、相對論、波動與振動、以及訊號處理,說明各主題背後的數學原理及應用。
透過系統性的導引與範例說明,幫助學生建立清晰的物理與工程圖像,並奠定後續專業課程所需的數學基礎。
本課程建議具備微積分基礎,並對物理有興趣的同學選修。「工程數學(一)」於下學期開設,「工程數學(二)」於上學期開設,鼓勵有興趣的同學於大一至大三期間開始修習,以有機會完整修習本系列課程。
objectives:
訓練數理邏輯以及推理計算的能力,亦可作為之後專業課程的基礎。
學習工程數學在物理、多學科領域及科技發展中的應用。

title: 計算思維與人工智慧應用導論 Computational Thinking and Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
description: 本課程旨在介紹計算思維與人工智慧的基本概念、原理和應用,為之後修習資訊相關課程奠下基礎。21世紀數位時代,如何具有應用人工智慧技術能力,培養計算思維是第一步,因為計算思維是分析問題、制定解決方法的思考過程,其中解決的步驟得依循電腦運算邏輯,因此在有了抽象思考能力後,將進一步介紹電腦具體運作架構,兩者的結合將由人工智慧程式應用來加以練習,此外也將介紹人工智慧的發展歷程和未來趨勢,以及人工智慧對社會、經濟和文化的影響。 This course aims to introduce fundamental concepts, principles, and applications of computational thinking and artificial intelligence, establishing a foundation for subsequent information technology-related coursework. In the 21st century digital era, developing computational thinking capabilities represents the essential first step toward effectively applying artificial intelligence technologies. Computational thinking encompasses the analytical processes for problem identification and solution formulation, wherein problem-solving procedures must adhere to computer operational logic. After developing abstract thinking skills, we will explore concrete computer operational architectures in more detail. The integration of these elements will be practiced through artificial intelligence programming applications. Additionally, we will investigate the developmental trajectory and future trends of artificial intelligence, and evaluate its impact on society, the economy, and culture.
objectives:
本課程目標在闡明數位世界中資訊科技的內涵、網路世界的發展與數位世界大數據的挑戰,培養同學資訊專業知能、簡單程式邏輯、跨領域知能、自我反思、公民素養等核心能力。此外,並透過期末的AI與永續專題,提升學生AI知能、永續素養、溝通表達、領導力及團隊合作等水平。
This course aims to clarify the connotations of information technology in the digital world, the development of the internet world, and the challenges of big data in the digital world. It cultivates students' core competencies, including information technology knowledge, basic programming logic, interdisciplinary knowledge, self-reflection, and civic literacy. Furthermore, through final AI and sustainability projects, it enhances students' AI knowledge, sustainability literacy, communication skills, leadership, and teamwork abilities.

title: 人工智慧程式設計 Artificial Intelligence Programming
description:
本課程著重「如何使用 Python 程式語言,以人工神經網路架構,撰寫 AI 相關之應用軟體」,內容相當於坊間的「深度學習」課程。課程目標包含:如何利用人工神經網路,針對影像、以及人類使用的自然語言(如:英文、中文),進行特徵抽取後,找出其中的規律與趨勢,並加以運用至手寫辨識、人機對話等場合。
本課程特色為:全程使用「AI 模型」,來輔助您程式碼的撰寫。每一個單元會先講解一種神經網路模型背後的原理,讓您了解模型背後運作的流程。接著您就可以把流程,轉化為用白話文撰寫而成的「提詞」,要求 AI 產生您想要的神經網路程式碼。
課程中,會使用 Python 來撰寫程式。因此選修此課程的同學,必須對 Python 語言有一定的認識。包含分支、迴圈等基礎語法,Tuple, List, Dict 等資料結構,以及函數的設計與撰寫等。若對物件導向程式設計的製作熟悉者更佳。
由於神經網路非常倚賴「機率與統計」這門學問。所以課程講解過程中,難免會談論到「平均值、標準差、常態分佈」等名詞。雖講師會在授課過程中,提供簡單的說明,唯同學們仍須對統計學的一些基本名詞有所認識,以取得更好的學習成效。
完成課程後,您將熟悉下列神經網路模型:
(1) 基本人工神經網路(ANN, Artificial Neural Networks):此乃一切神經網路的基礎模型。包含如何使用 Keras 套件,執行迴歸、分類等任務。
(2) 卷積神經網路(CNN, Convolutional Neural Networks),可以從影像自動抽取特徵,讓神經網路學會辨識照片裡的物體。
(3) 循環神經網路(RNN, Recurrent Neural Networks),能從人類日常使用的「自然語言」中,理解人類想要表達的意圖。其間會以 RNN,來辨識一則留言到底是「正評」還是「負評」,做為本小節的範例。
(4) 生成式神經網路(GNN, Generative Neural Network),包含如何用神經網路,生成各式圖片、文字之技術。包含「變分自動編碼器(Variational Autoencoder)」、「生成對抗網路(Generative Adversarial Networks, GAN)」、「擴散式模型(Diffusion Models)」等。
期待您學完本課程後,能對如何使用神經網路解決問題,有更深一層的認識。
附註:
由於歷年來修課人數眾多,為了維持修課的公平性,本課程恕無法受理同學透過私訊向老師提出的個別加簽請求。依學程主任的指示,若修課人數超出上限,將依「愛政大」系統內所顯示的遞補順序,於第二階段加退選期間,依序進行加簽。若因此造成不便,還請同學多多包涵,感謝您的理解與配合!
objectives:
能了解如何使用 Python,對資料進行「載入、切分、清理、補遺...」等前處理。以便讓資料能夠用於人工神經網路的模型訓練之用。
可以了解人工神經網路的運作原理。包含如何建構一個神經網路、神經網路如何學習與訓練...等主題。
能撰寫一個人工神經網路,做到依據現有資料集,猜測未來趨勢的程式(亦即以人工神經網路,解決「迴歸」問題)。
能訓練出一個人工神經網路模型,依照使用者的輸入值分類(如:輸入蘑菇外觀、氣味,判別它是否可以食用)。
能夠架構出「卷積神經網路(Convolutional Neural Networks,CNN)」,辨識一張照片的內容為何。
能夠架構出「循環神經網路(Recurrent neural network,RNN)」,依照過往行為,猜測下一步的行動之程式(如:明日股票漲跌、看懂留言情緒...等)。
利用「生成對抗網路(Generative Adversarial Network,GAN)」,讓電腦產生出各種圖形(如:手寫數字...等)。
利用現有的 AI 模型(如:ChatGPT),撰寫出夠聰明的應用程式。
grading:
60%:作業與課堂實作
30%:期末評量
10%:課程出席與參與度

title: 人工智慧實務專題 Special Topics in Artificial Intelligence Applications
description:
本課程課堂中討論人工智慧相關議題與研讀相關研究,結合學生跨領域背景,學習提出以人為本的人工智慧應用,並結合機器學習相關技能,完成 AI 專題。
* 先修課程:AI 技術相關課程,如機器學習觀念與技術、人工智慧方法與工具、人工智慧程式設計、機器學習概論、資料科學、資料採掘、深度學習等課程。
* 先備技術:AI 技術相關工具, 如 RapidMiner、Python/R - ML/DL 相關套件等。
本課程小組專題討論時間為每週二34C或另約討論時間(中午時段也可以),請於 8/31 前完成表單填寫 https://forms.gle/3XYamrfebLpNuKvRA(使用政大Gmail帳號),專題討論地點將寄信通知,如果同學的專題團隊尚未確定,請於 9/8 (二) 第一堂課12:10到課,以利分組, 第一堂課未到課且未完成分組者請自行退選,未退選該科成績以零分計算。
* 已確定團隊成員的同學請事先討論團隊共同時段再填寫表單,謝謝。:)
objectives: 認識以人為本的人工智慧應用,了解人工智慧相關研究進展,學習人工智慧實務應用開發與測試,完成期末專題。
grading:
課程參與 60%、專題成果 40% (包含期末報告與展示35%、同儕評量 5%)。
本課程可認列 AI 學程與 AI 微學程學分。

title: 社群媒體探勘 Social Media Mining
description: 社群媒體探勘是一門專注於從社群媒體平台上提取有價值的資訊與知識的學科。本課程將介紹社群媒體的基本概念、數據探勘技術以及網路分析等方法,並探討如何應用這些技術來分析和理解社群媒體數據。學生將學習到如何從社群媒體中收集數據、進行數據預處理、應用探勘技術並解釋結果,以幫助解決實際問題。本課程將包括YouTube、Twitter、Facebook、Instagram等平台的數據探勘實作與專題,適合對數據科學、社群媒體和網路分析有興趣的同學。
objectives: 這門課程將通過討論、實作、分組專案來幫助學生全面掌握社群媒體探勘的理論與實踐技能。包括對社群平台的探勘實作與專題,讓學生能夠運用所學知識解決實際問題。

title: 金融科技的網路安全:理論與應用 Cyber Security in FinTech: Theory and Application
description:
//本課程可讓學生加簽
1.金融科技的網路安全
(1)金融資安行動方案
(2)金融科技安全

(1)資安解壓縮Podcast
(2)國際資安證照:Security+、CEH、CHFI
(3)資安實習與攻防搶旗賽
3.資訊安全管理與實務應用
(1)CYBERSEC 臺灣資安大會:勒索軟體、供應鏈資安、雲端安全、零信任資安、工控安全、金融資安、資安治理、人工智慧資安、Blue Team、Red Team、上市櫃資安標竿論壇。
(2)資安治理與管理

objectives:
一、課程目標
1.培養資訊安全相關的基本核心能力
強化資訊安全領域專業知識,期許學生能瞭解資訊安全國際發展與應用趨勢,解資訊安全倫理與法律,以具備策劃及執行專題研究能力、並兼備跨領域創新與溝通能力。
2.個案探討與分析
經由實務個案,經驗法則與論理法則後的易位思考,探討理論與應用的實務差距與磨合可能性,開拓未來職場發展。
(1)「好」學生可能承受不了職場現實的失敗與壓力。
(2)會「讀書」,能應付考試;會「做人」,能應付職場。
(3)感謝「敵人」,並將敵人視為「朋友」,無形中增加「貴人」相助的潛在機會。
4.推薦實習或就業:適時提供實習或就業推薦機會與諮詢建議。
5.準備就業:為鼓勵同學自動自發學習課業、規劃未來職(志)業並正向積極準備就業,提升準備
金融科技或網路安全等相關就業機會的能力。
二、學習成效
1.具備規劃學習地圖與生涯發展路徑的能力
2.具備有效運用大學各項學習資源
3.具備深度閱讀的能力
4.具備探索、熟悉新型態的數位學習模式
5.養成自主與終身學習的態度與策略
6.具備團隊合作與專題製作能力
三、未來職場KSA + Attitude
1.Knowledge: Teamwork Enhances Personal Growth.
(1)一個人走很快、一群人走更遠
(2)好一時不是真的成功,好一世才是終極成功。
(3)產業共利及讓利平台:共利及讓利是牽(千)手合作之本。
甲方角度:產業資安聯防(情資分享)
乙方角度:資安產業聯盟(人員、程序、技術、治理)
2.Skill: Keep Learning All the Time.
(1)資安類別:沒有人是局外人,區分政策、管理、技術型資安人
(2)Chances are always ready for those who are prepared.
(3)Be ready for the next jump.
3.Ability: Stay Hungry. Stay Foolish.
(1)跳脫舒適圈:跳脫框架,產生改變。
(2)從反思經驗中學習:火車開了,不要停在月台上。
(3)培養個人競爭力:無可取代的優勢,輔以偷不走技能。
(4)培養後進:授人以魚,不如授人以漁
4.Attitude: Develop a Positive Mindset and Attitude.
Positive thinking is a mental and emotional attitude that focuses on the bright side of life and expects positive results.
(1)量入為出:花錢一時爽,還債火葬場
(2)正向循環:沒事互通有無,有事相互扶持。受之小惠,回以大德。
(3)工作亮點:從未來的簡報開始;管住嘴,邁開腿。
(4)積極心態:所願所不願,不如心甘情願;所得所不得,不如心安理得。
(5)禍從口出:讚美的話,需要字字反思;批判的話,不需句句反駁。

title: 現代密碼學 Contemporary Cryptography
description:
1.理解資訊安全的重要性
2.對密碼理論及演算法有初步的理解
3.學習現代密碼學的主流技術
objectives: 密碼學技術為區塊鏈的關鍵核心技術之一。比特幣利用雜湊函數(hash function)演算法來進行工作量證明。而ECDSA橢圓曲線數位簽章標準則用來確保交易的安全性與不可否認性。除此之外,密碼學亦是現代電子商務、網路安全等必備之工具。本課程將介紹密碼學的基本理論及其實務。基本理論將介紹公開金鑰密碼技術、數位簽章及電子認證的技術、秘密分享機制、橢圓曲線密碼、多方安全計算、零知識證明等密碼協定的設計與安全性分析。

title: 資訊理論 Information Theory
description: 本課程介紹資訊理論與資料壓縮的基本概念,涵蓋資訊量、熵、編碼理論,以及無失真與有失真壓縮技術。課程內容包含 Huffman Coding、Arithmetic Coding、LZ-Coding、Predictive Coding、Transform Coding、Wavelet Coding,以及視訊壓縮等主題,並探討資訊理論在多媒體資料壓縮中的應用。透過理論講解、數值計算與案例分析,使學生理解各種壓縮技術背後的原理與設計理念,並培養分析與評估資料壓縮方法的能力。
objectives: 本課程旨在介紹資訊理論與資料壓縮的基本概念與核心技術,使學生理解資訊量、熵、編碼效率與通道容量等資訊理論基礎,並進一步學習無失真與有失真壓縮技術之原理與應用。課程內容涵蓋多種編碼技巧以及視訊壓縮等主題,培養學生對多媒體資料壓縮方法的理解與分析能力。修習本課程後,學生應能計算資訊熵、平均碼長與編碼效率等相關指標,理解各類資料壓縮技術的設計原理與特性,分析不同壓縮方法在壓縮率、計算成本與資料品質之間的取捨,並能以資訊理論觀點探討多媒體資料壓縮技術於實際應用中的設計、限制與安全性相關議題。

title: 工業物聯網與營運技術安全 IIoT and OT Security
description:
本課程首先介紹工業物聯網及相關技術、發展趨勢,協助學生了解相關應用。接下來介紹工業物聯網之架構及元件,從感知、收集、傳輸、至處理,及相關協定與對應資安議題,讓學生具備工業物聯網全觀認知。課程接續介紹OT營運技術之資安架構、標準、並透過案例說明OT資安防護應用。課程另擬規劃國內工業物聯網相關企業參訪、以及業師共同授課,增進課程產學聯結並促進學生就業觀。
This course first introduces the IIoT (Industrial Internet of Things), the related technologies, and development trends, to help students understand related applications. Next, the architectures and components of the IIoT are introduced, from sensing, collection, transmission, to processing, as well as related protocols and corresponding cybersecurity issues, so that students can have a comprehensive understanding of the IIoT. Then the course introduces the cybersecurity architectures and the international standards of OT (Operation Technology), and illustrates the application of OT security protection through cases. The course also plans to visit IIoT-related enterprise, and include co-lecturing by industry experts, to enhance the connection between industry and academia and promote students’ prospects.
objectives:
1. 具備了解與分析工業物聯網系統概念。
2. 具備跨域整合、解析工業物聯網領域資安議題能力。
3. 具備發掘問題、分析歸納、與解決問題能力。
4. 洞悉工業物聯網資安發展趨勢及並瞭解國際標準。
1. Understand and analyze the concepts of IIoT systems.
2. The ability to integrate across domains and analyze information security issues in the field of IIoT.
3. The ability to explore problems, analyze, summarize, and solve problems.
4. Understand the development trends of IIoT cybersecurity and international standards.

description: 本課程以現場鑑識分析為主軸,帶領學員瞭解案件現場作業項目及要點、實做蒐集揮發及非揮發性資料,並演練現場鑑識流程,充實學員可用於就業或面試之實戰技能。

title: 可信任人工智慧 Trustworthy AI
description:
可信任人工智慧的議題範圍相當廣泛。本課程主要聚焦於人工智慧中的模型安全與資料隱私;至於公平性、可解釋性、透明性以及分布偏移等主題,僅在必要時作概括性介紹。
本課程之先修要求為深度學習。課程內容並非以教授深度學習為目標,雖然在涉及相關專有名詞時會進行簡要回顧,但仍建議學生在修課前已具備基礎概念,例如 contrastive learning、transformer 與 meta-learning 等。
Trustworthy AI covers a broad range of topics. This course focuses primarily on model security and data privacy in artificial intelligence. Other topics—including fairness, interpretability, transparency, and distribution shift—will be mentioned only when necessary.
The prerequisite for this course is deep learning. The course is not designed to teach deep learning itself; although key concepts will be briefly reviewed when mentioned, students are expected to have a basic understanding of terms such as contrastive learning, transformers, and meta-learning prior to attending the course.
objectives:
本課程旨在培養學生理解人工智慧中的模型安全與資料隱 私之核心概念,並能分析 AI 系統在不同階段的潛在風險與其與效能之權衡。學生將學習基本的隱私保護與安全技術,並具備閱讀相關研究與應用於實務場景的能力;其他如公平性、可解釋性與分布偏移等議題,則作為輔助性理解。
This course aims to develop students’ understanding of model security and data privacy in AI, and their ability to analyze risks across system stages and trade-offs between privacy and utility. Students will learn fundamental protection techniques and gain the ability to read research and apply these concepts in practice. Topics such as fairness, interpretability, and distribution shift are covered as supplementary material.

作業(60%)、期末專題報告(40%)。
Assignments (60%), Final Project Presentation (40%)

title: 國際關係理論 International Relations Theory
description:
国際関係理論と称する講義、著作は、米国だけでなく台湾、日本でも相当数にのぼる。
台湾の学生にとって身近な国際関係は、戦後最も緊密な関係を有した対米関係、あるいは最も身近な隣国である対日関係、そして、冷戦終結後に生まれた世代にとっては両岸関係も国際関係の範疇に属するとみなせるかもしれない。極論すれば、台湾にとって、最も重要な国際関係とは台米関係、両岸関係、台日関係であろう。
本講義は、社会科学的視点から日本研究を学ぶ台湾人学生を念頭において設計しており、具体的には、国際政治史と国際関係理論への知識の習得と応用においている。
はじめに、「国際政治学」、「国際関係理論」をリードしてきた欧米研究者の文献を読み、20世紀以降の国際政治の大きな流れを掌握し、リアリズム、リベラリズム等の代表的な理論や概念を理解し、国際関係の中で起きてきた事象を理解、分析する。
また日本(台湾)においては、「欧米の理論を直輸入し、紹介している」という批判を意識し、国際社会における日本の現状や日本の国際政治に対する問題意識を反映した視点を採りこむために、日本人研究者による文献を読み、日本の視点から国際関係への視角を概観する。
objectives:
講義で使用する文献を読むことによって、以下の成果が上がるよう目標とする。
1.20世紀以降の国際政治の大きな流れを習得する。その際に、その時の台湾、日本はいかなる存在であったのかということを常に意識する。
2.現代国際関係理論におけるパラダイムであるリアリズム、リベラリズム、コンストラクトヴィズムのほか、主要分析レベル(国家、個人、国際システム)の概念を理解する。
3.既存の理論、視角を通じて日本と特定の国家、あるいは日本の行為を分析する。大学院における講義における一般的な目標としては、実証的な日本研究をするための基盤を整えるとともに、明確な問題意識を持ち、仮説を立て、分析するという流れの習得も目指す。
4.課外学習 政府機関などを訪問して実務的現場に触れる。
grading:
1.出欠、関連活動への参加20%(全出席の場合は18点以上、他は表現で+-)
2.講義における報告40%(担当週の報告と評論週の表現)
3.期末報告40%(8000字前後、論文発表会試案を目標 締切12/30(水)夜12時厳守。)
テーマは、本講義で学んだ理論や視点を通じて日本(台湾でも可)をめぐる国際関係から選ぶ。
最低限必要な内容は1先行研究の整理2問題の視角3心得・展望。期末報告など他講義提出の報告からの無断引用は厳禁、発覚時には当該学期の成績は不合格とする。

title: 研究方法 Research Methodology
description:
學期:114(上)
單位:俄羅斯研究所、日本學程,國際事務學院
時間:每週三上午9:10~12:00
教室:綜合院館270810
學分:3
修別:俄羅斯研究所、日本學程,碩一必修
授課教師:薛健吾
電子信箱:〔聯絡資訊已移除〕
(請把老師的email加入聯絡人,避免系統檔信)
教師研究室:綜合院館271301
面談時間:每週三下午2:00~4:00 or by appointment
objectives:
在學術的研究中,常見的研究題目的類型主要有詮釋型、探索型、描述型、解釋型以及評估型這幾種,這一堂課的主要目的是指導同學們該如何對「描述型」(descriptive)、「解釋型」(explanatory)以及「評估型」(evaluative)這三種題目進行「社會科學」的「實證研究」,並且培養同學們學術論文寫作與發表的基本技巧。
本課程主要涵蓋三大部分的內容:第一個部分是關於如何作一個「科學的」研究,包括如何尋找因果關係、如何透過文獻形成研究問題、如何透過文獻建構一個「可以在經驗上被否證的」理論(theory)或是論點(argument),以及如何透過研究設計(research design)來檢證因果關係(也就是你所建構的理論或是論點所聲稱的內容);第二個部分為一些常見的主要研究方法,研究者可根據「是否可以進行實驗」、「案例數目的多寡」以及「分析單位」這三個標準,來選擇其中的一種或多種研究方法在研究中使用,其背後共享的邏輯為「如何在各種不同的情況之下盡可能地逼近『實驗法』的研究設計」,以及「如何讓你的研究設計有辦法被其他的研究者進行複證」;第三個部分則是關於論文寫作與發表的技巧,包括論文的基本格式、引用文獻的格式與方法、論述的過程、一些常犯錯誤的避免,以及如何對自己與別人的研究做出專業的發表和評論。由於我們俄研所和日本學程注重的是對俄國和日本的黨政、經濟、社會與外交等相關問題的研究,因此在研究問題的性質上,「比較研究法」(comparative method)與「個案研究法」(case study method)很可能會是各位同學們所必須採用的主要研究方法(為什麼呢?),因此本課程也將在各週提及這兩個研究方法如何與各週的主題相輔相成。
在課程進行的過程中,同學們將分段完成自己的期末研究論文計劃的各個重要部分,並且將在期末在課堂上舉辦一個模擬學術研討會,由同學們分別擔任主持人、發表人、評論人與聽眾,培養進行學術研究與發表的專業能力。
同學們應可在課程中發現,社會科學的實證研究基本上就是一連串你如何去justify「你如何發現問題」與「你如何解決問題」的過程,這個方法論與研究設計的訓練,除了對同學們的研究與寫作有幫助之外,對於我們思考每天的社會現象與日常生活中的切身問題也都會帶來很多的啟發。
grading: 參見SYLLABUS。

title: 日本古典文法1 Grammar of Ancient Japanese Literature I
description:
日本古典文法是一套和現代日文大不相同的文法體系,卻又是現代日文的根源與先驅。現存日文的相關資料中,除了日本古典文學等領域之外,台灣殖民文學、近現代日本文學、台日政治史等相關文獻,甚至是日本媒體廣告、動漫中,也存在著為數不少的古典文法。因此培養解讀日本古文的能力,不僅是有助於學習者理解日語文法體系的歷史脈絡、掌握日語的特色,更是進行日本研究、理解日本文化時的重要先行工作。本課程分上下學期,欲修下學期課程者,請務必修上學期課程。
教材: 教師自製教材
objectives:
(一)本課程之課程目標:
習得日語古典文法之基礎知識
認識著名之日本古文文章。
習得基本知閱讀古文能力。
建立現代與古典一脈相承的語法體系與概念。
奠定處理日治時代文獻資料的能力。
理解日本媒體、動漫等文化產業中的古文表現。
(二)基於上述之課程目標,本課程主要以古文讀解、活用語之文法為主,由淺入深進行教學以及實作練習。內容可分以下五部份:
古文讀音之介紹與練習
形容詞活用
形容動詞活用
動詞活用
(三)透過前述之課程目標和課程內容,本課程預計能為學習者帶來以下的學習成就:
能夠解讀日本古文,理解日語文法體系的歷史脈絡、掌握古典日語的特色。
了解現代日語和古文之異同點。
處理日本古典文獻。
處理古文與現代日文混用的文獻。
處理圖書館、出版社以及台灣總督府所留存之日治時代文獻。
處理日本媒體、動漫等文化產業中的古文表現。
grading:
每單元預計進行約四週,上課時會先進行文法結構之系統教學,進而搭
配文章做練習。
每單元會先複習現代日語之文法結構,再循序近入古典文法,借此理解現代日語和古文一脈相承之系統。
兩次筆試。

title: 日美安保條約的歷史與現狀 History and Current Status of the U.S.–Japan Security Treaty
description:

title: 日本軍事力量發展與戰力建構 Development of Japan's Military Power and Capacity Buildind
description:
本課程旨在從國際安全、國防政策與軍事戰略的整合視角,分析日本軍事力量的歷史演變、制度轉型與戰力建構。
課程首先說明戰後和平憲法、專守防衛原則及日美安全體制,探討日本自衛隊如何在法律限制、國內政治與區域安全環境交互下逐步發展;並分析日本《國家安全保障戰略》、《國家防衛戰略》及《防衛力整備計畫》等國安三文件,掌握日本由本土防衛轉向跨域整合、機動部署、反擊能力與聯盟協同的戰略變化。
在戰力建構方面,課程將檢視陸上、海上及航空自衛隊的兵力結構、指揮體系、主要裝備與作戰任務,並討論飛彈防禦、遠程精準打擊、反潛作戰、兩棲機動、太空、網路、電磁頻譜及無人系統等新興能力。同時分析日本國防科技、軍工產業、武器出口、供應鏈安全及國際共同研發對防衛自主的影響。
此外,本課程將日本軍事發展置於美中戰略競爭、朝鮮半島、俄羅斯遠東活動及台海安全脈絡中,評估日美同盟及多邊安全合作對日本戰略角色的塑造。透過政策文件研讀、案例分析與情境推演,培養學生分析軍事力量建構、國防資源配置及印太安全變化的能力。
objectives: 課程目標與學習成效:一則是,講解日本軍事力量發展與戰後和平憲法、專守防衛原則及日美安全體制之關聯,掌握日本自衛隊在法律、政治與安全環境限制下的發展脈絡。二則是,介紹日本《國家安全保障戰略》、《國家防衛戰略》與《防衛力整備計畫》等政策文件,理解日本由本土防衛轉向跨域整合、機動部署、反擊能力及聯盟協同的戰略轉型。三則是,分析陸上、海上及航空自衛隊的兵力結構、指揮體系、主要裝備與作戰任務,並探討飛彈防禦、遠程打擊、反潛作戰、兩棲機動、太空、網路、電磁頻譜及無人系統等新興戰力。四則是,探討日本國防科技、軍工產業、武器出口、供應鏈安全與國際共同研發對防衛自主的影響。五則是,引導學生從美中競爭、朝鮮半島、俄羅斯遠東及台海安全等脈絡,評估日本軍力發展對印太秩序的影響。六則是,透過政策研讀、案例分析、分組報告與情境推演,培養學生蒐集資料、戰略分析、團隊合作及口頭簡報能力,並進一步思考台灣國防建設與安全政策的借鑑方向。

title: 日美同盟與印太區域安全 Japan US Alliance and Indo Pacific Regional Security
description: 本課程主要是利用同盟理論(Alliance of Theory)、權力平衡(Balance of Power)、以及威脅平衡(Balance of Threat)等現實主義的觀點,講授以下三大主題,包括冷戰期間推動日美同盟演進的內外因素,日美兩國推動與中共關係正常化的聯中制蘇國際大環境,後冷戰時期中共崛起衍生印太區域的權力結構變化,以及日美同盟因應此一變化與威脅之強化合作措施。由本課程授課內容,可以呈現出日本在美中戰略競爭或長期博弈過程中,扮演著美國不可或缺的同盟夥伴,而日本則基於無力單獨抗衡崛起的中共挑戰或威脅之戰略思考,必須確保日美同盟對中共之嚇阻力,為此積極拉攏美國持續留駐印太地區。
objectives:
本課程目的在於讓學生習得同盟理論(Alliance of Theory)、權力平衡(Balance of Power)、以及威脅平衡(Balance of Threat)等現實主義的觀點,作為探討冷戰期間推動日美同盟演進的內外因素,後冷戰時期中共崛起衍生印太區域的權力結構變化,以及日美同盟合作因應此一變化與威脅的概念性分析架構。
由本課程授課內容,可以呈現出日本在美中戰略競爭或長期博弈過程中,扮演著美國不可或缺的同盟夥伴,而日本則基於無力單獨抗衡崛起的中共挑戰或威脅之戰略思考,必須確保日美同盟對中共之嚇阻力,為此積極拉攏美國持續留駐印太地區。學生將可透過本課程的學習,正確認識日美安保體制或同盟合作在確保包括台海在內的印太區域安全的表色扮演及其重要性。

title: 當代日本外交專題研究 Research on Modern Japanese Foreign Policy
description:
一、講義の説明(課程簡介)
台湾にとって日本は、1972年の断交後も緊密な人文、経済関係を積み上げてきただけでなく、昨今では政治外交の関係も重要性を増しており、現代日本が直面する外交問題を理解することは、必要不可欠な問題である
本講義では、日本外交の概説となるように戦後日本外交の流れを理解した後、現在直面するホットなイシューである日本の安保、近隣諸国との平和と安全、国際社会の平和と安全、国際協力、国際経済文化のイシューにつき検討する。
objectives:
二、講義目標と学習成果(課程目標與學習成效)
日本外交を学ぶ教材や講義は数多く存在しているが、本講義では、限られた時間の中で基本的な内容を習得するため、歴史:戦後外交の流れ、現代日本が直面する幅広いシュー、日本外交議題としてはあまり触れらない、兵器輸出管理、国際犯罪、難民のほか、世界遺産や捕鯨問題などにまで広げて言及し、日本国内の立場や相反する見方の存在を確認する。
大学院の講義であることに鑑み、安倍→菅→岸田政権で現在進行中の対外政策の変化については、最新情勢を講義において随時取り上げる。

title: 日本近代政治外交史專題研究3 Seminar in Modern Japanese History of Political and Diplomatic 3
description:
(一)日本政治方面以日本近代政治家(大久保利通、木戶孝允、伊藤博文、陸奧宗光、井上馨、山県有朋、大隈重信、小村寿太郎、加藤高明、寺内正毅、高橋是清、井上準之助、原敬、新渡戶稻造、幣原喜重郎、児玉源太郎、後藤新平、渋沢栄一)等人為中心,探討近代中日關係史上重大的政治外交、歷史重要事件等相關課題,同時講授近代日本與東亞的關係。
(二)日本外交方面則以條約改正及日清、日俄戰爭為主軸,共同討論相關議題。
(三)與同學共同解讀近代日本政治外交重要大事紀及近代日中關係史研究入門(日清戰爭、日俄戰爭、二十一條條款、第一次世界大戰、第二次世界大戰)。
(四)課堂中配合課程內容,觀看日本NHK有關中日近代政治外交史相關教學影片(例如:條約改正、日本最長的一日、我的1919),觀看後與同學共同討論相關議題及交換心得,並要求同學針對重要人物與事件進行報告。
objectives:
一、研讀基本資料,並透過共同討論方式,培養學生收集、解讀分析基本資料的能力。
二、推薦評價良好的專書、工具書鼓勵學生自習,培養學生對近現代日本政治外交史之理解並能累積相關專業知識。
grading:
1.參與討論及主題發表40%
2.出席率20%
3.期末報告40%

title: 日本與東亞 Japan and East Asia
description:
日本是東亞的一個主要國家,是從歷史脈絡、抑或地緣政治、全球政治角度來看,日本在東亞與亞太地區都是不容忽視的國際政治行為者。本課程規劃從歷史演進過程中強化學生對日本與東亞關係的理解。
本課程規劃從總論、個論、互動學習三個層面切入規劃學習,並分為以下五大部分:歷史脈絡下的日本與東亞、近代史時期的日本與東亞、戰後的日本與東亞、國家研究、學生報告。
objectives: 日本是東亞的主要國家,也是東亞地區面對中國的、歷史上唯一曾經成為東亞核心的國家。歷史相關問題也是日本當前對外關係關係中必須嚴重的問題之一。本課程許學生能從歷史的角度切入理解不同時期日本與東亞的,首先能增強學生在研究日本對外關係政策選擇時的分析能力。

title: 日本外交專題:層次分析途徑 Japanese Foreign Policy: Levels of Analysis Approaches
description: 本課程將分為兩部分,第一部分介紹層次分析途徑,聚焦在國際關係(以下簡稱國關)理論各學派分別如何由國際體系、國內政治、決策者層次來分析國際政治及外交關係。第二部分為專題討論,由學生先發表該專題的背景、事件經過,之後在課堂討論適用的分析層次及理論,是否有其他相似的議題,是否有其他的切入角度?課程前半部將著重閱讀文本及課堂討論,後半部著重在課程發表及雙向討論。本課程將分為兩部分,第一部分介紹層次分析途徑,聚焦在國際關係(以下簡稱國關)理論各學派分別如何由國際體系、國內政治、決策者層次來分析國際政治及外交關係。第二部分為專題討論,由學生先發表該專題的背景、事件經過,之後在課堂討論適用的分析層次及理論,是否有其他相似的議題,是否有其他的切入角度?課程前半部將著重閱讀文本及課堂討論,後半部著重在課程發表及雙向討論。
objectives: 主要針對國際關係理論及其在日本外交研究上的應用。目標有二:在學術訓練上,希望能為本校有志從事日本政治及外交研究的學生,奠定理論研究的基礎。在人才培育上,藉由課堂發表及撰寫報告,培養學生統整知識及獨立思考的能力,為撰寫學術論文作準備。
grading:

第1週 課程簡介
分配課堂研讀資料、課堂發表分組。
第一部分:層次分析的讀物研讀

Hudson, Valerie M. 2020. Foreign Policy Analysis: Classic and Contemporary Theory. 3rd edn. Lanham, MD: Rowman & Littlefield. Ch1.

title: 近代日本的形成與發展 The Formation and Development of Modern Japan
description:
本課程是以「公論」、天皇、立憲政治三者為主軸,來探究從幕末維新期至第二次世界大戰結束為止近代日本的形成與發展,進而思考近代日本天皇制國家的本質,以及國家與社會的統合問題。
在此所謂的「公論」,意指以打破江戶時期世襲身分制為前提的人才登用及政治參與。而「公論」又與天皇制國家的建立與立憲政治的形成密不可分。因此,本課程的重點將放在幕末「公論」慣習的發生、天皇大權的摸索,以及近代「天皇的官僚」、明治憲法體制、家族國家觀、政黨政治的形成與發展上。
同時,鼓勵同學從臺灣之「他者」的角度,重新思考日本近代史、甚至是日治時期的臺灣史或同一時期的東亞史。
以有中級日語閱讀能力及基本日本近代史知識者為佳。
課程進度及課堂口頭發表的方式,會依同學的日語能力適時調整。
objectives:
1.理解近代日本天皇制國家、社會的形成及其構想。
2.理解19世紀以來日本立憲主義的建構過程及其特徵。
3.透過課堂的平時的口頭發表及討論,培養統整論點及分析能力。
4.透過撰寫期末書面報告,訓練論文寫作能力。
※期末書面報告之要求:本學期的主題,自由選擇;需遵循論文寫作格式(問題意識、本論、結論、注釋、出處)。
中日文不拘(中文:至少6000字,日文:至少6500字)。
※旁聽生須得到任課教師的同意,並且必須要預習及參與課堂討論,若未能做到此要求,任課老師會適時拒絕旁聽。

title: 日本經營管理 Management of Japan
description: 歷經高度成長期與泡沫經濟之後,日本企業的組織型態以及日本式的經營管理,即成為企業管理學領域的重要課題。本課程即聚焦於當代日本經營管理的特色與面臨之挑戰,深入探討日本企業的領導、戰略與組織。

一、深化理論基礎:探討傳統「日本企業經營」之核心元素。

title: 日本經濟安全保障 Economic Security of Japanese
description: 戰後的日本雖有《日美安保條約》保障國家安全,但如何倚靠「非軍事力量」來構築有利於日本經貿活動的國際環境,是戰後日本在外交層面上持續摸索的關鍵課題。在此一特殊國際政治經濟狀況下,日本國內逐漸形成以政府的力量,透過經濟的手段來維護國家安全的「經濟安全保障」(economic security)概念,並在不同的階段以不同的政策思維呈現。本課程聚焦於經濟因素對近代日本國防與外交政策的意義,以及經濟安全保障概念對戰後日本國家安全的政策影響。
objectives:
一、釐清日本國家安全政策中的經濟因素,以及日本經濟安全保障概念的理論意涵。
二、綜合分析戰後日本所處之國際環境與國內環境的變遷,探討日本在面臨各種經濟威脅時的對應思維與措施,闡述戰後日本經濟安全保障的政策內涵與意義。

title: 國際關係理論 International Relations Theory
description:
The world is changing faster than our maps of it. Hegemonic competition now spans chips and shipping lanes; wars are redrawing borders in Europe and the Middle East; great-power rivalries stretch across the Indo-Pacific and Asia-Pacific regions; artificial intelligence advances by the month; and the climate system is breaching thresholds once thought to be decades away. We now live in a world of unknowns, where yesterday’s certainties expire before the semester ends. In such a world, no subject is more critical than International Relations: it is the discipline that asks why states fight or cooperate, why international orders rise and unravel, and how power, ideas, and institutions shape the fates of nations—and of all of us who live in them. This course might not offer you predictions. But it will attempt something more durable: to equip you with the theories and analytical tools needed to ask better questions of a world that refuses to stand still.
Against this backdrop, this graduate seminar is intended to provide an advanced introduction to the major theoretical traditions, analytical approaches, contemporary problems, and emerging frontiers in International Relations (IR). As a seminar, the course expects each student to complete the assigned readings before coming to class and to participate actively in course discussions and simulation activities.
Rather than organizing the course exclusively around the traditional “isms,” the course proceeds in four stages. Part I (Long-Standing Foundational Paradigms) examines the foundational theoretical traditions of IR, including realism, liberalism, institutionalism, constructivism, critical approaches, and psychological and behavioral extensions. Part II (New Analytical Perspectives) turns to the analytical toolkits that reoriented the field around domestic politics and strategic interaction, as well as to theorizing from outside the great powers. Part III (Critical Phenomena in Modern International Relations) applies theory to the central empirical problems of contemporary world politics: war and political violence, the global economy, energy, and geopolitical and economic competition. Part IV (New Frontiers: Challenges of the Anthropocene) confronts the planetary and technological transformations—climate change and migration, emerging technologies, and artificial intelligence—that test the limits of inherited IR theory. The course will also feature invited talks, which will be announced later in the semester.
Throughout the course, students will be asked to identify the assumptions, causal mechanisms, scope conditions, and empirical implications of competing theories. The aim is to encourage students to read critically, participate actively, connect theory to evidence, and design original research.
objectives:
Master the core concepts, debates, and theories of contemporary IR.
Identify the principal actors, mechanisms, and international dimensions of each substantive area.
Apply IR theory to analyze current international developments.
Design and write an original, theoretically grounded research paper.
grading:
Weights may be adjusted before the term begins.
SCourse Participation: 35%
SNews Presentation of International Relations : 5%
SDiscussion Leader (once) :10% (Prepare Presentation Slides and upload to the course website 24 hours before the course)
SGeneral Course Participation (do the reading and come to the class with questions or comments): 20%
SMidterm: 20% (Oct. 8)
SReview Article: 10%
SFinal Research Paper:35% (5% for Oral Presentation and 30% for Paper)
weeklyText:
Note: The number of readings of each week might seem challenging, so there is a chance of adjusting the required amount. Send your feedbacks to me from now on and I will consider potential adjustment by week 2.
Week 1(9/10) — Introduction — What Is IR Theory? Science, Paradigms, and Levels of Analysis
Goal: Course logistics, the role of theory in social science, the levels-of-analysis problem, and the politics of paradigms.
1. Kenneth N. Waltz, Man, the State, and War (New York: Columbia University Press, 1959), Introduction and ch. 1.
2. Jack Snyder, “One World, Rival Theories,” Foreign Policy, no. 145 (2009): 52–62.
3. David A. Lake, “Why ‘Isms’ Are Evil: Theory, Epistemology, and Academic Sects as Impediments to Understanding and Progress,” International Studies Quarterly 55, no. 2 (2011): 465–480.
Central Question: What makes an explanation a theory of international relations, and what are the appropriate units and levels through which world politics should be explained?
Week 2 — Realism — Anarchy, Power, the Security Dilemma, and International Order
Classical and structural realism; offensive vs. defensive realism; hegemonic order and power transition; the contemporary polarity debate.
1. John J. Mearsheimer, The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (New York: W. W. Norton, 2001), chs. 1–2.
Recommended to read & conpare/contrast the following reading: Kenneth N. Waltz, Theory of International Politics (Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1979), chs. 5–6.(this is not required)
2. Rosato, Sebastian. 2026. “Competition Under the Security Dilemma.” International Security 50(4): 36–73.
3. Graham Allison, "The Thucydides Trap: Are the U.S. and China Headed for War?," The Atlantic, September 24, 2015; Robert Gilpin, "The Theory of Hegemonic War," Journal of Interdisciplinary History 18, no. 4 (Spring 1988): 591–613; C. Raja Mohan, "The Multipolar Delusion," Foreign Affairs, February 19, 2026.
Central Question: Is great-power competition primarily produced by capabilities, intentions, status, technological change, or the structural uncertainty inherent in anarchy?
Week 3 — Liberalism, International Institutions, and Global Governance
Neoliberal institutionalism and the study of international cooperation, institutional design, global governance, and the rise—and contemporary crisis—of the liberal international order.
1. Keohane, John J. Robert O. After Hegemony: Cooperation and Discord in the World Political Economy (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1984), ch. 4+ ch.6(most critical).
2. Robert O. Keohane. 2001. “Governance in a Partially Globalized World.” American Political Science Review 95(1): 1–13; Barbara Koremenos, Charles Lipson, and Duncan Snidal, “The Rational Design of International Institutions,” International Organization 55, no. 4 (2001): 761–799.)
3. David A. Lake, Lisa L. Martin, and Thomas Risse. 2021. “Challenges to the Liberal Order: Reflections on International Organization.” International Organization 75(2): 225–257; Jeff D. Colgan and Robert O. Keohane. 2017. “The Liberal Order Is Rigged: Fix It Now or Watch It Wither.” Foreign Affairs 96(3): 36–44; Goddard, Stacie E., Ronald R. Krebs, Christian Kreuder-Sonnen, and Berthold Rittberger. 2025. “Liberalism Doomed the Liberal International Order.” Foreign Affairs.
Recommended to read Ikenberry, G. John. 2018. “The End of Liberal International Order?” International Affairs 94(1): 7–23..(this is not required, but this give you a sense about what LIO is about)
Central Question: Can liberal institutions create durable cooperation and international order in a world still defined by anarchy, unequal power, and domestic political conflict?
Week 4 — Constructivism and Beyond: Norms, Identity, Critique, Everyday Politics, and Psychology
The social construction of anarchy, identity, and security, joined with feminist and racial critiques of the discipline and with the political psychology and behavioral revolution in IR. The week also explores how international politics is constituted through everyday practices, affect, and lived experience.
1. Alexander Wendt, “Anarchy Is What States Make of It: The Social Construction of Power Politics,” International Organization 46, no. 2 (1992): 391–425; Nyman, Jonna. 2021. “The Everyday Life of Security: Capturing Space, Practice, and Affect.” International Political Sociology 15(3): 313–337.
2.J. Ann Tickner, “Hans Morgenthau’s Principles of Political Realism: A Feminist Reformulation,” Millennium 17, no. 3 (1988): 429–440; Brown OR. The Underside of Order: Race in the Constitution of International Order. International Organization. 2024;78(1):38-66. doi:10.1017/S0020818324000018
Recommend to read Bulley, D. (2026). Fair play? Hostile environments and everyday immigration ethics. Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1080/1369183X.2026.2675344; (Not required, but it is helpful to make sense of everyday politics)
3. Emilie M. Hafner-Burton, Stephan Haggard, David A. Lake, and David G. Victor, “The Behavioral Revolution and International Relations,” International Organization 71, no. S1 (2017): S1–S31; Wayne, Carly, Mitsuru Mukaigawara, Joshua D. Kertzer, and Marcus Holmes. 2025. “Diplomacy by Committee: Assessing Resolve and Costly Signals in Group Settings.” American Journal of Political Science 69(4): 1218–1234;
Recommended to read Landau-Wells M. Building from the Brain: Advancing the Study of Threat Perception in International Relations. International Organization. 2024;78(4):627-667. doi:10.1017/S0020818324000328((Challenging the field: this is not required, but highly recommended))
Recommended to read Kertzer, Joshua D., Ryan Brutger, and Kai Quek. 2024. “Perspective Taking and the Security Dilemma: Cross-National Experimental Evidence from China and the United States.” World Politics 76(2): 334–378..(this is not required, but highly recommended)
Central Question: Where should IR explanations begin—with social structures and shared meanings, with everyday practices and power relations, or with the cognitive processes of individuals?
Week 5(10/7) — Mid-term Examination
Take-home examination covering Part I (Weeks 1–4). No assigned readings.
PART II — NEW ANALYTICAL PERSPECTIVES
Week 6 — Strategic Choice and Domestic Politics — Open Economy Politics, Bargaining and War, and the Democratic Peace
The strategic-choice reorientation of the field: domestic sources of foreign economic policy (OEP), rationalist explanations for war, and regime type/democratic peace.
1. David A. Lake and Robert Powell, “International Relations: A Strategic-Choice Approach,” in Strategic Choice and International Relations (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1999), 3–38; James D. Fearon, “Rationalist Explanations for War,” International Organization 49, no. 3 (1995): 379–414.
2. Lake, David A. 2009. “Open Economy Politics: A Critical Review.” Review of International Organizations 4(3): 219–244; Frieden, Jeffry A. 1991. “Invested Interests: The Politics of National Economic Policies in a World of Global Finance.” International Organization 45(4): 425–451.
3. Bueno de Mesquita, Bruce, James D. Morrow, Randolph M. Siverson, and Alastair Smith. 1999. “An Institutional Explanation of the Democratic Peace.” American Political Science Review 93(4): 791–807.; Schultz, Kenneth A. 1999. “Do Democratic Institutions Constrain or Inform? Contrasting Two Institutional Perspectives on Democracy and War.” International Organization 53(2): 233–266.
Central Question: How do preferences, strategic interaction, and domestic institutions combine to shape international economic and security outcomes?
Week 7 — IR Theory of Middle Powers and Small States
How small and middle powers acquire a theoretical place in a great-power-centric discipline: agency under power asymmetry, autonomy, hedging, soft balancing, role adaptation, and international order—with particular attention to Global South perspectives on nonalignment and strategic autonomy.
1. Robert O. Keohane, “Lilliputians’ Dilemmas: Small States in International Politics,” International Organization 23, no. 2 (1969): 291–310; Long, Tom. 2017. “Small States, Great Power? title: 研究方法 Research Methods
description:
This course teaches students how to complete a research design and basic research methods, including both qualitative and quantitative methods. We will discuss the process of writing a research proposal and cover issues such as framing your research question, collecting data, and analyzing and interpreting data. In addition to introducing widely-used qualitative and quantitative methods in social sciences and international studies, this course will focus on how to practically answer your research questions using different qualitative or quantitative methods.
This course is divided into two parts. Before the mid-term exam, our focus is on quantitative methodology, and every week we will have a one-hour R section in which you will use statistical software R to finish some tasks and analyze data. After the mid-term exam, we will focus on qualitative methodology and cover a number of methods. From Week 2 onwards, you will be given homework to work on every other week, and are expected to submit your answers to the Moodle by the next class (i.e., 9:10am on Friday). Late submissions will not be accepted. There will be a total of four homework throughout the semester. At the end of the semester, you also need to complete a research proposal no longer than 4,000 words and present it in class. The paper is due on December 18th, 5pm, to the Moodle.
objectives: Upon completing this course, students are expected to (1) understand how to complete a research design and collect data, (2) be familiar with basic qualitative and quantitative methods, (3) acquire the essential ability to analyze data, and (4) finish a research proposal and apply an appropriate method to answer your research question.
grading: Attendance and participation: 10%; Homework: 20%; Midterm exam: 30%; Final research proposal: 40%

title: 全球政治經濟中的東亞發展 East Asian Development in the Global Political Economy
description: This course examines the political economy of East Asia’s remarkable transformation from a relatively poor and war-torn region into one of the central engines of the global economy. It explores how states, markets, and societies have interacted to shape distinctive development trajectories across Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, China, and Southeast Asia, and how these experiences challenge orthodox theories of development and globalization.
objectives:
Beginning with classic debates on the developmental state and regional production hierarchies, the course traces the rise, evolution, and diversification of state-led development models in East Asia. It compares democratic and authoritarian variants of developmentalism, analyzes China’s economic rise and its integration into the global political economy, and assesses how late developers have navigated industrialization, globalization, and institutional change. Attention is given to trade and production networks, financial and currency cooperation, urban transformation, and the role of cities as global economic hubs.
The final part of the course focuses on contemporary challenges, including economic statecraft, geoeconomic competition, technological rivalry, and the growing fusion of economic and security concerns. By the end of the course, students will be able to critically evaluate competing explanations of East Asian development, understand variation across national cases, and assess how East Asia’s political economies are reshaping the global economic order.

title: 俄烏衝突研究 Special Topics on the Russia-Ukraine Conflict
description: The ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict represents a defining moment in 21st-century history, offering the world unprecedented opportunities to advance theoretical understanding, develop innovative methodologies, and contribute to knowledge that will inform policy and practice for decades to come. With such a “critical historical moment”, however, we have learned not only the mass media but also many scholars analysis have continuously failed to access critical information so to give insightful views on the undergoing international unrest and international power conflict normally invisible during peacetime. In face of all kinds of biased war information and propaganda, this war therefore provides a unique laboratory but also a challenging task for understanding how political institutions, identities, and relationships stage warfare under extreme duress. This course aims to revisit selected aspects of researches on the Russia-Ukraine conflict, through class discussion and then to develop an insightful approach for understanding the origins of geopolitical tensions, conflict prevention, humanitarian response, and international security. Hopefully the course participants can contribute to evidence-based policy-making and humanitarian practice, providing further research with broader social impact beyond academic circles.
objectives:
Firstly, students to learn how recent scholarship emphasise the importance of Realist and Liberal theories provide competing explanations for the conflict’s origins and development. Comparative analyses using these frameworks help illuminate different aspects of the war’s causes and conduct.
Secondly, through learning the phenomenological approaches to own valuable knowledge for studying critical thinking in academic institutions during the war; in addition, students are also expected to check on qualitative thematic analysis has been employed to understand coping strategies among key findings.
Thirdly, theoretical frameworks such as constructivist approaches offer insights into identity formation and perception-based motivations in the conflict. This theoretical framework emphasises how Russian and Ukrainian identities have shaped the war’s trajectory.
In addition, students may experience how a proper politico-sociological analysis in understanding the war’s impact on Ukrainian society. Research methodologies include semi-structured interviews with displaced populations, and survey research examining social attitudes during wartime.
In general, developing expertise in Russia-Ukraine conflict studies positions young scholars at the forefront of an emerging and important academic specialisation. As the conflict’s implications continue to unfold over decades, scholars with deep understanding of its insightful dimensions will be increasingly valuable to academic institutions, policy organizations, and international agencies.

title: 抗爭、衝突與戰爭:東南亞的抗爭政治與暴力 Protest, Conflict, and War: Contentious Politics and Violence in Southeast Asia
description:
The course “Protest, Conflict, and War: Contentious Politics and Violence in Southeast Asia” straddles International Studies, Political Science, and Political Sociology, engaging with key debates on contentious politics and political violence through an interdisciplinary lens. It draws on foundational scholars such as Charles Tilly and Sidney Tarrow on contentious politics, Sidney Tarrow on social movements, James C. Scott on state power and resistance, Karl Marx on structural inequality, Henri Tajfel on social identity, René Girard on mimetic desire and scapegoating, Stathis Kalyvas on civil war violence, and Martha Crenshaw on terrorism. In doing so, the course examines how protest, conflict, violence, and war are interconnected processes rather than discrete phenomena.
The course is designed for graduate students in International Studies broadly, where increasing attention to political instability, identity conflict, and violence requires stronger integration between political sociology, comparative politics, and international relations. It speaks directly to the need for analytically rigorous frameworks capable of explaining how collective action escalates across different political contexts, from everyday protest to organized armed conflict.
Within the International Master’s Program in International Studies (IMPIS – NCCU), this course enriches and extends the existing Southeast Asia-focused curriculum by offering a more systematic and theoretically integrated treatment of contentious politics in the region. It complements existing courses such as Hybrid Regimes: Democratic Challenges in Southeast Asia, Civil and Uncivil Societies in Southeast Asia, Ethnicity, Religion, Nationalism: Violence and the Politics of Belonging in the Global World, and Religion and Politics in the Modern World, forming part of a coherent intellectual cluster on political order, identity, and conflict.
The course is structured in two parts. The first half develops theoretical foundations in contentious politics and theories of conflict and violence, applied through illustrative cases from Indonesia, Myanmar, Thailand, and the Philippines. The second half functions as a Southeast Asia laboratory, in which these frameworks are tested and refined through deeper comparative engagement with these four cases, alongside selected references to Cambodia and Timor-Leste where relevant to post-conflict trajectories and state formation dynamics.
objectives:
This course is grounded in interdisciplinary literatures from political sociology, comparative politics, and international relations, and is designed to equip students with conceptual, theoretical, and empirical tools for analyzing contentious political phenomena. It brings together scholarship on contentious politics (Tilly, Tarrow), structural inequality (Marx, Scott), identity formation (Tajfel, Horowitz), psychological and cultural theories of conflict escalation (Girard, Atran), political violence (Kalyvas, Brass), and terrorism studies (Crenshaw, Hoffman), with sustained empirical engagement in Southeast Asia.
At the end of the course, students will be able to critically analyze the dynamics of protest, conflict, violence, and war using multiple theoretical frameworks; compare escalation trajectories across Southeast Asian cases; evaluate the strengths and limitations of competing explanations of political violence; and apply interdisciplinary concepts to contemporary empirical developments in the region. Students will also develop the ability to synthesize theoretical and empirical materials into coherent analytical arguments appropriate for graduate-level research in International Studies.

title: 貨幣、金融與國家安全的國際政治經濟分析 International Political Economy of Money, Finance, and National Securi ty
description:
This seminar examines the political processes through which the contemporary international monetary and financial system is constructed and operated, and how national security relationships are intertwined with the international and monetary relationships. It introduces the theoretical frameworks and the empirical literature that allow students to analyze the major issues of international monetary, financial and security politics, and it supports students in developing an original research project of their own.
Few would deny that the integration of international monetary and financial markets is among the most consequential features of globalization. Susan Strange saw early that international relations and foreign policy would be increasingly constrained by monetary and financial affairs. Today firms and individuals can invest in, or withdraw from, distant economies almost instantaneously. High capital mobility has reshaped national economic policy and social order, and has unsettled the territorially bounded relationship between state, market and society. The systemic risks generated by financial globalization — the crisis of 2007–08 above all — have shaken established paradigms of national and global governance, and the anti-globalization backlash, protectionism, and trade and currency conflict that followed have become principal drivers of power transition and order change.
The seminar is organized in five parts. Part I introduces the core analytical problem — the ‘unholy trinity’ of exchange rate stability, capital mobility and national policy autonomy — together with the classical IPE paradigms, Open Economy Politics, constructivist and Everyday IPE, and the “securitization of geoecnomic/geopolitical economy” turn of the past few years. It then traces the historical construction of the modern order: the gold standard, the Great Depression and the Second World War; the rise and collapse of Bretton Woods; and the globalization of financial risk.
Part II turns to international monetary relations: the politics of exchange rate policy, the operation and limits of central banks, monetary regionalism, and international monetary power and currency statecraft. Part III addresses the international financial system: capital account liberalization and re-regulation, financial and sovereign debt crises and their governance, private authority and inequality in financial markets, and the challenge of digital money.
Part IV is new to this iteration of the seminar and takes up two developments that have moved to the centre of the field since the syllabus was last taught. The first is artificial intelligence: compute, semiconductors and data centres have become chokepoints in the global economy, AI is reshaping asset management and financial governance, and states are responding by building techno-blocs. The second is resilience and economic security: investment screening, export controls and supply-chain de-risking are now instruments of monetary and financial statecraft, and ‘resilience’ has become a governing category with its own distributive politics.
Part V concludes with the security implications of money and finance. As Cicero observed, the sinews of war are infinite money. International monetary relations and financial systems have always been bound up with military power, and this connection is now among the most active research frontiers in the field. We examine war finance, rearmament, and the relationship between financial capacity and power transition.
There are no prerequisites. Students who have not previously taken a seminar in international political economy can keep pace by completing the weekly readings, participating in discussion, and fulfilling the written requirements. Questions and requests for supplementary material are welcome in class, during office hours, or by email.
** NoteThis course is a highly intensive, research-focused seminar. The goal of this course is to help each registered student complete a publishable project related to the themes of the course by the end of the semester. Students who took this course are expected to develop a clear research topic and be prepared to immerse themselves in a substantial amount of IPE literature.
.
objectives:
By the end of the course, registered students are expected to have the following competencies:
1. be familiar with the political processes that underlie the construction and functioning of international monetary relations and the financial system, and understand the key issues affecting the governance of international money and finance, such as the Unholy Trinity, exchange rate stability, capital mobility, and national policy autonomy, as well as other important themes such as financial crises, monetary power, and monetary regionalism.
2. understand the key actors, modes of interaction, and international dimensions of each theme
3. apply the theories learnt in this course to explain the politics of international money and finance from the perspective of international political economy
4. design and write original, published research papers.
grading:
1 Class Participation (30%)
Active participation is essential. Students must complete the assigned readings before each session and contribute to discussion. Participation is assessed in two parts.
Discussion Leader (20%). Each student serves as Discussion Leader twice (10% each). The Discussion Leader introduces and critically evaluates the assigned readings for that week and prepares questions for the seminar. The presentation may take the form of an in-depth critique of a single reading or a comparative synthesis of several. Slides must be uploaded to the course site at least 24 hours before class.
General participation (10%). In weeks when they are not Discussion Leader, students are still expected to have completed the readings and to participate actively.
2 Country Macro-Monetary Brief (10%)
Each student selects one country at the start of the semester and spends approximately five minutes each week following its major economic, monetary and financial developments — macroeconomic performance, central bank decisions, exchange rate and capital flow news. At the beginning of each session, students briefly report on developments in their assigned country. The purpose is to build the habit of reading current monetary and financial news through an analytical lens.
3 Literature Review Essay (10%; maximum 1,500 words)
From Week 3 onwards, each student writes one literature review essay on the readings of a single week. The essay may be an in-depth analysis of one reading or a thematic comparison of several. A strong essay includes:
A concise summary that states the core argument clearly. (A summary alone does not constitute a good review.)
A critical evaluation: why you agree or disagree with the argument; whether the empirical evidence is reliable and valid; whether the case selection adequately answers the research question; and how the argument might be strengthened.
Students may choose the week in which they serve as Discussion Leader, but are not required to do so.
Submission: by email to the instructor no later than 48 hours before the class session on the week being reviewed. Late submissions are not accepted.
4 Research Paper and Presentation (50%)
The seminar is designed to help students identify a research topic, design a project and write an original paper. Students submit a research paper of no more than 20 pages related to the themes of the course, and present it in Week 16. The presentation is worth 10% and the written paper 40%.
A one-page statement of the research topic (question, case, method) is due by the end of Week 8 (28 October).
A three-page outline of the research design is due by the end of Week 11 (18 November).
The instructor will circulate a short guide to writing a research proposal in Week 9.
Students are encouraged to discuss their topics with the instructor early in the semester.
The final paper is due by 17:00 on the Friday one week before grades are uploaded, submitted by email. Early submission is strongly encouraged.
