title: 永續發展與全球挑戰 Sustainable Development and Global Challenges
description: 當前人類面臨許多相互關聯的全球挑戰,包括氣候變遷的威脅、日益加劇的不平等、資源枯竭以及生物多樣性喪失等多重危機。聯合國不斷強調採取行動的急迫性與必要性,而聯合國永續發展目標(Sustainable Development Goals, SDGs)代表了全球共同的行動藍圖 。本課程將深入探討永續發展的核心概念、歷史脈絡等多重維度,並探討不同行為者在推動永續發展中的角色,以及永續發展在全球性層面的不同挑戰。本課程特別融入太平洋島國案例,智慧城市與AI等特色議題,透過文獻理論與實務個案的雙軌辯證,培養學員全面性的國際戰略思維與永續決策能力。
objectives:
1.了解永續發展的核心概念、原則與發展歷程。
2.分析全球環境、社會、經濟挑戰的相互關聯性。
grading:
課堂參與(20%): 針對每週主題、指定文獻及實務個案之思辨、發言與職場經驗分享。
小組期中簡報(30%): 選擇真實世界的永續發展或全球挑戰案例進行分析與報告。
個人期末專題報告/政策建議書(50%): 於第16週進行成果發表(口頭發表 20%,書面報告 30%)。結合學員自身專業領域,撰寫一份具備戰略建議性質的政策建議書。

title: 全球化與經濟整合 Globalization and Economic Integration
description:
從1980年代開始,全球化成為最受到注目的發展趨勢,也是一個時代的潮流。在全球化的大屋頂之下,全球主要的經濟部門快速的融合,連帶的經濟整合的進程也為之挺進,歐洲聯盟快速的擴張,拉美國家持續推動(例如,南方共同市場、太平洋聯盟),而東亞國家在建立經濟共同體上也大步向前邁進(例如,RCEP)。
由於川普執意退出,使得TPP面臨到發展的困境,在日本領導下將之改造為CPTPP,這展現出亞太國家仍努力於進行經濟整合。儘管如此,川普的路線和拜登政府無積極作為都使得國際社會懷疑美國對經濟整合的真正意圖。換言之,全球化逐漸的出現裂解。
值得注意的是中國大陸所扮演的角色。相對於美國川普總統追求重商主義的策略,重回到孤立主義路線,中國大陸卻是展現出擁抱自由主義市場經機,其主導的RCEP已經全面生效,且正式提出申請加入CPTPP,這使得東亞經濟整合未來的發展更具動態性,有許多可能的變化。尤有甚者,中國大陸在與其他國家簽署自由貿易協定已經開始逐漸升級,例如與秘魯、東南亞國協的自由貿易協定已進展到3.0,這更強化了其對整合的支持。而歐洲聯盟也在推動與其他國家或國家集團簽署自由貿易協定,例如,歐盟完成了與南方共同市場、日本的自由貿易協定,這都對經濟整合產生正面影響。這個發展趨勢不但影響到國家本身的發展,更在全球層次上衝擊到國際秩序的權力分配。
因之,本課程的設計一方面瞭解全球主義和全球化的意義、經濟整合的相關理論,另外一方面探討各區域整合進行的狀況,特別是比較西半球拉丁美洲國家及東亞國家在理論和實踐上的異同。值得注意的是影響全球化的兩大因素:其一是川普總統執意要重新建立以「美國再度偉大」(MAGA)為中心的國際貿易體系;其二是新冠狀病毒肆虐及俄烏戰爭導致國際供應鏈走向區域化的現象。我們也要探究這一現象,以及可能對經濟整合產生的影響。
objectives: 基於從1980年代到目前國際政治經濟情勢的快速變遷,本課程的目標使同學從理論上和實務上充分掌握此一轉換的流程趨勢及其內涵。透過自我學習、同儕思辮、以及老師的點評,期望同學能夠充分理解,並從政治經濟學的角度來分析並理解當前國際社會的頻繁互動、激烈競爭和無休止的爭霸。

title: 傳播、文化與外交 Communication, Culture and Diplomacy
description: 本課程專為外交系策略與國際研究高級碩士課程學員設計,旨在幫助中階專業人士提昇在溝通、文化和外交領域的知識,並分享經驗。教學安排以本科生國際傳播與國際關係課程為基礎,但更側重於實踐應用,提供案例研究和其他實例。

title: 發展中國家國際關係研究 Seminar on International Relations of the Developing Nations
description:
本課程旨在介紹發展中國家國際關係研究,重大國際事件之發生經過和影響,課程並主要以大師級相關中文譯作作為課堂討論內容,以期培養同學對國際安全與國際政治經濟問題之獨立思考、分析能力。
同學修習本課程之預期收穫為:國際關係如何運作、政治與經濟如何交互作用、國際關係各種成員之間又如何互動及影響、以及我們應如何養成正確的國際觀,進而思考如何維護我國的外交與戰略利益,都是本課程所要探討的主題。
以課程講授為主,並隨堂抽問同學指定網站中外文資料及個人意見,此外亦要求同學在期中考週交付學期報告綱要,期末報告請於期末考週交付。
objectives: 發展中國家或譯為開發中國家,泛指南方國家和第三世界國家。就地理範圍而言,開發中國家一般包括亞洲、非洲和拉丁美洲的大部份國家。本課程亦以此項分類方式為準,分別說明相關區域的重大議題。不過發展中國家成員眾多,而且個別國家差異性極大,大國如巴西者,國土面積比美國本土(不包括阿拉斯加)還大,小國如亞太地區的海島國家,即使在地圖上也不容易尋找。有鑑於此,本課程將先從拉丁美洲國家和亞太國家切入,並對與我有邦交國家,作進一步的說明,俾使同學對相關發展中友邦有進一步的認識。此外本課程亦以美國著名政治學者杭廷頓(Samuel P. Hungtington)第三波民主化、文明衝突、誰是美國人,以及弗里曼(Thomas L. Friedman)世界是平的、世界又平又熱又擠、我們曾經輝煌等中譯出版品作為主要參考教材,以期同學從大師級著作中,擷取智慧的精華,從而形塑自己的世界觀。
grading: 本課程評分標準如下:課堂參與20%、期中綱要說明和摘要及心得報告40%、期末口頭和書面報告40%。若有報告遲繳或抄襲等事宜,皆依學校相關規定處理。

title: 比較外交政策 Comparative Foreign Policies
description:
在此國際關係瞬息萬變,經貿科技進入超級競爭與充滿不確定性的時代,更不用說通貨膨脹長期化與氣候變遷的衝擊已成常態,而長達三年多的俄烏戰爭,再加上中東戰事已從以哈戰爭擴及以色列與伊朗的軍事衝突,凸顯各國和平相處與協力合作已成為解決國際衝突與化解誤解誤判的唯一途徑。
本課程主旨即在引介比較分析的方法來研究外交政策與國際關係,探討何以不同國家的外交政策行為有所差異,而這些差異往往就是國家發生衝突與戰爭誤判的主要原因。因此,若能正確瞭解與掌握這些導致衝突與對抗的原因就可制訂有效的外交政策策略來增進國家利益、找出解決國際紛爭的方案,促進和平,且進而達成國際政經科技合作與彼此獲利的目標。教學內容分兩部分,前半段介紹比較研究分析的主要學說與學派,後半段則是實證分析個案。除剖析大國間的競合,利益的交集與相衝以及心理矛盾與衝突外,更特別著重於探討中小型國家的存活與永續之道。所討論分析的對象國含括分裂國家外交政策模式(台海兩岸與兩韓互動之比較)、美中新冷戰時代所引發的供應鏈重整對中小型國家外交模式的衝擊(澳洲、加拿大、印度、印尼、越南、墨西哥)以及亞歐互動新模式(德國外交政經困境、東北亞與中東國家以及V4國家經貿互動)等。
objectives:
Course Objectives:
提供學生有用的分析方法,且以不斷更新的知識與例證來驗證研析個案以助學生建構分析架構及其應用與活用
Learning Outcomes
學生將可進行獨立思考分析,制訂符合自己的多學門整合(外語+國際關係+國際安全+經貿科技等)的策略組合(strategic portfolio),終而增進國際競爭力,可更貼近就業市場所需
grading: Grade will be based upon 1. individual paper presentation (40%); 2. written paper (50%) plus 4. class performance and participation(10%).

title: 國際政治經濟學 International Political Economy
description: 這門課程主要是設計給外交學系戰略與國際事務碩士在職專班,想要初步瞭解國際政治經濟領域中主要議題與發展的同學研習。國際政治經濟的發展已逾四百年,國內與國際政治與經濟行為之間如何交互影響,一直是世界政治與政治經濟學學者的研究興趣之一。國政經的研究議題相當廣泛,從區域貿易協定如何影響全球整合?貿易互賴(或是依賴)如何影響國際衝突行為?跨國公司如何形塑母國與投資國的國內政治?等. . .,都是國際政治經濟學者持續探討的議題。而近年來受到發展議題的影響,國家如何展現與其他國家不一樣的發展方向,也是學界與政策界主要關切的焦點之一。
objectives: 透過這堂課程,我們預期同學可以學習國際政治經濟中的重要議題、應用國際政治經濟理論來解釋、預測與分析世界政治經濟活動。更重要的是,同學們可以獨立發展與思考可能的國際政治經濟議題與解決方案。

title: 環境影響評估專題 Seminar on Environmental Impact Assessment
description:
授課內容(中文)
本課程主要內容包括:
環境影響評估制度與發展歷程
我國環境影響評估法規與審查機制

永續發展與ESG導向之環評思維
氣候變遷、淨零碳排與韌性評估
都市更新、重大建設與土地開發環評案例
環評報告書架構與撰寫方法
GIS、大數據與AI於環評分析之應用
國內外重大環評爭議案例研討
專題研究與成果發表(期中報告與期末報告)
Course Description (English)
The course covers the following topics:
Development and theoretical foundations of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)
Taiwan’s EIA regulations and review procedures
Identification of environmental impacts in development projects
Ecological, hydrological, air quality, noise, and transportation impact assessments
Social impact assessment and public participation
Sustainability and ESG-oriented EIA frameworks
Climate change adaptation, net-zero transition, and resilience assessment
EIA cases related to urban redevelopment, infrastructure, and land development
Structure and preparation of EIA reports
Applications of GIS, big data, and AI in EIA analysis
Domestic and international controversial EIA cases
Final project research and presentations
教學方式
課堂講授
文獻閱讀與討論
案例分析
分組專題研究
學生口頭報告
專家演講與實務交流
objectives:
本課程旨在培養學生對環境影響評估(Environmental Impact Assessment, EIA)制度、理論與實務操作之整合能力,透過國內外案例分析、政策法規研討、專題實作及跨領域議題探討,使學生理解大型開發計畫對自然、生態、社會、經濟與都市環境之影響。課程亦將結合永續發展、氣候變遷調適、淨零轉型、ESG治理、公民參與與智慧科技等新興議題,強化學生在都市規劃、土地開發、公共工程與環境治理領域之專業分析與決策能力。
This course aims to cultivate students’ integrated understanding of the theories, regulatory frameworks, and practical applications of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). Through case studies, policy discussions, project-based learning, and interdisciplinary analysis, students will examine the environmental, ecological, social, and economic impacts of development projects. The course further incorporates emerging issues such as sustainable development, climate adaptation, net-zero transition, ESG governance, public participation, and smart technologies, enabling students to develop professional competencies in environmental governance, urban planning, land development, and infrastructure assessment.

title: 量化分析方法與城鄉研究 Quantitative Methods in Urban and Rural research
description: 本課程的目的在引介本系研究常用的計量分析工具,讓學生學習如何將資料(data)變成資訊(information)並產生知識(knowledge),以供決策(decision making)之用。包括量化研究設計、量化資料蒐集、與量化資料分析等基本概念與方法。課程中廣泛的教授迴歸分析、多變量分析、多準則評估分析、多目標規劃分析、線性規劃分析、及格體選擇模型等分析方法,以利同學應用於現況分析歸納、未來發展預測、發展方案規劃以及方案評估及決策工作之計量方法。
objectives: 除了統計學概念的說明之外,本課程也強調統計軟體的操作。藉由實作,修課者一方面能夠更加熟悉統計概念的意義,另一方面也能夠運用軟體實際進行經驗資料的分析。本課程將以EXCEL、SPSS資料分析軟體及相關的空間計量分析軟體。另從政府統計資料(大數據)切入,結合適宜之量化分析方法,培養同學運用科學方法、嚴謹推理、獨立思考的能力。

title: 不動產交易管理與法律專題研究(一) Seminar on Real Estate Deal Management and Law(I)
description:
「不動產交易管理與法律專題研究」之課程,係以不動產交易過程中所涉及之主要法規作為研究對象,探討其理論與實務上有關之法律問題。由於我國並無一部稱之為「不動產交易法」之法律,故所謂不動產交易法係指「法律領域」而言。舉凡與不動產交易有關之法律,皆可納入此一法律領域,而本課程將篩選與不動產交易有關主要法規以為研析及討論。由於可能涉之法規甚多,本課程將以一學期探討一項法規之相關問題為原則。
本學期之研討主題為「不動產交易與公平交易法」。公平交易法是各產業市場競爭之遊戲規則,不動產交易相關產業之從業人員,對於此一經濟基本法亦應有基礎之認識。此外不動產交易案件中涉及諸多公平交易法上之問題,諸如不動產交易之不實廣告、不實促銷、資訊揭露以及對仲介業者之規範等,不僅對於事業之營業競爭行為甚為重要,對於購屋消費者之保護亦關係密切。熟悉公平交易法對於不動產交易之規範內容與理論實務,對於從事不動產交易之當事人可謂十分重要。本學期之課程內容,即在深入探討上述相關議題。
objectives: 本課程之目標在於使修習課程之同學瞭解公平交易法之基本架構、內容,以及公平法對於不動產交易之規範及理論實務。透過報告、討論及老師之說明講解,期盼在修完此一課程後,同學們能夠清楚掌握不動產交易與公平交易法之密切關連性,並具有處理相關問題之基礎法律知識。
grading: 本課程以同學之書面及口頭報告內容及上課參與討論之情形作為評分標準。報告時應準備PPT檔或書面之討論資料。同學除應報告其所分配到之題目外,對於其他同學報告之題目亦應盡量參與討論,出席與參與討論之情形亦列為評分之重要參考。學期末應依據上課討論情形,修訂完善後繳交書面報告(5000字以上)。報告之撰寫,不得使用AI代撰。

description: 這是一門理論與操作並重的課,藉由基本理論的講授以及相關軟體的操作,可讓修課學生對空間分析有較為完整的認識。
objectives:
本課程針對地政系碩士班學生所設計,課程設計目的為應用GIS與統計工具於國土、區域、都市、及社區的空間型態分析,亦可應用於與空間型態相關的領域,如交通與土地使用規劃、估價。
最終應具備空間分析應有之概念與操作分析能力。

title: 不動產金融研究 Real Estate Credit Market
description: 本課程主要教導學生了解財務與投資原理在不動產標的之應用,以及不動產在金融市場之角色 (如融資擔保品及證券化), 課程自基礎之一般財務、公司財務、個人投資理財、至不動產財務與投資分析、以及相關之衍生性商品(如不動產與資產證券化Real Estate Investment Trust, REIT; Mortgage-Backed security, MBS; Collateralized- Mortgage Obligation, CMO)等,均進行深入淺出之探討。而在不動產估價方法中之「收益法」,即需紮實的財務基礎俾利此法之進行。最後以財務觀點針對不動產、股票、債券、基金、期貨與選擇權及其他商品進行各標的投資抉擇之比較探討。而在美國次級房貸風暴後,高度財務槓桿之投資或購屋之風險及不動產與金融市場之關係尤為各界所矚目。又在風暴後的量化寬鬆(Quantitative Easing, QE)貨幣政策,及新冠肺炎(COVID-19)疫情後實施的"無限QE",均因資金充沛而分別引發了不動產的漲勢。因此課程總結將以財務分析之觀點及對政策之分析(如貨幣政策或財政政策等)預測不動產及金融市場之走勢及投資契機之時點,與金融風暴發生的可能。
objectives:
不動產財務與金融分析涉及不動產與財務金融兩專業領域的整合, 雖然不動產是眾多投資標的之一, 但因金額龐大常需向金融機構融資, 且流動性低, 而除了投資需求外, 相較於股票或債券等金融商品, 不動產尚具實質使用功能, 如居住或營業等, 因此在價格波動上, 不動產市場通常在市場下跌趨勢下具"僵固性" (rigidity).
因此本課程將教導修課不動產之特性、財務分析及不動產與金融市場間之整合與交互關係, 除了應用在不動產標的之價格評定及投資決策外, 亦能再與其他標的(如股票, 債券及黃金等), 以培養本身為所有資產標的分析之整合性人才.
除了訓練不動產及金融之相關專業外, 本課程亦藉著帶領修課學員研析及導讀相關文獻的過程, 培養其獨立研究、撰寫論文的能力. 使學員兼具不動產與金融專業實務與學術發展之能力.
最後補充不動產與金融市場之新研究與新技術, 及林教授在"好房網"撰寫的文章與國際最新文章之探討(如經濟學人The Economists): 如大數據(Big Data), 金融科技 (FinTech), 及不動產科技(PropTech)等.

title: GPS定位測量專題研究 Seminar of GPS Surveying
description:
在土地管理與規劃的專業領域中,精確的空間定位技術是決策與研究不可或缺的基礎。全球定位系統(Global Positioning System, GPS)作為最廣泛應用的全球導航衛星系統(GNSS),已徹底改變了傳統測量方式,並深刻影響到都市規劃、土地利用、資源管理與災害防治等多元領域。
本課程將引導同學深入理解 GPS 的原理、定位方法與誤差來源,並學習如何透過差分定位(DGPS)、即時動態定位(RTK)、精密單點定位(PPP)等技術,提升定位精度,滿足土地規劃與管理的專業需求。課程同時強調 跨領域整合,結合地理資訊系統(GIS)、遙測影像與空間資訊分析,培養學生在土地使用變遷監測、交通運輸規劃、區域發展研究及生態環境管理等方面的應用能力。
透過理論與實務並重的學習,學生將能:
掌握 GPS 與 GNSS 的核心技術與應用模式
了解定位誤差來源並具備修正能力
將定位成果整合至土地管理與規劃的決策流程
提升在自然資源經營、災害監測及社會經濟研究中的專業競爭力
本課程不僅提供技術知識,更強調 實務應用與策略思維,讓同學能在未來的土地規劃與管理工作中,善用精準定位技術,解決複雜的空間問題,並創造更具前瞻性的規劃成果。
objectives:
課程目標
建立定位技術基礎:系統性介紹 GPS 與其他 GNSS 的組成、訊號特性、定位原理與誤差來源,讓學生掌握空間定位的核心知識。
強化誤差修正能力:學習差分定位、RTK、PPP 等誤差消除方法,培養精準測量與土地規劃所需的技術能力。
拓展跨域應用視野:結合 GIS、遙測與空間資訊分析,探索 GPS 技術在土地使用監測、交通運輸規劃、災害防治與區域發展研究中的應用。
培養問題解決能力:透過案例分析與專題研究,訓練學生將定位成果整合至土地管理決策流程,提升專業實務操作能力。
學習成效
修習本課程後,學生將能:
理解定位原理:熟悉 GPS 與 GNSS 的運作機制,並能解釋定位精度差異與誤差來源。
應用修正技術:具備使用差分定位、RTK 等方法提升精度的能力,達到土地規劃與管理所需的專業標準。
整合空間資訊:能將定位成果與 GIS、遙測影像結合,進行土地使用變遷監測與區域規劃分析。
展現專業競爭力:在自然資源管理、交通規劃、災害監測及社會經濟研究等領域,展現前瞻性的規劃與研究能力。
完成專題研究:透過期末報告,展現理論與實務整合成果,培養獨立研究與專業表達能力。
grading:
1、各單元講授完畢後,將有作業或報告。
2、期末請提出報告乙篇。
3、學期總成績包含2部分,平時成績50%與期末報告50%。

title: 農地利用與農村規劃 Farm Land Utilization and Rural Planning
description:
近年全球氣候變遷加劇,加以COVID-19疫情、俄烏戰爭及中東地區衝突等國際事件影響,導致全球糧食供應鏈受到衝擊,農業生產環境面臨嚴峻挑戰,糧食安全議題遂成為各國政府高度關注的重要課題。歐美國家逐漸體認農業除具有糧食生產功能外,亦兼具生態保育、環境維護、景觀塑造及社會文化等多元價值,因此透過農地利用規劃與農村發展政策,推動農業與農村地區之永續發展。
我國於2016年公布《國土計畫法》,將農業發展地區列為重要國土功能分區之一,以確保糧食安全、維護優良農地資源及農業生產環境為核心目標,並透過國土功能分區劃設、鄉村地區整體規劃及鄉村計畫等制度,強化農地利用管理與農村空間治理,避免土地零星開發及資源錯置利用。
本課程以農地利用與農村規劃為主軸,探討農地資源管理、土地利用規劃理論、農村發展策略及空間治理機制等重要議題,並結合國土計畫制度、鄉村地區整體規劃及國內外實務案例分析,透過相關理論與文獻閱讀,培養學生理解農地利用與農村規劃之基本原則、規劃方法及執行策略,進而掌握農業發展與農村永續治理之重要課題。
objectives:
一、本課程的教學目標為:
本課程旨在介紹農地利用與農村規劃之理論基礎,探討相關政策制度、法規架構及規劃實務,並從國土空間治理與永續發展觀點,理解農地利用與農村規劃於糧食安全、農地保育、環境維護及地方發展中的角色與功能。課程將透過國內外案例分析,檢視理論與制度於實際執行過程中可能面臨之課題及其影響,進一步探究理論與實務間之落差及其形成原因,並研擬可能之因應策略,以培養學生問題分析、政策評估及規劃研擬之能力。
此外,本課程將善用數位學習平台進行教材分享、資訊交流及課後討論,以提升學習成效與互動品質。由於本課程為研究所課程,將採取師生互動與議題討論並重之教學方式,鼓勵學生主動思考、批判分析及意見交流,以深化對農地利用與農村規劃相關議題之理解。
二、本課程希能達成的學習成效為:
(一)透過課堂討論與專題報告,提升學生論證思辨、口語表達及學術交流能力,並強化同儕間之學習與互動。(二)藉由師生定期交流課程內容與學習心得,尊重學生對課程安排與教學方式之建議,提升課程參與度與學習認同感。
(三)培養課前閱讀、課後反思及自主學習之習慣,強化文獻蒐集、整理與分析能力,奠定研究基礎。
(四)結合理論探討與相關實務案例分析,培養學生從農地利用、農村發展、國土規劃及空間治理等面向進行問題分析與政策評估之能力,以提升專業素養與國際視野。
(五)透過課堂報告、同儕互評及教師指導,增進學術論文撰寫能力,協助學生將研究成果發展為研討會論文或期刊投稿作品。

title: 社會科學研究方法 Research Methods for Social Sciences
description: This class is designed to provide solid training for graduate students to conduct scientific research and publish the results. It starts with the introduction of ontology, epistemology, methodology, and eventually research methods for decent qualitative research. It also covers the issues of identifying workable research topics from daily life observations.
objectives: Research methods should be learned by doing. It is a craft that can hardly be expressed in words. Nevertheless, understanding the logic behind the choices of research designs, data collection tools, and fieldwork dynamics would help the researchers gain the tacit knowledge needed to do things right. This course starts with possible approaches to studying human phenomena and strategic thinking about research designs, from identifying a potential topic to matching it with appropriate research methods. The course would also provide some technical details on fieldwork. It will further demonstrate how to wrap up the research results for publication.
grading:
1. Class Attendance and Active Participation and Assignments (40%):
All students are required to attend each class meeting and be ready to discuss the reading materials and major issues with others. This course will be taught in a diagnostic mode in which students’ own work will be put under examination in the class; the discussion demands basic politeness and courtesy.
2. Field Trip Report (20%)
A field trip will be arranged in the middle of the semester. Specific empirical data will be assigned to be collected on the trip and reported right after the trip. Classmates will conduct the investigation in a group of 3 members.
3. Final Paper (40%):
By the end of the semester, students have to hand in a research result that has the potential to be published in professional journals in the future. The final write-up needs to include research interests, a theoretical framework (with literature review), propositions or proposed arguments, methods to collect empirical evidence, a preliminary survey, and a conclusion. This proposal needs to be presented in front of all classmates in 15 minutes, and you need to take criticism and advice from the audience for at least 5 minutes. References need to be carefully documented, and all academic ethics faithfully followed.

title: 全球議題在亞洲 Global Issues in Asia
description:
"Global Issues in Asia" offers junior and senior undergraduate students and graduate students an exploration of major global issues within the framework of Asian studies and anthropology. This is an advanced course continuing from the Anthropology course (ZU1007001). We will explore five “foreshadowed problems”: history, subject, structure, difference, and perception. Each section contains three global issues. Throughout the course, we will examine issues including imagination, pop culture, algorithms, precarity, inequality, political unrest, ethnic conflicts, technology and innovation, the Anthropocene, and diverse forms of life. We ask how emerging global issues manifest in Asian societies and explore the distinctive ways these societies engage with key challenges. We will also engage with foundational dialogues and emerging themes in Asian studies, analyzing contemporary ethnographies from anthropology, sociology, and media studies that trace the evolution of these debates and concerns. This is a reading-intensive course with a strong emphasis on interactive ethnographic practices, laying the groundwork for introductory fieldwork experience.
「全球議題在亞洲」是針對創新國際學院大三、大四學生、研究生開設的專題課程,其內容聚焦於全球重大議題,藉此探索當代亞洲社會與文化所面臨的挑戰與機遇。這是一門進階人類學的課程,我們將延續人類學課程(ZU1007001)裡的五個「預示性問題」(foreshadowed problems):歷史、主體、結構、差異、認知,課程的每個單元將聚焦三個全球議題。這個學期我們將討論以下議題:想像、流行文化、演算法、不穩定階級、社會不平等、政治抗爭、族裔衝突、科技創新、人類世以及多樣的生命樣態等。一方面,課堂上將探討全球共同面對的新興課題如何在亞洲社會浮現,以及思考這些議題在亞洲呈現的特殊性。另一方面,我們也將討論不同的亞洲國家與社會如何回應全球議題的挑戰。修習本課程,學生將能了解當代亞洲研究中關鍵的全球議題、問題意識與理論,並透過人類學、社會學、媒介研究等領域的當代民族誌,了解這些議題如何浮現與轉變。這是一門著重於民族誌閱讀的理論課程,同時將搭配課堂中的互動式民族誌實作,奠定初階田野實作的能力。

title: 科技法律與資料治理 Technology Law and Data Governance
description:
I. Course Objectives
This course is designed to help students understand the legal and governance issues arising from the development of digital technologies, with data governance as its central focus. It addresses major emerging topics, including personal data protection, artificial intelligence governance, digital platform accountability, open government data, data sharing, cybersecurity, cross-border data flows, and the European Union(EU)’s data governance framework.
Taught entirely in English, the course introduces students to core concepts in contemporary international technology law. It examines legal issues that arise throughout the data life cycle, from collection, processing, use, retention, and sharing to deletion. The course also considers the legality of artificial intelligence systems in model training and content generation, and analyzes the respective responsibilities and obligations of governments, businesses, digital platforms, and data intermediaries in data governance.
The course further incorporates Taiwan’s legal framework, the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Data Governance Act, Data Act, Artificial Intelligence Act, and other significant legislative developments and international trends. Through this comparative approach, students will develop a stronger interest in technology law and acquire the analytical skills needed to address practical legal issues.
II. Course Description
This course begins with legal issues related to data use as an entry point into technology law. It introduces key legal concepts, including personal data protection, informational self-determination, privacy, and data governance, before moving to issues such as open government data, data sharing, data intermediary services, data altruism, data access for Internet of Things devices and connected products, cloud switching, regulation of artificial intelligence technologies, algorithmic transparency, disclosure obligations, and legal requirements for cross-border data transfers.
The course focuses on recent developments in the EU’s data governance regime and explains how the GDPR, Data Governance Act, Data Act, and Artificial Intelligence Act together shape a technology law framework grounded in trustworthiness, data access, and risk management. In addition to introducing major international technology laws, the course includes weekly case discussions to help students examine the relationship between data governance, personal data protection, public interest, industrial innovation, digital market competition, national data sovereignty, and the protection of fundamental rights.
objectives:
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:
Understand the foundational theories and regulatory structure of technology law and data governance.
Examine legal issues concerning personal data protection, data sharing, digital platform regulation, risk-based regulation of artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity safeguards.
Compare Taiwan’s digital legal framework with the GDPR, Data Governance Act, Data Act, and other major technology laws of the EU.
Assess, from legal and governance perspectives, personal data protection risks and appropriate levels of regulatory oversight arising from artificial intelligence and other technological applications.
Analyze current disputes and cases involving the application of technology law from an independent perspective and propose appropriate legal or policy reforms.

title: 地緣科技:後全球化時代的半導體供應鏈 Geo-technology: Understanding Semiconductor Supply Chain in the Post G lobalisation Era
description: This course examines the political economy of the global semiconductor industry through the analytical framework of geo-technology. Rather than focusing on technological or commercial aspects alone, it explores how semiconductors have become central to national security, industrial policy, global governance, and geopolitical competition in the post-globalization era. The first half of the course introduces major theories of international political economy, including neorealism, liberalism and developmental state theory, providing students with a strong analytical foundation. The second half compares the semiconductor development trajectories of the United States, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, and China, emphasizing the interaction between state capacity, industrial policy, and geopolitical change. Through comparative analysis and debates on issues such as the return of industrial policy and technological decoupling, students will develop critical analytical skills and a deeper understanding of the global political economy of semiconductors.
objectives: This course applies the framework of geo-technology to examine the global political economy of the semiconductor industry. Through International Political Economy theories and comparative case studies of the United States, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, and China, students develop analytical skills to understand the interaction between industrial policy, state capacity, and geopolitical competition.

title: 語言人類學 Linguistic Anthropology
description:
This is a theoretically oriented seminar course focusing on the historiography, theories, and contemporary developments of linguistic anthropology, including the emerging linguistic anthropology of AI. The purpose of this course is to explore how linguistic anthropologists conduct research to foreground language practices within a matrix of cultural dynamics, power relations, social inequality, and identity construction. Different from formal analyses of language, linguistic anthropologists view language as social action through which meaning, language ideology, subjectivity, identity, voice, and power are constituted, contested, and transformed across time and space.
The course also examines how artificial intelligence, especially large language models and other AI-based language technologies, challenges and extends core questions in linguistic anthropology. AI-generated language raises important issues about interaction, communicative competence, authorship, voice, authority, knowledge production, and human–machine communication. By bringing classical theories of linguistic anthropology into dialogue with contemporary debates on AI, this course asks how language continues to mediate social life in an increasingly machine-mediated communicative world.
本課程為EMI課程,以語言人類學的學術知識史、理論發展與當代理論思潮為核心,開放給大學部高年級與碩士班學生選修。本課程旨在引導學生理解語言人類學如何研究語言實踐,並將語言置於文化動態、權力關係、社會不平等、身分建構、主體性與聲音等問題的交織脈絡中加以分析。不同於以語言形式結構為主要對象的語言學分析,語言人類學將語言視為一種社會行動,關注語言如何在具體互動情境、社會文化脈絡與歷史過程中,參與意義、語言意識形態、身分認同、主體性、聲音與權力關係的形成、協商與爭辯。本課程將系統性討論人類學與語言學在「語言與文化」研究中的主要論述與基礎理論,並透過民族誌案例與實際語言資料,訓練學生連結理論概念與經驗分析。
此外,本課程也納入近年以來語言人類學對人工智慧(AI)與大型語言模型的諸多討論,思考 AI 生成語言如何挑戰並延伸語言人類學關於互動、溝通能力、作者性、聲音、知識生產與人機溝通的核心問題。透過將語言意識形態、符號學、互動分析、民族誌方法與 AI 語言技術研究相互對話,本課程進一步探討在日益由機器中介的溝通世界中,語言如何持續形塑社會關係、權力結構與文化意義。
objectives:
A. To cultivate students’ understanding of the historiography, classical theories, and contemporary developments of linguistic anthropology through the systematic reading of foundational texts, and to help them grasp how linguistic anthropologists analyze language practices within broader contexts of cultural dynamics, power relations, social inequality, and identity formation.
B. To train students to use core concepts in linguistic anthropology to analyze language as social action, through which meaning, language ideology, subjectivity, identity, voice, and authority are constituted, negotiated, contested, and transformed across time and space.
C. To develop students’ ability to connect micro-level linguistic practices with broader political-economic, sociocultural, and historical processes, and to cultivate more nuanced and critical forms of observation and analysis.
D. To guide students in examining how artificial intelligence, especially large language models and AI-based language technologies, challenges and extends central questions in linguistic anthropology, including interaction, communicative competence, authorship, voice, authority, knowledge production, and human–machine communication.
E. To cultivate students’ ability to bring classical theories of linguistic anthropology into dialogue with contemporary debates on AI, and to critically analyze the sociocultural assumptions, language ideologies, power relations, and knowledge limitations embedded in AI-generated language.
F. To strengthen students’ ability to read original English-language academic texts and to express their analytical perspectives on language, culture, power, and technology through academic writing, oral presentations, and classroom discussion.

title: 治理中國:政治變遷、社會轉型與台港澳關係 Governing China: Political Change, Social Transformation, and Relation s with Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau
description:
This course examines the rise of China as the defining force shaping politics and society across the Greater China region. Over the past four decades, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has transformed from a poor, isolated polity into the world’s second-largest economy and a leading geopolitical power — with profound consequences not only for its own governance but for its relationship with Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan, three societies bound to the mainland by deep cultural and historical ties yet possessing distinct institutional inheritances. The course asks: how has China’s rise reshaped the political institutions, social fabric, and external relationships of each of these polities, and what does the resulting variation tell us about the reach and the limits of Chinese-style governance?
The first half of the course maps the mainland system that drives these dynamics: major theoretical traditions for understanding Chinese politics (authoritarian resilience, fragmented and consultative authoritarianism, adaptive governance, party-state institutionalism); the organisation, ideology, and cadre system of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) under Xi Jinping; political change and policy implementation under the post-2012 leadership; the social transformation generated by urbanisation, hukou reform, demographic change, and growing inequality; and state–society relations including civil society, religion, ethnic politics, surveillance, and platform politics.
The second half traces how the rise of China has reshaped — and is being reshaped by — its peripheries. In Hong Kong, the asymmetric integration of the Special Administrative Region into the mainland’s political and economic order has accelerated since 2014, culminating in the 2020 National Security Law, the 2021 “patriots-only” electoral overhaul, and the 2024 Safeguarding National Security Ordinance (Article 23). In Macau, the rise of China has been managed through a quieter politics of accommodation, with deepening integration into the Greater Bay Area and continued reliance on a gaming economy increasingly aligned with Beijing’s strategic priorities. In Taiwan, China’s rise has driven both deepening economic interdependence (trade, investment, ECFA, semiconductors) and an intensifying security competition, with democratisation, identity politics, the 2024 presidential election, and the role of the United States all shaping the cross-Strait equation. The final two weeks are reserved for student case presentations.
objectives: By the end of the course, students should be able to: (1) compare leading theoretical models of Chinese governance and assess their analytical reach; (2) explain how the CCP organises power and recruits, monitors, and disciplines cadres; (3) trace the principal directions of political change under Xi Jinping; (4) analyse social transformation and state–society contention in mainland China; (5) compare the post-handover political trajectories of Hong Kong and Macau; (6) account for the trajectory of Taiwan’s democratisation and cross-Strait relations; and (7) deliver a research-grade case study and reflection note that engage critically with primary scholarship.
grading:
Class Participation (10%): Students are expected to read the assigned reading materials and attend all the classes.
In-class discussions (20%): Students are encouraged to participate actively, and each student is expected to lead or co-lead at least one reading discussion during the semester.
Presentation (35%): Students are expected to give a presentation (around 20–30 minutes) in Weeks 15 and 16 respectively. Presentation topics should be related to the substance of this course and will be confirmed in the consultation session in Week 8.
Final project (15%): Following the presentation, a written final project (around 4,000 words) should be submitted by 31 December 2026. The paper should develop the argument made in the presentation, situate it in the relevant scholarly literature, and apply at least one theoretical framework discussed in class.

The note should demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the academic literature on a specific topic placed in context. The note must be submitted by WEEK 10. title: 從鹿皮到半導體:臺灣的對外貿易與社會發展經驗 From Deerskins to Semiconductors: Taiwan's Experience in Foreign Trade and Social Development
description: This interdisciplinary course explores Taiwan’s transformation from a marginal entrepôt trading deer hides to a key player in the global semiconductor industry. Through historical, economic, and technological lenses, it examines how foreign trade, colonial legacies, and global networks shaped Taiwan’s social and economic development. Topics include early maritime trade, Japanese colonial infrastructure, the rise of small and medium-sized enterprises, and Taiwan’s pivotal role in the global tech economy. The course also introduces foundational concepts in the history of science and traces the evolution of modern physics leading to the semiconductor revolution. Field trips and guest lectures enrich the understanding of Taiwan’s dynamic trajectory.
objectives:
To provide students with a historically grounded understanding of Taiwan’s role in global trade networks from the 17th century to the present.
To critically examine how colonialism, war, and industrial policy shaped Taiwan’s economic and infrastructural development.
To introduce key economic sectors—such as agriculture, transport, and manufacturing—and analyze their transformation over time.
To investigate Taiwan’s transition into a technological hub through the lens of science, education, and innovation.
To foster interdisciplinary thinking by connecting historical events with scientific advancements, particularly the rise of the semiconductor industry.
By the end of the course, students will be equipped to understand the broader socio-economic forces behind Taiwan’s development and its position within global capitalism and technological innovation.

title: 東亞冷戰中的文化與性別 Culture, Gender and Sexuality in Cold War East Asia
description: This course surveys the discourses on hot wars, culture, gender, and sexuality in Cold War East Asia, and speaks to recent work in global “New Cold War” and historiography on the potential for rethinking the legacies of Cold War. The course strives to provide students with a strong understanding of some of the major actors shaping the development of states and the everyday experiences of people who lived in Asia during the period known as the Cold War. To this end, we will read scholarship on the legacies of imperialism and colonialism, Anti-Communism, Korean War, cultural and literary production on promoting Cold War ideology, and the gender/sexual politics in the artifacts or policies. Through the readings and discussions, we will challenge the existing world view of binarism, which is constructed by the ideology of Cold War Division (capitalism / communism, modern / tradition, gender dichotomy, progressive / backward...), and to approach a better understanding of the current geopolitical situation.
objectives:
Review important and classic works in the field of East Asian Cold War studies.
Investigating the histories of WWII, Korean War, and Vietnam War.
Understanding how the Cold War system operates, and is maintained through the norms of "sexuality/gender," and vice versa.
Understanding the issues and knowledge production of "Cultural Cold War" and "Cultural Imperialism".
Establishing preliminarily knowledge on "Cold War" and "sexual politics" in literary representations across East Asia.

title: 思辨:當代社會議題 Contemporary Social Problems and Justice
description:
This course is designed to introduce the benefits and methods of interdisciplinary study and research for exploring complex social problems and justice. Starting with the U.S. and Taiwan contexts as its foundation, this course expands its global context and weekly discussions by featuring several talented guest lecturers specializing in public administration and management. Their diverse international insights and perspectives provide a rich learning environment.
Students will be guided through the process by learning and applying critical thinking, problem identification, and problem-solving skills to discuss and explore creative policy approaches that integrate differing perspectives.
* Course Schedule and Adjustments:
The course topics and schedule may be adjusted based on speaker availability and details, field trips, as well as students' learning progress and needs. Changes such as rescheduling sessions or extending class time until 12:30 PM may occur when necessary. Any modifications will be announced in advance. As the course includes engaging and diverse activities, your cooperation is essential. Please carefully consider the course schedule and commit to full participation.
* Class Time and Attendance:
Classes begin promptly at 9:20 AM. Please arrive on time and follow the teaching assistant’s instructions at the start of class to complete the required activities, which will help facilitate the day’s lesson. There will be one scheduled break during the session, depending on the course progress.
* Attendance Policy:
Students who plan to enroll in or add to the course must attend the first class. Failure to do so will result in a final grade of zero (0) for the semester, and you will be responsible for withdrawing from the course. Only students who are physically present and complete the First-Day class attendance survey and self-introduction will be considered to have fully attended. First-day attendance and Regular Participation are required. Please read the course schedule carefully.
* Absence and Leave Policy:
Students who are absent without a valid reason, as outlined in the university’s leave policies, will not be allowed to participate in in-class activities, group presentations, or any graded assignments for that day. If you are unable to attend, please notify both the instructor and teaching assistant in advance via email (other forms of communication, such as messaging apps, will not be accepted) and obtain approval. Supporting documentation is required, and you must also complete the official leave process through the university’s system.
* This syllabus is a guide for the course and is subject to change with advance notice. Please pay attention to the newest course announcements, email notifications, and Moodle for updated course materials.
*AI tools may be used only when permitted and in strict accordance with assignment instructions; students must clearly disclose their use, take full responsibility for the content, and ensure academic integrity through proper citation.
*This course is highly participatory, integrative, and collaborative. All assignments are designed to guide students in building critical thinking, problem identification, and problem-solving skills.
objectives:
This course is highly participatory, integrative, and collaborative. Please note that this course is designed as a project-based learning approach with relevant tasks at different phases to help you develop your project and respond to feedback. All assignments are designed to guide students in completing their final project, developing critical thinking, problem identification, and problem-solving skills.
At the completion of this course, students will be able to:
Understand the process and language of interdisciplinary study and research.
Build tolerance for dissonance in conducting interdisciplinary study and research.
Build a deeper understanding of diversity, inclusion, and social justice embedded in the context of interdisciplinary social problems.
Analyze and apply perspectives of multiple disciplines to shape your understanding of complex social problems and social justice.
Critically examine, interpret, and explain the multiple perspectives from disciplines of social science that apply to complex social problems and creative policy solutions/resources.
Practice collaborative, interdisciplinary approaches to problem identification and disciplinary integration.
grading:

Actively participate in course discussions, in-class activities, and group project assignments
Complete all required assignments and activities on time
* All the assignments are designed to guide you in completing your final project with your critical thinking, problem identification, and problem-solving skills.
* All students are required to attend each class meeting and be ready to discuss the reading materials and assigned social problems with others.

Weekly Questions (Due every Tuesday at 23:59, 1-2 meaningful questions based on required readings and weekly topics), and Weekly Notes and Reflective Journals (Due the following Tuesday at 23:59)

Group Project and Final Integration Presentation
* Group assignments will be graded based on your role(s) and contributions in each assignment, as well as self & peer evaluation. Non-participation will result in a zero for your group project grade.

If you have any questions, challenges, or special learning needs, contact Dr. Shie to discuss your situation and a learning plan before any deadlines for this course. At the same time, you have to reach out to NCCU resources and/or other relevant sources to support your situation and be able to request a letter of support.
Students who are unable to attend classes due to illness or other university-approved reasons are required to apply for a leave of absence, providing documentary evidence. Please email both Dr. Shie and the teaching assistant for approval before leaving.
Without an excused absence, no late work will be accepted. From the due date, students with an excused absence have 24 hours to submit missing assignments, unless otherwise arranged with the instructor. If you have any questions or difficulties, contact Dr. Shie as soon as possible before the due dates. title: 國際遷移與照顧 Transnational Migration and Care
description:
The advanced undergraduate, graduate, and Ph. D courses will introduce and elaborate the crucial concepts, comparative policy analysis, and research findings (such as a systematic review) in transnational migration and care. Understanding the phenomena of international migration and care influences contemporary relations between individuals, families, communities, civil society groups, governments, and states (including sending and receiving countries including sending countries (such as Indonesia, Philippines, and Vietnam) and receiving countries (such as Korea, Japan, Singapore, and Taiwan). The course discusses issues related to the following:
Migration theory and pattern.
Varieties, im/mobilities, and precariousness of migrant workers, mainly migrant industrial and welfare/care workers.
Care regimes: How are the lives of migrants/persons who move across national borders influenced by international laws, national policies, and social exclusion or inclusion practices?
Rights and various abuses of migrant care workers
Runaway/unaccounted-for migrant care workers, stateless children, and family members lag behind
To explore these above topics of migration, the classical and latest research published by major academic presses in recent years, as well as reports from international organizations (such as the International Labor Organization, ILO), will be examined carefully and critically to inquiry the complicated issues that migrant workers face with the lived experiences of those impacted by migration.
objectives:
This course requires class participants to critically read, comprehend, write, and engage with interdisciplinary scholarship in transnational migration studies. This class will be facilitated as a seminar, and participants are expected to take responsibility for creating a collaborative, operative learning environment. Class participants are anticipated to engage thoughtfully, critically, and self-reflexively with course readings. Most of the classroom time is spent discussing every week’s reading of these textbooks and Journal articles. Thus, students are expected to obtain all the required books and complete all the assigned tasks before the class period in which they will be discussed. Leading discussions, class participation, and graded assignments are designed to encourage active, critical engagement with readings and other course materials. Class participants are also encouraged to observe and do fieldwork in practice related to migration and migrant workers’ issues. The Lecturer may use classroom time to engage students with documentary films, academic blogs, and popular media (such as YouTube), and guest speakers may also be invited to lecture to deepen our understanding of the issues in the assigned readings.
Learning Outcomes
Advanced skills in critical thinking and writing related to transnational migration, initiating an oral presentation related to a global migration issue, and generating a term paper related to international migration and care using a full-length final paper adopting the academic style and source
Comprehend the complexities of global migration and its impact on contemporary social and cultural life, national and international policies, governmental and non-governmental responses
Engage critically with academic theory related to worldwide migration and apply this knowledge to gain a deeper understanding of various outcomes that global migration caused
Identify the significant contemporary “push” and “pull” factors shaping international migration, displacement, and settlement, particularly for the migrant live-in care workers
Understand how international migration is changing contemporary forms of relationships (gender, kinship, and other forms of intimacy) and care as well as affected by the intersectionality of multiple policies/ regimes
grading:
The use of AI generation tools is prohibited in this course except for academic purpose
Course participation 15%
Observation report 15%
Leading class (article summary presentation) 30%
PPT presentation 20%
Final group project 20%

title: 種族、宗教、民族主義:全球的暴力與歸屬政治 Ethnicity, Religion, Nationalism:Violence and the Politics of Belonging in the Global World
description:
Notes:
Essays: Students write 1 essay (1000 words), due at the mid-term. This essay is written in a style of policy commentary. For this essay, students choose for themselves at least 2 theories from the 16-week course, and a case study.
Final paper: Students write 1 individual final paper (4,000-5,000 words) due at the end of the course. Students choose the topic of these final papers themselves.
Presentations: Students present twice: 1 on the weekly topic of their choice, 1 very short 5-minute presentation on the framework of their final papers.
The course includes stimulating activities such as debates, games, simulations, and watching a film. Film Title: Argo (2012), a three-Oscar-winning film about the rescue of US embassy employees from the siege of the American embassy in Tehran, Iran. Director: Ben Affleck. This film shows how Iran’s religious nationalism and US secular nationalism clashed during the 1979 Iranian revolution.
Alternatively the course is planned to introduce an innovative learning method which includes visits to religious civil society organizations to discuss with religious leaders/activists on the interplay between “religion” and “nationalism”, the organizations are: the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan (PCT) or the Tzu-Chi Foundation.
In light of the prolonged Israeli-Hamas war and the ongoing tensions between the United States and Iran, observers have warned of the possibility of a serious regional escalation and renewed global instability in the near future. The course “Ethnicity, Religion, Nationalism: Violence and the Politics of Belonging in the Global World” provides a structured space for students to critically examine how ethnic and religious identities shape nationalism and contribute to political conflict and violence in different regional and international contexts.
The course explores the interaction between religion and ethnic identities in Asia (East Asia, South Asia and Southeast Asia), the Middle East, and the United States, and their impact on the construction of nationalism. It addresses critical questions of identity and citizenship, inclusion and exclusion, emotional and symbolic attachments, and the linkage between local and global political dynamics. The course asks how ethnicity and religion shape political interaction, how ethnic and religious identities may aggravate conflict or strengthen cooperation, and how they are mobilized in processes of nation-building and political legitimation. It further examines how relevant dimensions such as sacralization and symbolic forms of legitimation may lead to conflict and violence.
The course is divided into two parts. The first part introduces key concepts of ethnicity, religion, identity, nation, and nationalism, and examines major theoretical explanations for the emergence and persistence of nationalism. The second part focuses on the political consequences of nationalism for belonging and identity, including religious nationalism, fundamentalism, and identity-based conflict, through case studies from China, Myanmar, Thailand, Indonesia, India, Turkey, Israel, and the United States.
The course also considers the role of digital technologies and artificial intelligence in shaping contemporary identity politics and nationalist mobilisation. Social media platforms, algorithmic systems, and AI-generated content increasingly mediate the circulation of ethnic and religious narratives, often amplifying polarization and reshaping boundaries of inclusion and exclusion in the process.
On Week 12 students will watch the film “Argo” (2012, Director: Ben Affleck), an Oscar-winning film which depicts the 1979 rescue of six U.S. State Department employees during the siege at the American embassy in Tehran, Iran. Alternatively, the course will include an Innovative Learning Method Week with Study Visits to religious organizations. Planned visits include the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan (PCT), or Tzu-Chi Foundation, where students will engage with religious leaders and practitioners to discuss the interplay between “religion” and “nationalism”, and conflict.
objectives:
After completing the course, students will:
Understand the meaning of key concepts, such as ethnicity, religion, identity, nation, nationalism, religious nationalism and fundamentalism.
Understand the interaction and complex relations between these key concepts and their role in the politics of belonging and citizenship in various countries.
Understand the interaction and complex relations between these key concepts and their role in fundamentalism and/or political violence in various countries.
Be able to analyze current and/or past conflicts by examining how ethnicity and religion generate nationalism, which in turn may produce violence and political conflict in the global world.
Be able to critically assess how digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) shape the circulation, amplification, and contestation of ethnic, religious, and nationalist narratives, and how these processes influence contemporary forms of identity politics and conflict.
grading:
Evaluations
Attendance and active participation : 15%
2 Presentations (1 on week topic, 1 on final) : 30%
1 Essay : 25%
1 Final paper : 30%
Criterion
Attendance and active participation: quality and frequency of contribution to class discussions and intervention. Excellence is marked by continuous contributions to class discussions and interventions which show high levels of analysis. Students should complete the assigned readings prior to the meetings and therefore are prepared to discuss the readings.
Presentations: Students present twice: the first one is on the essay topic of their choice; the second one is a short 5-minute presentation on the outline of their final paper. Evaluation is based on the quality of argument, evidence of research, presentation structure and cohesiveness, speech flow and quality of oral delivery. Excellence is marked by structured delivery, clear and analytical argument, fluent speech, and use of PowerPoint or other tools. The short final presentation can be done within the last four lecture weeks of the course (thus, starting on week 11).
Essay at mid-term: The essay is 1,000 words long. Students choose at least 2 theories and a case study on which they would like to write essays. Students apply these theories on a case study, thus the essay is not only a summary of the readings. The essays are submitted on mid-term.
Final paper: The final paper is 4,000-5,000 words, focusing on a case study which is analyzed using the theories and concepts learned in the class. Students should consult the instructor about the topics at least four weeks before the paper is due. Evaluation is based on the quality and structure of the written piece, evidence-based and conceptually grounded argument, and adequate literature review. The usage of relevant additional materials not listed in this syllabus is encouraged. Excellence is marked by analytical argument, usage of relevant theories and concepts, understanding of current events, well-argued position.

title: 地理資訊系統與社會科學 GIS for Social Science
description: This course focuses on the principles of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) as a way of analyzing and understanding society. GIS is a tool to provide geospatial information analysis and display results. Industry-standard GIS software will be used in this course. Students learn the concepts of spatial analysis with GIS; use techniques in importing and creating spatial and attribute data; recognize critical components of cartography to design maps, and build attribute and spatial queries for problem-solving based on spatial relationships. Laboratory exercises incorporate the use of GIS software (ArcGIS) in the analysis of social issues.
objectives: The objectives of the course are to acquaint graduate students with methods to analyze spatially-referenced data with the procedures appropriate for a social science’s theoretical base. The course contact hours are organized into three major foci: (a) essential theoretical concepts and the constituent reference to social science GIS applications; (b) the visualization of social data facilitated by Geographic Information Systems software; and (c) techniques to construct or analyze social point, line, and polygon data using exploratory and confirmatory spatially centered procedures to actual social theories and data using a pedagogical analytical approaches. Weekly readings and homework will emphasize applications of these procedures to actual social theories and data using a pedagogical model of application, interpretation, and presentation of empirical analyses by students. The semester-length project is a key instrument by which students will demonstrate competence in spatial analysis methods covered in the course.

title: 人性與存有:民族誌與人類學觀點 Being Human: Ethnography and Anthropological Perspective
description:
The rapid development of artificial intelligence has created ethical debates about whether a robot, if one day it has self-consciousness, should be treated like a human being. Likewise, a growing demand for psychological therapies has resulted in/from the quest for meanings and purposes of being alive. Underlying these contemplations is a fundamental question: What makes a human a human? This course aims to facilitate discussions and provide potential answers from academic literature.
Based on anthropological theory, ethnography, and cross-cultural comparison, this course introduces the formation of human society, life stages, and the phenomenology of ‘being human’. In the past ten years, there has been a trend of thought in the humanities and social sciences, debating the social and personal aspects of the positive sides of social life, such as expectations, dignity, values, ethics, empathy, care, freedom, and hope. This course will examine the subjective and objective conditions of well-being, reflecting on how well-being is perceived, defined, and created. Through lectures, class discussions, student presentations on the required readings, and field trips/documentaries/guest speeches, this course attempts to cultivate students’ ability to care for society and themselves.
This course begins with introducing basic concepts and epistemology of anthropological theory and ethnography. We will unpack what anthropologists have called ‘culture’ and ‘society’ and consider how themes of this kind lead to a reconsideration of how anthropological theory and ethnographies might be useful for comprehending the development of humanity. After providing an overview, each week’s topic will focus on key issues discussed in the sub-fields of Cognitive and Psychological Anthropology, Medical Anthropology, Religious Anthropology, Environmental Anthropology, and Positive Anthropology. Throughout, this course will focus on the relationship between self and society and that between mind, body, and the more intangible aspects such as emotion and spirit. We will look at how universal human capabilities develop and are used during different stages of life to create unique cultural understandings and practices.
objectives: This course contains lectures, student presentations and in-class discussions. These activities are based on reading materials and the instructor's lecture slides. Apart from lectures, students are expected to summarise reading materials on the topic(s) they sign-up for at the beginning of the term and present their thoughts in the class (at least 1 presentation, depending on the class size). This course will emphasise analytical perspectives and critical thinking. Students are required to read before classes and bring their reflections and questions to in-class discussions. In addition to presentations, students are expected to write reading notes. Finally, this course encourages students to apply their knowledge to the real world by analysing a case related to the topics mentioned in this course. Students are expected to demonstrate their findings both in presentations and written works.

title: 中國政治經濟發展 The Political Economy of China's Development
description: This course aims to provide students with a fundamental understanding of China's economic, social, and political development since 1978. Four main themes are involved. The first is the introduction. We will introduce this course with a discussion on the universality and particularity of the "China Model" from a comparative perspective. The second theme is economic transformation. We will explore China's industrialization and engagement with the world economy after the 1978 reform and opening up by examining the roles of the central government, local governments, the financial system, the fiscal system, state-owned enterprises, private enterprises, and foreign enterprises. The third theme is social changes. We will investigate the impacts that economic transformation brought to society in many aspects, including the urban-rural divide, social stratification, the one-child policy and its impact on demographics, as well as environmental issues. The fourth theme is political development. We will explore the implications of economic development for the prospect of democracy in China, as well as the impact that China's rise might bring to international political development. Moreover, we will show to and discuss with students selected movies related to the topics in the course, with an aim to improve students' understanding of some critical scenarios in the processes of China's political and economic development.
objectives: Students will be equipped with the ability to interpret and analyze the causes, logic, and consequences of China's political and economic development. Considering the current trend of China's rise, such capacity will be beneficial to students' career development whether in academic circles or practical fields.
grading:
Attendance (10% of course grade): Students are required to come to classes. The grade is decided by the student's level of attendance.
Participation (20% of course grade): Students are expected to read assigned readings and participate in class discussions. The grade is decided by the quantity and quality of the student's engagement in the class.
Reading guides (20% of course grade): Each student will have the opportunity to serve as a lead discussant for about two assigned readings during the semester. He or she must present the assigned reading, provide comments, and raise questions to facilitate class discussions.
Essay papers (50% of course grade): Each student must independently write two 4-page essay papers based on assigned readings to respond to the teacher's questions. The two papers are respectively due in the midterm and final exam weeks. The questions will be announced one week earlier. There will be one week for students to work on their essays at home. The papers must be submitted to Moodle by the deadline set by the teacher.
*To ensure fairness and enhance the learning experience, the use of generative AI tools for writing mid-term and final essays is prohibited in this course. The teacher will reference the results of detection software and may meet with students suspected of using AI for writing. If it is confirmed that the report was generated by AI, it will be scored as zero.

title: 混合政體:東南亞的民主挑戰 Hybrid Regimes: Democratic Challenges in Southeast Asia
description:
Notes:
Essays: Students write 1 essay (1000 words), due at the mid-term. This essay is written in a style of policy commentary. For this essay, students choose for themselves at least 2 theories from the 16-week course, and a case study. The best essays will be chosen for publication submission at prominent policy platforms of Southeast Asia politics, such as ISEAS’ Fulcrum in Singapore or East Asia Forum in Australia, after sufficient editing.
Final paper: Students write 1 individual final paper (4,000-5,000 words) due at the end of the course. Students choose the topic for these final papers themselves.
Presentations: Students present twice: 1 on the weekly topic of their choice, and 1 (very short, 5-minute presentation) on the framework of their final papers.
The course includes stimulating activities such as debates, games, simulations, and discussing a film. Two alternatives: (1) “The Kingmaker” (2019) an award-winning documentary film portraying the political career of Imelda Marcos of the Philippines, the widow of the former president of the Philippines, with a focus on the efforts to rehabilitate the family's image and to return to political power (2) “I Not Stupid” (小孩不笨) (2002), an award-winning Singaporean political satire comedy about the lives, struggles and adventures of three elementary school students. The film sparked public discussions and parliamentary debates that led to real reforms in the education system.
The course is also tentatively planned to include an innovative learning method called “Learning Together”: in one of the weeks, our students will be learning together with students from NTNU’s Department of East Asia Studies. This will be done either by receiving NTNU’s students in our classroom or by visiting NTNU’s class on politics in Southeast Asia.
The course “Hybrid Regimes: Democratic Challenges in Southeast Asia” is designed as a standalone course or as a follow-up course for students who have completed the introductory course “Politics in Southeast Asia: Change and Continuity”. The course examines the socio-political development of authoritarian and hybrid regimes in Asia, enabling students to survey, compare, and analyze the persistent challenges of democratization in the region. While the empirical focus is Southeast Asia, the course also situates regional political dynamics within broader geopolitical relations, particularly with East Asian actors such as China, Taiwan, and Japan. Cambodia’s limited democratization, for instance, has been analyzed by some scholars in relation to its close ties with China. From this perspective, democratization in Southeast Asia may also be influenced by engagement with consolidated democracies, such as Taiwan and Japan. The course further engages with Taiwan’s foreign policy initiative, the NEW SOUTHBOUND POLICY, through which Taiwan seeks to deepen economic, political, and cultural relations with Southeast Asian countries.
In the aftermath of the Cold War, a global wave of democratization reshaped political systems across Asia, Central and Eastern Europe, Latin America, and Sub-Saharan Africa. The dissolution of the Soviet Union weakened the legitimacy of many authoritarian regimes, leading to transitions toward multiparty systems and liberal reforms. However, regime transitions did not always result in democratic consolidation, and many states experienced stalled or reversed democratization processes.
While pure authoritarian regimes have become less common in Asia, many states are better understood as “hybrid regimes” or “electoral autocracies”, positioned between liberal democracy and authoritarian rule. These regimes typically maintain the formal structures of electoral competition, including multiparty elections, while systematically limiting opposition voices through institutional manipulation, uneven political competition, and selective enforcement of rules. In these nations, the thin veneer of quasi-democratic institutions and multi-party elections became a façade for abuses of power, manipulation and corruption. In Thailand, following the 2019 election, the military-backed government dissolved an opposition party and arrested activists, triggering widespread student-led protests demanding constitutional reform and greater civil liberties. In 2023, although the opposition Move Forward Party won the election, it was prevented from forming a government due to institutional constraints and entrenched political interests. In the Philippines in 2016, voter dissatisfaction with crime and entrenched elite politics contributed to the election of Rodrigo Duterte, whose administration was associated with an extensive “war on drugs” involving extrajudicial killings. In 2022, voters elected Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the son and namesake of the former dictator, signaling the persistence of dynastic politics. In Myanmar, the military coup in 2021 marked a reversal of electoral democratization and a return to direct military rule.
The course also incorporates analysis of the role of digital technologies in shaping political competition and state-society relations in Southeast Asia. Social media platforms have become central arenas for electoral mobilization, political communication, and contestation in hybrid regimes. Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), further amplify these dynamics by enabling new forms of political communication and information manipulation at scale. In several cases, coordinated online networks, including troll activities and disinformation campaigns, were deployed during election periods to influence public opinion and delegitimize opposition actors. Concurrently, states have introduced regulatory frameworks such as anti-fake news legislation and cybersecurity laws, which, while formally justified in terms of public order and information integrity, may also function as instruments of digital surveillance and constraints on freedom of expression. These developments underscore how hybrid regimes are sustained not only through formal institutions and coercive mechanisms, but also through digital infrastructures and information environments.
Some of the questions the course seeks to answer are: What is democracy good for? Why do some states democratize while others continue to exhibit authoritarianism? How do highly corrupt political regimes survive for decades? How do populist leaders gain and maintain power in Asia? What is the legacy of political violence in newly democratic states? What is the legacy of military rule in the region? How do global human rights values and “Asian values” shape political development in the region? How do digital technologies, including social media platforms, disinformation networks, and state regulatory frameworks, reshape political competition, state-society relations, and the boundaries of free expression in hybrid regimes? The course begins by introducing core concepts, regime typologies, and indicators for assessing democratization. It subsequently examines in-depth developments in Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Myanmar, Vietnam, and Cambodia.
grading:
Evaluations
Attendance and active participation : 15%
2 Presentations (1 on week topic, 1 on final) : 30%
1 Essay : 25%
1 Final paper : 30%
Criterion
Attendance and active participation: quality and frequency of contribution to class discussions and intervention. Excellence is marked by continuous contributions to class discussions and interventions which show high levels of analysis. Students should complete the assigned readings prior to the meetings and therefore are prepared to discuss the readings.
Presentations: Students present twice: the first one is on the essay topic of their choice; the second one is a short 5-minute presentation on the outline of their final paper. Evaluation is based on the quality of argument, evidence of research, presentation structure and cohesiveness, speech flow and quality of oral delivery. Excellence is marked by structured delivery, clear and analytical argument, fluent speech and use of power point or other tools. Depending on how many students are enrolled in the course, the short 5-minute final presentations can already be done in any of the last four weeks of the course (thus starting on Week 13), based on the students’ own preference.
Essay at mid-term: students choose at least 2 theories and a case study on which they would like to write essays. The essay is 1,000 words long, based on the theories in at least 2 (two) of the readings, plus apply them to a case study that is relevant, thus not only a summary of the readings. The essays are submitted at mid-term. The best essays will be chosen for a revision and submission to policy platforms on Southeast Asia politics, for example: ISEAS’ Fulcrum in Singapore, or East Asia Forum in Australia.

title: 亞洲主權:人類學視角 Sovereignty in Asia: Anthropological Perspectives
description: This class will examine the institution of sovereign rule from the bottom up, taking stock of the emergence of ancient states and attending to three distinct, but shifting registers in which sovereignty emerges in modern formations. One addresses the nation-state as a territorially and ideologically bounded entity, another engages with indigenous understandings of social relationships with the earth, which folds into the third register of Indigenous People’s sovereign claims to territory. To unpack these interconnected strands, we begin by examining ancient sovereigns form from East and Southeast Asia using anthropological and archeological data to complicate the story of civilization. We will attend to god kings and emperors, as well as the modern forms of territorial control that emerged from those ancient states. With this, we will turn the assumption of teleological progress into a question. Is the institution of the sovereign nation part of an evolutionary process of human social life? To address this question, we turn to the cults of soil and water common to indigenous communities across the region. There are elements of these practices that are directly connected to ancient forms of sovereignty. Part of our work will be to identify this connective tissue, as well as what possibilities are severed in the shift to sovereignty. From this perspective, we can follow the trail of sovereignty as it emerges out of the resources it consumes and, in this context, will consider the contested spaces where contemporary Indigenous Peoples make sovereign claims. The purpose of this examination is to consider alternative ways to frame contemporary questions about territory, resources, and the organization of place and society. We will ask more questions than we answer in this class, and participants should come prepared to think together about the creative process of social organization.
objectives:
Course Objectives:
In the context of changing planetary systems and unchanging political and economic activities, students will understand some of the historical processes that inform our current challenges
Students will understand the history and development of modern sovereign nations
Students will be able to make connections between sovereign nations and the geo-bio processes that sustain them
Sovereign claims by Indigenous Peoples will be understood in the context of their deep history.
grading:
Course Requirements
Class Participation 30%
Midterm exam 30%
Final Paper 30%
Pop Quiz 4 10%
Three-credit course
To achieve the three-credit course requirement, this course offers at least 54 hours of instruction.
We will meet physically in class for 3-hour sessions weekly (42 hours). Week 8 is a mid-term take-home exam. Week 16 is the final take-home exam.
Office hour instruction is offered each week (3 hours/wk. adding 48 hours of additional instruction opportunities).
Class Participation
Show up, on time, prepared to discuss the week’s readings. Computers or cell phones are for note taking, translation assistance, or researching course-related things. Do not do other work during class time. Be respectful of others’ opinions, share interesting things related to the discussion, be mindful of others who may be more shy than you. Students are invited to prepare presentations for class related to course material or to their own explorations of sovereignty. Presentations will be considered extra credit toward enhancing the class participation grade.
Midterm Exam
Short answer, open book essay exam. You will be provided 6 questions, you will choose 4 and write no more than 1000 words to answer each question. Your answers should be in the form of an academic argument, not a summary of readings, and will be graded on the demonstrated understanding of the material and the ability to blend the ideas of various authors together into one synthesized, short essay.
Final Paper
Write 15-20 pages on a topic related to the course materials and your own research project. This will be graded on the extent to which it makes an original argument, attends to course materials, has a sophisticated literature review, and provides convincing evidence in support of the argument. The paper should be in a formal academic style and should be considered a draft essay for a journal publication.
Pop Quiz
At random moments during the course, the professor will announce a pop quiz. Students will be given 15 min at the beginning of class to answer a question related to the week’s readings. AI use will not be tolerated for these quizzes. Quizzes are scored on a 10-point scale according to the extent to which the question is answered and the student demonstrates having read and understood the assignment.

title: 全球衛生治理 Global Health Governance
description:
Today’s world is becoming more interconnected and globalized. Public health issues — such as infectious diseases, non-communicable diseases, climate change, and emerging technologies — are no longer national or regional problems; they are increasingly addressed through a global, integrated, and multidisciplinary approach.
This course empowers students, future policy-makers, and practitioners to analyze and engage with global health issues. Each week introduces a topic in global health governance — such as the World Health Organization and the International Health Regulations, pandemic preparedness, climate change and human health, health technology and digital health, health financing, and One Health — led by the instructors or invited guest speakers. Reflecting recent World Health Assembly priorities, the 2026 edition gives expanded attention to climate change and human health, health technology, and the financing of global health.
In the final weeks, the class executes a simulated public health emergency under the World Health Organization framework (the WHO Simulation), joined by outside experts, civil society, and journalists. Students are divided into four to five countries and assigned roles as key legal, policy, and public health decision-makers responding to the scenario. The simulation consolidates what students learn across the term and builds their competencies in global health governance.
objectives:
• Understand current global health issues and risks, including emerging infectious diseases, non-communicable diseases, climate change, and the role of new health technologies.
• Understand how global health governance works — its institutions, strengths, and weaknesses in addressing global health challenges.
• Develop the ability to participate in international conferences, deliver oral presentations, and collaborate in teams.
• Build research capabilities using media, literature, and databases, and gain front-line experience of health policy-making through the WHO Simulation.
• Broaden horizons beyond students’ own disciplines, deepening understanding of public health, biomedicine, law, and international relations.
grading:
• Class participation — 10%
• Project presentation and report — 30%
• WHO Simulation — 40%
• Final report — 20%

title: 中國大陸的政治發展 Political Development of Mainland China
description: China is the second largest economy in the world and is gorwing in influence at the global stage. And yet, the country is traversing in a very different path of development as with many countries in the West. The Political Economy of China class is designed to help students who may not have profound knowledge of China to get to know the country’s basic political system, processes, ideology, leadership, institutions, and developments. Important history of develpments at various stages as well as key leaders such as Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, and Xi Jinping will be emphasized. Especially attention will be prioritized to characteristics of the leadership and decision-making process. China's political structure of one-party dictatorship will also be examined, along with the meaning of China model.
objectives: The purpose of the class is to build a fundamental knowledge base of China for students so that they might be able to feel more comfortable in the future when employment demands professionalism. The class will also provide solid foudation for students who want to advance their studies in China in the future.

title: 會計學 Accounting for International Managers
description:
Course Description
This course consists of two subjects: fundamental financial accounting and managerial accounting. Financial accounting is the process of recording, summarizing and reporting a company's business transactions through financial statements. Managerial accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, analyzing, interpreting, and communicating information to managers for the pursuit of an organization's goals. This course introduces basic principles of accounting theory and practice and emphasizes on how to analyse, process, and apply accounting information in decision-making from the perspective of managers and financial statement users. Topics covered include accrual basis accounting, the accounting cycle, cost accounting, product pricing, capital expenditures, performance evaluation, preparation of financial statements, and financial statement analysis. Students will study the nature of assets, liabilities, owners’ equity, and budgeting while learning to use reported financial information for purposes of making decisions about the company.
objectives:
Aims & Objectives
Accounting is the language of business, facilitating communication of the financial aspects of business. This module provides an introduction to the financial and managerial accounting. The activities and events of a business entity are summarised by the financial accounting process into financial statements to be used by external users such as investors and creditors and internal users such as executives and controllers. Such users would need to understand both the financial accounting process and its outputs in order to make investing or production decisions. Therefore, students will learn how to prepare simple financial statements and how to read, understand and analyze financial data for decision-making. Published financial statements of listed companies will be used as examples.
Learning Outcomes
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
Understand the basic concepts and principles underlying financial accounting.
Comprehend the process that results in published financial statements.
Account for common elements of the financial statements.
Prepare simple financial statements in an appropriate International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) format
Analyse and interpret financial statements using financial analysis techniques.
Utilize cost accounting information in an organization's operation.
Develop the ability to use various tools and models to support business decisions and to analyze the issues related to the implementing of the decisions.
