title: 海外學習 Overseas Learning
description:
As a core component of the GCIT curriculum, students are required to fulfill this program requirement by completing either Overseas Learning or a Domestic Internship. This course option is available only to GCIT students from their second semester of enrollment onward.
This course supports students in participating in overseas internships or GCIT-organized study tours, academic visits, and conferences. Through these experiences, students gain first-hand international exposure to media, communication practices, and cross-cultural environments.
This course accommodates two types of overseas experiences for GCIT students:
students who obtain their own overseas internships, and
students participating in GCIT-organized study tours, academic visits, or conferences.
All overseas experiences must have a minimum duration of one month. There is no regular class session for this course; instead, students are expected to maintain communication with the instructor throughout their overseas experience.
As this is a subsidized course supported by the Ministry of Culture, students are required to submit a clear and well-structured proposal in advance. The proposal must include the name and contact information of a supervisor or mentor who can evaluate the student’s performance during the overseas period.
This course is evaluated on a Pass/Fail basis, based on the successful completion of the overseas experience and all required deliverables. The goal of the course is for students to gain first-hand international experience and develop the ability to reflect on and present their learning outcomes.
objectives:
This course aims to:
Support students in planning and completing overseas learning experiences
Develop students’ understanding of global media and communication environments
Strengthen students’ ability to reflect on and present international experiences
Learning Outcomes
Upon completion of the course, students will be able to:
Complete an overseas internship or academic experience
Analyze and reflect on communication practices in an international context
Present their overseas experience in a clear and structured format

This course is evaluated on a Pass/Fail basis.
To receive a Pass, students must complete the overseas experience and fulfill the following requirements:

Maintain communication with the instructor

title: 國際智慧財產權法專題研究(一) Seminar on International Intellectual Property Law (I)
description:
Being independent of Seminar II, the course (Seminar I) is designed to examine intellectual property (IP) law and policy in the international arena by addressing the core international agreements governing intellectual property, such as the Paris Convention, and the Berne Convention; and the TRIPS Agreement (Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights). We will focus on the legal and economic implications of the international intellectual property standards in the light of prior Conventions, with particular regard to such topics as copyrights, patents, trademark, and trade secrets.
There is no pre-requisite for this course. Background in intellectual property laws is not necessary, although it may occasionally help you understand the subject. The materials for class will be assigned according to the instructor's class schedule.
objectives:
This course aims to help students understand the essential IP issues in the international arena. Through reading, discussion, instructor’s questions, and class presentations, this course should help students recognize the economic, political, and technological dimensions associated with international IP. A minor goal is to equipped students with the basic language capabilities to deal with international IP issues.
This is an English-taught course. By and large, during the first half of this semester, each meeting day will be proceeded via Socratic approach to help students understand the essence of reading assignment. Students have the obligation to read the assignment before class, and are strongly encouraged to participate in the discussion over the background and legal issues under the assignment. All students, divided to 6 groups, will normally be invited by the instructor to serve as teaching assistants, at turns, to present the assignment and lead the classmates to answer questions in class. Of course, those who are not on duty are always welcome to participate as well.
Another half of this semester is a seminar on IP. Students will be separated into the presenting groups. Each group has to present once in the semester a draft developed in an International IP-related topic. Presenters are responsible for answering questions raised by commentators and other colleagues. Presenters are required to email the abstract of their presentation by 5:00 pm Wednesday before the class. Moreover, each group has to serve as commentators once for their colleague’s presentation.
A final paper has to be submitted in the end of the semester on a group base. It is preferred that this final paper derives from the students’ presentation, and incorporates their own responses, and their colleagues’ comments. Papers should be printed on A4 size papers. Ideally, a final paper written in English should be around 3500-5,000 words, the due day of final papers is December 31, 2026.
grading:
Class Participation 35%
Presentation of the Assignment (TA Session) 20%
Comment on Your Colleague's Presentation (TA Session) 10%
Final Paper 35%
It should be noted that the grading is not based on the fluency of English speaking, but rather on the willingness to express your idea in English. Those who don't speak English well can still perform well in this class if they do work hard and are willing to participate.

title: 創新領導與新興科技 Leadership for Innovation in Emerging Technologies
objectives:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
Define and describe eight leadership styles and four organizational frames. (Bloom’s Taxonomy: Remember, Understand)
Apply frame–leadership pairings to analyze challenges and opportunities in emerging technologies. (Apply)
Analyze and interpret the strengths and growth areas of various leadership styles in the context of emerging technology adoption. (Analyze)
Evaluate leadership strategies for responsible technology adoption. (Evaluate)

title: 生成式AI及資料科學應用實作 Capstone: Practice of Generative AI and Data Science
description:
In recent years, Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an important tool for solving social problems. However, due to its ongoing development, many gaps still need to be filled to meet the professional requirements of various industries. This course aims to train students to utilize the latest technologies in Generative AI and data science to develop projects that can address real-world challenges. The technology covered includes, but is not limited to, diverse content (such as text, audio, and video) connections, fine-tuning, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
This course is offered in collaboration with AMD and other partner institutions, which will provide students with access to the latest AI computing equipment and real-world AI projects. Students will use tools such as Claude Code and Codex to build AI agents and complete project-based assignments. However, students who wish to enroll are expected to have completed prior coursework in Python programming so that they can evaluate and verify code generated by GenAI tools.
objectives: The capstone course is divided into three main sections: AI computing equipment training, AI project introduction, and hands-on practice. In the first section, students will be introduced to the AMD server, the ICI NVIDIA server, the installation and use of Claude Code and Codex, and AI agents and workflows. In the second section, partner organizations will present AI projects based on current industry needs and define the objectives of each project. In the third section, students will follow detailed guidelines provided by instructors and professional mentors to complete their assigned projects.

title: 人工智慧、媒體與資訊完整性 AI, Media, and Information Integrity
description: This course offers a critical examination of the intersection of artificial intelligence, media, and information integrity. It equips students with conceptual frameworks and analytical lenses to critically appraise the role and impact of AI in contemporary media ecosystems. Students will explore how AI technologies shape the production, dissemination, and perception of information in digital spaces, while interrogating the assumptions, narratives, and power structures embedded in these systems. Topics include AI’s role in misinformation, conspiracy theories, deepfakes, persuasion, journalism, ethics, and democracy. Emphasis is placed on critically reading both media representations of AI and the socio-technical dynamics underlying its development and use. Through lectures, discussions, and assignments, students will evaluate how AI reconfigures trust, authority, labor, and responsibility in media, and assess its broader implications for information integrity and democratic life.
objectives:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
Understand the role of AI in shaping media and information integrity.
Critically analyze AI-driven misinformation, conspiracy theories, and deepfakes.
Evaluate ethical and political implications of AI in journalism, advertising, and democracy.
Develop strategies to foster trust and integrity in online spaces influenced by AI.
Apply theoretical and analytical frameworks to assess AI’s cultural and societal impact.

Individual Class Discussion Lead (15%)

Critical examination of AI chatbot, details to be discussed in class (due July 10).
Final Group Project (presentation 20%, research report 20%)
Students will work in teams to examine how generative AI is socially represented across different platforms (presentation on July 22, research paper due July 24)

description: This course is specifically designed to thoroughly explore the theoretical foundations of communication, with a particular emphasis on media effects. description: This graduate-level course explores the conceptual foundations, design principles, and practical applications of immersive technologies, including Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR), and Mixed Reality (MR). Students will engage with theoretical frameworks such as experiential learning, embodied cognition, and affordance, while critically examining how these principles guide the design and evaluation of immersive experiences. The course follows a two-cycle learning design: each conceptually focused week features group-led discussions on assigned readings, followed by a group-based case study application the following week. Through this iterative approach, students actively connect theory with practice, developing hands-on skills in designing, analyzing, and critiquing immersive technology applications. The course also incorporates site visits, guest lectures, and expert panel presentations to broaden perspectives and foster interdisciplinary understanding...
objectives:

Understand Core Concepts: Explain the foundational principles of AR, VR, and MR, including experiential learning, embodied cognition, and affordance.
Apply Design Principles: Demonstrate the ability to apply design principles in immersive environments, integrating theoretical knowledge into practical solutions.
Engage in Iterative Learning: Participate effectively in group-led discussions and case study analyses, using the two-cycle structure to deepen understanding and problem-solving skills.
Critically Analyze Applications: Evaluate AR/VR/MR systems and experiences using evidence-based criteria, including usability, affordances, and user engagement.
Communicate Insights: Present project outcomes, provide constructive peer critique, and articulate design rationale in both written and oral formats.
Integrate Multidisciplinary Perspectives: Examine immersive technologies in educational, industrial, and creative contexts, recognizing the interplay of technical, cognitive, and social factors.

title: 女性影像與新媒體 Women's Cinema and New Media: From Gaze to Play
description:
What is Women’s Cinema? In Women’s Cinema: The Contested Screen, Alison Butler argues that “’Women’s cinema’ is a complex critical, theoretical and institutional construct, brought into existence by audiences, film-makers, journalists, curators, an academics and maintained only by their continuing interest: a hybrid concept, arising from a number of overlapping practices and discourses...” (Alison Butler, 2003, 2)
The course tackles such complex, hybrid, constructed term by not only understanding it as “works made by women” or “films designed for the female audience,” but by learning about the history and social context in which women have engagd with cinema and new media, both as creators and consumers, and consider the complex interplay between production, consumption, and representation in relation to women and film/media texts.
To do so, the course examines women’s roles, rerpesentations, and experiences from early cinema to comtemporary digital culture. Students are introduced to a diverse set of methodologies and theoretical frameworks which will allow them to explore works from films, television, aniem, video games, and other media forms from various cultures; from the perspectives of film history, auteur, spectatorhsip, genre, feminist criticism, industry, circulation, globalization, and (trans)nationalism. By combining these interdisciplinary approaches, the course introduces a feminist intevention to the existing paradigms and provides studenst with a thorough grasp of women’s cinema and media culture from its historical origins to its current manifestations.
Final projects may take the form of traditional research papers, creative media work, or essay films, encouraging students to engage with course materials through critical and/or creative expression.
objectives:
Identify key figures and movements in the history of women’s cinema.
Analyze films and media texts from a feminist perspective, considering the role of gender, genre, and cultural context.
Evaluate the impact of women filmmakers and media creators in world cinema and media culture.
Engage with critical theories and debates surrounding women and film/media in diverse perspectives.
Develop research and presentation skills through class discussion, assignments and a final research project, which may take the form of a written paper, creative media work, or essay film.

description:
Design Thinking for Innovative Talent and Teams in the AI Era
— Build your purposeful career and abundant life
📌 Important Notice Before the First Class
Students who wish to take this course should carefully read the description and policies below, and complete the registration form.
Mandatory Attendance: You must attend the first class (9am Sep. 8, 2026) to be considered a candidate for enrollment.

Course Format: This is a highly interactive course featuring extensive teamwork and collaborative activities. Full engagement and active participation are expected throughout each session.
Class Capacity: : The standard enrollment limit is 25 students (for credit). An additional 5 slots are available for exchange students and visiting scholars.
Enrollment Notification:

🌟 Testimonials
"It’s very satisfying knowing that I am not alone in this journey. I have a group to share my daily achievements and support each other... It feels like life consultation; each class allows us to reflect on our path more and more. Thanks for this amazing journey!!"

— Inspiring feedback from NCCU DT Class of 2024–2025!
🌟 Course Introduction
In an AI era defined by rapid change and ambiguity, this course equips advanced undergraduate and graduate students with Design Thinking (DT) principles and innovative problem-solving tools to build effective teams and thrive in both life and career.
To avoid the pitfall of learning theory without practice, every single session in this course is divided into a "Two-Half Structure":
The Macro Track (1st half): Master macro-level design methodologies, cross-disciplinary tools, and tech-AI mindsets applicable to corporate and global ecosystems.
The Micro Track (2nd half): Turn the lens inward. You will use your own life as a sandbox for a semester-long Personal Project, executing real-world behavior design experiments.
Our curriculum spans 16 transformative weeks, structured into three golden phases:
Phase 1: DT Fundamentals & Habit-Forming Project (Weeks 1–5): Master classical d.school methodologies while executing a SMART habit-design experiment to optimize your personal energy.
Phase 2: AI-powered DT & Good Life Upgrade (Weeks 6–10): Navigate the digital age. Learn to leverage AI as a high-performance collaborative peer while scaling your habits into a Good Life Project Prototype anchored in Purpose, Achievement, and Enjoyment.
Phase 3: Re-engineering of Life, Career & Resilience (Weeks 11–15): Apply design mindsets to your future career blueprint. Tackle your life priorities, navigate unchangeable limitations, map out alternative pathways, and establish your personal "Life Board of Directors" to bounce back gracefully from setbacks.
🧭 Guidance & Expectations
🧭 For Introverts:
About one-third of our past students identified themselves as introverts before joining. By the end of the semester, every single one of them successfully found their rhythm and navigated the course beautifully. Many were pleasantly surprised by how many genuine friendships they formed along the way!
🧭 For busy students with heavy credit loads or extracurriculars:
"I really appreciate the engaging courses you’ve designed. I never thought I would have this much fun in a college classroom. Thank you!!"
This course is designed to be a space where you can pause, recharge, have fun, and create something inspiring for yourself, your team, and the world. Most students find our sessions to be a rewarding break from their usual academic stress.
🧭 Regarding Attendance (Can I maintain the commitment?):
Last year, 50% of the students maintained near-perfect attendance (100%, or missing only 1 class due to medical reasons). Only 5% struggled to meet the course standards. Please note our attendance policy: 3 absences will trigger a formal warning, and a 4th absence will automatically result in a failing grade (no credit).
🎯 Three Major Takeaways:
DT & Tech Mastery: Master the core mindsets of Design Thinking (e.g., Embrace Ambiguity, Defer Judgment, Bias toward Action) while learning to co-ideate with AI, giving you a distinct competitive edge in the technological era.
Elevated Teamwork Confidence: Foster advanced communication, psychological safety, and leadership skills through hands-on collaboration simulations and peer feedback frameworks.
Life Resilience & Navigation: Reframe life's bottlenecks, map out adaptive alternative pathways, and intentionally design a sustainable future—discovering a beautifully iterated "new version of yourself" along the way.

week 1 | Course Introduction & Icebreaking
Instructional Objectives | • Familiarize students with course expectations, grading policies, and the interactive dynamic. • Build early psychological safety and connection among peers.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Lecture on the course blueprint, the "Two-Half Structure," and instructional objectives. • Micro Track: Rapid networking simulation and team formation roles overview.
week 2 | Phase 1: Empathy & Self-Awareness
Instructional Objectives | • Master foundational empathy map and journey map tools. • Discover hidden personal needs and energy drains in daily routines.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Lecture on user research methodologies, Empathy Maps, Journey Maps, and case studies. • Micro Track: Launching the Habit-Forming Project by defining personal "Fundamentals" (sleep, movement, energy).
week 3 | Phase 1: Problem Definition & Root Causes
Instructional Objectives | • Reframe chaotic raw data into actionable "How-Might-We" (HMW) design statements. • Identify root causes of personal inconsistency rather than surface symptoms.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Workshop on 2x2 definition tables, drafting Need Statements, and mastering the art of problem reframing. • Micro Track: Executing the "6A Self-Awareness Framework" to pinpoint the primary obstacles in personal habits.
week 4 | Phase 1: Ideation & Trigger Design
Instructional Objectives | • Practice deferring judgment and brainstorming high-volume, unconventional solutions. • Design environmental triggers and psychological cues to sustain habits without pure willpower.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Brainstorming drills focused on "Wild Ideas" and leveraging diverse peer perspectives for creative problem-solving. • Micro Track: Deconstructing the "7 Core Desires" to creatively design attractive psychological triggers for personal habits.
week 5 | Phase 1: Prototyping Daily Rituals
Instructional Objectives | • Shift from overthinking to rapid execution (Bias toward Action). • Build a tangible, visual tracker for personal morning or evening rituals.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Hands-on "Six-Thinking-Hats" simulation to systematically evaluate and refine experimental ideas. • Micro Track: Visualizing an ideal day's ritual as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) utilizing mindful anchors (Smile, Breathe, Align).
week 6 | Phase 1: Iteration & Habit 2.0 Launch
Instructional Objectives | • Learn to harvest and synthesize experimental data from feedback loops. • Formulate a resilient, long-term habit framework based on behavior science.

week 7 | Phase 2: Tech Mindsets & Attention Economy

Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Exploration of AI as a collaborative peer and the psychological impacts of constant digital notifications. • Micro Track: Auditing personal tech habits and tracking screen-time triggers utilizing the Internal Family Systems (IFS) "Thoughts are Clouds" concept.
week 8 | Phase 2: Core Self & Reclaiming Attention
Instructional Objectives | • Master info-architecture and data-synthesis using advanced prompting mindsets. • Design structural boundaries to protect mental workspace and emotional energy.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Practice prompting as a tool for structuring information and clarifying core intent (The "Lead-from-Within" mindset). • Micro Track: Establishing personalized digital boundaries and building an emotional fortress against notification anxiety.
week 9 | Phase 2: Human-AI Collaboration
Instructional Objectives | • Evaluate human-AI partnerships through the lens of Self-Determination Theory. • Leverage generative AI to break team groupthink and solve bottlenecked problems.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Deep dive into Self-Determination Theory (Autonomy, Competence, Relatedness) within the context of automated technology. • Micro Track: Using AI as a personalized coaching partner to analyze and optimize project hurdles without losing human agency.
week 10 | Phase 2: Shaping the Good Life Blueprint
Instructional Objectives | • Transition from micro-habits to macro life design across Purpose, Achievement, and Enjoyment. • Sketch the initial vision and milestone markers for a short-term life project.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Deconstructing the "Happiness Triangle" and mapping personal alignment with Ikigai principles. • Micro Track: Mapping out the 5 Gold Elements of the Good Life Project Prototype via a structured mind map.
week 11 | Phase 2: Tech Audit & Constructive Feedback
Instructional Objectives | • Master rapid digital prototyping using integrated tools. • Practice d.school feedback frameworks to refine project frameworks with peers.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Strategic breakdown of tech-team roles (Hacker, Goal-Getter, Visionary) and digital prototyping workflows .• Micro Track: Conducting a comprehensive Tech Audit for the Good Life blueprint and practicing the "i like, i wish, i wonder" peer-review matrix.
week 12 | Phase 3: The Well-being Triangle
Instructional Objectives | • Audit the dynamic tension between external career achievements and internal psychological health. • Formulate immediate interventions to correct lifestyle imbalances.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Interactive debate on the conflicts within the Well-being Triangle (Life Priorities, Career Focus & Resilience) .• Micro Track: Striking a radical balance in individual project timelines to actively protect personal mental well-being.
week 13 | Phase 3: Dynamic Reframing & Constraints
Instructional Objectives | • Distinguish between structural "Gravity Problems" and solvable design challenges. • Reframe unchangeable realities into creative boundaries for career pivot options.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Introducing the "Three Arrows for Decision Making" and categorizing career/life constraints. • Micro Track: Mapping out Alternative Pathways (Plan B & C) for individual projects to successfully bypass major bottlenecks.
week 14 | Phase 3: Failure Immunity & Self-Compassion

title: 科技社會與文化 Technoscience, Society & Culture
description:
本課程從科學與技術研究(Science and Technology Studies, STS)的視角,探討科學、技術與社會文化、政治之間複雜交織的關係。課程將從技術研究與科學研究作為出發,系統性介紹STS的多元分析觀點,包括科學知識社會學、技術的社會建構與形塑、行動者網絡理論、科技的政治性、公民科學中的專家與常民知識、女性主義科技研究,以及本體論與物質的轉向等。這些理論工具將幫助學生深入理解科技與社會的互動過程,並培養批判性思考能力。
課程強調科技變遷與社會變動的共構關係,通過具體案例說明兩者如何相互塑造。例如,英國工業化過程中運河開鑿與工程師專業的形成、英國的會計師的客觀性建構,以及美國電網發展等大型社技系統的案例,都展示了技術、材料、法律、政策和管理等多面向的交互作用。這些案例將幫助學生理解科技發展如何深刻影響社會結構,同時社會因素又如何塑造科技的發展方向。
透過本課程,學生將理解科學家、工程師和產業市場如何緊密連結,形成穩固的社會技術體制。同時,課程也將探討科技內在的政治、文化與性別特性,以及專家知識在公共事務中的權威地位和操作:這將使學生認識到科技並非中立的工具,而是特定價值觀和權力關係的社會媒介。希望學生以氣候變遷與太陽光電、離岸風電等,來說明STS理論如何應用於理解現實問題。
objectives:
辨識科技內生的政治、文化與性別特性,科技不僅只是工程師與科學的事情,科技與我們日常生活的種種選擇與安排有著持續的相互鞏固關係。
明白科學知識與專業所帶有的公共權威意涵,與理解技術物的設計與操作中的性別建構。
學習台灣在能源轉型上所面臨的最新議題,例如電網與儲能設施、光電與生態衝突、離岸風電中的白海豚、候鳥的生態保育等等。
明白專家知識如何介入與操作技術性的公共議題,這當中充滿權衡與詮釋與協商彈性。
grading:
(50%) 課堂口頭摘要報告
以檔案形式呈現,一週兩人,進行詳細的文獻摘要、提出讀後問題與議題回應。
(50%) 課後心得與課堂參與
共需繳交10次的課後心得,每篇約一頁,主要針對當週文章的核心論點與課堂內容進行說明,並提出個人最具啟發的部分。課堂的參與討論表現是主要評分項目。
本課程以課堂的持續參與為主,並希望能啟發碩士論文研究方向。

title: AI與倫理 Artificial Intelligence and Ethics
description:
Recent advances in computing may place us at the threshold of a unique turning point in human history. Soon we are likely to entrust management of our environment, economy, security, infrastructure, food production, healthcare, and to a large degree even our personal activities, to artificially intelligent computer systems.
The prospect of "turning over the keys" to increasingly autonomous systems raises many complex and troubling questions. How will society respond as versatile robots and machine-learning systems displace an ever-expanding spectrum of blue- and white-collar workers? Will the benefits of this technological revolution be broadly distributed or accrue to a lucky few? How can we ensure that these systems respect our ethical principles when they make decisions at speeds and for rationales that exceed our ability to comprehend? What, if any, legal rights and responsibilities should we grant them? And should we regard them merely as sophisticated tools or as a newly emerging form of life?
隨著近期AI與自動化設備之技術發展,已達到人類歷史發展之轉折點,人類非常可能大規模地將環境、經濟發展、安全、基礎設備、食物生產與分配、健康照護與保險交由AI與自動化設備安排與執行。
本課程目標在介紹AI技術對於倫理與法律制度之衝擊。此次邀請國內外法學者與學生一同參與線上課程,營造國際化學習環境,豐富學生學習資源,增進臺灣與各國學生對於AI技術將造成的社會、政治、經濟與文化衝擊等議題,例如:AI與自動化設備取代白領與藍領勞工工作機會之社會衝擊評估與對應?AI與自動化設備之技術革命帶來之整體利益,是否能公平分配?如何在AI與自動化設備進行自動決策時,確保道德原則?法律是否該賦予AI與自動化設備法律權利與責任,抑或僅是工具或輔助物?進行學術與文化交流,並由臺灣學者介紹臺灣與美國現行與正在研擬之相關法律制度與政策以資比較,藉此使學生能瞭解AI所帶來的衝擊,增進學生到東協國進修或就業的動力,同時也能開展臺灣與東協國家間學術互動與合作的契機。
objectives:

The goal of this course is to equip students with the intellectual tools, ethical foundation, and psychological framework to successfully navigate the coming age of intelligent machines.

title: 台灣近代史 Modern Taiwanese History
description:
本課程以台灣為觀察範例,使來自台灣、東亞、中南美洲及歐洲學生,回顧東亞自19世紀中期起,至20世紀80年代後期止,在西方衝擊下,於政治、經濟、社會、文化四個面向近代化回應。本課程分為三個時期:近代化初期(1860-1895); 日治時期(1895-1945); 中華民國政府威權統治時期 (1945-1987)。近代化初期,本課程探討台灣在清領時期既存之政經結構及社會脈絡,以及中、日兩國於19世紀中後期啟動近代化歷程,對台灣及東亞之影響。其後,本課程介紹日本帝國統治台灣後,推行近代化治理及亞洲主義,對台灣與西太平洋各地的衝擊及其回應。最後,本課程介紹二次大戰後,台灣因冷戰結構以及國共對抗,進入威權統治及經濟、社會結構調整,逐步邁向民主化過程。本課程也探討19世紀中葉以來,分別探討西方在各時期,對東亞/西太平洋區域政治、經濟、社會、文化的衝擊、回應與相互調整,及對當代東亞政治、經濟、社會層面之影響。
This course focuses on the evolution of modernity in Taiwan and East Asia from the mid-19th century to the 1980s. This course analyzes how the concept of modernity was applied to and impacted Taiwanese society in three periods: the late Ching Imperial Rule Period (1860-1895), the Japanese rule period (1895–1945), and the period of strict control by the ROC government (1945–1987).
After the Second Opium War, Taiwan engaged in the global capital market via opening the treaty ports in 1860. The preachers and business people from the west and Asian pacific areas substantially transformed the existing eco-political landscape in Taiwan. The Ching government had implemented modern governing and changed its negative defensive strategies. And the local elites in Taiwan coordinated with the Ching government to aggregate capitals and enhanced their political autonomy.
After the Sino-Japanese War, in 1895, the Ching Empire ceded Taiwan to Japan. The Empire of Japan established a colonial regime in Taiwan. The Government-General of Taiwan (GGT) used its power to implement modern and colonial governing in Taiwan. In addition to maximizing economic capital in metropolitan Japan, the colonial government also lingered between the strategies of assimilation and non-assimilation. This debate led identity crisis among local elites in Taiwan for social movements.
After World War II, the Republic of China (ROC), dominated by the ruling party, the Kuomintang (KMT), took over Taiwan. After the Chinese Civil War outbreak, the Temporary Provisions During the Period of National Mobilization for Suppression of the Communist Rebellion (temporary provisions) were enacted in 1948, suspending the human rights provisions within the ROC Constitution. In 1949, the ROC moved its central government to Taiwan, transforming Taiwan from a vast territory to a de facto nation. Meanwhile, the ROC government changed the industry to integrate into the global market more optimal, leading to the Taiwan miracle and people consciousness in the 1980s. With the end of the temporary provisions, the ROC revived its constitution in 1991 and turned Taiwan to a new page.
objectives:
1. 協助學生理解現代性概念,及台灣與東亞/西太平洋區域,近代化的起源及特徵。
2. 協助學生培養具有歷史思維之分析當代政治、經濟、法律與社會議題之能力。
1. Be able to identify and critically analyze the concept of modernity, the origin of modernization, and its implications in East Asia.
2. Be able to apply historical thinking to critically discuss and analyze the political, economic, social, and legal issues in East Asia.

title: 機器人與AI互動專題:理論與研究 Seminar on Human-Robot Interaction and Human-AI Interaction: Theories and Research
description:
請注意:此門課程將以英語授課,所有的課間報告與討論也將以英文進行。Note: This course will be taught in English. All the in-class presentations and discussions will also be in English.
This seminar course explores advanced theories and research in Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) and Human-AI Interaction (HAI). Students will examine cutting-edge studies and core concepts in the field, including interaction dynamics, social implications, and the evolving roles of robots and AI agents in human environments. Through in-depth discussions and analyses of academic papers, students will critically evaluate the theoretical and empirical foundations of HRI and HAI while considering their applications in diverse contexts. The course also emphasizes understanding how these technologies influence communication, collaboration, and social structures.
objectives:
By the end of this course, students will:
Understand foundational and emerging theories in HRI and HAI.
Develop a comprehensive knowledge of key frameworks and concepts in the field.
Critically analyze academic literature.
Engage with research papers to evaluate methodologies, findings, and implications.
Examine social and ethical impacts of HRI/HAI technologies.
Discuss how robots and AI agents shape societal norms and values.
Apply theoretical insights to real-world scenarios.
Consider how research findings can inform future design and applications.
Communicate academic ideas effectively.
Lead and contribute to seminar discussions with clear and critical perspectives.
grading:
The total score of 100 points will be the accumulation of these activities:
Leading a class (20%): Each student will lead one class over the course of the semester. (Students may form a team to co-lead. I will decide the size of the teams in the first week.) The class lead(s) will be responsible for the assigned readings and, if preferred, selecting 1-2 additional articles for students to read that apply concepts from that week’s readings to current work in Human-AI Interaction (HAII), Human-Robot Interaction (HRI), Computer-mediated communication (CMC), human-computer interaction (HCI), or a related area. Readings must be assigned to the rest of the class a week in advance. During the class session, the student(s) will be the class lead(s) to lead the discussion. The class lead(s) are encouraged to include multiple activities and up-to-date examples (such as short videos, memes, recent popular SNS posts, other student’s online discussion) to facilitate the discussion.
Online Discussion (15%): Each week (except for Week 1, team project presentation, team project data collection, and final poster sessions), students are expected to post comments on the topic in the online forum set up for that week.
Each post should include (a) a short description of one surprising or interesting point from the readings assigned for that week, something you did not know before or had not thought deeply about; and (b) some implications of this interesting point for your own research or experience. Posts should be about 150-300 words and must be completed by 6 PM one day before the class to receive credit.
Students should also comment on two other student's posts by 10 PM one day before the class to receive full credit.
Each student is allowed to miss two weeks without any need for explanation, but no late submission will be accepted. If a student misses more than two assignments, no excuses will be accepted for subsequent missed assignments.
Team Research Projects (55%): Students will work in teams to conduct a research project on an HRI or HAII topic. This project can be design-oriented, theoretical analysis, or related to human’s behavior related to intelligent agents.
Students are expected to work on:
Idea Pitch (5%): Students will prepare 2-3 research topics, why they find these topics interesting and important, supported by key previous studies (2-4 for each topic). Every research topic should be less than 1 page, double spaced, excluding tables and figures.
Midterm Research Proposal Presentation (15%): Students will present (1) one chosen research topic, (2) a refined introduction of research motivation supported by a brief literature review (with clear definitions of the main concepts, and at least 4 relevant studies), and (3) proposed research methods. The presentation should be between 8-12 minutes, followed by 5 minutes of Q&A.
Final Poster Session (15%): Each research project team will present its research and results to the class via a short oral presentation and a poster. Students also need to prepare a 1-2 minute of short video and upload it onto YouTube to attract attention to their research. Further details will be provided later in the semester.
Final Report (20%): Students will write a report of the project using standard report-writing style (e.g., introduction, related work (literature review), hypotheses, method, results, discussion). The research report should be 10-15 pages, double spaced, excluding tables and figures.
Class participation (10%):
Active participation is essential for this course. Students are expected to come to each class prepared, having read and taken notes on the assigned materials. You may be called on to summarize the main arguments, strengths, weaknesses, or critiques of any assigned reading.
To receive full participation credit, each student must contribute verbally at least twice per class session. Simply attending class without speaking will result in zero points for participation that day.
Each student may miss up to two classes without explanation. However, no additional absences will be excused, regardless of the reason. In addition, students must not miss the class sessions during which they are responsible for leading discussions, presenting team projects, collecting data, or participating in the final poster session.
Bonus (2%): Participating in any user studies related to communication, design, psychology, and human-computer interaction at NCCU will lead to +0.5 of the final semester points. Students can participate in up to 4 studies. (If a study takes more than 30 minutes, it counts as 2 studies.)

title: 影音媒體創新與互動科技 Audiovisual Media Innovation & Interactive Technologies
description:
生成式AI、XR等科技迅速發展,促使影音產業企製與行銷之創新轉型,產製虛擬融合的影音內容,透過自媒體品牌策略性經營,透過跨平台社群媒體影音行銷推播,網路影音能病毒式迅速傳播,吸引觀眾眼球及網路聲量。
本學期授課包含兩層面:1) 知識面: 了解AI、XR新科技在影音媒體產業、組織與內容企製之創新因素、流程與影響,本學期授課重點為虛擬製作(virtual production)、生成式AI(Gen-AI); 2) 實務面: 同學創立自媒體影音品牌,企製網路影音內容(結合virtual production & Gen-AI),藉由社群行銷推廣頻道內容,解讀網路數據洞悉觀眾與評估成效。
本產學合作創新課程涵括新媒體影音企製、經營、行銷及成效評估整體學習目標,與專家實驗AI及XR科技在影音自媒體上之創新應用,讓同學透過虛擬製作與生成式AI工具做出有區隔性、質量兼優的創新內容,體驗如何將新科技融合於影音企製,汲取自媒體品牌經營之實戰經驗,並理解現行新媒體產業生態與作業流程,提升未來出社會競爭力,預先與業界接軌。
objectives:
課程目標
生成式AI時代來臨,影音媒體新科技發展出虛擬結合創新內容,提高臨場感與互動性,帶來使用者沉浸式體驗,Gen-AI在影音實驗性應用也不斷發展。本課程藉由實務分享及實戰教學,讓同學們了解Gen-AI、XR及互動科技在影音媒體創新應用。課程重點包括:自媒體影音企製(結合Gen-AI與XR科技)、影音媒體品牌規畫與影音社群推廣。
影音創新與科技:協助學生了解生成式AI、XR、5G等熱門新科技發展,以及它們對影音產業及生態所帶來衝擊,同時了解多螢、虛實融合的觀影新趨勢,並進一步認識影音媒體結合新科技進行創新、調整或轉型之作法與成效。
影音媒體企製:結合GenAI、XR科技規劃自媒體影音品牌、企製內容,並進行社群行銷,結合知識、know-how及實作經驗,最後以數據評估作品成效,並邀請專家講評企製內容。掌握虛擬製作訣竅,融合生成式AI工具於創新影音內容企製與宣傳工作。

title: 全球傳播與文化 Global Communication and Culture
description: This course is designed to give students an introduction to cross-cultural research and the theories that govern global communication practices. They will have the opportunity to explore their own cultural backgrounds and how that impacts the way they work and communicate with others internationally; they will have the same opportunity to put themselves in others’ shoes to see the world from new perspectives, enabling them to develop sensitive business and marketing strategies, or develop sensitive journalistic stories that will reach their target audience more effectively. The final project will also give them the chance to practice their media skills on a topic related to culture and understanding cultural perspectives on varying issues.
objectives:
Students should be able to discuss basic theories of cross-cultural psychology and apply them to global communication settings.
Students should be able to take the perspective of people from other cultural backgrounds in order to better communicate with internationals.
Students should be able to communicate respectfully and effectively in writing and in new media contexts to a variety of audiences from different cultural contexts.

title: 數位影像媒體實作 Digital Video Media Practices
description: This course introduces students to the principles and practices of video design and dissemination through an integration of theory and application. The course first engages students with a range of theoretical perspectives—including cognitive psychology, multimedia design principles, communication theories, and storytelling frameworks—to develop a solid conceptual foundation for understanding how videos are perceived, processed, and communicated. Building on these theories, students will then apply their knowledge through hands-on activities using digital video tools, experimenting with design techniques and production strategies. By moving from theory to practice, students will critically examine and refine their own video projects, gaining both analytical insight and practical competence in video design and planning.
objectives:
Explain key theoretical perspectives—including cognitive psychology, design theories, and communication frameworks—relevant to video design and dissemination.
Analyze video examples using theoretical principles to evaluate effectiveness in learning, engagement, and communication.
Apply digital video tools and techniques to plan, design, and produce short video projects.
Integrate theory and practice by critically reflecting on the alignment between conceptual frameworks and their own video design choices.
Demonstrate competency in video planning and dissemination, presenting projects that balance theoretical insight with creative execution.
grading:

Class engagement (20%)
Group presentation (25%)
Final report (35%)
Peer review (10%)

description: The goal of the course is to both introduce students to research methodologies within the broad field of Communication Science and give them hands-on experience analyzing data obtained from these varied study types. Students will learn about qualitative (i.e., interviews, focus groups, content analyses) and quantitative (e.g., surveys, experiments) research methodologies, their strengths and weaknesses, and how to consider both methodology and theory when engaging in study design.

Students will be able to design and execute a qualitative research design.
Students will be able to design and execute a quantitative research design.
Students will be able to present study design ideas effectively to grant-givers and reviewers.

title: 人機互動設計 Human-Computer Interaction and Design
description:
This course uses lectures and assignments to help students understand the interaction process between people and products, so that they can learn how to design the best possible interaction experiences with digital media. Here, "products" refers broadly to any object, digital content, or service in our environment.
The course consists of the following units:
The Nature of Interaction. In all things interactive, interaction takes place through an "interface" defined by several core elements. Interacting through interfaces is one of the fundamental ways the world works. This unit takes an analytical approach to what various interface concepts have in common, how they form the basis of human-computer interaction, and how HCI concepts apply across a range of phenomena.
The Psychological Basis of HCI. "Human" is at the core of HCI, but what does that really mean, and what constraints does it impose? What principles guide how people process information within interfaces and interactive processes? Starting with the visual system, this unit introduces perception, memory, cognition, and the laws of human factors engineering — and asks what "intuitive" actually means.
HCI and Communication. This unit covers classical communication theory and the principles of human-to-human dialogue, showing how these principles underlie HCI and how they can be applied to understand the successes and failures of an interaction.
The Context of HCI and Design. This unit introduces basic design-research methods and data presentation, and shows how data can deepen our understanding of both the user (human) and the function (machine).
Methods and Tools for Designing HCI. This unit covers task design axes and goals, along with the design elements of human-computer interfaces — graphical interface elements and conventions, information visualization, perceptual design, and information architecture.
Prototyping and Evaluation of HCI Design. A prototype is a tool for verification and optimization, and effective prototyping must go hand in hand with effective evaluation. This unit introduces a range of prototyping techniques and evaluation methods.
New HCI Technologies. This unit covers the foundational technologies of the metaverse — Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) — and their impact on the future of HCI.
Note: This course will be taught in English by two faculty members: Prof. Yihsiu Chen (陳宜秀) for Weeks 1–8, and Prof. Tsung-yu Yoyo Ho (侯宗佑) for Weeks 9–16.
objectives:
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:
Understand the principles and applications of HCI as a foundation of digital media
Understand the structure, design process, and value of HCI
Apply course content to observe and make sense of everyday phenomena
Apply course content to professional design and production work
Recognize emerging interactive technologies and their possibilities for future development
grading:
Your final grade (out of 100 points) will be based on the accumulation of the following components:
Individual homework (1 assignment): 10 points maximum (10%)
Group assignments (5 assignments): 10 points maximum each (50% total)
Final poster session: 40 points (20% determined by the instructor and TA, 20% determined by your fellow students)

title: 國際新聞報導 International News Reporting
description: This course focuses on learning both fundamental and advanced skills in international news reporting, including essential principles of journalistic ethics and practical simulations of international reporting. The curriculum covers understanding different types of international news, familiarizing oneself with the characteristics of various issues, international relations and geopolitics, and the impact of digital journalism on international reporting. The course will also feature case studies and practical challenges discussed in collaboration with professional instructors with media expertise.
objectives:
The objective of this course is to enable students to understand how international news topics are developed and stories produced. Students may be able to manage and conduct international coverage via news-editing skills and planning.
Through a midterm report and a final project involving simulated reporting, students will demonstrate their comprehension of the course content and achieve the intended learning outcomes.

title: 新媒體與資訊科技 New Media and Information Technology
description: This graduate-level course explores the dynamic intersections of new media, emerging technologies, and their impact on learning, communication, and human interaction. Students will critically engage with topics including smart classrooms, AI and chatbots, mobile devices, virtual worlds, online communities, digital storytelling, eye-tracking techniques, video games, digital curation, and digital ethics. The course also features invited talks and a field trip to EdTech Taiwan 2025, giving students opportunities to connect theoretical insights with real-world practices. In addition to seminar discussions and critical readings, students will explore and observe the functionality of new technologies to deepen their understanding of how they influence education, human behavior, and social interaction.
objectives:

title: 全球研究導論 Introduction to Global Studies
description:
Course Description:
Introduction to Global Studies is a foundational, required course for first-year students at the International College of Innovation (ICI). This course provides students with an interdisciplinary knowledge base in global studies. Together, we will explore three core themes:
Theme 1: What is Global Studies? This section examines the historical context and formation of Global Studies, offering an overview of how the global order has evolved from the modern era to contemporary times. This builds the fundamental knowledge infrastructure for students. Upon this foundation, students will design their own ideal Global Studies curriculum maps during the first roundtable forum.
Theme 2: Why Study Global Studies? In this section, we explore why global issues necessitate interdisciplinary interventions. Through issue-oriented discussions, students will step-by-step become familiar with ICI's three major specialized tracks: Global Governance (GG), Sustainability and Society (SS), and Data Analytics (DA). For the second roundtable forum, students will select a contemporary issue and dissect it through the lenses of these three tracks. These discussions will help students understand how the tracks intertwine within our complex world, while preparing them to choose their specialization within the college in the future.
Theme 3: What Can Global Studies Do? This theme focuses on the “liberal skills” and career possibilities within Global Studies. We will invite ICI alumni, as well as experts from think tanks and NGOs, to share how they apply global studies in their respective professional fields. The third roundtable forum will challenge students to answer “What can global studies do?” through various creative presentations.
In addition to the three themes, three continuous threads of core curriculum designs run throughout the course:
Academic and Career Blueprinting: We will introduce ICI faculty members and their courses, providing students with a panoramic overview of the four-year curriculum at ICI to assist them in mapping out their future studies and career paths.
Collaborative Skill-Building: Through the roundtable forums and extensive teamwork, this course fosters essential communication and coordination skills crucial for interdisciplinary learning.
Reflective Practice: Students will maintain a semester-long Reflexive Study Journal to document their challenges, breakthroughs, and personal growth throughout their interdisciplinary journey.
Enrollment Policy: This foundational course is exclusively reserved for ICI freshmen, double majors, minors, and transfer students. To preserve class capacity and the cohort-based learning experience, students from other departments are kindly discouraged from enrolling.
全球研究導論是ICI(創新國際學院)大一的入門必修課,這門課將為學生們提供一個跨學科、跨領域的全球研究知識基礎。我們將會共同探索「全球研究是什麼」、「為什麼要學習全球研究」以及「全球研究可以做什麼」等三大主題。
第一個主題「全球研究是什麼」,將探討全球研究的形成脈絡,概覽從近代到當代全球秩序的形成及變化,提供學生對全球研究的知識基礎建設。在此基礎之上,學生也將在第一次的圓桌論壇設計自己理想中的全球研究課程地圖。
在第二個主題「為什麼要學習全球研究」,我們將了解為什麼全球議題需要跨領域研究的介入。透過議題導向的討論,我們將逐步認識全球研究的三大專軌(track):「全球治理」 (Global Governance)、「永續與社會」(Sustainability and Society)、「資料分析」(Data Analytics)。
第二次的圓桌,學生們將選擇一個當代議題,透過三軌的視角進行討論。這些討論將引領學生們認識這三個專軌如何在我們複雜的生活世界中相互交織,同時也為學生未來選擇學院的三項專軌預作準備。
第三個主題「全球研究可以做什麼」,我們將了解全球研究的文理技能(liberal skills)和職涯可能性。我們將邀請 ICI 的畢業生、智庫和NGO領域的專家,分享全球研究在他們職涯中的應用。第三次圓桌邀請學生透過各種創意發想,回答「全球研究可以做什麼」。
除此以外,有三個設計將貫串全球研究導論課程。首先,我們將介紹ICI的老師和他們開設的課程,使學生們全景式地概覽 ICI四年課程,藉以協助學生規劃未來的課程修習和職涯藍圖。其次,透過上述圓桌論壇和大量的團隊合作,這門課將串起跨領域的學習不可獲缺的溝通和協調能力。最後,學生將透過全學期的反思學習日記(Reflexive Study Journal)記錄下跨領域學習過程中的困惑和成長。
選課政策: 此一導論課程專為創新國際學院(ICI)的大一新生、雙主修生、輔系生及轉學生開設。為維持課堂人數上限並保障同儕共學之授課品質,懇請非本院學生選修ICI其他豐富的課程。

title: 全球衛生治理 Global Health Governance
description:
Today’s world is becoming more interconnected and globalized. Public health issues — such as infectious diseases, non-communicable diseases, climate change, and emerging technologies — are no longer national or regional problems; they are increasingly addressed through a global, integrated, and multidisciplinary approach.
This course empowers students, future policy-makers, and practitioners to analyze and engage with global health issues. Each week introduces a topic in global health governance — such as the World Health Organization and the International Health Regulations, pandemic preparedness, climate change and human health, health technology and digital health, health financing, and One Health — led by the instructors or invited guest speakers. Reflecting recent World Health Assembly priorities, the 2026 edition gives expanded attention to climate change and human health, health technology, and the financing of global health.
In the final weeks, the class executes a simulated public health emergency under the World Health Organization framework (the WHO Simulation), joined by outside experts, civil society, and journalists. Students are divided into four to five countries and assigned roles as key legal, policy, and public health decision-makers responding to the scenario. The simulation consolidates what students learn across the term and builds their competencies in global health governance.

title: 台灣近代史 Modern Taiwanese History
description:
本課程以台灣為觀察範例,使來自台灣、東亞、中南美洲及歐洲學生,回顧東亞自19世紀中期起,至20世紀80年代後期止,在西方衝擊下,於政治、經濟、社會、文化四個面向近代化回應。本課程分為三個時期:近代化初期(1860-1895); 日治時期(1895-1945); 中華民國政府威權統治時期 (1945-1987)。近代化初期,本課程探討台灣在清領時期既存之政經結構及社會脈絡,以及中、日兩國於19世紀中後期啟動近代化歷程,對台灣及東亞之影響。其後,本課程介紹日本帝國統治台灣後,推行近代化治理及亞洲主義,對台灣與西太平洋各地的衝擊及其回應。最後,本課程介紹二次大戰後,台灣因冷戰結構以及國共對抗,進入威權統治及經濟、社會結構調整,逐步邁向民主化過程。本課程也探討19世紀中葉以來,分別探討西方在各時期,對東亞/西太平洋區域政治、經濟、社會、文化的衝擊、回應與相互調整,及對當代東亞政治、經濟、社會層面之影響。
This course focuses on the evolution of modernity in Taiwan and East Asia from the mid-19th century to the 1980s. This course analyzes how the concept of modernity was applied to and impacted Taiwanese society in three periods: the late Ching Imperial Rule Period (1860-1895), the Japanese rule period (1895–1945), and the period of strict control by the ROC government (1945–1987).
After the Second Opium War, Taiwan engaged in the global capital market via opening the treaty ports in 1860. The preachers and business people from the west and Asian pacific areas substantially transformed the existing eco-political landscape in Taiwan. The Ching government had implemented modern governing and changed its negative defensive strategies. And the local elites in Taiwan coordinated with the Ching government to aggregate capitals and enhanced their political autonomy.
After the Sino-Japanese War, in 1895, the Ching Empire ceded Taiwan to Japan. The Empire of Japan established a colonial regime in Taiwan. The Government-General of Taiwan (GGT) used its power to implement modern and colonial governing in Taiwan. In addition to maximizing economic capital in metropolitan Japan, the colonial government also lingered between the strategies of assimilation and non-assimilation. This debate led identity crisis among local elites in Taiwan for social movements.
After World War II, the Republic of China (ROC), dominated by the ruling party, the Kuomintang (KMT), took over Taiwan. After the Chinese Civil War outbreak, the Temporary Provisions During the Period of National Mobilization for Suppression of the Communist Rebellion (temporary provisions) were enacted in 1948, suspending the human rights provisions within the ROC Constitution. In 1949, the ROC moved its central government to Taiwan, transforming Taiwan from a vast territory to a de facto nation. Meanwhile, the ROC government changed the industry to integrate into the global market more optimal, leading to the Taiwan miracle and people consciousness in the 1980s. With the end of the temporary provisions, the ROC revived its constitution in 1991 and turned Taiwan to a new page.
objectives:
1. 協助學生理解現代性概念,及台灣與東亞/西太平洋區域,近代化的起源及特徵。

2. Be able to apply historical thinking to critically discuss and analyze the political, economic, social, and legal issues in East Asia.

title: 統計學(一) Statistics(I)
description:
This course introduces undergraduates to the fundamental terminology, concepts, interpretation, and communication of the descriptive and inferential statistics most commonly encountered in scientific research.
Learning statistics is like learning an everyday language that is widely used in the scientific community. For example, many researchers use surveys, public opinion polls, censuses, and other quantitative data sources to document, describe, and explain a wide range of social phenomena. Statistics is also a crucial cornerstone of data science. To join the conversations being conducted in this realm of research, you must be literate in the vocabulary of research, data analysis, and scientific thinking. Knowledge of statistics will enable you to understand professional research literature, communicate with experienced social scientists, conduct quantitative research, and help you access the growing body of social science knowledge. Additionally, the course will enable students to learn how to utilize data from international data archive projects, such as the World Value Survey, the International Social Survey Program or the Asian Barometer, to explore significant social or political issues in the region.
objectives:
This course is a required foundational course for all students at the International College of Innovation. It introduces students to the essential statistical tools and shows how they are used to analyze quantitative data. A fundamental understanding of these tools is a critical foundation for scientific research. This course is designed mainly as AI-mediated learning, which means that you, as a student, will be responsible for learning key concepts and skills most of the time using an AI tool of your preference, guided by a prepared list of questions for each session. The instructor and TAs will be facilitators to help you learn.
The course covers descriptive statistics, inference from samples, hypothesis testing, and various basic statistical analyses. The course will also introduce R, a free software for statistical computing and graphics. You will need to bring a laptop or notebook to the class to use R. We will have practice time to use R almost every week.
Upon successful completion of this course, you will be able to complete the following tasks:
1. Explain basic concepts of social statistics (e.g., population vs. sample, sampling distribution).
2. Summarize numeric data by computing descriptive statistics (e.g., mean, variance) and creating tables and graphs. For each procedure, you will learn a hand calculation method (using calculators) and a computer method (using software such as R).
3. Compute various inferential statistics (e.g., t-score) using hand calculation and computer methods.
4. Apply probability theory to test research hypotheses.
5. Explain the differences among various statistical techniques and identify an appropriate method for a given set of variables and research questions.
grading: Attendance: Class attendance is required. Statistics learning requires you to gradually but constantly build your knowledge and skills. It is tough to catch up once you fall behind. You are also expected to contribute to the class by asking questions, participating in class discussions, and collaborating on in-class exercises. Therefore, your attendance is essential for making these contributions. Reading Assignments: You are expected to read the assigned chapters and related materials uploaded on Moodle before each session (see the class schedule above). To complete reading assignments successfully, you need to understand what is in each chapter. Therefore, in addition to highlighting the text and taking notes, I suggest you write down any specific questions. It would be helpful if you plan to spend 3 hours before and 3 hours after the weekly class. You may find some chapters challenging to follow. Don't worry if this happens. It is crucial to finish reading the assigned chapter before each session to gain a general understanding, and to review it after class to ensure deeper comprehension of the materials. Homework Assignments: Learning by doing is crucial for understanding statistics. You will be given homework exercises at the end of most sessions. Homework questions for each chapter will be uploaded to Moodle. You will have at least a week to complete each assignment. If you start working on your homework early, you will have a chance to ask questions in the next class session before submitting your assignments. I will collect assignments at the start of each scheduled class session. You will lose points if you turn in your homework late (any time after the class session starts and before 4:00 pm on the next day). Upload your assignments to Moodle as PDFs. Group Project: There will be a one-week group project at the end of the semester (Week 15). You'll need to form project groups. Each group may have up to 5 students and should include members from at least 2 countries. Honor Code: Please help each other by exchanging notes for missed class sessions, studying for exams, and so on. However, the assignments (homework or quizzes) you turn in should result from your own hard work. You should not copy your peer's work in any way. In short, No Plagiarism or Cheating. title: 資料科學 Data Science
description:
This course introduces the full process of data science, from collecting raw data to building useful insights and models. Students will learn how to gather data from sources like websites and APIs, clean and prepare it for analysis, and label image or text data when needed. The course covers key steps in data science, including data wrangling, exploration, visualization, modeling, and evaluation.
In the image section, students will learn how to label and explore image data, apply clustering techniques like K-means to group visual patterns, and understand how to move from basic clustering to using pre-trained models for classification. For each method, students will learn how to evaluate performance using metrics such as accuracy and Intersection over Union (IoU).
In the text section, the course begins with text cleaning and basic techniques like TF-IDF. Students will then explore more powerful models like BERT, and learn how different models can be used for classification and language understanding tasks. Along the way, students will compare results using standard evaluation metrics.
Rather than focusing only on model training, this course emphasizes how to use data to answer real questions, communicate findings, and build end-to-end data science workflows. Students will use Python tools such as Pandas, Scikit-learn, Matplotlib, and Hugging Face Transformers to work on real datasets and complete hands-on projects.
This course is designed for students with basic Python and AI knowledge who want to deepen their understanding of the data science pipeline.
objectives: This course aims to help students understand the full process of data science, from collecting and preparing data to building and evaluating models. Students will learn how to handle different types of data, including text and images, and apply both basic and advanced techniques such as K-means clustering, TF-IDF, and classification. By the end of the course, students will be able to use Python tools to explore data, label datasets, apply machine learning models, and evaluate results using metrics like accuracy and IoU. They will also complete a small project to apply what they have learned in a real-world context.

title: 國際人權法 International Law of Human Rights
description:

⚠️ MUST READ BEFORE REGISTRATION ⚠️
🚨 If you cannot attend the keynote speech scheduled 12:10-14:00 on 10 December, PLEASE DO NOT TAKE THE COURSE. 🚨
Languages: The course is part of NCCU’s English-as-a-medium-of-instruction (EMI) program, co-organised by the Department of Political Science, the College of Law, and the International College of Innovation. Given students’ pragmatic needs for their future careers, Chinese Mandarin also serves as a supporting language in the running of discussions. However, language proficiency does NOT affect the evaluation of students' performance.
Prerequisites: The course is open to NCCU senior undergraduates and graduate students WITH prior higher education coursework in constitutional law or public international law, plus a foundational understanding of legal concepts and terminology.
objectives:
Students will explore multidisciplinary perspectives on human rights institutions and jurisprudence. Through analysing controversial issues and bridging domestic and international dialogues, the course prepares students to navigate contemporary challenges to peace, democracy, the rule of law, and competing interests.
Method, Requirements, & Assignments
The seminar comprises a combination of lectures, guided readings, and discussions.
Google Classroom Participation #so4fv67w
All students must join the course communication platform and enable notifications. To join it, please first set up your NCCU Google Workspace account via personal settings in iNCCU https://i.nccu.edu.tw.
Designated Readings and Rapporteur Podcast
- Structure & Format: Each rapporteur team—consisting of 3 members from diverse cultural and disciplinary backgrounds—will produce a 20-minute AUDIO PODCAST summarising the week's designated readings. Podcasts must be uploaded to Google Classroom at least 24 hours before class.
- Objective: This assignment is an exercise in audio-only storytelling. The goal is to translate dense academic literature or case law into an accessible, engaging narrative without relying on slides or visual aids.
Mid-term Oral Examination (Individual Session)
- Scheduling: The presentation order will be randomly generated and published one week prior to the examination.
- Format: On the day of the exam, each student will draw a random question and will have 20 minutes to prepare the response, during which open-resource research, references, and peer consultations are fully permitted.
- Presentation: Each student will deliver a 3-minute oral response to the instructor. Please note that this is a Socratic-style examination; the instructor may interrupt students’ presentations at any point with follow-up questions.
Term Oral Examination (Moot Court Session)
- Structure: Rapporteur teams will be organised into different rounds of moot court simulation, playing either the applicant council or the respondent State (assignment to be determined randomly).
- Materials & Rules: Case facts and simplified oral arguments rules will be published on Google Classroom by late November.
- Requirements: Robust invocation and citation of the course jurisprudence are essential. Written memorials are only required to be communicated to the opposing party team.
grading:
Assessment
General evaluation (30%) includes rapporteur podcast, in-class and Google Classroom participation.
Mid-term oral examination (35%) is evaluated based on comprehension and argumentation quality.

title: 設計思維 Design Thinking
description:
Design Thinking for Innovative Talent and Teams in the AI Era
— Build your purposeful career and abundant life
📌 Important Notice Before the First Class
Students who wish to take this course should carefully read the description and policies below, and complete the registration form.
Mandatory Attendance: You must attend the first class (9AM, Sep 8th, 2026) to be considered a candidate for enrollment.
Pre-registration: You must complete the registration form before coming to the first class.
Course Format: This is a highly interactive course featuring extensive teamwork and collaborative activities. Full engagement and active participation are expected throughout each session.
Class Capacity: : The standard enrollment limit is 25 students (for credit). An additional 5 slots are available for exchange students and visiting scholars.
Enrollment Notification (via email):

Early decision (2nd tier): Before Sep. 8th
Final admission decision: within 24 hours after the first class.
🌟 Testimonials
"It’s very satisfying knowing that I am not alone in this journey. I have a group to share my daily achievements and support each other... It feels like life consultation; each class allows us to reflect on our path more and more. Thanks for this amazing journey!!"

— Inspiring feedback from NCCU DT Class of 2024–2025!
🌟 Course Introduction
In an AI era defined by rapid change and ambiguity, this course equips advanced undergraduate and graduate students with Design Thinking (DT) principles and innovative problem-solving tools to build effective teams and thrive in both life and career.
To avoid the pitfall of learning theory without practice, every single session in this course is divided into a "Two-Half Structure":
The Macro Track (1st half): Master macro-level design methodologies, cross-disciplinary tools, and tech-AI mindsets applicable to corporate and global ecosystems.
The Micro Track (2nd half): Turn the lens inward. You will use your own life as a sandbox for a semester-long Personal Project, executing real-world behavior design experiments.
Our curriculum spans 16 transformative weeks, structured into three golden phases:
Phase 1: DT Fundamentals & Habit-Forming Project (Weeks 1–5): Master classical d.school methodologies while executing a SMART habit-design experiment to optimize your personal energy.
Phase 2: AI-powered DT & Good Life Upgrade (Weeks 6–10): Navigate the digital age. Learn to leverage AI as a high-performance collaborative peer while scaling your habits into a Good Life Project Prototype anchored in Purpose, Achievement, and Enjoyment.
Phase 3: Re-engineering of Life, Career & Resilience (Weeks 11–15): Apply design mindsets to your future career blueprint. Tackle your life priorities, navigate unchangeable limitations, map out alternative pathways, and establish your personal "Life Board of Directors" to bounce back gracefully from setbacks.
🧭 Guidance & Expectations
🧭 For Introverts:
About one-third of our past students identified themselves as introverts before joining. By the end of the semester, every single one of them successfully found their rhythm and navigated the course beautifully. Many were pleasantly surprised by how many genuine friendships they formed along the way!
🧭 For busy students with heavy credit loads or extracurriculars:
"I really appreciate the engaging courses you’ve designed. I never thought I would have this much fun in a college classroom. Thank you!!"
This course is designed to be a space where you can pause, recharge, have fun, and create something inspiring for yourself, your team, and the world. Most students find our sessions to be a rewarding break from their usual academic stress.
🧭 Regarding Attendance (Can I maintain the commitment?):
Last year, 50% of the students maintained near-perfect attendance (100%, or missing only 1 class due to medical reasons). Only 5% struggled to meet the course standards. Please note our attendance policy: 3 absences will trigger a formal warning, and a 4th absence will automatically result in a failing grade (no credit).
🎯 Three Major Takeaways:
DT & Tech Mastery: Master the core mindsets of Design Thinking (e.g., Embrace Ambiguity, Defer Judgment, Bias toward Action) while learning to co-ideate with AI, giving you a distinct competitive edge in the technological era.
Elevated Teamwork Confidence: Foster advanced communication, psychological safety, and leadership skills through hands-on collaboration simulations and peer feedback frameworks.
Life Resilience & Navigation: Reframe life's bottlenecks, map out adaptive alternative pathways, and intentionally design a sustainable future—discovering a beautifully iterated "new version of yourself" along the way.
