weeklyText:
week 1 | Course Introduction & Icebreaking
Instructional Objectives | • Familiarize students with course expectations, grading policies, and the interactive dynamic. • Build early psychological safety and connection among peers.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Lecture on the course blueprint, the "Two-Half Structure," and instructional objectives. • Micro Track: Rapid networking simulation and team formation roles overview.
week 2 | Phase 1: Empathy & Self-Awareness
Instructional Objectives | • Master foundational empathy map and journey map tools. • Discover hidden personal needs and energy drains in daily routines.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Lecture on user research methodologies, Empathy Maps, Journey Maps, and case studies. • Micro Track: Launching the Habit-Forming Project by defining personal "Fundamentals" (sleep, movement, energy).
week 3 | Phase 1: Problem Definition & Root Causes
Instructional Objectives | • Reframe chaotic raw data into actionable "How-Might-We" (HMW) design statements. • Identify root causes of personal inconsistency rather than surface symptoms.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Workshop on 2x2 definition tables, drafting Need Statements, and mastering the art of problem reframing. • Micro Track: Executing the "6A Self-Awareness Framework" to pinpoint the primary obstacles in personal habits.
week 4 | Phase 1: Ideation & Trigger Design
Instructional Objectives | • Practice deferring judgment and brainstorming high-volume, unconventional solutions. • Design environmental triggers and psychological cues to sustain habits without pure willpower.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Brainstorming drills focused on "Wild Ideas" and leveraging diverse peer perspectives for creative problem-solving. • Micro Track: Deconstructing the "7 Core Desires" to creatively design attractive psychological triggers for personal habits.
week 5 | Phase 1: Prototyping Daily Rituals
Instructional Objectives | • Shift from overthinking to rapid execution (Bias toward Action). • Build a tangible, visual tracker for personal morning or evening rituals.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Hands-on "Six-Thinking-Hats" simulation to systematically evaluate and refine experimental ideas. • Micro Track: Visualizing an ideal day's ritual as a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) utilizing mindful anchors (Smile, Breathe, Align).
week 6 | Phase 1: Iteration & Habit 2.0 Launch
Instructional Objectives | • Learn to harvest and synthesize experimental data from feedback loops. • Formulate a resilient, long-term habit framework based on behavior science.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Executing the d.school "Wallet Activity" to master rapid, user-centric feedback loops and testing cycles. • Micro Track: Finalizing and publishing the 5 core pillars of the individual Habit 2.0 Guidebook.
week 7 | Phase 2: Tech Mindsets & Attention Economy
Instructional Objectives | • Critically analyze the impact of generative AI and the mechanics of the attention economy. • Diagnose how digital tools enhance performance versus how they hijack attention.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Exploration of AI as a collaborative peer and the psychological impacts of constant digital notifications. • Micro Track: Auditing personal tech habits and tracking screen-time triggers utilizing the Internal Family Systems (IFS) "Thoughts are Clouds" concept.
week 8 | Phase 2: Core Self & Reclaiming Attention
Instructional Objectives | • Master info-architecture and data-synthesis using advanced prompting mindsets. • Design structural boundaries to protect mental workspace and emotional energy.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Practice prompting as a tool for structuring information and clarifying core intent (The "Lead-from-Within" mindset). • Micro Track: Establishing personalized digital boundaries and building an emotional fortress against notification anxiety.
week 9 | Phase 2: Human-AI Collaboration
Instructional Objectives | • Evaluate human-AI partnerships through the lens of Self-Determination Theory. • Leverage generative AI to break team groupthink and solve bottlenecked problems.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Deep dive into Self-Determination Theory (Autonomy, Competence, Relatedness) within the context of automated technology. • Micro Track: Using AI as a personalized coaching partner to analyze and optimize project hurdles without losing human agency.
week 10 | Phase 2: Shaping the Good Life Blueprint
Instructional Objectives | • Transition from micro-habits to macro life design across Purpose, Achievement, and Enjoyment. • Sketch the initial vision and milestone markers for a short-term life project.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Deconstructing the "Happiness Triangle" and mapping personal alignment with Ikigai principles. • Micro Track: Mapping out the 5 Gold Elements of the Good Life Project Prototype via a structured mind map.
week 11 | Phase 2: Tech Audit & Constructive Feedback
Instructional Objectives | • Master rapid digital prototyping using integrated tools. • Practice d.school feedback frameworks to refine project frameworks with peers.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Strategic breakdown of tech-team roles (Hacker, Goal-Getter, Visionary) and digital prototyping workflows .• Micro Track: Conducting a comprehensive Tech Audit for the Good Life blueprint and practicing the "i like, i wish, i wonder" peer-review matrix.
week 12 | Phase 3: The Well-being Triangle
Instructional Objectives | • Audit the dynamic tension between external career achievements and internal psychological health. • Formulate immediate interventions to correct lifestyle imbalances.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Interactive debate on the conflicts within the Well-being Triangle (Life Priorities, Career Focus & Resilience) .• Micro Track: Striking a radical balance in individual project timelines to actively protect personal mental well-being.
week 13 | Phase 3: Dynamic Reframing & Constraints
Instructional Objectives | • Distinguish between structural "Gravity Problems" and solvable design challenges. • Reframe unchangeable realities into creative boundaries for career pivot options.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Introducing the "Three Arrows for Decision Making" and categorizing career/life constraints. • Micro Track: Mapping out Alternative Pathways (Plan B & C) for individual projects to successfully bypass major bottlenecks.
week 14 | Phase 3: Failure Immunity & Self-Compassion
Instructional Objectives | • Deconstruct Impostor Syndrome and high-achievement anxiety • Cultivate resilience by treating setbacks as objective pivot data rather than personal definitions.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Interactive breakdown of the Five Building Blocks of Self-Esteem, Shame Deconstruction, and Self-Compassion practices. • Micro Track: Authoring a personalized "Good Life Failure Resume" to systematically wire an internal bounce-back mechanism.
week 15 | Phase 3: Ecosystems & Personal Board
Instructional Objectives | • Move away from the "lone wolf" mentality to map out strategic stakeholder networks. • Practice approaching high-profile mentors using tactical networking frameworks.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Formulating stakeholder maps and applying the "Link, Learn, Leverage" framework to engage high-value networks. • Micro Track: Finalizing the individual "Board of Directors" blueprint and initiating outreach for alternative project pathways.
week 16 | Phase 3: Final Launch, Storytelling & Gratitude
Instructional Objectives | • Synthesize 15 weeks of personal data into a compelling, transformative narrative .• Formally commit to an autonomous, long-term action experiment beyond campus boundaries.
Content & Activities | • Macro Track: Master storytelling techniques to present the evolution of the self and leveraging psychological capital (HOPE /HERO). • Micro Track: The New Version of Self Launch Ceremony, integrated with mindfulness gratitude rituals

title: 科技與當代社會 Technoscience and Contemporary Society
description:
This course introduces students to the sociological study of technoscience and society. You will explore and analyze what it means to live in a contemporary technological society. A major goal will be to answer several questions: (1) What are the social, structural, and cultural influences on our behavior, attitudes, and technological change? (2) What are the sources, dynamics, and consequences of social inequality and of how we are organized? (3) What are the implications of materials and technology for social change? We will then discuss fundamental social processes and concepts—culture, organization and management, social identity, and social interaction.
In the later part of the semester, you will study how technology and society have been intertwined. While technology has always been an intricate part of any society, in the second half of the 20th-century technological change became a defining characteristic of the way societal structures, and technological politics are constituted and organized. In this part, you will investigate and unravel this distinctive condition. You will study different areas where questions about technology’s role in society are central: economy, transportation, and corporations. In this course, you will learn that technological development is not just about technology.
objectives:
You will examine and challenge your own experiences, observations, and assumptions about society with sociological reflections.
You will develop a more sophisticated understanding of your social worlds and your identities.
You will learn to recognize and apply analytical perspectives to analyze the entanglement of technology, media, and politics in our contemporary society.
You will be able to make a reasoned contribution to academic and societal debates on the role of technology in society.

title: 科技社會與文化 Technoscience, Society & Culture
description:
本課程從科學與技術研究(Science and Technology Studies, STS)的視角,探討科學、技術與社會文化、政治之間複雜交織的關係。課程將從技術研究與科學研究作為出發,系統性介紹STS的多元分析觀點,包括科學知識社會學、技術的社會建構與形塑、行動者網絡理論、科技的政治性、公民科學中的專家與常民知識、女性主義科技研究,以及本體論與物質的轉向等。這些理論工具將幫助學生深入理解科技與社會的互動過程,並培養批判性思考能力。
課程強調科技變遷與社會變動的共構關係,通過具體案例說明兩者如何相互塑造。例如,英國工業化過程中運河開鑿與工程師專業的形成、英國的會計師的客觀性建構,以及美國電網發展等大型社技系統的案例,都展示了技術、材料、法律、政策和管理等多面向的交互作用。這些案例將幫助學生理解科技發展如何深刻影響社會結構,同時社會因素又如何塑造科技的發展方向。
透過本課程,學生將理解科學家、工程師和產業市場如何緊密連結,形成穩固的社會技術體制。同時,課程也將探討科技內在的政治、文化與性別特性,以及專家知識在公共事務中的權威地位和操作:這將使學生認識到科技並非中立的工具,而是特定價值觀和權力關係的社會媒介。希望學生以氣候變遷與太陽光電、離岸風電等,來說明STS理論如何應用於理解現實問題。
objectives:
辨識科技內生的政治、文化與性別特性,科技不僅只是工程師與科學的事情,科技與我們日常生活的種種選擇與安排有著持續的相互鞏固關係。
明白科學知識與專業所帶有的公共權威意涵,與理解技術物的設計與操作中的性別建構。
學習台灣在能源轉型上所面臨的最新議題,例如電網與儲能設施、光電與生態衝突、離岸風電中的白海豚、候鳥的生態保育等等。
明白專家知識如何介入與操作技術性的公共議題,這當中充滿權衡與詮釋與協商彈性。

共需繳交10次的課後心得,每篇約一頁,主要針對當週文章的核心論點與課堂內容進行說明,並提出個人最具啟發的部分。課堂的參與討論表現是主要評分項目。
本課程以課堂的持續參與為主,並希望能啟發碩士論文研究方向。

title: AI與倫理 Artificial Intelligence and Ethics
description:
Recent advances in computing may place us at the threshold of a unique turning point in human history. Soon we are likely to entrust management of our environment, economy, security, infrastructure, food production, healthcare, and to a large degree even our personal activities, to artificially intelligent computer systems.
The prospect of "turning over the keys" to increasingly autonomous systems raises many complex and troubling questions. How will society respond as versatile robots and machine-learning systems displace an ever-expanding spectrum of blue- and white-collar workers? Will the benefits of this technological revolution be broadly distributed or accrue to a lucky few? How can we ensure that these systems respect our ethical principles when they make decisions at speeds and for rationales that exceed our ability to comprehend? What, if any, legal rights and responsibilities should we grant them? And should we regard them merely as sophisticated tools or as a newly emerging form of life?
隨著近期AI與自動化設備之技術發展,已達到人類歷史發展之轉折點,人類非常可能大規模地將環境、經濟發展、安全、基礎設備、食物生產與分配、健康照護與保險交由AI與自動化設備安排與執行。

title: 全球議題在亞洲 Global Issues in Asia
description:
"Global Issues in Asia" offers junior and senior undergraduate students and graduate students an exploration of major global issues within the framework of Asian studies and anthropology. This is an advanced course continuing from the Anthropology course (ZU1007001). We will explore five “foreshadowed problems”: history, subject, structure, difference, and perception. Each section contains three global issues. Throughout the course, we will examine issues including imagination, pop culture, algorithms, precarity, inequality, political unrest, ethnic conflicts, technology and innovation, the Anthropocene, and diverse forms of life. We ask how emerging global issues manifest in Asian societies and explore the distinctive ways these societies engage with key challenges. We will also engage with foundational dialogues and emerging themes in Asian studies, analyzing contemporary ethnographies from anthropology, sociology, and media studies that trace the evolution of these debates and concerns. This is a reading-intensive course with a strong emphasis on interactive ethnographic practices, laying the groundwork for introductory fieldwork experience.
「全球議題在亞洲」是針對創新國際學院大三、大四學生、研究生開設的專題課程,其內容聚焦於全球重大議題,藉此探索當代亞洲社會與文化所面臨的挑戰與機遇。這是一門進階人類學的課程,我們將延續人類學課程(ZU1007001)裡的五個「預示性問題」(foreshadowed problems):歷史、主體、結構、差異、認知,課程的每個單元將聚焦三個全球議題。這個學期我們將討論以下議題:想像、流行文化、演算法、不穩定階級、社會不平等、政治抗爭、族裔衝突、科技創新、人類世以及多樣的生命樣態等。一方面,課堂上將探討全球共同面對的新興課題如何在亞洲社會浮現,以及思考這些議題在亞洲呈現的特殊性。另一方面,我們也將討論不同的亞洲國家與社會如何回應全球議題的挑戰。修習本課程,學生將能了解當代亞洲研究中關鍵的全球議題、問題意識與理論,並透過人類學、社會學、媒介研究等領域的當代民族誌,了解這些議題如何浮現與轉變。這是一門著重於民族誌閱讀的理論課程,同時將搭配課堂中的互動式民族誌實作,奠定初階田野實作的能力。

title: 科技法律與資料治理 Technology Law and Data Governance
description:
I. Course Objectives
This course is designed to help students understand the legal and governance issues arising from the development of digital technologies, with data governance as its central focus. It addresses major emerging topics, including personal data protection, artificial intelligence governance, digital platform accountability, open government data, data sharing, cybersecurity, cross-border data flows, and the European Union(EU)’s data governance framework.
Taught entirely in English, the course introduces students to core concepts in contemporary international technology law. It examines legal issues that arise throughout the data life cycle, from collection, processing, use, retention, and sharing to deletion. The course also considers the legality of artificial intelligence systems in model training and content generation, and analyzes the respective responsibilities and obligations of governments, businesses, digital platforms, and data intermediaries in data governance.
The course further incorporates Taiwan’s legal framework, the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Data Governance Act, Data Act, Artificial Intelligence Act, and other significant legislative developments and international trends. Through this comparative approach, students will develop a stronger interest in technology law and acquire the analytical skills needed to address practical legal issues.
II. Course Description
This course begins with legal issues related to data use as an entry point into technology law. It introduces key legal concepts, including personal data protection, informational self-determination, privacy, and data governance, before moving to issues such as open government data, data sharing, data intermediary services, data altruism, data access for Internet of Things devices and connected products, cloud switching, regulation of artificial intelligence technologies, algorithmic transparency, disclosure obligations, and legal requirements for cross-border data transfers.
The course focuses on recent developments in the EU’s data governance regime and explains how the GDPR, Data Governance Act, Data Act, and Artificial Intelligence Act together shape a technology law framework grounded in trustworthiness, data access, and risk management. In addition to introducing major international technology laws, the course includes weekly case discussions to help students examine the relationship between data governance, personal data protection, public interest, industrial innovation, digital market competition, national data sovereignty, and the protection of fundamental rights.
objectives:
Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:
Understand the foundational theories and regulatory structure of technology law and data governance.
Examine legal issues concerning personal data protection, data sharing, digital platform regulation, risk-based regulation of artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity safeguards.
Compare Taiwan’s digital legal framework with the GDPR, Data Governance Act, Data Act, and other major technology laws of the EU.
Assess, from legal and governance perspectives, personal data protection risks and appropriate levels of regulatory oversight arising from artificial intelligence and other technological applications.
Analyze current disputes and cases involving the application of technology law from an independent perspective and propose appropriate legal or policy reforms.

title: 治理中國:政治變遷、社會轉型與台港澳關係 Governing China: Political Change, Social Transformation, and Relation s with Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau
description:
This course examines the rise of China as the defining force shaping politics and society across the Greater China region. Over the past four decades, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has transformed from a poor, isolated polity into the world’s second-largest economy and a leading geopolitical power — with profound consequences not only for its own governance but for its relationship with Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan, three societies bound to the mainland by deep cultural and historical ties yet possessing distinct institutional inheritances. The course asks: how has China’s rise reshaped the political institutions, social fabric, and external relationships of each of these polities, and what does the resulting variation tell us about the reach and the limits of Chinese-style governance?
The first half of the course maps the mainland system that drives these dynamics: major theoretical traditions for understanding Chinese politics (authoritarian resilience, fragmented and consultative authoritarianism, adaptive governance, party-state institutionalism); the organisation, ideology, and cadre system of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) under Xi Jinping; political change and policy implementation under the post-2012 leadership; the social transformation generated by urbanisation, hukou reform, demographic change, and growing inequality; and state–society relations including civil society, religion, ethnic politics, surveillance, and platform politics.
The second half traces how the rise of China has reshaped — and is being reshaped by — its peripheries. In Hong Kong, the asymmetric integration of the Special Administrative Region into the mainland’s political and economic order has accelerated since 2014, culminating in the 2020 National Security Law, the 2021 “patriots-only” electoral overhaul, and the 2024 Safeguarding National Security Ordinance (Article 23). In Macau, the rise of China has been managed through a quieter politics of accommodation, with deepening integration into the Greater Bay Area and continued reliance on a gaming economy increasingly aligned with Beijing’s strategic priorities. In Taiwan, China’s rise has driven both deepening economic interdependence (trade, investment, ECFA, semiconductors) and an intensifying security competition, with democratisation, identity politics, the 2024 presidential election, and the role of the United States all shaping the cross-Strait equation. The final two weeks are reserved for student case presentations.
objectives: By the end of the course, students should be able to: (1) compare leading theoretical models of Chinese governance and assess their analytical reach; (2) explain how the CCP organises power and recruits, monitors, and disciplines cadres; (3) trace the principal directions of political change under Xi Jinping; (4) analyse social transformation and state–society contention in mainland China; (5) compare the post-handover political trajectories of Hong Kong and Macau; (6) account for the trajectory of Taiwan’s democratisation and cross-Strait relations; and (7) deliver a research-grade case study and reflection note that engage critically with primary scholarship.

title: 學術寫作的邏輯與研究設計 Designing and Understanding Research
description: The goal of this course is to prepare undergraduate students for writing and designing their own independent research either for a capstone, honors thesis, or future master’s/PhD applications. Through the combination of philosophy and academic writing, as well as the instructor’s own shared experience designing and publishing pieces of research, students will learn how to construct effective argumentation in their own ideas and understand others’ published arguments. Students are also provided with ample practice time they can use to work in class and ask the professor questions. By the conclusion of the course, students should be confident in reading and understanding research and be able to correctly apply the knowledge gained into their own work.
objectives:
Students should be able to understand existing research that aligns with their interests in the social sciences and/or humanities.
Students should understand and apply academic standards of writing.
Students should be able to defend and explain their own ideas when questioned by scholarly peers.
grading:
The course is structured around the creation of a research proposal, and it is this proposal that will constitute 80% of the course grade. However, this grade will be divided into four subsections that each have a different due date.
Introduction – 20%
Theoretical Background – 30%
Methodology – 20%
Final proposal – 10%
The final proposal will be graded based on your edits of the feedback given on the previous three parts. This will not constitute writing a new proposal, but rather putting together and editing the three previous sections upon which you have already received feedback.
Individual rubrics will be presented in class for each assignment, but generally speaking, you will be graded on 1) formatting, 2) English quality, and 3) content accuracy/mastery for each of the three subsections of the proposal that are handed in.
Proposal Defence – 20%
This will be a 20-minute presentation in which students will present their research proposal and answer questions from their peers about their proposed research.
Within this presentation slot, students will need to:
Introduce their topic
Explain the urgency behind their research (why it’s important)
Describe what existing literature has to say about their topic
State their research questions and/or hypotheses
Explain their methodology of choice
Justify that methodology
Explain how that methodology will answer their research questions/hypotheses
Students will also need to answer questions from the professor and their peers. Students will be marked based on their questions for other students during their presentations as well.
Grades can be expected for each assignment within 2-3 weeks of handing in the assignment. If you do not receive your grade in that timeframe (and the professor has not indicated that it will be taking longer), please contact the professor to ensure that the original submission was received.
All due dates are indicated in the syllabus, and all assignments (except the defense) can be handed in by email to 〔聯絡資訊已移除〕.

title: 實證經濟學與資料分析 Empirical Economics and Data Analysis
description: The goal of this course is to show students how to do research using the tools of empirical microeconomics. We will use STATA to do data management and microeconometric analysis. We will also discuss microeconometric tools commonly used in empirical work, including regression analyses, treatment effect estimation, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, and panel data methods. Recent advances in causal inference methods, such as event study and staggered intervention, will also be included if time permits. Selected papers will be discussed and replicated in the class such that students can learn how to complete empirical microeconomics research from the beginning to the end. Students are expected to complete a research project at the end of the course.
objectives:
Ability to conduct empirical analysis using STATA.
Ability to understand papers using empirical analysis.
Ability to locate proper research topics.
Ability to find and manage datasets.
Ability to propose and conduct empirical strategies.

title: 量化的環境治理:永續指標的實作與政治 Governing Environment by Numbers: the Practices and Politics of Sustai nability Metrics
description:
Course Description
This course has two aims. On one hand, It intends to help ICI (International College of Innovation) students acquire basic knowledge of sustainability reporting and carbon accounting. These are two popular tools in the corporate world of sustainability and in the field of environmental governance. On the other hand, this course also aims to equip ICI students with critical and historical perspective to understand the quantification logic behind the current trend of global environmental governance.
This course interweaves technical training and critical analysis throughout the semester: you will read sustainability reports learn the standards behind them, examine how metrics are constructed, and learn directly from practitioners’ insights. Specifically, this course collaborates NCCU's own Sustainability Office. We will use NCCU’s own Sustainability Report as a companion case and interact with the authors who craft the report from office. Furthermore, we will use the global higher education sector as our focus and collectively analyze how different universities develop their own Sustainability Reports and what the implications are.
Course Format
Class Activity & Group Discussion & Short Lecture:
I employ a student-centered learning approach in this course rather than a traditional lecture format (i.e., you listen to lectures to learn knowledge). My role will be a facilitator who supports your learning. In particular, this course is built on group discussion and collective learning. Most learning will be based on reading assigned materials, discussion, and class activities. I will supplement these activities with short lectures that help contextualize readings, articulate learning themes across weeks, and move the discussion forward.
Learning Activities
Collective Annotation:
For most of the weeks, there is one assigned reading you need to finish reading before coming to the class. You will also be required to make 3 comments on a collective reading document. Your comments will be incorporated into the classroom activity and discussion.
Weekly online discussion
Each week, we are going to have TWO threads of discussion online. The platform we are going to use is the LinkedIn private group. The first thread is based on the weekly assigned reading and the collective annotation. The second thread is based on an existing LinkedIn post that is chosen by a designated student. You will be responsible to provide at least ONE response on each thread (meaning TWO responses in total). And you will also have a chance to share one LinkedIn post as our basis of discussion.
The design of this class activity also means each students need to create your own LinkedIn account. The goal is to help students get familiar with the platform and the content on the platform. LinkedIn is also an important source for the course topic – substantiality reporting, carbon accounting, and global environment management and governance.
While the use of LinkedIn in this course is a strategic choice intended to strengthen your learning, you should be mindful of a longer-term consequence of this design. Unlike a comment posted on a course platform that disappears when the semester ends, your contributions in this private LinkedIn group carry a "real stake": they are attached to the professional profile you will take with you into job-seeking, and they may persist beyond this course. This is deliberate. Part of the aim is for you to practice speaking thoughtfully in a professional setting where your name and your words are connected—which is also why participation should be a considered choice, not an afterthought. If you would prefer not to hold a LinkedIn account or not to post under your own name, you may want to avoid enrolling in this course.
Class participation and end-of-class exercise
It is critical to come to the class on time and participate in class activities. My assumption is that a fair proportion of your learning will come from your interaction and collaboration with your classmates during the class. Thus, it is imperative to attend every class except for legitimate reasons (e.g. sick leave or other types of leave permitted by the university).
Collaborative project – Surveying Sustainability Reporting in the Global Higher Education sector
Throughout the semester, our class will collectively produce a critical report on how higher education institutions around the world account for their environmental impacts. Working in groups, you will each analyze sustainability reports from universities in different countries, especially including reports written in languages other than English. We will examine the choices behind them: which frameworks they adopt, how they define what counts, what they measure, and what they leave out. Rather than scoring or ranking universities, our goal is to map the varieties of sustainability reporting practices in the higher education sector and to ask what these documents reveal about how universities understand their environmental responsibilities. More importantly, the goal is not to produce separate analysis by different students but to put together all the analysis as a coherent report. Ideally, we will publicly launch the initial draft of our collective report at the end of the semester. There will be different tasks throughout the semester to craft the report together. I will announce these tasks at the beginning of the semester.
Study Journal:
Study Journal is a Google document you share with me. I will provide detailed instructions later for how to create your Study Journal. I hope this Study Journal will serve as a platform for you to monitor and track your learning progress. It will also be a good way for me to know how you are doing during these four months and what measures I could do to support your learning. You will be responsible for maintaining this Study Journal throughout the 4-month course. In specific, this Study Journal will include four components.
At the beginning of the course, you will need to develop your learning schedule for all the course assignments stated in the syllabus. (mandatory)
In the 9th week of the course, you will need to do a mid-term reflection to evaluate your learning so far and how you may adjust your study plan in the next two months. (mandatory)
At the end of the course, you will need to write a brief report evaluating your learning during these four months. (mandatory)
You are welcome to write an update on your learning progress and status any time during the semester (e.g., once a week) on the same document. (optional)
objectives:
Learning Outcome
During this course, you will have the opportunity to learn how to:
Explain the rationale, structure, and major frameworks of sustainability reporting.
Describe the basic principles of carbon accounting.
Analyze how quantification logic shapes and constrains environmental governance.
Situate sustainability reporting and carbon accounting within their historical and political contexts.
Evaluate the limitations of quantification-based governance and propose alternative approaches.
Produce a collectively authored critical assessment of higher education sustainability reporting at the global scale.
Engage in a professional learning community by immersing in sustainability trends and discussing with peers on LinkedIn.
grading:
Evaluation
Accumulative
There are five types of assignments you will finish during the course. As you can see, there is NO mid-term or final exam. All the grades are accumulative. This means you will accumulate your grades with each task you accomplish. But this also means you need to spend an equal amount of time on the course each week, and you will NOT have the chance to “cram” all the coursework at the end of the semester.
Grade Calculation
(1) Collective Annotation | 13% | 13 readings, 1% each | the end of every Sunday
(2) Online Discussion | 26% | 13 weeks, 2% each

Planning for the entire semester | 2% | once | The end of W2
Mid-term self-assessment | 2% | once | The end of W8
End-of-Semester Reflection | 2% | once | The end of W16
Total | 100%

title: 數位賦能教育科技管理研究 Study on Digital Empowerment and Education Technology Management
description:
The course focuses on digital technology enhanced education innovation and management with applications. Over the past several years, the field of Educational Technology Management has undergone a significant transformation. The advancements in digital technologies have led to new educational paradigms, and the need for efficient management and effective implementation of these technologies has never been more pressing. This course provides opportunities for students to explore these changes and share experiences and knowledge to improve educational technology management practices.
This course will help students to reflect on the role various forms of electronic and digital technology can play in the teaching/learning process and how you can engage these processes in your classroom. Students will become skilled in some of the many digital tools used in today's schools, including MIT’s System Dynamics modelling and simulation-based scenario planning.
This course also consider how a small-scale Educational Technology research project can be conducted in an education environment. Case studies and project-based learning with Education for Sustainable Development and organizational learning will be reviewed to offer practical tools and applied research strategies to students prior to conducting their own Educational Technology research project.
objectives:
This course is designed for students to develop their understanding of educational technology and digital empowerment and to learn how to manage educational technologies for better educational practices. Therefore, the objectives of this course are for the student to:
Understand the principles of digital empowerment and trends of educational technology with education innovation issues.
Manage educational technologies for teaching and curriculum development.
Manage educational technologies for e-learning systems.
Develop ideas, steps, and apply digital innovations for organizational learning.

Second, each student must prepare an article review (or case review) and present the articles/case to the class. The review should be an analysis of the authors’ theory, methods, and findings. title: 大型跨國調查資料之分析與應用 Analysis and Application of Large-Scale International Survey Data
description:
Have you ever wondered if people in different countries really live differently? They often think differently about family, work, money, trust, happiness, and politics. They may also behave differently, follow different ways of life, and reach different results in education and health. For example, how many hours do people work, and are shorter working hours linked to more happiness? How do couples share housework across countries? How healthy do people stay as they grow older? And how well do students do in math and science in different school systems and education cultures? In this course, we use real survey data collected from people all around the world to study questions like these.
You will work with several famous international survey projects, including the World Values Survey (WVS), the East Asian Social Survey (EASS), the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP), the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), and the WHO Study on Global AGEing and Adult Health (SAGE).
This course gives you the tools to study that world with real evidence. Step by step, you will learn how these surveys are made, how to clean and prepare the data, how to compare answers fairly across countries, and how to turn your results into a clear report and a short presentation.
You do not need to be a “statistics person” to do well here. We start from the basics and build up slowly. Every new idea comes with a hands-on example, and we review the key statistics together in class before you need to use them. Class demonstrations use R (and Python templates will also be shared), but you may use any software you like for your own work, including R, Python, Stata, SAS, or SPSS. There are no required prerequisites. Having taken (or currently taking) an introductory statistics or research methods course is helpful, but it is not mandatory.
The skills you build here are useful far beyond the classroom and beyond academic research. You will learn how to work with large and messy real-world data, how to ask a clear question and find the answer in the numbers, how to make simple charts and tables that tell a story, and how to explain your findings to people who are not experts.
objectives:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
Understand how the major international surveys (WVS, EASS, ISSP, PISA, and SAGE) are built, and why they are useful for studying how people think, behave, live, and learn in different countries.
Prepare and clean real survey data, and run basic to intermediate analysis using the software of your choice.
Ask a clear research question and test it with care, while watching for common problems in comparing countries (for example, sampling, and whether a question means the same thing in each country).
Write and present your own short research that compares countries or studies a topic in an international setting.
Turn data into a clear story: make simple charts and tables, draw honest conclusions, and explain your findings to people who are not experts.
grading:
Evaluation Items
Problem Sets (30%): Three problem sets (each 10 %). For every assignment, you will analyze one or more of the international datasets introduced in class, applying techniques covered in lectures. Submit both your code (R, Python, Stata, SPSS, or another software) and the resulting output. Collaboration is encouraged, but each student must run the code independently and turn in their own work. Because an answer key is released immediately after the deadline, late submissions are accepted only when an extension is approved in advance or, in an unforeseen emergency, retroactively.
Paper Reading Notes (20%): Two assignments (each 10 %). For each, select a journal article that meets the instructor’s criteria and complete structured reading notes by answering guided questions. These tasks build your ability to read research critically and extract insights relevant to your own work.
Research Project (40%): Group project for undergraduates (you are also welcome to submit individual work if preferred); individual project for graduate students. Design and carry out an original empirical study with an international dimension—either a cross-national comparison or an analysis that combines samples from at least two countries. The study must present clear research questions, theory-based hypotheses, appropriate data analysis, and conclusions drawn from the findings. The final paper, written in English, should be about 4,000–8,000 words (excluding references).
(1) Proposal (5%): Proposal Workshop on Nov. 12. Written proposal due Nov. 18.
(2) Presentation (10%): Presentations will take place on Dec. 24.
(3) Final Paper (25%): Due Dec. 30.
Attendance and Participation (10%): You may miss up to three classes without explanation. Additional absences must comply with the National Chengchi University Student Leave of Absence Rules (國立政治大學學生請假規則). Late arrival or early departure without approval may result in a partial deduction from the attendance grade.
Late Submission Policy: Written works are due at 23:59 on the stated date. Problem sets cannot be submitted late. For paper-reading notes and research projects, late submissions will lose 10 percent of the available points for each 24-hour period past the deadline, unless the instructor has approved an extension in advance or grants a waiver afterward due to an unforeseen emergency. An unexcused absence from a scheduled presentation without prior arrangement earns a grade of zero for that component.

Allow the use of AI for other purposes (such as generating ideas, content, or visual design) with full acknowledgment.

title: 公共政策分析與倡議 Public Policy Analysis and Advocacy
description: This course introduces the foundational concepts and practical approaches in public policy analysis and advocacy. Public policy is any decisions and actions (or indecisions and inactions) of governments. Public policy analysis is a tool to inform policymakers’ decisions, and policy advocacy is the technique to engage with stakeholders and communicate with the public to pursue policy change. This course will cover key stages in policy analysis and advocacy, such as problem identification, policy formulation, decision-making, advocacy, and adoption. Through case-based learning and theoretical grounding, students will explore how policy problems are defined, options developed and evaluated, and stakeholder interests negotiated. Students will complete a comprehensive policy analysis project and participate in a mock press conference, developing analytical, communication, and civic leadership skills.
objectives:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
Explain core concepts in public policy, including problem definition, policy formulation, and the adoption process.
Apply theoretical and practical tools in public policy analysis and advocacy to analyze practical problems and assess policies, such as evaluation matrices, cost-benefit analyses, and stakeholder analyses.
Communicate policy ideas and proposals effectively through both oral and written formats to inform policymakers and the public.
grading:
Reading Mind Map (15%): You will choose any 3 weeks between Week 2 and Week 14 to submit a mind map summarizing that week’s assigned readings, prepared before class; each submission is worth 5%, for a total of 15% (if you submit more than 3, your top 3 scores will count). Due by 12:00 noon the day before class (i.e., due on Tuesday). You may use AI tools to help draft the mind map, but you must fully understand its content yourself. Students who submit a mind map may be asked to present and explain their mind map in class.
Public Policy Analysis Project (50%): In this assignment, you will take on the role of a policy analyst, completing three written assignments and one oral presentation that carry a single policy problem from definition through alternatives comparison to political feasibility assessment. This project may be completed individually or in groups of 2 or 3 students; in-class time will be reserved in Week 3 for group formation, and assignment requirements will be adjusted based on group size (see Moodle for details).
(1) Problem Statement (10%). Due 10/13. In this assignment, you (or your group) will define and explain the public policy problem you have chosen to analyze, addressing its jurisdiction, significance, scale, and root causes.
(2) Alternatives Evaluation (15%). Due 11/10. In this assignment, you (or your group) will propose three policy alternatives and evaluate them using a multi-criteria matrix or cost-benefit/cost-effectiveness analysis to reach a clear policy recommendation.
(3) Stakeholder Analysis (10%). Due 12/15. In this assignment, you (or your group) will analyze the key stakeholders and political context surrounding your recommended alternative, applying an analytical approach (e.g., stakeholder matrix, advocacy coalitions, iron triangle, framing, or social construction) to assess its political feasibility.
(4) Oral Presentation (15%). Policy Advocate Press Conference, held over Weeks 15–16 (12/16 and 12/23). Present your policy proposal and recommendation to the class as if briefing the media, defending your analysis and fielding questions.
Peer Interaction Activity (25%) (Individual Assignment): In these assignments, you will take on the role of a policymaker, completing two assignments that require you to set policy priorities and make policy decisions based on your classmates’ submissions.
(1) Issues Ranking (10%). Due 10/27. In this assignment, you will act as the president (or key leader) of a fictional country, rank five classmates’ policy issues by agenda priority and justify your decision.
(2) Decision Making (15%). Due 11/24. In this assignment, you will act as a policymaker of your choice (the president, legislators, city mayor, etc.), decide how to respond to a classmate’s Policy Analysis Project and reflect on your decision-making model.
Attendance (10%): You are allowed up to three absences without needing to provide a reason. title: 海洋法-法律框架、國家實踐、及挑戰 The Law of the Sea-Legal Framework, State Practice, and Challenges
description:
Course Description:
The legal regime regulating the rights and obligations of States in their use of the seas has long been one of the most dynamic and important areas of International law. Various economic activities of humankind take place in the seas and oceans, and, at times, they are also hot spots for regional tensions and conflicts. The law of the sea provides the legal framework reflected in the wealth of customary laws, treaty laws, and judicial opinions dealing with this subject.
This course provides a full picture of the legal framework of the state practice in the seas, mainly the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Emphasis will be given on the issues of state sovereignty and their sovereign rights in maritime zones, due regard when when states exercise maritime freedom and rights, mechanism of dispute settlement, and enviroment aspects regarding climate change and living resources. Law enforcement and military activities on the seas will also be equally addressed, among others.
The theories and state practice will be introduced through the rulings of international judicial bodies and academic treatises. Students will have a chance to examine the balance of rights and interests between states and between states and the international community and identify the challenges to the legal framework from emerging issues on environment protection, climate change, and maritime security.

本課程將以聯合國海洋法公約為主,提供海域國家實踐法律框架全貌。置重點於海域之主權及主權權利、國家行使各項海域自由及權利時,對沿岸國及第三國之適當顧及義務、以及氣候變遷與生物資源等環境議題。海上執法以及海域軍事活動,亦同時為授課重點。
藉由觀察國際司法見解以及學術主張,學生得以檢視國與國之間、個別國家與國際社會間之權益平衡,並認知肇因於環境保護、氣候變遷及海域安全,對海洋法法律框架帶來的挑戰。

title: 永續發展商業模式:選擇、實施與最佳案例分析 Sustainable Business Strategy: Choice, Implementation and Best Practices Sharing
description:
Sustainable Business Strategy: Choice, Implementation, and Comparative Benchmarking in Corporate Governance
永續商業策略:全球標竿企業之 ESG 選擇、實施與治理合規對比
This course aims to lead students into a deep exploration of the core values of Social Responsibility (S) and Corporate Governance (G) within the ESG framework, while critically benchmarking key environmental (E) performance indicators. The curriculum systematically covers the structural impact of the net-zero transition on corporate operations, operational standards for social sustainability, and best practices for implementing corporate governance across distinct industry environments. Special emphasis will be placed on Social Responsibility (such as international human rights, Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion [DEI], and employee family-care benefits) and Corporate Governance (including legal compliance, supply chain governance, and tax transparency).
The core training of this course centers on "Strategic Choice, Implementation Evaluation, and Comparative Industry Benchmarking." Students will systematically read and analyze the English Sustainability Reports of top global tech giants (Apple, TSMC, Microsoft, HP, Google), alongside traditional sectors and global luxury brands (textile/apparel industries and the LVMH Group). The course will guide students to focus on and dissect the differentiation and implementation across three critical dimensions:
Environmental (E) Commitment and Execution: Examine the strategic choices regarding water stewardship and net-zero carbon emission commitments across various industries, and critically track their latest implementation progress.
Strategic Depth of Social Responsibility (S): Deconstruct how corporations align with International Human Rights standards, implement DEI policies—specifically focusing on family-care mechanisms (e.g., parental leave, maternity/paternity leave, and family support)—and manage labor rights within complex global supply chains.
Corporate Governance (G) and Compliance Thresholds: Integrating fiscal and strategic thinking, this dimension explores legal and internal corporate Compliance, and how such compliance is extended to global Supply Chain Governance and corporate tax transparency.
Through domestic and international case studies of both success and failure, expert forum debates, and quantitative/qualitative analysis of sustainability reports, students will learn to objectively evaluate corporate sustainability performance and propose forward-looking strategies and policy recommendations for practical challenges.
本課程專為創新國際學院、財政學系高年級與研究生設計,是一門兼具國際視角、ESG實務規範與公司治理評估的英語教學(EMI)核心進階課程。
本課程旨在引領學生深入探討 ESG 中的社會責任(Social, S)與公司治理(Governance, G)的核心價值及其對現代組織的重要性,同時精準對比環境(E)維度的關鍵績效。課程內容涵蓋氣候變遷淨零轉型對組織運作影響的系統性分析、社會責任的實務操作規範,以及如何在不同產業環境中落實公司治理的最佳實踐。本課程特別針對企業在社會責任(如國際人權、多元平等包容 DEI、員工福利與家庭照護等面向)及公司治理(如法律遵循合規性 Compliance、供應鏈管理與租稅透明度)等提供深入的剖析與探討。
課程的核心訓練在於「實戰報告研讀、利害關係人分析與跨產業比較」。學生將系統性地閱讀並分析頂尖科技巨頭(Apple, TSMC, Microsoft, HP, Google)、自行車產業、傳統產業與國際精品品牌(紡織/成衣業與NIKE, Addidas, LVMH 集團, Zara等)的英文永續報告書(Sustainability Reports)。課程將帶領學生聚焦並剖析三大維度的落實程度與差異化:
環境(E)承諾與實踐: 檢視各產業在水資源管理、零碳排(Net-Zero)承諾上的積極度,並批判性地追蹤其最新的執行進度(Implementation Progress)。
社會責任(S)的策略深度: 深度剖析企業如何因應國際人權(International Human Rights)標準、落實多元平等包容(DEI)政策,特別是家庭照護機制(如適親假、產假、育嬰假等工作與生活平衡機制),以及在複雜的全球供應鏈中進行勞工權益管理。
公司治理(G)與合規底線: 結合財政與策略思維,探討企業在法律與內部規範的合規性(Compliance),以及如何將合規延伸至供應鏈管理(Supply Chain Governance)與國際租稅透明度。
透過國內外成功與失敗案例研究、企業專家分享、以及永續報告書的量化與質化分析,學生將學習如何客觀評估不同產業標竿企業在永續治理上的表現,並能針對實務問題提出具前瞻性的策略與改善建議
objectives:
Learning Objectives and Outcomes
Objectives
Mastering Transition and Governance: Comprehend the impacts of net-zero transitions and water scarcity on corporate operations, and master the best practices of social responsibility, regulatory compliance, and corporate governance.
Connecting Social Strategy with Performance: Deeply explore the practical execution of social responsibility (particularly international human rights, family care, and DEI) and its long-term impact on corporate reputation, talent attraction, and financial/fiscal health.
Advanced Sustainability Report Deconstruction: Cultivate the ability to independently read and critically analyze quantitative E, S, and G metrics and implementation timelines within the sustainability reports of tech, textile, and luxury retail sectors.
Strategic Proposal and Critical Thinking: Develop problem-solving capabilities to combine fiscal tools and organizational strategy to formulate concrete, actionable solutions for corporate governance deficiencies and supply chain vulnerabilities.
Outcomes
Critical Evaluation of Cross-Industry Sustainability Strategies Students will be able to independently read, deconstruct, and critically analyze the English sustainability reports of multinational corporations across tech, traditional manufacturing, and luxury retail sectors. They will develop the practical capacity to precisely evaluate actual implementation progress against environmental (E) commitments (e.g., water stewardship and net-zero targets) and effectively identify potential greenwashing practices.
Strategic Planning for Social Responsibility and Inclusive Governance Students will be able to proficiently apply international human rights and Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) frameworks to deeply dissect the variations in employee welfare and family-care strategies across diverse industries. They will acquire the skills to formulate forward-looking strategic plans and actionable solutions for multinational organizations aiming to protect labor rights and optimize work-life balance
Audit and Assessment of Corporate Governance, Legal Compliance, and Supply Chain Management Risks: Integrating finance and business strategy perspectives, students will be able to systematically evaluate a corporation's compliance thresholds, tax transparency performance, and the execution of its global supply chain governance. They will be equipped to accurately identify and assess potential fiscal risks and reputational damages arising from governance failures or regulatory non-compliance.
教學目標
掌握轉型與治理精髓: 理解淨零轉型與水資源壓力對企業運營的影響,並熟練掌握社會責任、合規性及公司治理的最佳實踐。
深掘社會責任與績效關聯: 深入探討社會責任(尤指國際人權、家庭照護與 DEI)的實務操作,及其對企業形象、人才吸引力與財務績效的長期影響。
具備跨產業報告書解構能力: 培養獨立閱讀並批判性分析科技業、紡織成衣業與奢侈品零售業英文永續報告書中 E、S、G 數據與執行進度的能力。
展現策略提案與批判思考: 培養學生分析和解決問題的能力,能結合財政工具與組織策略,針對企業在供應鏈管理及合規缺陷上提出具體的建議方案。
學習成效
跨產業永續戰略之批判性評估能力 學生將閱讀並批判性分析跨國企業(包含科技巨頭、傳統製造業與國際精品品牌)的英文永續報告書,並能精準評估其在環境(E,如水資源與零碳進度)承諾上的真實執行成效,具備識別「綠洗(Greenwashing)」的實戰辨析能力。
社會責任與包容治理之策略規劃能力 學生能熟練運用國際人權與多元平等包容(DEI)框架,深度剖析不同產業在員工福祉與家庭照護(如親職假、產假與育嬰假等)的布局差異,並能針對跨國組織在保障勞工權益與優化工作生活平衡上,提出具前瞻性的策略規劃與改善方案。
公司治理、法律遵循合規性與供應鏈風險之審查能力 結合財務,法務與商業策略視角,學生能系統性地評估跨國企業的法規遵循合規性(Compliance)、財務透明度表現,以及其將合規機制延伸至全球供應鏈治理的成效,並能準確識別與評估組織因治理失當或違反法規所面臨的潛在風險與商譽損失。

description:
In recent years, Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an important tool for solving social problems. This course aims to train students to utilize the latest technologies in Generative AI and data science to develop projects that can address real-world challenges. The technology covered includes, but is not limited to, diverse content (such as text, audio, and video) connections, fine-tuning, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
This course is offered in collaboration with AMD and other partner institutions, which will provide students with access to the latest AI computing equipment and real-world AI projects. Students will use tools such as Claude Code and Codex to build AI agents and complete project-based assignments. title: 科技地緣政治時代的半導體產業 Semiconductor Industry in the Era of Techno-Geopolitics
description:
Technical innovation has the potency to significantly alter the economic and military landscape. Thus, the US and China are competing over the next breed of technology since the year of 2018. New national level regulation on technology transfer such as export control and restriction on foreign investment are being rolled out by the US, United Kingdom, Australia, Japan, Taiwan, and China itself as well. Such landscape change on regulating technology will change not only current global economy, but also the technological supply chain and global order. Taiwan, as one of the most critical tech hubs of global tech supply chain, is becoming one of the key players of these grand competition in the coming era of geo-technology. Our future decision makers from government to enterprise need to be cultivated more knowledge and strategy to take charge the leadership of Taiwan’s leading technology, economy and sovereignty.
Therefore, our discussions focus especially on recent legal and policy issues related to the grand transformation of global geo-technological environment: technology law and policies related to resent geo-technological trends focus on the US-China high-tech competition and impact of the reconstructing of global tech supply chain, the rising idea of implementing regulation to protect cutting edge technology through reforms on security export control, investigation and restriction on foreign investment, data and information protection, intellectual property and trade secret from an intersectional perspective.

title: 創新與全球發展 Innovation and Global Development
description:
Course Description
Contemporary society seems to be grappling with numerous crises and challenges! In 2000, United Nations member states collectively signed the Millennium Declaration, aiming to tackle major global issues such as poverty and hunger through collaborative efforts. In a similar vein, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation launched the Grand Challenges initiative in 2003, seeking to identify significant contemporary challenges and promote the development of innovative solutions. Coinciding with this, in 2008, the U.S. National Academy of Engineering announced 14 Grand Challenges for engineering, aimed at driving research to solve complex and intractable social problems, often referred to as "wicked social problems." Following this approach, the European Union in 2014 identified seven major societal challenges to guide technological development policies. Finally, in 2015, the United Nations updated the global challenges and introduced the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), outlining seventeen major challenges that the global community should overcome by 2030. It is evident that the international community increasingly relies on the concept of "Grand Challenges" to define and address the various social problems facing humanity.
As the world confronts various "Grand Challenges," there is a growing tendency to look toward potential "innovations" as solutions to these global crises. Increasing resources are being allocated to promote diverse innovations aimed at addressing these significant challenges. This reliance on technological advancements to solve major social issues is also reflected in international policy-making. In 2014, the European Union introduced the Horizon 2020 research and innovation program, with the primary objective of using "Responsible Research and Innovation" to tackle key societal challenges. Similarly, in 2015, when the United Nations unveiled the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), it also released a policy white paper detailing how science, technology, and innovation (STI) can be harnessed to achieve these goals.
Various issues arise following this trend. What are these innovations being promoted by international agencies? How could we discern whether these innovations could really solve the social and environmental problems without unintended consequences? In short, how could we develop a deeper understanding of these innovations as solutions to global problems?
These are questions that constitute the basis of this course. In this course, relying on perspectives from different disciplines in social sciences, we are going to collectively explore the landscape of innovation in the international development field. We will also learn to develop various analytical tools to assess potential and existing innovations poised to solve grand challenges.
Course Format
Class Activity & Group Discussion & Short Lecture:
I employ a student-centered learning approach in this course rather than a traditional lecture format (i.e., you listen to lectures to learn knowledge). My role will be a facilitator who supports your learning. In particular, this course is built on group discussion and collective learning. Most learning will be based on reading assigned materials, discussion, and class activities. I will supplement these activities with short lectures that help contextualize readings, articulate learning themes across weeks, and move the discussion forward.
Learning Activities
Collective Annotation:
For most of the weeks, there is one assigned reading you need to finish reading before coming to the class. You will also be required to make 3 comments and reply to 3 comments on a collective reading document. Your comments will be incorporated into the classroom activity and discussion.
Class participation and end-of-class exercise
It is critical to come to the class on time and participate in class activities. My assumption is that a fair proportion of your learning will come from your interaction and collaboration with your classmates during the class. Thus, it is imperative to attend every class except for legitimate reasons (e.g. sick leave or other types of leave permitted by the university).
Case Study – Exploring Taiwan’s innovation beyond the semiconductor sector
Throughout the course, you will also need to pair with the other student and investigate a specific innovation in Taiwan beyond the semiconductor sector. At the end of the semester, each group of students will need to produce a 3000-word piece of essay. Your essay will have the chance to be included in a special issue in the Taiwan Insight online magazine website if it meets the standard.
To prepare each group to work on your case study, we will learn a series of analytical questions and different kinds of “stakeholder analysis” mapping tools that could allow you to carry out the analysis. You will also have the opportunity to carry out some fieldwork to study the case better.
I will also assist you to finish this essay every step of the way. There are NINE assignments throughout the semester to help you craft the essay. I will also provide a more detailed guideline for each assignment during the course. These assignments include:
Initial proposal

title: 蓋婭政治與戰時生態學 Gaiapolitics and War Ecology
description:
The notion of Gaia-politics challenges traditional approaches to sovereignty by taking more seriously the geo of geopolitics, that is to say its environmental dimension. War ecology is another concept that aims to address the concomitance of the climate emergency with more traditional threats on national security including military and civilian defense. Through guess lectures, off campus visits and negotiation theaters, the class focuses on the case of Taiwan in comparison with other countries.
In 2023, this course focused on conflicts between humans and non-humans. In 2024, we paid attention to the role of social movements (such as environmental protection and antinuclear mobilization), and how they connect with national politics, in particular state agencies and the parliament. In 2025, we explored with a critical eye the catchwords of ‘social resilience’, ‘technological innovation’ and ‘energy transition’, and how these effectively influence collective preparation to climate change and war scenarios.
In 2026, while continuing our research on these topics, we will also conduct an educational experiment that requires us to spend most of our time out of the classroom. The idea is to take a pause, detox from our overuse of electronics and AI, and return to the basics of ethnographic fieldwork with our eyes and ears wide open, using handwritten notes and drawings.
「蓋婭政治」(Gaia-politics)的概念挑戰了「主權」 概念的傳統取徑,因為蓋婭政治更認真看待「地緣政治」中的「地緣」,也就是其環境面向。「戰爭生態學」(war ecology)則是另一個概念,旨在面對氣候緊急狀態與傳統國安威脅(包括軍事與民間防 衛)共存的局勢。
透過客座課程、校外參訪與協商劇場的形式,本課 程將聚焦於台灣相較於其他國家的情勢。2023年, 本課程聚焦於人類與非人類之間的衝突。2024年, 我們更注重社會運動(如環保與反核運動)的角 色,以及它們如何與國內政治——特別是政府機構與國會——產生連結。
2025年,我們將在延續對跨物種正義、社會運動與 國家政治的關注之餘,進一步批判性地探討「社會 韌性」、「科技創新」與「能源轉型」這些關鍵詞,並檢視它們如何實質地影響集體面對氣候變遷與戰爭 情境的準備與應對能力。
2026年,我們除了將繼續探索上述議題,亦會將多數時間移至教室之外,進行一項教育性實驗計畫。本計畫旨在按下暫停鍵,戒斷我們對3C產品與人工智慧的過度使用;並以敏銳的觀察與傾聽,透過手寫與手繪紀錄,回歸民族誌田野工作的基礎。
objectives:
The goal of this mixed-method approach—using ethnographic fieldwork and negotiation theater—is to improve our capacity to detach from electronic devices and increase our focus while reading scientific papers, attending lectures, participating in group discussions, and conducting ethnographic fieldwork. In other words, this means listening and observing, taking valuable notes, and turning these observations into social capital and political will through class discussions. Meanwhile, protests against the environmental cost of electronic waste and the huge carbon footprint of AI data centers provide further reminders and incentives to detox from electronics. Last but not least, as Taiwan’s civil defense organizations train their members, we must also learn to cope with electricity shortages or blackouts in the event of a military emergency, natural hazard, or industrial disaster (such as earthquakes, typhoons, or gas explosions).
課程目標與預期成果:本課程透過民族誌田野工作與協商劇場的混合途徑,旨在幫助我們降低對電子產品的依賴,藉此提升在閱讀文獻、參與講座、小組討論與田野工作時的專注力。具體而言,我們將練習觀察與傾聽、作好筆記,並透過課堂討論將這些觀察轉化為社會資本與政治動能。此外,遠離 3C 也是對當前社會與環境議題的反思。電子垃圾的環境代價與 AI 資料中心的巨大碳足跡,不斷提醒並促使我們減少對電子設備的依賴。最後,正如台灣民防組織對其會員的訓練,我們也必須透過這門課學會:在遭遇軍事衝突或天災人禍(如地震、颱風、氣爆)時,如何面對並適應缺電或停電的狀態。
grading:
Regular attendance and participation: 60%
Attending the class regularly.
Listening and watching attentively during the class, and taking handwritten notes (including simple drawings, charts, etc.), and participating to the class discussion (small group discussion and negotiation theaters).
Reading the printed papers that will be distributed in advance (the quantity is small).
Final report (scrap book) based on field notes: 40%

title: 政治學概論 Introduction to Political Science
description:
‘Introduction to Political Science’ is a one-semester module for undergraduate students. It aims at (1) presenting the scope and core areas of political science to students, (2) nurturing their abilities to reflect on politics, and (3) developing their abilities to express their analysis and interpretation of politics through coherent arguments.
The module, therefore, is organised into two major themes: political phenomena and ideas, with a strong emphasis on the theory and history of political science. Apart from the first two weeks that introduce the theme of the module and its historical origins, the module unfolds with (1) the mapping of key political phenomena (week 3-7), before moving onto (2) the essential aspects of politics (week 9-15). To conclude the module, the last two weeks will include an open discussion on the future of political science (week 15), and a three-round debate (week 16).
objectives:
The objectives of the module include (1) familiarising the students with the core analytical or interpretative objects and approaches of political science, (2) cultivating the students’ ability to think critically about the political environment they find themselves in, and (3) encouraging students to form and present their political arguments in public in a debate.
The design of the assignments, including the essay abstract (mid-term), class debate (week 16), and term paper (end of term), aims to help students develop the ability to form coherent and succinct arguments and present them in an articulate, well-informed, and academically sound term essay.
grading:
Class Attendance (10%)
Participation (10%)
Group presentation in debates (30%)
Term paper (1500-2000 words) (50%)

title: 永續發展數據分析:理論與應用 Data Analysis for Sustainable Development: Theory and Applications
description:
Sustainable development has been ardently advocated by numerous international institutions, governments, NGOs, and corporations in recent years. Despite its growing prominence, the concept of sustainable development is broad and complex. One illustrative example of its scope is the United Nations' 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). These cover a wide array of interconnected objectives, ranging from poverty eradication and climate action, to ensuring inclusive education and beyond.
Navigating these multifaceted and often nebulous concepts can pose a significant challenge. The tasks of defining these goals, assessing progress, and crafting effective strategies are no small feats. Yet, the advent of advanced data analysis tools and techniques provides a promising pathway to address these complex issues. Especially in the recent years, GenAI's development has offered opportunities for the analysis of sustainable issues.
objectives:
This course is designed to illuminate this intersection. Its goal is to equip students with the necessary knowledge and skills to apply data analysis in the context of sustainable development. Through this journey, students will cultivate a robust understanding of how to define, evaluate, and address sustainable development goals using data-driven approaches and AI agents.
This course is designed to leverage data analysis in order to evaluate the ways in which various groups and classes mobilize to promote their agendas, ultimately impacting the progress of sustainable development. These social actors encompass corporations, trade associations, social classes, racial and ethnic groups, as well as the state. Through this course, you will embark on a journey into a dynamic and rapidly evolving field that has the potential to drive significant change on corporate, national, and even global levels.
grading:
1. It is essential that you complete all required readings before attending the classes.
2. This course is structured into different sections, each consisting of both literature classes and practice classes.
3. In the literature classes, students are expected to write critique papers. For the short paper, students should review all the assigned readings for a given week. The critique should include a clear identification of the research question(s), the cause, the effect, theoretical argument, empirical design, and findings of the readings. It is important to focus on identifying one central theoretical limitation or one central empirical limitation that has significant conceptual implications for the analysis. Furthermore, students should provide a thorough analysis of the weakness and present a plausible argument for possible improvements. Each short paper should be two single-spaced pages and must be submitted by 5 pm prior to the day of the course. Additionally, students are expected to read and provide feedback on other teams' critique papers. Authors are responsible for sharing their short papers with the entire class.
4. During the practice classes, the instructor will assign several projects for the students. Students should prepare the necessary data and codes before the classes and complete the projects during the practice sessions.
5. All students are required to utilize data analysis techniques to develop individual final project papers on a topic within the field of sustainable development. Students should carefully follow the guidelines provided by the instructors to effectively develop their final proposals and papers.

Work independently on assignments, particularly in coding.
Seek help when facing challenges or in need of inspiration.

title: 種族、宗教、民族主義:全球的暴力與歸屬政治 Ethnicity, Religion, Nationalism:Violence and the Politics of Belonging in the Global World
description:
Notes:
Essays: Students write 1 essay (1000 words), due at the mid-term. This essay is written in a style of policy commentary. For this essay, students choose for themselves at least 2 theories from the 16-week course, and a case study.
Final paper: Students write 1 individual final paper (4,000-5,000 words) due at the end of the course. Students choose the topic of these final papers themselves.
Presentations: Students present twice: 1 on the weekly topic of their choice, 1 very short 5-minute presentation on the framework of their final papers.
The course includes stimulating activities such as debates, games, simulations, and watching a film. Film Title: Argo (2012), a three-Oscar-winning film about the rescue of US embassy employees from the siege of the American embassy in Tehran, Iran. Director: Ben Affleck. This film shows how Iran’s religious nationalism and US secular nationalism clashed during the 1979 Iranian revolution.
Alternatively the course is planned to introduce an innovative learning method which includes visits to religious civil society organizations to discuss with religious leaders/activists on the interplay between “religion” and “nationalism”, the organizations are: the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan (PCT) or the Tzu-Chi Foundation.
In light of the prolonged Israeli-Hamas war and the ongoing tensions between the United States and Iran, observers have warned of the possibility of a serious regional escalation and renewed global instability in the near future. The course “Ethnicity, Religion, Nationalism: Violence and the Politics of Belonging in the Global World” provides a structured space for students to critically examine how ethnic and religious identities shape nationalism and contribute to political conflict and violence in different regional and international contexts.
The course explores the interaction between religion and ethnic identities in Asia (East Asia, South Asia and Southeast Asia), the Middle East, and the United States, and their impact on the construction of nationalism. It addresses critical questions of identity and citizenship, inclusion and exclusion, emotional and symbolic attachments, and the linkage between local and global political dynamics. The course asks how ethnicity and religion shape political interaction, how ethnic and religious identities may aggravate conflict or strengthen cooperation, and how they are mobilized in processes of nation-building and political legitimation. It further examines how relevant dimensions such as sacralization and symbolic forms of legitimation may lead to conflict and violence.
The course is divided into two parts. The first part introduces key concepts of ethnicity, religion, identity, nation, and nationalism, and examines major theoretical explanations for the emergence and persistence of nationalism. The second part focuses on the political consequences of nationalism for belonging and identity, including religious nationalism, fundamentalism, and identity-based conflict, through case studies from China, Myanmar, Thailand, Indonesia, India, Turkey, Israel, and the United States.
The course also considers the role of digital technologies and artificial intelligence in shaping contemporary identity politics and nationalist mobilisation. Social media platforms, algorithmic systems, and AI-generated content increasingly mediate the circulation of ethnic and religious narratives, often amplifying polarization and reshaping boundaries of inclusion and exclusion in the process.
On Week 12 students will watch the film “Argo” (2012, Director: Ben Affleck), an Oscar-winning film which depicts the 1979 rescue of six U.S. State Department employees during the siege at the American embassy in Tehran, Iran. Alternatively, the course will include an Innovative Learning Method Week with Study Visits to religious organizations. Planned visits include the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan (PCT), or Tzu-Chi Foundation, where students will engage with religious leaders and practitioners to discuss the interplay between “religion” and “nationalism”, and conflict.
objectives:
After completing the course, students will:
Understand the meaning of key concepts, such as ethnicity, religion, identity, nation, nationalism, religious nationalism and fundamentalism.
Understand the interaction and complex relations between these key concepts and their role in the politics of belonging and citizenship in various countries.
Understand the interaction and complex relations between these key concepts and their role in fundamentalism and/or political violence in various countries.
Be able to analyze current and/or past conflicts by examining how ethnicity and religion generate nationalism, which in turn may produce violence and political conflict in the global world.
